units.tr: To my most gracious Lord, grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: ACERBISSIMVM quidem, Princeps Illustrissime, luctum intulit Deus familiæ vestræ, quum Illustrissimum Principem parentem tuum ex hac misera commoratione ad se in stationem beatam evocavit. Quem luctum eo acerbiorem T.C. scio accidisse, quòd eo semper optimo parente & duce fidefidelissimo usus sis ad totam rationem vitæ & studiorum tuorum institutum.
units.tr: Most bitter indeed, most illustrious Prince, was the grief God brought upon your household when he called your most illustrious father from this wretched sojourn to his blessed station. I know that your Highness has been grieved all the more because you always used that best of fathers and guides as your most faithful guide in ordering the whole course of your life and studies.

units.la: Quòd si tristis ille & funestus casus aut solus exstitisset, aut solam T.C. affecisset, æquiore animo fuisses laturus ipse, & minus sensura Germania tota: de cuius pace & tranquillitate semper quàm fidelissimè optimus ille parens laboravit. At quàm multa funera in Germania vidimus anno uno! quàm multis casibus fuit Germania de ira Dei minante, & terrores & plagas & mala gravissima denunciante certior facta à Domino! Intus sunera, foris bella utrinque in fines indignissimè & atrocissimè irrumpentia: quæ T.C.(scio) afficiunt vehementiùs quàm vel domestica hæc calamitas. Etsi in domestica hac calamitate id est incommodi, quòd dum Germaniæ commune ex malis tantis laborat, eodem tempore illa subsidio, immò præsidio pacis & tranquillitatis firmissimo, parente tuo, orbata est. Quid dicam, nisi iram Dei exardescere? minari ferulam? ad veram pacem cum Deo, cum Ecclesia, cum fratribus Germaniam totam revocare! Nam gravia quidem illa, adeoque gravissima. Sed Video (prob dolor) malum Germaniam exedens longè gravissimum: Scindi Germaniam non tam per hostes exteros, mundo, carni, ambitioni, & tyrannidi iniustissimae servientes, quàm per eos ipsos Germaniae partus & alumnos, qui ex natura conscientia pacem corporis ut membra, ex gratiae conscientia pacem Ecclesiae ut filij pacis procurare debent. Video eos ipsos quos receptui canere quam religiosissimè oporteret, administros pacis evangelizaturos pacem in Domino, eos ipsos inquam bellicum canere quam ardentissimè, & primos in ordines Ecclesiae, ordines pacis, contrà quàm Deus pacis mandavit, contentione summa incurrere. Quid? nonne vident discidia nostra esse amicorum dispendia, b[?]ostium compendia (ut cum Hieronymo dicam) & publica irae divinae incendia: Miseretur Dominus: me quidem miseret secundum Dominum: & quamuis iam absentem à Germania solo per voluntatem Dei, tamen ut præsentem animo graviter afficit istorum malorum, quæ video & prævideo, cogitatio. Atque his quidem malis provisurum confido Deum, & provisuros pios Principes amantes pacis publicæ & suæ, amantes pietatis, amantes patriæ. Sed quia tu, Mauricii Illustrissime, non postremus es in eorum numero, qui studio meditantur pacem, officio procurant, & exemplis (quibus abundas domi ab avo, à parente tuo) incitantur: non potui quin & Germanię communi vestræ & T. C. animum meum constantem & studiosum vestræ pacis vobis exponerem à discessu meo. Scripsi de pace documenta communia, quæ in mente sunt, in ore omnium; sed non sunt aut comparént usquam in opere. Nam eo ipso quòd communia sunt, negliguntur, teruntur pedibus : curant singuli singularia & particularia, vt vocant. Latinè scripsi, vt Germaniæ vestra aliqua saltem [?]τερψεια[?] renumerem, qui annos amplius XXV. in ea vixerim. Optimo animo cupiui [?]ἀνπολαργῆν[?]. Hæc causa me adduxit vt hoc opusculum, qualecunque est, T. C. inscriberem, & per manus eius offerrem Germaniæ tuæ. T. C. oro vt hoc meum officium sibi exhibitum in bonam partem accipiat, studiumque interpretetur bene : Deum vero opt. max. auctorem pacis & charitatis verae, vt benedicens precibus & labori meo, Ecclesiam suam Germaniamque ipsam vestrum stabiliat in pace & sanctimonia, & omnium animos, procerum ac popularium, in primis T. C. regat in consiliis, atque ad pacem dirigat constan-tissimè, tissimè, ut instrumentum pacis sancti-ficatum à Domino ad gloriam ipsius, Ecclesiæ & Reipub. utile futurum ac salutare quàm diutissimè.
units.tr: If that sad and deadly event had stood alone, or had touched only your Highness, you would have borne it with a calmer mind, and all Germany would have felt it less. Yet that excellent father had laboured as faithfully as possible for the peace and tranquillity of Germany. But how many deaths have we seen in Germany in a single year! How often has Germany been warned by the Lord of the anger of God threatening, and of terrors, plagues and most grievous evils to come! Deaths within, wars without, bursting into our borders from every side in the most unworthy and savage way: these, I know, afflict your Highness more deeply than this domestic calamity itself. Yet this domestic calamity has the added misfortune that, while Germany suffers from so many evils in common, she has at the same time lost that most firm support, or rather protection, of peace and tranquillity, your father. What can I say, except that the wrath of God is kindled, that he threatens the rod, and that he calls all Germany back to true peace with God, with the Church, and with her brothers! For those troubles are grievous, and indeed most grievous. But I see (alas) a far graver evil eating away at Germany: Germany is being torn apart, not so much by foreign enemies who serve the world, the flesh, ambition and most unjust tyranny, as by those very offspring and nurslings of Germany, who ought to pursue the peace of the body, as members, by natural conscience, and the peace of the Church, as children of peace, by the conscience of grace. I see those very men who ought most devoutly to sound the retreat, the ministers of peace who should preach peace in the Lord, I say those very men sounding the call to war as eagerly as they can, and, contrary to what the God of peace has commanded, rushing with the utmost contention into the first ranks of the Church, the ranks of peace. What? Do they not see that our divisions are the losses of friends, the gains of enemies (as I may say with Jerome), and public fires of the divine wrath? "The Lord have mercy": I indeed have mercy on them, according to the Lord. And although I am now absent from Germany by the will of God alone, yet in spirit I am deeply moved, as if present, by the thought of these evils, which I see and foresee. And I trust that God will provide against these evils, and that pious princes will provide, who love public and their own peace, who love piety, who love their fatherland. But since you, most illustrious Maurice, are not the least among those who earnestly work for peace, who promote it by their duty, and who are stirred by examples (of which you have many at home, from your grandfather and your father), I could not refrain from setting before your Highness and before the common good of your Germany my constant and eager mind for your peace, since my departure. I have written on peace the common teachings which are in everyone's mind and on everyone's lips, but which are nowhere to be found or are not set out in a work. For precisely because they are common, they are neglected and trodden underfoot: each man cares for the singular and particular, as they call them. I have written in Latin so that I might repay Germany, where I have lived for more than twenty-five years, with at least some [τέρψις] delight. With the best of intentions I wished to [ἀνπολαργῆν] make a return. This reason led me to dedicate this little work, such as it is, to your Highness, and to offer it through your hands to your Germany. I beg your Highness to take this duty of mine kindly and to interpret my zeal favourably; and I pray to God, the best and greatest, the author of true peace and charity, that, blessing my prayers and labour, he may establish his Church and Germany itself with you in peace and holiness, and may guide the minds of all, nobles and common people, and above all your Highness, in counsel, and direct them most steadfastly to peace, so that this instrument of peace, sanctified by the Lord to his glory, may be useful and salutary to the Church and the commonwealth for as long as possible.

units.tr: THE FIRST PART OF THE EIRENICUM.

units.la: NATURALE studium est omniumi ut fruantur bono; & ad fructum boni consequendum depellunt à se contraria naturæ luce, quibus oppugnatur bonum. Hunc autem appetitum, qui rebus omnibus naturalis est, multa insuper accidētia solent acuere; inprimis autem molestæ malorum infestantiū moles & fluctus procellarum: qui quo grauius impendent atque exagitant, eo plus animi humani premuntur sollicitudine. Ac sollicitudo quidem de proprio & singulari bono ita est singulis indita, ut moneri quemquam non sit opus de bonis singularibus & privatis cōmodis persequendis, aut propulsandis incommodis. Sed cùm à natura ita fit comparatum, ut singula quæque ad unum aliquod commune bonum referantur, homines verò supra res creatas cæteras per singularem Dei gratiam luce rationis, & quàm plurimis ad bonum adiumentis instructi sint: quod indignum aliis rebus existimát, eas à bono cōmuni discedere, id multo amplius de se ipsi debent statuere: qui & bono proprio instructi, & ad commune documentis tam multis provocati, tam tám fugiunt quàm qui maximè suauissimum illum fructum communis boni,&in publicum malum velut coniurati ruunt pertinaciffimè.
units.tr: Every creature naturally desires to enjoy the good; and to attain the fruit of the good, people drive away from themselves whatever opposes the good, by the light of nature. This appetite, which belongs naturally to all things, is commonly sharpened by many further circumstances; above all by the troubles of hostile evils and the waves of storms, which, the more heavily they hang over and harass us, the more they weigh down the human mind with anxiety. Now the anxiety about one's own particular good is so implanted in each person that no one needs to be reminded to pursue his private advantages or to repel his private misfortunes. But since nature has so ordained that each single thing is referred to one common good, and since human beings, set above all other created things by God's singular grace, are furnished with the light of reason and with so many aids to the good, it is unworthy of them, when other things are deemed not to turn away from the common good, that they should think this of themselves; they who, though furnished with their own good and summoned to the common good by so many teachings, flee from it as far as they can, and, as if in conspiracy against the public welfare, rush headlong with the utmost obstinacy away from that most sweet fruit of the common good.

units.la: Etsi quid de bono illo naturæ ponendo ante oculos omnium,aut de malitia hominum dicamus multis,commune bonum,quod natura exhibet,oppugnante? Est bonum longè præstabilius, fúnimum bonum, optimum bonum in Deo positum, &ab eodem expositum; velut principio omnis boni, cum in natura, tum supra natúram rerum creatarum omnium: ad cuius boni conscientiam, exspectatione, & apprehenfionem à Deo regignimur, instituimur, prouocamur, ducimur, trahimurq. vi quadam salutari, & incredibili misericordia: & quò Deus impium hunc mundum prouocat, suos transmissurus ad participationē supernaturalis suæ & diuinæ gloriæ. Huius tanti boni fontem fe exponit Deus, plenitudinem in Christo exhibet,riuos in mundo statuit, aquas salutares in ecclesia distribuit suis, omnes denique in communionem sanctorum omnibus modis salutaribus prouocat,ad ipsius æterna bona æternùm percipienda in Christo Iesu, & hic etiam in terris, dum peregrè absumus à Domino, in vnitate corporis & spiritus vnà fide per vinculum pacis degustanda.
units.tr: Should I say something about placing before the eyes of all that good of nature, or about the malice of many men who oppose the common good which nature offers? There is a good far more excellent, the highest good, the best good, placed in God and set forth by him, as the beginning of all good, both in nature and above the nature of all created things. To the knowledge, expectation and apprehension of this good we are begotten, instructed, summoned, led and drawn by God, by a certain saving force and incredible mercy; and by this means God calls this impious world, so as to bring his own into participation in his supernatural and divine glory. God sets himself forth as the fountain of this great good, displays its fullness in Christ, establishes its streams in the world, distributes the saving waters among his own in the Church, and finally calls all into the communion of the saints by every saving means, to receive his eternal goods eternally in Christ Jesus, and here on earth also, while we are absent from the Lord as pilgrims, to taste them in the unity of body and spirit, in one faith, through the bond of peace.

units.la: Hic verò quid dicturi sumus, cùm miserabilem istam sanctissimam q. mundi ruentis constitutionem animaduertimus? finiul videmus, simul horremus: & iusto dolore, si quidem verè Christiani sumus, in isto Christianitatis sunere ac busto contabescimus. O si quis daret caput meum esse aquas, & oculum meum scaturiginem lacrymarum, ut deflerem interdiu & noctu tot funestos casus mundi & cruentissima ecclesiæ vulnera, intus, foris, à domesticis, ab exteris indignissimè imposita! O si quis poneret me in deserto, in deuersorio viatorum, ut derelinquerem populū istum rebellem, & abirem ab eo migraturus ad dominum meum, Deum veritatis quæ exulat, & Deum pacis quæ à filiis pacis oppugnatur! Libet enim, adeoque iuftiffimus dolor cogit me erumpere in illa Ieremiæ Prophetæ verba: quibus funestum gentis suæ, ac potius prisçæ illius ecclesiæ statum deplorabat. Nam si hæc tempora cum illis comparem, omnino statuo illa vetera, vtcunq. fuerint misera, ab his nostris omni malorum genere, ut cùm maximè, superari: Quibus neque ad summum illud & vnicum verè bonum communi studio aut zelo priuato contenditur, neque via certa ad illud pertinente insistitur, neque pietatis ratio ante mundi peruersi oculos versatur, neque inclinatio ad iustitiam vllam, neq; amor veritatis ad omnia hæc consequenda tenendaque perfecceffariæ, neque prudentiæ modus ad publicum priuatumque bonum in pace & sanctimonia promouendum: Sed contrà (ut verbis prophetæ utamur) omnes omnino cor-
units.tr: But what shall we say here, when we observe this wretched and most holy state of the collapsing world? We see and at the same time shudder; and with just grief, if indeed we are truly Christians, we waste away in this funeral and pyre of Christianity. O that someone would give my head to be waters and my eye a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for so many deadly calamities of the world and the bloodiest wounds of the Church, inflicted most unworthily from within and without, by its own members and by outsiders! O that someone would place me in the wilderness, in a travellers' inn, so that I might leave that rebellious people and depart from them, going to my Lord, the God of truth, who is in exile, and the God of peace, who is assailed by the sons of peace! For indeed, such a just grief compels me to burst out into those words of the prophet Jeremiah, in which he lamented the deadly state of his own nation, or rather of that ancient Church. For if I compare these times with those, I firmly judge that those old times, however wretched they were, are surpassed by ours in every kind of evil, as never before. In our times the highest and only true good is not sought with common zeal or private earnestness, nor is a sure path leading to it trodden; the principle of piety is not kept before the eyes of a perverse world; there is no inclination to any justice, no love of truth sufficiently strong to pursue and hold all these things; no measure of prudence to promote the public and private good in peace and holiness. But on the contrary (to use the prophet's words) all have utterly corrupted their ways,

units.la: rumpunt vias suas, in mente ipsorum impietatem colunt,& abominandas actiones animo perpetrant, reipsa non est qui faciat bonum sibi[?] ipsi, nedum fratri & conferuo suo.
units.tr: they worship impiety in their minds, and commit abominable deeds in their hearts; there is none who does good, not even to himself, much less to his brother and fellow-servant.

units.la: In hac tanta strage ruinâque miserabili orbis Christiani, quem sua ipsius membra, tum aduersus seipsa,tumvero inter fe pugnátia,praefertim religionis & pietatis nomine, lacerant indignissimè, & porrò peffumdatura sunt, nisi salutaris è cælo manus Dei fccerit medicinam: Quid agerem,nisi ut oculos meos[?] in cælum attollerem ad Deum salutis nostræ, & illa arma militiæ nostræ spiritalia cælitus emissa corriperem, ut in Dei nomine ( cui seruio,& Ecclesiæ catholicæ eius fecundum ipsum) fratres meos, & membra Christi,tâ quæ vocata fan&a,quàm quæ vocanda per Dei gratiam, sermone & exemplo (fi quid exemplo possum) ad pacem unitatemque spiritus reuocem, in unitate corporis illius quod Deus redemit sanguine suo?
units.tr: In this so great slaughter and wretched ruin of the Christian world, which its own members tear apart most unworthily, fighting both against themselves and among one another, especially in the name of religion and piety, and which will be utterly destroyed unless the saving hand of God from heaven provides a remedy: what should I do, except lift my eyes to heaven, to God of our salvation, and seize those spiritual weapons of our warfare sent down from heaven, so that in the name of God, whom I serve, and of his Catholic Church, according to his will, I may recall my brothers and the members of Christ, both those who are called saints and those who are to be called by the grace of God, by word and by example (if I can do anything by example), to peace and unity of the Spirit, in the unity of that body which God redeemed with his own blood?

units.la: Quam ad rem primùm Deum omnipotentem oro supplex, Patrem domini nostri Iesu Christi, ex quo omnis cognatio nominatur in cælo & terra, Deum veritatis & pacis, ut abiectâ ratione peccatorum tot & tantorum, quibus majestaté ipsius & alij alios plus fatis offendimus, veritatem suam demonstret errantibus, & veram pacem intus & foris stabiliat, quâ alij alios ferre, & omnesad Deum contendere vno animo possimus in Christo Iesu redemptore & seruatore nostro. Deinde verò fratres omnes meos, fratres (inquam) & vniuersali naturæ lege, & communi vocatione gratiæ, & singulari spiritus communicatione, rogatos volo quàm diligentissimè per summas illas Dei miserationes, quæ nobis perituris affulserunt, & adhuc nos circumfulgent in malis nostris (proh dolor) pereuntes: si qua est consolatio in Christo, si quod solatium charitatis, si qua communio spiritus, si quæ viscera ac miserationes, vt de exsplendo sanctorum gaudio mecum laborent diligentissimè; vt itidem sint affecti, eandem charitatem habentes, vnanimes & sententiis vni; nihil gerentes per contentionem aut per inanem gloriam, sed ex modestia alij alios sibi præstare existimantes, quisq. non sua spectent, sed etiam quæ sunt aliorum: Denique is sit affectus in nobis omnibus qui in Christo Iesu, velut capite & summo exemplari nostro. Postremò autem, quia de hoc ipso argumento, dum omnia inter Christianos miserè clamoribus & vociferationibus impotentissimis personant, artibus[?] evertuntur, & eruentantur cædibus, constitui secundùm Deum ex sanctissimo ipsius verbo aliquid pronunciare, quod secundùm veritatem & charitatem (quam omnibus imperauit Deus) ad utilitatem publicam iudico pertinere: Peto ab omnibus & singulis quàm possum amantissimè, ne quid aut de me homine abiectissimo, aut de scripto hoc instituto meo præiudicati conconcipiant in animis suis,tanquam si in harum aut illarum partium (quibus hodie Christianus orbis miserè scinditur ) odium,inuidiam, aut notam qualemcumq; sim allaturus, aut de me ipse magnificè suprà quàm decet aut oportet sentiam, aut meam operâ præsidenter [?] aliorum, quos amò,colo,venerorque,operæ anteponam: sed potiùs sic de me statuant, me omissa causarum, rerum, & actionum singularium , quæ in hoc tempore discutiuntur, ratione , citra præiudicatum vllius hominis , ex sola veritatis diuinæ cōtemplatione,de pace Christianorum,quæ communia sunt ( hinc enim traducimur particularibus studiis & occasionibus) dicturū esse: qui de mo [?] sic sentiam,nō solùm aliorum peccata,sed mea quoque ipsius in Deum grauissima his lamentabilibus Christianitatis discidiis castigari : qui denique de mea opera non aliud prædicem,quàm quòd sit tenuissima, & à fine proposito absit quam longissimè, sed tamen à Deo sit,qui etiam tenuès operarios & infirmos cū valentioribus occupat in domo suaextruenda,ad sanctorum coagmentationem & ædificationem corporis Christi. Deus nouit, cui seruio in spiritu mentis meæ,quantum incendium(vt ita dicam) in præcordiis & animo meo sentiam hac tristi facie Christianitatis excitari.: quantum me horum & illorum simul misereat, qui religionem imprudentes oppugnant religionis studio, naturam auctoritate naturæ , & Deum ipsum diuinæ auctoritatis specie ipsorum oculos, dum ad fe ipsi non fatis attendunt, præstinguente. Quod fi meam hanc opellam, cuius studium in me concitauit Deus, ille pater miserationum & omnis consolationis auctor sua benedictionis manu direxerit, vt & veritatem in se habeat, & omnibus præbeat, & bonis saltem aliquot testatam faciat veritatem hoc ossicio meo, maximum mihi operæ precium fecisse videbor per benedictionem illius.
units.tr: To this end I first pray humbly to Almighty God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and earth is named, the God of truth and peace, that, setting aside the reckoning of so many and so great sins by which we have all too much offended his majesty, one against another, he may show his truth to those who err, and establish true peace within and without, by which we may be able to bear with one another and all strive toward God with one mind in Christ Jesus our Redeemer and Saviour. Then I wish all my brothers, brothers I say, both by the universal law of nature and by the common calling of grace and by the singular communication of the Spirit, to be asked most diligently, by those supreme mercies of God which shone upon us when we were perishing and still surround us in our evils, which (alas) we are perishing in: if there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any bowels and mercies, that they labour most diligently with me for the fulfilment of the saints' joy; that they be likewise disposed, having the same love, being of one accord and one mind; doing nothing through contention or vainglory, but in humility each esteeming others better than himself, each looking not only to his own things but also to the things of others. Finally, let this be the disposition in all of us which was in Christ Jesus, as our head and highest pattern. Lastly, because on this very subject, while everything among Christians resounds miserably with clamours and most violent outcries, and is overturned by arts and dripping with slaughter, I have resolved, according to God, to declare from his most holy word something which, according to truth and charity (which God has commanded all), I judge to pertain to the public good: I ask of all and each, as lovingly as I can, that they not form in their minds any prejudgment either about me, a most lowly man, or about this writing of mine, as if I were about to bring hatred, ill will or any mark whatever against this or that party (into which the Christian world is wretchedly split today), or as if I thought of myself more highly than is fitting or proper, or set my own work before the work of others whom I love, honour and revere. Rather, let them judge of me thus: that, setting aside the reasoning of particular causes, matters and actions which are being debated at this time, and without prejudice to any man, I shall speak from the sole contemplation of divine truth about the peace of Christians, which is a common concern (for we are drawn away from it by particular interests and occasions); and that I think of myself as one who sees that not only the sins of others but also my own very grievous sins against God are chastised by these lamentable divisions of Christianity; and finally that I claim nothing for my work except that it is very slight and far from the purpose proposed, yet that it comes from God, who also employs weak and feeble labourers together with stronger ones in building his house, for the joining together and edification of the body of Christ. God knows, whom I serve in the spirit of my mind, how great a fire (so to speak) I feel kindled in my heart and soul by this sad aspect of Christianity; how much I pity both those who, in ignorance, attack religion under the pretext of zeal for religion, nature under the authority of nature, and God himself under the appearance of divine authority, and who, while they do not sufficiently attend to themselves, blind their own eyes. But if God, that Father of mercies and author of all consolation, shall direct this little work of mine, which he has stirred up in me, by the hand of his blessing, so that it both contains the truth and offers it to all, and at least makes the truth bear witness to some good men by this my office, I shall seem to have done for myself the greatest service of labour through his blessing.

units.la: Hanc autem scriptionem meam ita certum est temperare, vt à Deo omnia, à me nihil (cuius quidem conscius esse possim) in medium asseram. Quapropter materiam totius sermonis ex Dei verbo depromptu-rus sum, ne à forma veritatis illius quâ Deus expressit verbo, temerè abscedám: Tractationem verò diuinæ huius materiæ atque argumenti iusto ordini, quoad eius fieri poterit, conformatam pertexam breuiter, dilucidè, ac populariter.
units.tr: It is certainly my aim to shape this writing so that I bring forward everything from God and nothing from myself, of which I could be conscious. I will therefore draw the subject matter of the whole discourse from the word of God, so as not to depart rashly from the form of truth that God expressed in his word. I will then work out the treatment of this divine subject and matter briefly, clearly and plainly, arranged in due order as far as that can be done.

units.la: Summa argumenti ergo futura est: Iam plus satis in orbe Christiano dimicatum esse; pacem quærendam secundum Deum, inueniendam, amplec[?]tenda, & modis omnibus retinenda, vt fructus illius, quos Deus verbo proponit, amplissimos assequamur. Partes autem sermonis istius duæ futuræ sunt: Vna, de modo pacis: Altera, de fructu illius. Modum, ex veibis[?] Dauidis Psal. 122. Fructus ex Psalmo 133. eiusdem verbis exponemus. Antequam verò ad singularem venimus utriusque loci interpretationem, cùm utroq. in Psalmo communis extet inscriptio; de eâ prout ad rem præsentem attinet, nobis dicendum est. Inscriptio sic habet, Canticum excellentiarum, id est, omni excellentia instructum, Danidis[?]. quibus verbis modus, & res quæ agitur, & auctor proponitur: Auctor quidem, Danidis nomine: Res, excellentiarum: Modus verò, Cantici appellatione.
units.tr: The summary of the argument, then, will be this: enough fighting has already gone on in the Christian world. Peace must be sought according to God, found, embraced and kept in every way, so that we may attain the very ample fruits that God sets before us in his word. The discourse will have two parts: one on the manner of peace, the other on its fruit. We will explain the manner from the words of David in Psalm 122, and the fruit from Psalm 133, in its own words. But before we come to the particular interpretation of each passage, since both psalms bear a common inscription, we must say something about it insofar as it bears on the present matter. The inscription reads: "A song of excellences", that is, furnished with all excellence, "of David". By these words the manner, the thing treated and the author are set forth: the author by the name of David, the thing by "excellences", and the manner by the word "song".

units.la: Cùm autem ad iustam istarum rerum intelligentiam id primum ratio naturæ nostræ postulet in docendo, ut de Reipsa antequam de Auctore aut Modo cognoscamus, quam rem excellentiarum nomine diximus demonstrari: Duo hic nobis expendenda sunt, quæ in dubium adduci possent: nimirum Hebræi nominis interpretatio, & conditio rei quæ his Psalmis exponitur. Nomen enim Hebræū[?] plerique omnes interpretantur varie: Alij gradus: Alij adscensus: Alij denique excellentias, quod postremum sequuti sumus.
units.tr: Since right understanding of these matters in teaching requires first of all (as the nature of our mind demands) that we know the thing itself before the author or the manner, namely the thing we have said is signified by the name "excellences", two points must be weighed here that could be called into doubt: the interpretation of the Hebrew name, and the nature of the thing set out in these Psalms. Most people interpret the Hebrew name variously: some as "steps", others as "ascents", and others finally as "excellences", which last we have followed.

units.la: Qui gradus interpretantur, ex coniecturis & sine probatione certa, quæ quidem ex scripturis constare possit, narrant gradus in templo fuisse, secundum quos Leuitarum Musicam exercentium ordines in ministerio sacro consisterent, quo tempore fiebant sacra coram Domino. Alij verò diuersum tempus stationis illius ponunt, nempe tum Leuitas in musico opere per suos ordines fuisse occupatos, cùm sacerdotes & alij ad lectionem legis & tractationem Scripturæ S. comparabant sese, expectabantq; coram populo, dicturi de Cathedra Mosis: quam ad rem historia Nehemiæ 9,4. abutuntur. Sed nec factum illud, meo judicio, confirmari potest, nec testimonia quæ adferuntur, cum hac narratione facti consentire. Nam cùm Leuitarum ordines Musicam exercentium plures multo fuerint, ut ex 1.Chron.2s.[?] (quem locum adducunt vulgo) confirmatur, & secundum portas, ac non secundum gradus fuisse dicantur distributiones illorum passim: non video quo pacto res istæ differentia tam perspicua distinctæ confundi possint. Quod autem ad illum Nehemiæ locum, tantum abest ut de re musica exponi possit, cùm Leuitæ occupati fuisse dicuntur in sanctissimo illo ministerio, ut contra ex ipsius capitis argumento & narratione tota constet evidentissimè, nihil tum ad musicam, sed omnia ad flebilem luctum fuisse composita, cùm populus totus ad jejunium religiosissimum & sanctissimā cõfessionem peccatorum vocatus esset. Nam cùm in eodem Psalmorum libro fideles pronuncient, Quomodo cantaturi essemus canticum Jehovæ in regione extera, id est, in hoc luctu publico: quis putet illos ejusdem pietatis in altero luctu, coque acerbissimo, oblitos esse?
units.tr: Those who interpret it as "steps" say, on conjecture and without certain proof that could be drawn from Scripture, that there were steps in the temple, on which the orders of Levites performing the music stood in sacred ministry when the holy rites were performed before the Lord. Others place that standing at a different time, namely that the Levites were then occupied in their musical work by their orders while the priests and others prepared themselves to read the law and treat Holy Scripture, and waited before the people, about to speak from the seat of Moses; and for this they abuse the history of Nehemiah 9:4. But in my judgment neither that fact can be confirmed, nor do the testimonies adduced agree with this account. For the orders of Levites who performed music were far more numerous, as is confirmed from 1 Chronicles 25 (the place they commonly cite), and their distributions are said to have been made everywhere by gates and not by steps. I do not see how things so clearly distinct can be confused. As for that passage in Nehemiah, it is so far from being explainable as about music, since the Levites are said to have been occupied in that most holy ministry, that on the contrary, from the very argument and the whole narrative of that chapter, it is most evidently clear that nothing then was arranged for music but everything for mournful lamentation, since the whole people had been called to a most religious fast and a most holy confession of sins. For when the faithful in the same book of Psalms say, "How shall we sing the song of Jehovah in a foreign land?", that is, in this public mourning, who would think they forgot that same piety in another lament, and that most bitter one?

units.la: Hac igitur interpretatione omissa, statuunt alij adscensus hoc loco denotari: quorū adscensuum occasionibus circumfcribédis discrepant.
units.tr: Setting aside this interpretation, others hold that "ascents" is what is meant here, though they differ in determining the occasions of those ascents.

units.la: Hi enim hos Psalmos pertinere putant ad illa tempora, quibus pij singuli é suis stationibus adscendebant Hierosolyma, apparituri folenni modo coram facie Domini: quem ritum lex docet quamplurimis locis, & Prophera celebrat Psalmo 42. & 84. & 132. exemplaque docent in Vetere & Nouo Testamento passim.
units.tr: For these hold that the Psalms belong to those times when individual godly people went up from their homes to Jerusalem to appear solemnly before the face of the Lord. The law teaches this rite in very many places, the prophets celebrate it in Psalms 42, 84 and 132, and examples in the Old and New Testaments show it everywhere.

units.la: Illi veró ad tempus reuersionis ex Babylonia iudicant pertinere: fiue vt adscendentes Hierofolyma fe his meditationibus sanctis confirmarent, aliique alios inter fe hortarentur, fiue vt liberationis illius diuinæ memoriam his sacris cantionibus meditationibusque recolerent. Verùm cùm iftarù rerum, vtut speciosæ sint, nullum vestigium in scripturis compareat, mihi religio est ex narrationibus eiusmodi, quas sola coniectura gignit, interpretationes afferre, & res probandas tanquam probatas & compertas in medium adducere. Quod fi ex coniecturis solum agendum effet, mallem Hebræam vocem adscensus quidem exponere, sed ita vt de spiritali piorum eue&ione ad Dominú potius quàm de corporali motu intelligeretur: quæ interpretatio cum ea ipsa quam nos ampleétimur conuenientiam effet habitura. Sin gradus malit quis reddere, vt Efai.38. hos Psalmos fecundum horas solario distinctas cantatos in templodixerim (vt de Psalmo 22. testatur inscriptio) post reuersionē Babylone. His itaque omnibus oniissis, iudicamus Hebræa voce non gradus, aut adscensus, sed excellentias(ut ante diximus) denotari. Moris est autem apud Hebræos, vt quæ in summo & superlatiuo (vt loquuntur) gradu enunciãda sunt, ea substantiuis nominibus pluralis numeri exprimantur. Sic Canticum canticorum, Cant. 1. vir desideriorum, Dan. 9. & 10. desertum desolationum; Ierem. 12. verba venti; Iob 16. nimbus vocum Iob 38. quibus in isto genere nihil comparari possit. ac proinde Canticum excellentiarum illis cùm dicitur, tam sonat quàm si dixeris excellentissimum, vel Omni excellentiâ (quæ quidem vere excellentia est) & præstantiâ summâ instructum. Atque hæc interpretatio; quia vsui Hebræorum communi omnino respondet, & omnibus coniecturis narrationum factorumque carer, mihi omnium probatur maximè.
units.tr: Others judge that they belong to the time of the return from Babylon: either so that those going up to Jerusalem might strengthen themselves with these holy meditations and urge one another on, or so that they might recall that divine deliverance by these sacred songs and meditations. But since no trace of such things, however attractive, appears in Scripture, I scruple to bring forward interpretations drawn from narratives of this kind, which conjecture alone produces, and to lay before people things to be proved as if already proved and established. If it were a matter for conjecture alone, I would prefer to explain the Hebrew word as ascents, but so that it is understood of the spiritual elevation of the godly to the Lord rather than of bodily motion; that interpretation would agree just as well with the one we are defending. But if someone prefers to render it steps, I would say these Psalms were sung in the temple after the return from Babylon, according to the hours marked by a sundial, as in Isaiah 38 (as the inscription of Psalm 22 bears witness). Setting all these aside, we judge that the Hebrew word denotes not steps or ascents, but excellences, as we said before. Now it is the custom among the Hebrews that what must be expressed in the highest, superlative degree (as they say) is expressed by substantive nouns in the plural. Thus "the Song of Songs", Song 1; "man of desires", Dan. 9 and 10; "desert of desolations", Jer. 12; "words of wind", Job 16; "storm of voices", Job 38; compared with which nothing in that kind could be set. So when they say "a song of excellences", it sounds just as if you had said "most excellent", or "furnished with all excellence" (which is truly excellence) and "endowed with supreme pre-eminence". This interpretation, because it wholly corresponds to the common usage of the Hebrews and is free of all the conjectures of narratives and events, is by far the one I most approve.

units.la: Non sum nescias fore, qui obiiciant eandem quoque aliis psalmis & canticis sacris inesse excellentiam: propterea iniquum esse, vt præ illis excellentiæ laus his perbreuibus Psalmis adscribatur. Sed si ad rem pij attenderint, animaduertent in hoc inscriptionum genere duo quædam oportere obseruari; sine quibus indignus hic inscriptionis modus esse videretur. Vnum est, quòd apud Hebræos hæ inscriptiones absolutè, ac non comparatè accipiuntur, tanquam si dixeris Canticum omnem in se excellentiam continens: quæ res citra aliorum canticorum[?] comparationem ita prædicatur, vt his Psalmis sua excellentia adseratur, de aliis verò nihil derogetur plane. Alterum, quòd etiam certo quodam respectu singularis est his Psalmis excellentia, quam præ aliis obtinent, & Dei spiritus testificatus est. Est autem excellentia summa & aliis anteponenda in his Psalmis aut respectu auctoris sui siue principij, aut rei, aut modi ad eam pertinentis. Non autem auctoris: nam rerum excellentissimarū & vniuersam naturam quam longissimè superantiū omnium, & singularū, auctor vnus est Deus Pater in Filio per Spiritū. Restat igitur, vt dicamus excellentiam inesse his Psalmis propter rē aut modum ipsorum: Quæ duo secundum rationem & respectum quendam ducimus coiungenda.
units.tr: I am not unaware that there will be those who object that the same excellence is found also in other psalms and sacred songs, and that it would therefore be unfair to ascribe the praise of excellence to these very short Psalms. But if the godly attend to the matter, they will notice that two things ought to be observed in this kind of inscription, without which this manner of inscription would seem unworthy. The first is that among the Hebrews these inscriptions are taken absolutely, not comparatively, as if you had said a song containing in itself all excellence. The thing is asserted without comparison with other songs, so that excellence is claimed for these Psalms while nothing at all is taken away from the others. The second is that, in a certain respect, the excellence these Psalms have above others is singular, and the Spirit of God has testified to it. The highest excellence, the one to be preferred to all others, lies in these Psalms either in respect of their author or principle, or of the thing, or of the manner pertaining to it. Not of the author: for the author of all things most excellent, surpassing the whole nature of all things by the furthest distance, both general and particular, is one God the Father, in the Son, through the Spirit. It remains, then, that the excellence is in these Psalms on account of their thing or their manner, and these two we take to be joined together according to reason and a certain respect.

units.la: Nihil hic dicimus de horum Psalmorū comparatione cum exteris siue humanis cantionibus, secundū quam omnes Psalmi & spirituales odæ à Deo sanctificatæ in scripturis communem habent excellentiam, Principio, Re, & Modo simul omnia humanarū cantionum genera omnibus modis superantem: Etsi hanc quoque communem excellentiam his Psalmis adscribi necesse est, vel eo ipso quòd sunt in cantionum diuinarū & spiritalium genere. Sed tantūm hoc loco agimus de comparatione horum Psalmorum cum aliis eiusdem generis, qui omnes Principio, Re, & Modo spirituali communicant. Hi enim certo quodam respectu excellentiam sibi vindicant auctoritate & testimonio Spiritus, non in se aut respectu sui, sed in nobis potius & respectu nostri: quia si ad Rem quæ continetur illis respexeris, simplicissimam habent rei quæ agitur applicationem supra quam alij Psalmi aut Cantica Scripturis S. comprehensa: Si ad Modum, eandem habent breuissimam, ac proinde ad memoriam hominum commodissimam. Sed quia de his rebus perspicuo ordine dicendum est secundum eas partes quas ante inscriptione proponi docuimus, præstat iam ad excutiendas partes singulas veniamus.
units.tr: Here we say nothing of the comparison of these Psalms with other, outside or human songs, according to which all the Psalms and spiritual odes sanctified by God in Scripture have a common excellence, surpassing in every way all kinds of human songs in principle, thing and manner together. Although this common excellence must also be ascribed to these Psalms, simply because they belong to the kind of divine and spiritual songs, at this point we treat only of the comparison of these Psalms with others of the same kind, which all share in principle, thing and manner of the spiritual sort. These claim excellence for themselves in a certain respect, by the authority and testimony of the Spirit: not in themselves or in respect of themselves, but rather in us and in respect of us. If you look at the thing contained in them, they have the most simple application of the matter treated, beyond the other Psalms or Canticles comprised in Holy Scripture; if you look at the manner, they have the same very brief form, and therefore the most convenient for human memory. But since these things must be set out in a clear order, according to the parts which we showed before are to be put forward in the inscription, it is better now to come to examine the individual parts.

units.la: De excellentia itaq. dicturi principium illud à natura ingeneratum, quod ante diecebamus, toti huic argumento præstruimus[?]: Naturam quamq. bonum appetere. Huic autem principio alterû quoq. adiungi necesse est, Naturam quamque sic bonum appetere, vt appetat melius, si potest contingere: ac proinde vbi ad bonum quo melius nihil est, ad bonum (inquam) summum peruenerit, in eo conquiescere, vt quo nihil melius. Bonum autem particulare communi, & humanum diuino cedit, naturale supernaturali: quia commune supernaturale, & diuinum est excellentius. Hæc bona homines, prout sunt disciplinabiles, re sic assequuntur, vt certâ doctrinæ[?] via atq. ratione ad inuestiganda, noscenda, consequenda, tenendaque ea perducantur. Quapropter vt bonum vnum præcellit alteri, sic vna doctrina alteri pro cōditione obiecti illius circa quod ( vt loquuntur) doctrina quaeq. occupatur,& rationis (vt vocant) formalis ad obiectum pertinentis. Hic autem quis neget ipsissimam excellentiam in his verbis tradi? in quibus non quoduis particulare; sed commune:non naturale,sed supernaturale: non humanum,sed diuinum plane bonum hominibus exponitur?Res igitur est excellentissima, doctrina rei excellentissimae his Psalmis consignata[?]:ac proinde si ad res cæteras respexeris,communis est in his impressa (vt in cæteris quoque scripturis) supra res omnes excellen- tia. Quòd si excellentiam appetimus, Ergò & horum Psalmorum doctrinam ( quæ nihil nisi excellentia est) appetamus necesse est.
units.tr: Therefore, in speaking of excellence, we lay down as the foundation of this whole argument that principle, implanted in nature, which we mentioned before: that every nature seeks good. To this principle a second must also be added: that every nature seeks good in such a way that it seeks the better, if that can be attained. Accordingly, when it has reached the good than which nothing is better, the supreme good, it rests in that, as in the thing than which nothing is better. Particular good yields to common good, and human good to divine, natural to supernatural, because the common supernatural and divine good is more excellent. Men attain these goods, insofar as they are capable of instruction, by being led through a certain path and method of teaching to investigate, know, obtain and hold them. Therefore, as one good surpasses another, so one doctrine surpasses another, according to the condition of the object with which each doctrine is concerned (as they say), and of the formal reason (as they call it) that pertains to the object. Now who would deny that the very highest excellence is delivered in these words, in which not some particular good but a common good, not a natural but a supernatural good, not a human but plainly a divine good, is set forth to men? The matter, therefore, is most excellent, and the doctrine of this most excellent matter is set down in these Psalms. Accordingly, if you look at other things, a common excellence is impressed on these Psalms (as on the other Scriptures also), above all things. And if we desire excellence, we must necessarily desire the teaching of these Psalms as well, since it is nothing but excellence.

units.la: Deinde vero cum in rebus ipsis supernaturalibus & diuinis alia bona aliis præstantiora sint,id etiam nobis videndum est, vt singularem horum Psalmorum excellentiam sanctè recog- noscamus, & ad eam probè cognitam religiosè colendam & amplectendam accendamur. Est autem horum Psalmorum excellentia siue præstantia:Vna communis,Altera propria.Communis est,quòd à Deo auctore sunt, quòd res diuinas tradunt,& quòd diuino modo ad eam rem sanctificati sunt, vt reliqui Scripturæ loci. Præterea Psalmorū & hymnorum spiritualium in Scripturis eà ratio,vt respectu nostri excellentiores,aliis Scripturis in doctrinæ modo esse videantur. Nam res sanctas singulari quodam modo usui nostro accommodant, & quasi temperati sunt ad modulum naturae nostrae ex inscientia commodius informandae, ex infirmitate confirmandae, atq. in veritate, justitia & sanctimonia, aduersus omnes animi perturbationes & impedimenta intus forisq. obuenientia, per singulare illud applicationis modum constabiliendae: qui modus non ita est in aliis scripturarum generibus. Itaque & hanc excellentiam Psalmorum & canticorum spiritualium communem his psalmis adscribimus. Nam scriptura quidem illa diuina aliis omnibus antecellit: sed in scriptura respectu applicationis ad vulnera, perpessiones, actiones, & difficultates quasuis animorum nostrorum Psalmi aliis scripturae partibus anteponendi sunt.
units.tr: Next, since among the supernatural and divine things themselves some goods are more outstanding than others, we must also take care to acknowledge devoutly the singular excellence of these Psalms, and to be stirred to cherish and embrace it, once it is rightly understood. The excellence or pre-eminence of these Psalms is twofold: one common, the other proper. The common excellence is that they have God as their author, that they teach divine things, and that they are set apart for that purpose in a divine manner, like the other passages of Scripture. Besides, the Psalms and spiritual hymns have this character in Scripture: in relation to us they seem more excellent than other parts of Scripture in their mode of teaching. For they fit holy things to our use in a singular way, and are, as it were, tempered to the measure of our nature, so that it may be more conveniently formed out of ignorance, strengthened out of weakness, and established in truth, righteousness and holiness against all disturbances and hindrances of the mind arising within and without. This is done by that singular manner of application, which is not found in other kinds of Scripture. So we also ascribe this excellence, common to the Psalms and spiritual songs, to these psalms. For divine Scripture indeed surpasses all other writings; but within Scripture, with respect to application to the wounds, sufferings, actions and whatever difficulties of our souls, the Psalms are to be preferred to the other parts of Scripture.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem Scriptura S. aliis scriptis toto genere, & Psalmi reliquae scripturae secundum quendam applicationis modum antecellunt: ita etiam hi psalmi, quamuis perbreues; suo quodam iure aliis dicuntur antestare. Cur autem? quia etsi rem eandem cum aliis communem tradunt, & eodem modo: in re tamen & in modo ipso singulare aliquid recognoscendum est. In re enim Lux quaedam familiaritatis emicat supra quàm in aliis plerisque psalmis, & quasi à multis circumstantiarum singularium, quae alibi occurrunt, tenebris expurgata: In modo autem, breuitas ad facilitatem accedens, quam vel pueruli memoria facilè completi potuerint. Quæ cùm ita sint, non dubitamus quin pij omnibus expensis in eam sententiam nobiscum venturi sint: totius quidem scripturæ; tum in se, tum in nobis excellentiam esse homini psychico incredibilé, nobis admirabilem: sed psalmorum libro atque argumento singularem inesse modum excellentiæ: his autem inter cæteros summè singularem. Atque hæc quidem de excellentia, si comparationem huius cum illa ex inscriptione instituere quisquam voluerit: quam excellentiam Spiritus sanctus affirmauit prouidentissimè, ne illa breuitas atque facilitas (vt fit) in contemptum abire posset. Alioquin mihi non displicet, si (pront Hebraei plurimum faciunt) hanc excellentiæ prædicationem absolutè & citra comparationem acceperis.
units.tr: Just as Holy Scripture surpasses other writings in its whole kind, and the Psalms surpass the rest of Scripture by a certain manner of application, so these psalms, though very brief, are rightly said to excel others by a certain right of their own. Why? Because although they hand down the same matter as the others, and in the same way, something singular is to be recognised both in the matter and in the mode itself. In the matter, a certain light of familiarity shines forth more than in most other psalms, as if cleansed of many shadows of the singular circumstances that occur elsewhere. In the mode, brevity adds ease, so that even children can easily complete it by memory. These things being so, we do not doubt that the godly, weighing everything, will agree with us in this judgement: that of all Scripture, both in itself and in us, there is an excellence incredible to the natural man and admirable to us; but in the book and subject of the Psalms there is a singular mode of excellence, and among these psalms this is most singular. This is what I have to say about excellence, if anyone wishes to compare it with that excellence set out in the inscription, which the Holy Spirit affirmed most providently, lest that brevity and ease (as tends to happen) should pass into contempt. Otherwise I have no objection, if you take this proclamation of excellence absolutely and without comparison, as the Hebrews very much do.

units.la: Cæterùm quia excellentiâ huic doctrinæ & huic scriptorum generi attribuit Deus, cùm omnes tum naturâ iubente, tû Deo per Apostolû præcipiente ad viâ excellentiæ tenea-mur contendere:id nobis obseruandum est, Omnis doctrinæ præstantia esse in rebus duabus positam. Nam ante eo doctrina vna alteri anteponitur, quòd dignior in se ipsa est, aut quòd est certior. Dignitas, in re: Certitudo, in modo illius exploratur.
units.tr: Moreover, since God has attributed this excellence to this doctrine and to this kind of writing, and since we are bound, both by nature commanding and by God precepting through the Apostle, to strive along the way of excellence, we must observe this: the pre-eminence of every doctrine rests on two things. One doctrine is preferred to another either because it is more worthy in itself, or because it is more certain. Worth is examined in the matter; certainty in the mode of knowing it.

units.la: Ac rei quidem dignitas ad scientiæ dignitatem facit, si res aliàs multas dignitate superauerit. Scientia verò diuinarum rerum, non dico multâs, sed omnes alias omnino superat, & transcendit longissimè: adeò ut quod minimum est illius, sit maius quàuis humanarum scientiarum amplitudine. Cùm autem scientiarum, quæ quidem apud homines habentur dignifsimæ, aliæ in cõtemplatione, aliæ in actione versentur, & omnes scientia diuinorũ ex æquo superet: ex eo planè cõficitur quicquid dignitatis in Theoricis, quicquid in Practicis obseruari potest, id totũ plenissimè non naturali, sed supernaturali; non humano, sed diuino modo in hoc existere. Est autem Theoricarum dignitas partim ex Rei vel Materiæ natura, partimq. ex comprehensionis modo huiusmodi; quòd ea confiderant sua quadam ratione secundum naturam, quæ rationi subiecta sunt: Practicarum verò dignitas potissimùm iis tribuitur, quæ ad vlteriorem fine nõ sunt ordinatæ, sed in eo proprie conquiescunt[?]: sicut, exempli causa, ciuilis scientia militari præstat, quia militia ad bonum ciuitatis ordinata est. Hæc omnia si in doctrina facta religiosè expendamus, & ea ipsa quam ex his psalmis (Deo dante.) sumus percepturi; Deus bone, quantam dignitatem maiestatemq. cernimus ab omni parte circumfulgentem nos & diuinis illis radiis in mētibus collustrantem! Nam si ad rerũ contemplationẽ respexeris, hæc scientia, hæc doctrina est primò & principaliter de iis rebus, quæ sua altitudine & amplitudine transscendût rationem, supra omnes cælos euectæ sunt, & diuinitas è cœlo res omnes perfundunt sua luce quæ ad participationem eiufdem dignitatis cælesti gratia ordinatæ sunt. Sin ad finem ipsius animum & cogitationem noftram conuertamus, non eum finem proponi simpliciter animaduertemus, qui à natura rebus creatis omnibus, aut etiam humano generi propositus est; sed ad cognitionem, fructumque suauissimum nos perducit illius finis ultimi, ad quem omnes alij fines scientiarum & actionum sunt ordinati. Deum enim ut finem statuit & communem terminûm, cùm rebus creatis cæteris, tum hominibus singulariter destinatum: neque hoc solùm, sed finem cuiusque proprium in illo communi termino reuelat, quòd in eo apprehenso æternam salutè & beatitudinem simus adepturi: denique, ne quisquam aberrare possit, media singula ad finem illum pertinentia & necessario cum eo coniun&ta declarat sapientissimè. quibus rebus quid dignius, vel angustius cogitari potest?
units.tr: The worth of a matter adds to the worth of a science if it surpasses many other things in dignity. But the science of divine things surpasses all others altogether, I do not say many, and transcends them by far, so that even its smallest part is greater than the whole breadth of human sciences. Since among the sciences held most worthy among men some are concerned with contemplation and others with action, and the science of divine things surpasses all of them alike, it plainly follows that whatever worth can be observed in theoretical or practical matters, all of it exists here most fully, not in a natural but in a supernatural way, and not in a human but in a divine way. The worth of theoretical sciences depends partly on the nature of the thing or matter, and partly on the manner of comprehending it, in that they consider, in their own way and according to nature, things that are subject to reason. The worth of practical sciences is attributed chiefly to those that are not ordered to a further end but rest properly in it: civil science, for example, excels military science, because warfare is ordered to the good of the state. If we religiously weigh all these things in this doctrine, and in the very doctrine we are to receive from these psalms (God granting it), good God, what dignity and majesty we see shining on every side around us, and illuminating our minds with those divine rays! For if you look to the contemplation of things, this science, this doctrine, is first and principally concerned with those things which by their height and breadth transcend reason and are raised above all the heavens; and divinity pours light from heaven upon all things, which by heavenly grace are ordered to participation in that same dignity. But if we turn our mind and thought to the end itself, we shall see that it is not simply the end set before created things by nature, or even before the human race, but that it leads us to knowledge and the sweetest fruit of that ultimate end, to which all other ends of sciences and actions are ordered. For God has established himself as the end and common term, destined both for created things in general and for men in particular. And not only this: he reveals the proper end of each in that common term, namely that by apprehending it we shall obtain eternal salvation and blessedness. Finally, lest anyone should be able to go astray, he wisely declares each means that pertains to that end and is necessarily joined with it. What more worthy or more ample thing can be thought of?

units.la: Venio ad certitudinem. Quæcunque in hominibus scientiæ fieri solét plurimi, eæ certitudinem suam ex principiis & mediis cognitionis dicuntur habere. Principia earù naturalia sunt immota & immediata per vim quandam naturæ in humano intellectu ingenerata: quorum alia ab ipsis scientiis, alia ab aliis depromi solét tanquam à superioribus. Huic doctrinæ merito vindicatur omnis excellentiæ perfectio: quæ immediatè nó à natura, sed à Deo; nec per naturam, sed per revelationem gratiæ principia sua obtinet certa,immota,& immediata.Quòd si quæ interdum à natura & ratione humanâ adhibet, ea non tanquam mutuò aut precariò à superioribus, sed suo iure tanquâ ab inferioribus & ancillantibus assumit: nō quo perficiatur ab illis, sed quo perficiat illas; & in usu iustissimò singulas occupet. Nam cur non utatur hac via Dominus & seruator noster? cuius doctrinam non propter defectum vel insufficientiam (ut ita loquamur) ipsius, sed propter defectum intellectus nostri, ad quos hæc salutaris doctrina pertinet, his adiumentis instrui oportuit: ut ex iis quæ per naturalem rationem, velut scientiarum omnium humanarum matrem, innotescùt, facilius ad ea percipienda deveniamus atq. deducamur, quibus humana ratio & natura tota superatur. Media verò ad certitudinem doctrinæ huius pertinentia cum his principiis planè cōsentiunt. Illæ enim scientiæ quibus homines intumescunt, certitudinem suam habent ex illo naturali rationis humanæ lumine, quæ potest errare: prout euentus in hominibus singulis plus satis ostendit. Hæc verò scientia (ut cum Propheta loquar) excellentiarum, perfectam divinitus habet certitudinem ex lumine supernaturalis scientiæ & divinæ, quæ nec ipsa errare potest, nec ab ullo erroris spiritu circumduci. Sed quid multis probationibus aliunde accitis opus est? Doctrinâ excellentiarum rum appellat Deus: quis dubitet eam ita esse vt appellat Deus?Deus hanc esse dicit sapientiam nostram & prudentiā nostram ante oculos populorum, vsqueadeò vt isti audientes dicãt, Tantùm gens ista maxima populus sapiens est & prudens: quis contradicat Deo veritatis? Est igitur excellens,imò excellentissima, imò omni omnis excellentiæ perfectione absolutissima: quæ omnia locutione Hebræa designātur.Cùm autem hæc singula eiusmodi sint, vt hominem, vel naturâ teste, ad huius doctrinæ amores incredibiles debeât excitare: ô miserum hominem, qui aliis in rebus omnibus facilè cupit excellere, præterquam in iis quæ verâ excellentiam ,certam, plenamque Deo teste & auctore obtinent!
units.tr: I come to certainty. Whatever sciences are usually found among men, they are said to have their certainty from the principles and means of knowledge. Their natural principles are fixed and immediate, implanted in the human intellect by a certain power of nature; some of these are drawn from the sciences themselves, others from other sciences as from superiors. To this doctrine is rightly claimed the perfection of all excellence: it obtains its certain, fixed and immediate principles not immediately from nature but from God, and not through nature but through the revelation of grace. But if it sometimes employs things from nature and human reason, it takes them not as borrowed or on loan from superiors, but by its own right, as from inferiors and handmaids: not so that it may be perfected by them, but so that it may perfect them, and in its most just use it claims each of them for itself. For why should our Lord and Saviour not use this way? His doctrine needed to be taught with these aids, not because of any defect or insufficiency in himself, so to speak, but because of the defect of our intellect, to which this saving doctrine pertains; so that by means of what becomes known through natural reason, the mother of all human sciences, we may more easily come to perceive and be led to those things by which human reason and nature are wholly surpassed. The means pertaining to the certainty of this doctrine agree completely with these principles. For those sciences by which men are puffed up have their certainty from that natural light of human reason, which can err, as the outcome in individual men shows more than enough. But this science of excellences (as I speak with the Prophet) has a perfect certainty divinely, from the light of a supernatural and divine science, which itself cannot err nor be led astray by any spirit of error. But why need many proofs brought from elsewhere? God calls this doctrine a doctrine of excellences. Who would doubt that it is just as God calls it? God says that this is our wisdom and our prudence before the eyes of the peoples, so that those who hear it will say: "Surely this great nation is a wise and prudent people." Who would contradict God, the God of truth? It is therefore excellent, indeed most excellent, indeed most perfect in every perfection of excellence, all of which are expressed by a Hebrew idiom. Since each of these things is of such a kind that, even by the testimony of nature, it ought to stir a man to incredible love for this doctrine, O wretched man, who in all other things easily desires to excel, except in those things which by God's testimony and authority obtain true, certain and full excellence!

units.la: Huius autem excellentiæ tum adiuncta manifestissima,tum certissima testimonia sunt duo illa reliqua capita, quæ ex inscriptione horum psalmorum antè ostendimus.. Quisquis enim de excellentia hac necdū sibi videtur satis confirmatus ,ad auctorem , ad modum respiciat: Hic certè habituru est, unde suam illam fidei infirmitatem statuminet. Auctor est Deus: instrumentum, Dauid, à Deo sanctificatum & in perscribendis his psalmis occupatum. Ille rex, propheta θεόπνευστος[?], ille homo secundùm cor Dei ; vt scriptura loquitur, testis incorruptus, & publicus Dei in Ecclesia, Ecclesiæque apud Deum notarius, publica fide & auctoritate hos psalmos exarauit. Has operas , Dei inquam & Dauidis,in his psalmis concurrentes, excellen-tes esse, & de rebus excellentissimis credent, quicumque Deum, Ecclesiam, & tantum Dei seruum a Deo Ecclesiaque adhibitum ad istud opus verebuntur.
units.tr: Moreover, the clearest and most certain attestations of this excellence are those two remaining heads, which we showed earlier from the title of these psalms. Whoever does not yet feel sufficiently assured of this excellence should look to the author and the manner of the work: there he will certainly find something to prop up that weakness of faith. The author is God; the instrument is David, sanctified by God and engaged in writing down these psalms. That king, a prophet inspired by God [θεόπνευστος], that man after God's own heart, as Scripture says, an incorruptible witness and public officer of God in the Church, and the Church's notary before God, wrote down these psalms with public faith and authority. Whoever reveres God, the Church, and so great a servant of God, employed by God and the Church for this task, will believe that these labours, I mean God's and David's, meeting together in these psalms, are excellent, and that they deal with the most excellent matters.

units.la: Huic dignitati & certitudini alterâ adiunxit Deus, cùm hos ipsos psalmos & cantica esse voluit, eaque publicè in Ecclesia cani, & ab eadem asseruari. Primùm enim quanta sit vis numerorum & modulationis in mentibus hominum & animis excitandis, reuocandis, flectendis, firmandis, regendisque in omnem partem, nemo homo ignorare potest. Quod autem in natura fit, id Deus sanctissimè & sapientissimè in rebus sacris, & in his ipsis voluit obseruari. Deinde non parú momenti adferre videtur harum cantionum auctoritati, quòd Deus nō solùm ad cantum cōmodas in populo suo extare voluit, sed etiam in publicum auctoritatem earum diuinam testificatus est: nec illis solùm temporibus colendam & suscipiendam, sed in omnem praeterea posteritatem, hîs temporibus ultimis, hac luce Evangelij, ad secundum usque adventum Christi observandam. Quae cùm ita sint, cùm harum cantionum quas hoc tempore interpretandas suscepimus, ea fit Principio, Re, & Modo ipsarum auctoritas, ea rerum (utcunq. paucæ videantur) Veritas, Utilitas, Honestas, atque Necessitas ex Dei ipsius veracis atque fidelis testimonio, ut nihil in rebus humanis adæquari, nihil comparari possit, vt quæ toto genere ab eis differât, & res omnes humanas,quæ dici aut cogitari possunt, maximopere antecellant: excitemur per Deum immortalem ex illo infausto lethiferoq. veterno , quo nos communisille aduersarius salutis nostræ soporauit , & in quo nati,educati, alti conquiescimus plus fatis. Videamus tandem nihil in rebus omnibus mundi existere , quod nobis verà excellentiam præbeat,quamuis ostentet speciem: nihil attendi à nobis oportere , ad quod (vt certatim) faciemus)apprehendendum concurramus in his labentibus. & caducis rebus: præterit enim figura mundi huius,inquit Apostolus.quin potiús pro eo quod ita miserè in fluxis rebus naturá noftrâ & studio diffluimus; veram excellentiam rerum quæramus studiosissimè: veram doctrinam excellentiæ naturâ extinctam , sed gratiâ oblatam pereipiamus diligentissimè: & verum auctorem doctrinæ huius ( cuius beneficio ad veritatem rerum doctrinarumque salutarium quàm indulgentissimè prouocamur ) aufcultemus religiofiffimè : & in scholá eius hærentes, tamquam ad pedes ipsius, hauriamus de riuis veritatis,expectantes dum ad fontem illius plenissimum plenissimè perducamur.
units.tr: God added another attestation to this dignity and certainty, when he willed that these very psalms and songs should exist, that they should be sung publicly in the Church, and that the Church should preserve them. For first, no one can be ignorant of how great is the power of rhythm and melody in stirring, recalling, bending, strengthening, and steering people's minds and souls in every direction. What happens in nature, God willed to be observed in sacred matters most holily and wisely, and in these very songs. Next, it seems to add no small weight to the authority of these songs that God not only willed them to exist among his people, fit for singing, but also bore witness publicly to their divine authority; that they were to be honoured and received not only in those times, but also to be observed by all later generations, in these last times, in this light of the Gospel, until the second coming of Christ. Since these things are so, since the authority of these songs, which we have now undertaken to interpret, is such in principle, in matter, and in manner, and since their truth, usefulness, honour, and necessity (however few they may seem) rest on the testimony of God himself, who is true and faithful, so that nothing in human affairs can equal or be compared with them, since they differ from them in their whole kind and far surpass all human things that can be said or thought, let us be roused by the immortal God from that ill-omened and deadly lethargy with which that common adversary of our salvation has lulled us to sleep, and in which we are born, brought up, and nourished, and in which we rest more than enough. Let us see at last that nothing in all the things of the world exists that gives us true excellence, however much it may put on a show; that we ought to attend to nothing which we should hurry to grasp, as we eagerly do, among these fleeting and perishing things; for the form of this world passes away, says the Apostle. Rather, since our nature and zeal pour away so wretchedly into fleeting things, let us most eagerly seek the true excellence of things; let us most diligently receive the true doctrine of excellence, which nature has extinguished but grace has offered; and let us most reverently listen to the true author of this doctrine, by whose kindness we are most graciously called to the truth of things and of saving teachings. Clinging to his school, as at his feet, let us draw from the streams of truth, waiting until we are led most fully to his most full fountain.

units.la: Ex his itaque fontibus de cóhditione sanctæ pacis & Christianæ ductuti aliquos riuos ad communem ædificatiónem , Deum oramus vt nobis de ipsa excellentia dicturis ptæfit Spiritu ritu excellentiæ suò, & lecturos omnes afficiat eiusdem excellentiæ suæ studio ac conscientiâ, ut viam excellentem hanc insistamus omnes, & ad finem perfectionemque illius uno animo contendamus in Christo Iesu unico, æterno, & perfecto seruatore nostro. Cùm autem duo capita de Pace receperimus, ante[?] nos esse dicturos: Unum, de Re & Modo ipsius: Alterum, de Fructibus: Iam auctore Domino venturi sumus ad prioris explicationem, prout verba nobis sanctus ille Dei Spiritus præiuit olim per Dauidem Psalmo 122. & nobis in eundem Psalmum dicendi gratiam admensurus est.
units.tr: Therefore, drawing from these fountains some streams concerning the condition of holy and Christian peace for common edification, we pray God that his Spirit of excellence may be present with us who are about to speak of that excellence itself, and that he may move all who read them with the same zeal and conscience for excellence, so that we all may tread this excellent way and strive with one mind toward its end and perfection in Christ Jesus, our only, eternal, and perfect Saviour. Since we have undertaken to speak of two heads concerning peace, the first on its nature and manner, the second on its fruits, we now, with the Lord as our author, come to the explanation of the first, as that holy Spirit of God long ago set the words before us through David in Psalm 122, and will grant us the grace of speaking on that same psalm.

units.la: PSALMVS. 122.
units.tr: Psalm 122.

units.la: 1. Lætor de dicentibus mihi, Eamus in domum Iehoue.
units.tr: 1. I rejoiced when they said to me, Let us go into the house of Jehovah.

units.la: Huius psalmi Finis est, ut Deus in Ecclesia sua glorificetur intus fide, foris obsequio fidei omnibusq. officiis pietatis, in unitate Spiritus per vinculum pacis. Summa est, Fructum Spiritus in omnibus piis esse gaudium spirituale, & pacem in iustitia; quam pacem Deus in Christo publicè dedit ecclesiæ, & singulis membris illius, in se, atq. inter se colendâ cum Deo, & secundum Deum. Partes itaque duæ sunt: Nam primùm loquitur Psaltes de spirituali piorum gaudio in Christo & ecclesiâ eius: ad quod gaudium omnes homines sermone salutis & exemplo piotum[?] prouocantur, quinq. versibus: Deinde vero pax illa ostenditur quam ecclesia colit,ex quo cælesti illo gaudio (quod modò diximus ) perfusa est, quatuor versibus ultimis.
units.tr: The aim of this psalm is that God may be glorified in his Church: inwardly by faith, and outwardly by the obedience of faith and by all the duties of godliness, in the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace. The sum is that the fruit of the Spirit in all the godly is spiritual joy and peace in righteousness. God has publicly given this peace in Christ to the Church and to each of its members, to be cultivated both in themselves and among themselves, with God and according to God. There are therefore two parts. First, the Psalmist speaks of the spiritual joy of the godly in Christ and in his Church, to which all men are summoned by the word of salvation and by the example of the pious, in five verses. Then, in the last four verses, he sets forth the peace that the Church cherishes, since it has been filled with that heavenly joy just mentioned.

units.la: .Antequam vero de his partibus distinctè dicimus, nō est prætereunda silentio illa occasio, quæ suis temporibus Dauidé excitauit ut hunc sanctissimum psalmum ad gloriam Dei canendum Ecclesiæ traderet. Quisquis vel mediocriter in lectione historiæ sacræ versatus est, non ignorat quantis difficultatibus inde à morte Iosuæ populus Dei laborauerit, in peccatis suis mersus, & in malis quamplurimis varié pro-propter peccata sua à Deo exercitus : à quibus malis etsi interdum longo interuallo recreabatur, liberationes aliquas divinâ manu adipiscens, tamen ne Samuelis quidem ipsius aut Saulis temporibus fuisse piis refrigerium (ut cum scriptura loquar ) eiusmodi, ac pòst illis contigit quàm Dauid in regnum evectus est, atque in eo confirmatus. Hanc cóstitutionem Dauidem assecutum, cum sui officij, tum divinarum in lege promissionum recordantem, de arca fœderis in civitatem suam importanda, & domo extruenda ferò cogitauisse: quorum prius, id est,arcæ importatio in civitatem Dauidis,contigit[?] vivente ipso: posterius,domus ædificatio, in tempus filij reiectum est. Cùm autem re in consiliùm[?] missa, arca illa Dei in tentorium, quod Dauid parauerat, inferenda esset, celebritatem fuisse maximam à Dauide imperatam ad deducendum arcam Iehouæ in locum eius,quem parauerat ei:& alacritatem summâ tum à sacerdotibus Leuitisque,tum à popularibus singulis exhibitam, sibi,& ecclesiæ toti ; regnoq. hanc Dei gratiâ gratulantibus expertus est. Ad hanc igitur occasionem cùm Dauid anteactas gentis suæ & Ecclesiæ Dei calamitates memoriâ repeteret, præsentiaque beneficia cum illis compararet,ad hoc canticum exarandum deponendumque in ecclesia fuit auctore Dei spiritu adductus; vt eâ ratione testatum faceret, se tum rerum præsentium, quas videbat oculis, tum illarum quas animo cernebat in Ecclesia Dei; argumento ad hanc prædicationem diuinam excitari. Videbat enim populum suum ab hoste liberatum, seque regem tranquillum datum, locum electum à Deo designatum, Arcam Dei symbolum gratiosæ præsentiæ eius importatam in ciuitatem suam, populum Deo, Regi, & sibi gratulantem; omnia deniq; laudibus & plausu piorum personantia de tot tantisq. acceptis beneficiis. Sed hæc quantula fuerunt, si cum spiritalibus, quæ iam tum cernebat animo, comparentur? Cernebat populum Dei ab hoste Satanâ liberatum in Christo redemptore nostro: hunc regem datum à Deo, quem adumbrabat Dauid: Deum sibi & Ecclesiæ toti in Christo esse præsentissimum singulari præsentiâ gratiæ per communicationem spiritus, & mansionem apud se populumq. suum statuisse: pios omnes acclamantes huic sanctissimo Dei adventui: Denique hæc omnia plenissimè à Christo consummanda, tum priore adventu ipsius, cùm sermo factus est Caro, & consummavit in se quæcunque sunt opus ad salutem nostram; tum posteriore illo exoptatissimoque adventu, quo omnia in nobis consummatura est, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: Before we set out these parts in detail, we must not pass over in silence the occasion which, in its own time, moved David to hand this most holy psalm down to the Church to be sung to the glory of God. Anyone who has at least a moderate acquaintance with the reading of sacred history knows how greatly the people of God laboured in difficulties from the death of Joshua onward. Sunk in their sins, and variously afflicted with many evils by God on account of those sins, they were indeed sometimes refreshed after a long interval, obtaining some deliverances by the divine hand. Yet even in the times of Samuel or Saul, the godly did not have such refreshment (to speak in the words of Scripture) as came to them after David was raised to the kingdom and confirmed in it. When David had attained this settled state, mindful both of his office and of the divine promises made in the law, he thought long about bringing the ark of the covenant into his city and about building a house. The first of these, the bringing of the ark into the city of David, took place while he was still alive; the second, the building of the house, was put off to the time of his son. When that plan had been set aside and the ark of God was to be carried into the tent that David had prepared, David ordered the greatest solemnity for conveying the ark of Jehovah to the place he had prepared for it. He experienced the highest eagerness shown by the priests and Levites and by the people individually, and their rejoicing at this grace of God for himself, for the whole Church and for the kingdom. Therefore, on this occasion, when David recalled the past calamities of his nation and of the Church of God and compared them with the present blessings, he was moved by the Spirit of God to write this song and to deposit it in the Church. By this means he would show that he was stirred to this divine proclamation both by the present things he saw with his eyes and by those in the Church of God that he discerned in his mind. For he saw his people delivered from the enemy, himself given a peaceful king, a place designated by God as chosen, the ark of God, the symbol of his gracious presence, brought into his city, the people rejoicing with God, the king and himself; and finally, everything resounding with the praises and applause of the pious for so many and so great benefits received. But how small were these things, if they are compared with the spiritual things he already discerned in his mind? He discerned God's people delivered from the enemy Satan in Christ our Redeemer; this King, given by God, whom David foreshadowed; God being most present to himself and to the whole Church in Christ, by the singular presence of grace through the communication of the Spirit, and having established his dwelling and his people with himself; all the godly acclaiming this most holy coming of God. Finally, he discerned that all these things would be fully accomplished by Christ, both at his first coming, when the Word became flesh and accomplished in himself whatever is needed for our salvation, and at that most longed-for second coming, by which he will bring everything to completion in us, so that God may be all in all.

units.la: Hac igitur occasione diuinitus sibi oblata Dauid ad canendum hunc psalmum, & tradendum ecclesiæ productus est. Quæ occasio etsi his temporibus ultimis in typo minimè perseverat, omnino tamen in rei veritate perdurat constantissimè. Quapropter æquitas postulat, & jubet pietas, & cogit necessitas, ut dum aberrans à contemplatione huius sanctissimæ occasionis Mundus furit in sua ipsius viscera, ad sensum illius sapientiæ amorem, & studium provocetur: & omnes pios Dei administros ad rem hanc adlaborare necesse est, freto certa expectatione cælestis paterna benedictionis, si in hoc opus in fide incubuerint.
units.tr: Therefore David, offered this occasion by God, was led to sing this psalm and to hand it down to the Church. Although this occasion does not in these last times persist in its type, it nonetheless continues most steadfastly in the reality of the matter.
