Therefore justice demands, piety bids, and necessity compels, that while the world, straying from the contemplation of this most holy occasion, rages against its own vitals, the wise sense of this be stirred up in us, together with love and zeal for it; and all the godly servants of God must labour at this task, relying on the sure expectation of the heavenly and fatherly blessing, if they apply themselves to this work in faith.

units.la: Jam de illis duabus partibus quas ante statuimus, Gaudio inquam & Pace piorum, videndum est. Gaudium suum, quo pius perfunditur in spiritu Dei, exponit Propheta, cùm & asse-ctionem suam narrat, & causas illius. Assectionem proponit unico verbo, Lafor sive latatus sum. Causas verò percurrit sequentibus.
units.tr: Now we must look at the two parts we set out earlier, namely the joy and the peace of the godly. The Prophet sets forth the joy with which the godly man is filled in the Spirit of God, when he tells both of his disposition and of its causes. He states his disposition in a single word, "I rejoiced" (or "I was glad"). He runs through the causes in the verses that follow.

units.la: Non temerè autem à professione suæ illius lætitiæ siue gaudij Propheta exorsus est. Nam plurimæ ante illud tempus calamitates populum Dei peruaserant: neque dubium est, quin eo ipso tempore adhuc manarent vlcera tristitiam bonis adferentia, siue ad internas hominum infirmitates, siue ad mala foris accedentia respicerent. Sed cùm Propheta horum omnium malorum sensui opponit gaudium, eo ipso docet euidentissimè quàm verè sit à Tullio dictum, iniquam esse præteritis bonis malorum enumerationem: quæ res etsi à naturâ est, plurimum tamen ignorantiâ, infirmitate, & singularibus nostris studiis oppugnatur.{*} Nam quotusquisque est, obsecro, qui vrgente vno aliquo malo non eò abripiatur statim, perinde atque si omnia bona interuentu vnius mali concidissent? Vt ergo ex malo tristitia concipitur, sic ex bonis delectationem & gaudium, quamuis in malo præsentissimo, constanter àpiis teneri necesse est, quam vim si naturæ instinctu pecudes, & rationis luce homines, etiam à Deo alieni, omnibus seculis ostenderunt: indignum, turpe, flagitiosum est, hominem Christianum diuini spiritus virtute & veritatis luce circumfusum, in vno autaltero mali impendentis sensu. exutá bonorū quæ summa & plurima à Deo obtinet, conscientiâ mollescere. Hæc igitur illa vis est, qua sanctissimus Dei seruus præterita præsentiaque populi mala per fidem superuolans ad Deum assurgit hoc loco, & fructum sibi esse praedicat quē mundus non potest eripere: nimirum gaudium illud spiritus, cuius nos Deus facit participes communicatione gratiae, adeo ut etiam in ipsis afflictionibus nos gaudere narret Apostolus, & gaudere iubeat in Domino: neque id solum, sed etiam de nostris afflictionibus praedicet gloriari.
units.tr: The Prophet did not begin, without reason, by declaring this joy and gladness of his. For many calamities had overwhelmed the people of God before that time, and there is no doubt that the sores bringing sorrow to the good were still running at that very time, whether they pertained to the inner weaknesses of men or to evils coming from outside. But when the Prophet sets joy against the sense of all these evils, he shows most clearly how truly Tully said that the enumeration of past good things by evils is unfair. Although this is natural, it is nevertheless very much opposed by ignorance, weakness, and our own particular inclinations. For how few are there, I beg you, who, when one evil presses on them, are not at once swept away, just as if all goods had perished at the coming of that single evil? Therefore, just as sorrow is conceived from evil, so joy and delight from good things must constantly be held by the godly, even in the most pressing evil. Beasts by natural instinct, and men, even those alienated from God, by the light of reason, have shown this in every age. It is unworthy, shameful, and disgraceful for a Christian man, surrounded by the power of the divine Spirit and the light of truth, to grow soft in conscience through a sense of one impending evil, when he has been stripped of the goods that he holds in the greatest measure and in abundance from God. This, then, is the power by which the most holy servant of God, flying over the past and present evils of the people through faith, rises up to God in this place, and declares that he has a fruit which the world cannot take away: namely, that joy of the Spirit, of which God makes us partakers by the communication of grace. So much so that the Apostle also tells us that we rejoice even in our afflictions, and bids us rejoice in the Lord; and not only this, but he also says that we glory in our afflictions.

units.la: Sed quia gaudium non satis est imperari, nisi materia iusta illius extiterit (alioquin non gaudium, id est delectatio cum ratione coniuncta, sed opinio esset ac [illegible, ~8 letters]) ad causas veniamus illius gaudij, quod Dauid tum de se praedicabat, & quod Dei Spiritus inde ab eo tempore imperauit suis, cùm auctoritate sua hunc psalmum sanctificans seruandum & obseruandum in Ecclesia deponeret. Causarum quae sanctum illud gaudium Dauidi attulerunt, duo sunt genera: quarum aliae (vt ita loquamur) sunt particulares, & priuatum quendam respectum habent: Aliae verò communes sunt, ad bonum publicum pertinentes. Vtrumque genus Propheta distinctè explicat: nam priores versus 1. & 2. posteriores, tribus sequentibus versibus ostendunt. Quem ordinem conuenientissimum opus est obseruari, vt nunquam in suis priuatis commodis aut studiis conquiescant, sed ab iis semper ad communis & publici boni rationem gaudium referant. de eo (si quod obtulerit Dominus) attollantur.
units.tr: But since joy cannot be enjoined sufficiently unless it has a just matter (otherwise it would not be joy, that is delight joined with reason, but opinion and [illegible]), let us come to the causes of that joy which David then declared concerning himself, and which the Spirit of God, from that time on, commanded his people, when by his own authority he consecrated this psalm and deposited it to be kept and observed in the Church. Of the causes that brought that holy joy to David there are two kinds: some of them are (so to speak) particular and have a certain private reference; others are common and pertain to the public good. The Prophet explains each kind distinctly: the first two verses set out the former, and the three following verses set out the latter. This order must be carefully observed, so that men never rest in their private advantages or pursuits, but always refer their joy from these to the account of the common and public good, and are lifted up by it, if the Lord has granted it.

units.la: Has igitur causas ordine expendamus.
units.tr: Let us therefore weigh these causes in order.

units.la: Particularium, siue earum quæ ad singularia membra ecclesiæ pertinent, loci duo sunt. Nam est sermo cōsilij exhortationisq. verf. 1. est opus communionis sanctorum, verf. 2. Sermonem consilij & exhortationis Propheta explicat dicens, se de iis qui dicerent ipsi, eamus in domum Iehoua lætatū esse. Sensus est:duobus nominibus piùm illud & religiosum gaudium: in priuata sua causa à Dauide fuisse perceptum: nam & personarū dicentium respectu illum fuisse assectum gaudio, & rerum quàs dicebant illæ Dauidi consulentes àtque gratulantes.
units.tr: Of the particular causes, that is, those that belong to the individual members of the Church, there are two. For the one is the speech of counsel and exhortation (verse 1), and the other is the work of the communion of saints (verse 2). The Prophet explains the speech of counsel and exhortation when he says that he was glad concerning those who said to themselves, "Let us go into the house of the LORD". The sense is that David perceived this pious and religious joy in his own private affair for two reasons: he was moved to joy both by regard for the persons who spoke, and by the things they said, as they counselled and congratulated him.

units.la: Ac personarum quidem nobiscum de regno Dei laborantium respectu percipi gaudium à nobis oportete Natura & Scriptura docent.
units.tr: Nature and Scripture both teach that we ought to feel joy over the persons who labour with us for the kingdom of God.

units.la: Cùm enim ànaturâ omnes simus ab uno principio orti, omnes unius speciei, omnes sociales, omnes iisdem bonis naturalibus ac veluti pignoribus instructi, quæcunque ad conseruationem speciei & societatis humanæ pertinent; profectò & sibi, & speciei, & societati, & Naturæ denique toti putandus est adversari, quisquis suas facultates non studet eò conferre, & ex eis non sentit gaudium. Quid? nonne feræ in suo genere sic feruntur instinctu naturali, ut speciem suam curent, & propterea etiam, ubi opus fore senserint, congregentur? Cætera animantia (inquiebat ille) in suo genere probè degunt: congregari videmus, & stare contra dis-similia: Leonum feritas inter se non dimicat: serpentum morsus non petit serpentes: ne imaris[?] quidem bellue ac pisces nisi in diuersa genera seiuiunt[?]. Et tu, homo à feris, ratione præditus ab expertibus, & socialis à solitariis vincatris[?]? tu operā des, ut feritate & abalienatione vincas cætera, & in tuo ipsius naturæ funere triumphator tibi videaris?
units.tr: For since all of us are by nature sprung from one origin, all of one species, all social, and all equipped with the same natural goods, as it were pledges, whatever pertains to the preservation of the human species and society, then surely whoever does not strive to direct his abilities to this end, and does not feel joy from them, must be thought to be at odds with himself, with the species, with society, and finally with all of nature. What of it? Do not wild beasts, in their own kind, act by natural instinct in such a way that they look after their species, and for this reason also gather together whenever they perceive that there is need? Other living creatures, as that man said, live well in their own kind: we see them flock together and stand against unlike things. The fierceness of lions does not fight among themselves; the bite of serpents does not seek other serpents; not even the huge whales and fish separate except into different kinds. And you, man, endowed with reason, do you conquer the beasts by savagery, the unthinking by reason, and the social by isolation? Do you labour so that you conquer the rest by ferocity and estrangement, and seem to yourself a triumphant victor over the very funeral of your own nature?

units.la: In primis autem respectus hominum pios affecturus est gaudio, cùm aliorum studium erga Deum & erga se pium animaduerterint: quemadmodum Propheta nobis exemplum hoc loco statuit, dicens: so latari[?] de hominibus dicentibus sibi & se alloquentibus pio illo sermone, qui post exponitur. Nam fit quidé plurimum, ut si quis nos refugiat, à nostra communicatione abhorreat, nostraque ipsorum bona auersetur aut auertat, iustam nobis causam habere videamur cur non gaudeamus de illis, aut illorum bono. Etsi hæc ipsa abalienatio nullo iure probari potest, cùm particulare (ut vocant) factum, & particularis causa, id est, vitium huius aut illius de iure naturali non possit derogare, nedum abrogare, & hominis odium, inimicitias, simultates, iniurias excusare. Sed cùm homines eiusmodi sunt erga nos, ut quod bonum est, dicant, & nobis dicant; aut si aliud quàm bonum dixerint, tamen animo spectant ad bonū, quamuis decipiantur specie illius: inhumanum est, si quis eo hominum sacto non afficiatur gaudio, & de illa sancta ad bonum conspiratione, quamuis cæcâ aut cæcutiente, gratuletur. Atque hæc causa est cur priscos illos Corinthios hanc certissimam materiam gaudij relinquentes, & in suo ipsorum fastu & fratrum imperitiorum contemptu insolescentes, grauissimè Paulus monuerit dicens, De spiritualibus donis, fratres, nolim vos in ignorantia versari. scitis vos gentes fuisse, qui ad idola illa muta, prout rapi contigisset, abripiebamini. Quapropter notum vobis facio, nullum per spiritum Dei loquentem dicere Ie-sum Anathema, & neminè posse dicere Iesum Dominum, nisi per Spiritum S. tanquam si dicerèt, iniquam esse inter homines illam æmu-lationem qua alij alios videntur antestare, & primas sibi arrogant ex spiritualium donorum conscientiâ. Ná siue ad dona respexeris, siue ad eos ipsos qui ea obtinent; omnia ilti[?] humano fastui & arrogantiæ tepugnare[?]. Etenim ad ea quod attinet, omnino dona esse; ac proinde alienæ gratiæ, non virtutis nostræ. Præterea spiritualia esse non ergo carnis aut naturæ nostræ, sed spiritus & cælestis gratiæ, prout in eádem epist. dicebat Apostolus, Quis est qui discernit te? aut quid habes quod non acceperis? quod autem ad eos homines qui dona ista per Dei gratiam participant, eos cum natura, tum ar-teactâ[?] experientiâ, & præsente spiritus diuini testimonio in animis ipsorum ab ista iniquitate in suos fratres revocari. Natura enim omnes ignorantes rerum spiritualium esse, donec eas nos Deus docuerit: nec plus cognitionis de illis posse nobis contingere, quàm prout de suo lumine Deus accenderit demensum fidei. Experientia vero vitæ ante-actæ nostræ id ipsum testari luculentissimè cùm omnes à naturâ infideles se fuisse sibi sint conscij, &c abreptos fuisse post idola muta & mundi vanitate prout contigerit: neque tum fuisse futurum gratum iustumq. nobis officiu, dum illis tenebris circumclusi hærebamus, si quisinsolète[?] fastu nos in tenebris siuisset computrescere. Postremò autem præsentem gratiæ diuinæ infirmos sustinentis &c cæcos illustrantis conscientiam satis ostendere tenues illas scintillas diuinæ lucis non exsufflandas fastu, aut contemptu extinguendas esse; sed magni semper faciendas, velut spiritus Dei munera; quæ ne in minimis quidem puerulis oporteat contristari. Et quis dubitat, quin in eo ipso dicentium numero, quos hic commendat Dauid, fuerint homines omnis generis secundũ dona Spiritus & gradus scientiæ, qui temporibus illis poterant contingere, inter se distinguendi? fuerunt docti; indocti, firmi, infirmi, excelsi, mediocres, tenues, omnes in eodem sermone pro modulo donationis Christi occupati: de quibus omnibus prorsifcuè[?] Dauid lætatus est, ad Christum commune caput omnis boni nostri, nō ad commune malum vitiofitatemque naturæ nostræ respiciens, & in omnibus honorans Dei imaginem. Quæ res nobis omnibus esse documento debet, ut neque personarum ratione, neque tenuitatis, infirmitatis, aut ignorantiæ illarū abducamur à dono Dei (quantulumcumque fit) in ipsis recognoscendo: sed vel tenuissimam lucis diuinæ scintillam, quam gratiosè Deus communicauerit, propter Deum & Chriftū & Spiritum eius habitantem in ipsis foueamus diligentissimè, lætitiamque fraternam de illis capiamus in spiritu.
units.tr: Above all, the regard for pious men will move us to joy when we perceive their zeal toward God and toward ourselves that is pious. So the Prophet sets this example for us here, saying that he rejoiced over the men who spoke to him and addressed him with that pious speech which follows. For it does happen very often that if someone shuns us, shrinks from our fellowship, and turns away from or repudiates our own good things, we seem to have a just cause not to rejoice over them or over their good. Yet this very estrangement can be justified by no right, since a particular deed and a particular cause, that is, the fault of this or that person, cannot derogate from natural right, let alone abrogate it, nor excuse hatred, enmities, quarrels, and injuries. But when men are such toward us that they speak what is good, and speak it to us; or if they say something other than good, yet still look in their mind toward the good, even though they are deceived about its appearance, it is inhuman if anyone is not moved to joy by such an act of men, and does not rejoice over that holy agreement toward the good, even though it is blind or dimly seeing. And this is the reason why Paul, most gravely, admonished those former Corinthians, who were abandoning this most certain matter for joy and were growing proud in their own arrogance and in their contempt for the less learned brethren. He says: "Concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you be ignorant. You know that you were Gentiles, carried away to those dumb idols, however you happened to be led. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says, 'Jesus is accursed,' and no one can say, 'Jesus is Lord,' except by the Holy Spirit." As if to say that the rivalry by which some seem to surpass others, and claim first place for themselves from the awareness of spiritual gifts, is unjust among men. For whether you look to the gifts or to those very persons who possess them, all of these things are at odds with human pride and arrogance. For as far as the gifts are concerned, they are altogether gifts, and therefore of another's grace, not of our own virtue. Moreover, they are spiritual, not of our flesh or our nature, but of the Spirit and of heavenly grace, as the Apostle said in the same epistle: "Who makes you to differ? Or what do you have that you did not receive?" As for those men who share these gifts through the grace of God, we ought to be called back from that injustice toward our brethren, both by nature and by experience, and by the present testimony of the divine Spirit in our minds. For by nature we are all ignorant of spiritual things, until God teaches us; nor can we attain more knowledge of them than God kindles in us as the measure of faith from his own light. And the experience of our former life clearly testifies to this same thing: since we all were by nature unbelievers, aware of it, and were carried away after dumb idols and the vanity of the world as it happened; and then it would not have been a pleasing and just duty for us, while we were stuck in those darknesses, if someone had proudly allowed us to rot in the darkness. Finally, the present consciousness of divine grace, which sustains the weak and illumines the blind, sufficiently shows that those thin sparks of divine light are not to be blown out by pride, nor extinguished by contempt, but are always to be held in high regard, as gifts of the Spirit of God, which ought not to be grieved even in the smallest children. And who doubts that, among that very number of speakers whom David commends here, there were men of every kind, to be distinguished from one another according to the gifts of the Spirit and the degrees of knowledge that could befall them in those times? There were learned and unlearned, strong and weak, eminent and middling, humble, all occupied in the same speech according to the measure of Christ's gift. David rejoiced over all of them without exception, looking to Christ, the common head of all our good, not to the common evil and vitiated state of our nature, and honouring the image of God in them all. This fact ought to be a lesson to all of us, so that we are not drawn away, either by regard for persons or by the lowliness, weakness, or ignorance of those persons, from recognising in them the gift of God, however small it may be. Rather, even the most slender spark of divine light, which God has graciously imparted, we should cherish most diligently for the sake of God, of Christ, and of his Spirit dwelling in them, and take brotherly joy in them in the Spirit.

units.la: Quod autem Propheta dicit hanc sibi lætitiam fuisse allatam de dicentibus sibi, non est otiosum. nam Dauidem hoc verbo sibi, statuimus duo hominum genera innuisse: quorum alij vocatione communi, alij singulari hos fanctos sermones cum Dauide habuerint. Communis vocatio est Pietatis Charitatisque, quam Deo & proximo debemus singuli. Vocatio verò illa singularis est, muneris atque consilij, quo cum rege communicare in re tanta tenebantur quoscumque Deus ad consilium publicum ecclefiæ, & Rex ad consilium regni allegerat. Neque enim dubium est, quin Sacerdotum, Levitarum Prophetarumque consilium in rebus sacris Dauid acceperit; & in iis quæ ad ordinem publicum pertinuerunt, aliorum quoque sententias rogauerit quos ad publici ordinis curam & conseruationem adhibebat: quemadmodum ex verbis auctoris 1.Chron.13.& 15 & fequente cofirmatur. Atque hæc profectò maxima est (vt ita dicamus) messis fructufq. maximus spiritualis illius gaudij qui hic in terris poteft cotingere, cùm omnes ordines sancta confenfione diuinitus indicà suis Principibus dicunt,& illis vicissim Principes,ea quæ ad cóstitutionem regni Dei sentiunt pertinere: præfertim fi iusto ordine aguntur omnia, quem 1.Chron.13.& 15.legimus informatum. Nam. Deus primùm permouit Regis Dauidis animum ad sanctam hanc cogitationem, eumque spiritu suo intus allocutus est: hoc deinde auctore Dauid cum suo Consilio communicat, 1.Chronic.13. pòftde sententiâ Consilij omnibus indicit rem deliberatam: denique sic inftituuntur omnia,vt Deus ordini præsit, omnes Deum sequantur ordine, & ita conficiantur ea. quæ iam olim Deus lege promiserat. Sic multiplicem lætitiam percepit Dauid; cùm æque in consilio suo ac in vniuerso populo pietatis ftudium animaduerteret: Studium autem ? imò etiam officium studiosissimum, cùm inter fe, tum ipsi regi dicentium quæ religionis & pietatis studium imperabant.
units.tr: But the Prophet's saying that this joy was brought to him concerning those saying to themselves is not idle. For by this word "to himself" we hold that he indicated two kinds of men, of whom some held these holy conversations with David by common calling, and others by a special calling. The common calling is that of piety and charity, which each of us owes to God and to his neighbour. That special calling is one of office and counsel, by which those whom God had chosen for the public counsel of the Church, and whom the king had chosen for the counsel of the kingdom, were bound to share counsel with the king in so great a matter. For there is no doubt that David took the counsel of the priests, Levites, and prophets in sacred matters; and in those things that pertained to public order, he also asked the opinions of others whom he employed for the care and preservation of public order; as is confirmed from the words of the author in 1 Chron. 13 and 15 and what follows. And this is surely the greatest harvest, and (so to speak) the richest fruit of that spiritual joy which can befall us here on earth, when all orders, by holy agreement divinely indicated, say to their princes, and in turn the princes to them, what they judge pertinent to the establishment of the kingdom of God; especially if all things are done in the proper order, which we read was instituted in 1 Chron. 13 and 15. For God first moved the mind of King David toward this holy thought, and spoke to him inwardly by his Spirit. Then, at David's instigation, he communicated this to his council (1 Chron. 13); afterwards, by the judgment of the council, he announced the matter as decided to all; and finally all things were so arranged that God presides over the order, all follow God in order, and thus those things are accomplished which God had long before promised by law. So David received manifold joy, since he perceived zeal for piety both in his council and in the whole people; and this zeal, indeed even the most zealous duty, was shown both among themselves and toward the king himself, of those who spoke what the zeal of religion and piety commanded.

units.la: Hic verò fecundus locus est,qui lætitiam illam animo Dauidis informauit, quòd sanctè dicentes audiret, eamus in domum lehoua. Pauca verba consilij: sensus amplissimus. Hoc confilium procerum cum rege, idem consilium fuit populapopularium inter se adhortantium ad executionem illius: Eamus, inquiunt, in domum Iehoua. Huius autem consilij & hortationis eò pertinentis unicum est argumentū, nempe adiri ad Deum oportere, & una huius argumenti actio. Veruntamen huius actionis in hisce pauculis verbis tres leges comprehenduntur sanctissimo consilio fixæ: Prima est de Fine: Secunda, de Via ad finem pertendente :: Tertia, de Actu piorum iusta[?] via ad finem concurrentium. Finis est Iehoua. Via est ecclesia, domus Iehoua: Actus est, Ambulatio ad Iehouam per Ecclesiam ipsius.
units.tr: Here is the second point, which shaped David's joy: that he heard them speaking devoutly, "Let us go into the house of Jehovah." Few words of counsel, yet a very wide meaning. This counsel of the nobles with the king was the same counsel of the common people, who urged one another to carry it out: "Let us go," they say, "into the house of Jehovah." This counsel and exhortation has one argument, namely that God must be approached, and one action that follows from this argument. Yet in these few words three rules of this most holy counsel are contained. The first concerns the End; the second, the Way leading to the end; the third, the Act of the pious, who together make their way by the right road to the end. The End is Jehovah. The Way is the Church, the house of Jehovah. The Act is walking to Jehovah through his Church.

units.la: Ac de Fine quidem multa huc à nobis adferri nihil necesse est: Hunc enim finem sic natura docet rerum omnium, etiam vitæ & sensus expertium, ut non possit quisquam sine impia & iniquissima oppugnatione naturæ ad alium finem contendere. Quod autem natura res omnes perdocet; id recta ratio naturæ nostræ indita longè amplioribus documentis perceptura esset, nisi tum internæ tenebræ mentis (nam tenebræ fumus) tum particularia animi studia (nam infirmi & malitiosi fumus) tum innumerabilia mundi fallacis obiecta (nam figura mundi & fuco circumuenti fumus) rationem illam præstinguerent. Veruntamen, ut impedita est, restant in conscientiâ quædam scintillæ veri & iusti; quæ homines pietatem & iustitiam in mendacio detinentes, adeoq. diabolos ipsos Deo & saluti nostræ aduersantes, euincunt cuincunt hoc vnum principium, hunc finem singulare esse vniuersis & singulis natura duce propositum, à quo, in quo, per quem, & propter quem omnia sunt, & omnes quoque (vt verbis vtamur Apostoli) viuimus, mouemur, & sumus. Neque solum id natura nostra & rerum creatarum omnium contestatur, verumetiam natura Dei omnia circumfulget virtute admirabili, & fine testimonio sui, præcipuè apud homines, se non finit vnquam. Quapropter Iehoua Hebræis appellatus est, vt qui sit ἀυτὸν, vt loquuntur patres: ipsum ens absolutum, ad nihil extra se relationem habens, & ad quem omnia omnino ex necessitate referantur. Hunc autem finem omnes duobus modis docemur cognoscere: puta vniuersali naturæ luce, & communi testificatione scripturæ vel diuini verbi: secundum quæ testimonia nemo est qui non sit dicturus, si modo animum contra veritatem non obsirmauerit, Iehouam esse, & cognosci oportere, denique ad ipsum contendi vt verum salutarem nostrum.
units.tr: There is no need for us to bring much forward about the End, for nature teaches this end of all things, even those that lack life and sense, so that no one can strive for another end without an impious and most unjust assault on nature. But what nature teaches all things, right reason implanted in our nature would perceive from far fuller evidence, were it not that the inner darkness of the mind (for darkness is smoke), the particular affections of the soul (for the weak and malicious are smoke), and the countless allurements of the deceptive world (for the shape of the world, and those beguiled by its paint, are smoke) extinguish that reason. Nevertheless, although it is impeded, certain sparks of truth and justice remain in conscience. These convict men who hold piety and justice in falsehood, and even the devils themselves who oppose God and our salvation, of this one principle: that this end is set by nature as the single goal for all and each, from which, in which, through which and on account of which all things are, and all of us too (to use the Apostle's words) live, move and are. Nor does our nature and that of all created things alone bear witness to this; the nature of God shines through all things with admirable power and never allows itself to be without witness of itself, especially among men. For this reason Jehovah was called by the Hebrews, as the Fathers say, he who is in himself [αὐτὸν]: absolute being itself, having no relation outside himself, and to whom all things must necessarily be referred. Now we are all taught to know this end in two ways: namely by the universal light of nature and by the common testimony of Scripture or the divine word. According to these testimonies no one will fail to say, if only he has not hardened his mind against the truth, that Jehovah exists, that he must be known, and finally that one must strive towards him as our true salvation.

units.la: Ac illud quidem homines pij & instituti in verbo Dei facilè ferre possunt, imò de eo lætari cum animis suis, si fratres imbuti eâdem gratiâ & informati singulari reuelatione eius, cùm ipsi inter se, tum ipsis acclamauerint, Eamus ad Iehouam. Etsi non desunt in eorum ipsorum numero (proh dolor) æqui perinde acsi Deum, & mundum, & naturam sibi solis esse oportet, ret, indignè ferunt hanc lucem cognitionis inesse suis fratribus ; aut certè hanc præferre atque exhibere ipsis ex pietatis & charitatis lege: Quo malo repurget gratiosè Dominus membra sua,& corpus Ecclesiæ suæ virtute spiritus, quem iuris & ardoris spiritum in scripturis appellauit. Veruntamen si forte res nobis futura est cum hominibus eiusmodi , qui singularem illam inspirationem & revelatione gratiæ non sunt adepti à Domino,quid dicturi sumus ? Si auctoritate scripturæ quam legunt, dicant, Eamus ad Dominum , sed non dicant commodè, quia nō intelligūt: si auctoritate naturæ,quamuis nec singulari revelatione spiritus, nec communi illá ac publicâ testificatione scripturæ instructi : si igitur naturâ duce hac sancta acclamatione utentur, Eamus ad Dominum,quod iudicium de illis facturi? quam sententiam laturi sumus? Horret animus cogitanti immania illa iudicia,conatus, facta, quibus hic mundus, & ipse Christianus orbis plus satis circumfluit, Impietatem specie pietatis , inhumanitatem specie charitatis,iniustitiâ prætextu iuris intus spirantia & foris contestantia. Atqui de his ipsis lætari nos oporteret singulos , & errantibus lucernam accendere ; non offendicula pedibus illorum obtrudere , aut bene cupientibus vim afferre malè. Nónne lex maledictum cum pronunciat, qui cæco in viâ offendiculum posuerit? nónne id natura docet,quod olim cæcus
units.tr: Pious men, instructed in the word of God, can easily bear this, and even rejoice in their hearts if brothers imbued with the same grace and informed by his singular revelation cry out to one another and to themselves, "Let us go to Jehovah." Yet among those very people there are not lacking (alas) those who, as if God, the world and nature belonged to them alone, unworthily bear that this light of knowledge is present in their brothers; or at least they refuse to offer it to them, although the law of piety and charity requires it. By this evil the Lord graciously cleanses his members and the body of his Church by the power of his Spirit, whom in the Scriptures he called the spirit of judgment and of burning. But if perhaps we have to deal with men of this kind, who have not received that singular inspiration and revelation of grace from the Lord, what are we to say? If, by the authority of the Scripture they read, they say, "Let us go to the Lord," but do not say it properly, because they do not understand it; if, by the authority of nature alone, not instructed by any singular revelation of the Spirit nor by that common and public testimony of Scripture, they use this holy exhortation, "Let us go to the Lord," what judgment shall we make of them? What sentence shall we pass? My mind shrinks as I think of those monstrous judgments, attempts and deeds with which this world, and the Christian world itself, is more than sufficiently flooded: impiety in the appearance of piety, inhumanity in the appearance of charity, injustice under the pretext of law, breathing within and bearing witness without. Yet we ought instead to rejoice over these very men, each of us, and to light a lamp for those who wander, not to put stumbling blocks at their feet or do harm to those who wish well. Does not the law pronounce a curse on the one who puts a stumbling block in the path of the blind? Does not nature itself teach what that old poet Ennius once sang?

units.la: Note: the small printed mark beside "de his ipsis" in the right margin has no accompanying text. ille cecinit Ennius? Homo qui erranti comiter monstrat viam, Quasi lumen de suo lumine accendat facit: Nihilominus ipsi lucet, cum illi 'accenderit. Quod si haec in rebus corporis & vitae praesentis Deus, Natura, boni, omnes denique praeceperunt; longe amplius profecto & diligentius danda est opera, ut in rebus animi & ad futuram illam aeternam vitam pertinentibus prosimus omnibus, obsimus nemini. Et, per Deum immortalem, quid est quod nos impediat, ne miseris illis ex morbo & errore asimi[?] laborantibus acclamemus ad bonum, & a malefacientes abstineamus quā fidelissime? Nam si illi caeci sunt, at nos sumus[?]: Si oberrant caecitate, at nos oberrauimus: Si denique impedimento sunt, at impedimentum habent, ut nos habuimus: quo magis nostra commiseratione & alleuatione digni sunt. Si quis ergo de scriptura satis informatus, tamen bono animo ad Deum con- tenderit, etiam de eo laetandum est quod procurat bono animo, quamuis non procuret bonum: foueri oportet quod bonum est, errorem tollit; quemadmodum olim dicebat Augustinus, Errorem tolle, & serua hominem. Similiter si quis in medium producatur fretus sola naturae luce, qui Deum requirat simplice animo, non temere depellendus[?] de gradu, sed sollicitè appellandus est, & omni officio ac potius pietate ad pietatis notitiam perducendus: laetitia spiritualis de hoc homine capienda: neque solum ore & sermone testanda foris, sed ex corde & veritate intrinsecus effundenda, ut sanctissimum hunc Prophetam (qui fuit vir secundum cor Domini) ex animo & corde toto imitemur. Quod si huius exemplum non potest eò nos adducere, videamus saltem quid Apostoli apud infideles egerint: quanto labore, studio, fide, religione Paulus dicatur cum illis versatus esse, & quanta sollicitudine cum infirmis ea communicauisse quæ acceperat à Domino. Plenus est harum historiarum totus Actorum liber, plenæ documentorum epistolæ. Deniq. seruator ipse Christus, qui suis Apostolis sermone & exemplo præiuit, suosq. imitatores nos esse voluit, nonne illum ipsum iuvenem, qui se omnia observavisse dicebat à iuventute sua, intuitus dilexit & monuit officij? quamvis eo tempore non legatur illum amoris illius monitorumque fructum aliquem percepisse, nedum edidisse; sed contrà indoluisse propter sermonem Christi, & contristatum abiisse. Quamobrem cùm Dei, Naturæ, & Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis, & piorum omnium, adeoque Christi ipsius exemplis doceamur finem hunc esse homini cuivis propositum (est autem à natura propositus, & à Deo expositus, quà obscurius, quà evidentius pro voluntate ipsius) cur naturæ bonum, quamvis imperfectiffimum, in homine damnemus? Cur eum propter mala præteritis bonis impelamus in ruinam miserabile? cur subvertamus impotentriâ animi,& malitiâ nostrâ? Videamus potius, ut scintillam boni accendamus,quàm ut extinguamus;& accensam foveamus ac fortificemus studiosissimè, lætitiamque sanctam communiter de ea capiamus cum bonis omnibus & cum Angelis electis in cœlo: ne forte quod olim prædicabat Dauid de suo spiritali gaudio in hac causa, id nobis in horrendam condemnationem vertatur iudicio Dei; postquam vestigia Dauidis ex historiâ sacrâ, & ex verbis ipsius hoc loco didicimus ad omnè pietatem humanitatemque erga quosvis homines religione summá contendisse.
units.tr: "A man who kindly shows the way to one who wanders does as if he lit his own lamp from another's light: he shines none the less, once he has lit the other's." But if God, nature and goodness have taught these things in matters of the body and of the present life, then much more and much more diligently must we work to benefit all men in matters of the soul and those pertaining to that future eternal life, and to harm no one. And, by the immortal God, what is there to prevent us from calling those wretched men, suffering from the disease and error of the soul, to the good, and from keeping them from evil as faithfully as we can? For if they are blind, so were we; if they wander in blindness, so have we wandered; if finally they are an obstacle to others, they have an obstacle just as we did. So much the more are they worthy of our pity and our support. If therefore anyone, sufficiently informed by Scripture, nevertheless strives towards God with a good heart, we must rejoice even at what he pursues with a good heart, though he does not yet attain the good: what is good must be cherished, and error removed. As Augustine once said, "Remove the error, and keep the man." Likewise, if someone is brought forward relying on the light of nature alone, seeking God with a simple heart, he is not to be rashly thrust from his step, but earnestly called, and brought to the knowledge of piety by every duty and above all by piety. Spiritual joy is to be taken in this man, and it is to be expressed not only outwardly by mouth and speech, but poured out from the heart and truth within, so that we imitate that most holy Prophet, who was a man after the heart of the Lord, with all our soul and whole heart. But if his example cannot lead us so far, let us at least see what the Apostles did among unbelievers: with what labour, zeal, faith and devotion Paul is said to have dealt with them, and with what care he shared with the weak what he had received from the Lord. The whole book of Acts is full of such histories, and the epistles full of instruction. Finally, the Saviour Christ himself, who went before his Apostles in word and example and wished us to be his imitators, did he not look upon that young man who said he had kept all these things from his youth, and loved him and gave him the admonition of duty? Although we do not read that at that time he gained any fruit from that love and those admonitions, let alone produced any; rather he was grieved at the word of Christ and went away sorrowful. Wherefore, since by the testimonies of God, nature and holy Scripture, and by the examples of all the pious and of Christ himself, we are taught that this end is set before every man (it is set by nature and set forth by God, more obscurely or more clearly as his will pleases), why do we condemn in man the good of nature, however imperfect it is? Why do we drive him, wretched, into ruin on account of past evils, passing over the good? Why do we overthrow him through the weakness of our mind and our malice? Let us rather see to kindle the spark of good than to extinguish it, and once kindled, to cherish and strengthen it most diligently, and to take holy joy in it together with all good men and the elect angels in heaven; lest what David once proclaimed of his spiritual joy in this matter be turned against us into a dreadful condemnation at the judgment of God, since we have learned from sacred history and from his own words in this place that David strove with the utmost piety towards all goodness and humanity towards every man.

units.la: Hic verò respondebit fortasse quispiam, de Fine quem sibi omnes homines ante oculos ponunt,non admodum dubitari: sed totum laboré nostrum in eo esse, ut viam quà peruenitur ad Finem illum, teneamus. Recté: Bene est igitur si de Fine inter omnes constat. At quotusquisque est qui de miseris hominibus ignorantia aut infirmitate abreptis sic iudicet ex charitatis officio ? quàm multi propter opiniones de aliis conceptas fratres suos, alienos servos, propter quos Christus mortuus est, temerè condemnant, & palàm pronunciant eos linguâ testari contrà quàm animus sentiat, ut iniquitatem iudiciorum suorum proteruè tueantur? Apage istam insaniam, non homine Christiano, non naturali homine, non brutâ animantè dignam: quæ insania inde à seculis multas animas perdiditinnumerabiles. Veruntamen esto,de Fine conueniat,vt antè dictum est : ergo de Viâ qua ad finé peruenturi fumus, deinceps videndum est. Atque hic fecundus locus est, quem antè ad horum verborum interpretationem probè obseruari diximus oportere.
units.tr: Here perhaps someone will reply that there is scarcely any doubt about the End that all men set before their eyes, and that our whole labour lies in holding to the way by which that End is reached. Quite right: it is well, then, if all agree about the End. But how few are there who, when it comes to wretched men carried off by ignorance or weakness, judge in this way out of the duty of charity? How many, on account of opinions formed about others, rashly condemn their brothers, other men's servants, for whom Christ died, and openly declare that they bear witness with their tongues to what their minds do not think, so that they may boldly defend the injustice of their judgments? Away with that madness, unworthy of a Christian, of a rational man, of a brute animal; a madness which has destroyed countless souls from the earliest ages. Nevertheless, granted that we agree about the End, as was said before, we must now consider the Way by which we shall arrive at that end. And this is the second point, which we said must be carefully observed for the interpretation of these words.

units.la: Via quâ ad Deü opus est cõtendere , à nobis definita est Prophetæ verbis , cùm domũ Iehoue, id est , Ecclesiam pro viâ nobis habendam esse traderemus. Hoc illud est,inquiet fortasse quifpiam,quod tâtopere cupimus : & quidé eo ampliuscupimus , quo videmus amplius necessariam esse reipfa viâ,& tamē vanitate hominum controuersam . Nam Ecclesiam quidē viam ad Deum esse pleriq. omnes agnoscimus : Sed in circumscriptione & determinationeillius, fermè (quod vulgò dici solet)qüot capita, tot sententiæ. Ergo vt de re tam necessaria,& tamen plus fatis controuersâ,inter nos cõuenire poffit,duo ponenda sunt, quæ nemo bonus (dum sibi constabit mente) negaturus est. Vnum est, dum de hac circumscriptione Ecclesiæ fententiæ audiuntur & discutiuntur , oportere vt alij feramus alios,ac nó contrà quàm in optimis rebus publicis & iudiciis bene cõftitutis iure obseruari solet, ab executione statuamus rei exordiü.Alterü est,vt faciliùs de hac quæstione conuenire possit,etiā cõsentiamus inter nos de cortis mediis vel potiùs principiis cõfeffis vtrinq. inter diuersas partes opus esse, ex quibus paulatim, animis cōpofitis & rixis sepositis, ad assequendam illam circumscriptionem veniamus determinationemque Ecclesiæ. Interea verò ne in hac nostrâ opera aërem dicamur cædere,fine discrepantium inter fe partiû præiudicio, Principium confessum apud omnes cum bona pace omnium statuemus. Illud autem est Scriptura sacra, de qua optimè olim Augustinus cum Donatistis agens,In Scripturis inquiebat, didicimus Christum: In Scripturis didicimus ecclesiam: Cur non ergo in scripturis communem Christum atque ecclesiam retinemus? Ex his autē scripturis, velut immediatis à Deo, certis,atque immotis principiis delineaturi Ecclefiam, non colligemus hinc inde quæ ad hoc argumentum videntur pertinere: sed hærentes in hoc ipso cātico vestigia Prophetæ [illegible, ~8 letters] persequemur. Sic de Ecclesia dicemus,quæ hic ipse locus nobis fubininiftraturus est, & Dei Spiritus ex eo edocturus.
units.tr: The way by which we must strive toward God has been defined by us in the Prophet's words, when we taught that the house of Jehovah, that is, the Church, must be held by us as the way. "This is what we desire so much," someone may perhaps say; and we desire it the more, the more we see that the way is truly necessary and yet disputed through human vanity. For nearly all of us acknowledge that the Church is the way to God; but in its delimitation and definition there are, as the common saying goes, as many opinions as heads. So that we may agree about a matter so necessary and yet more than enough disputed, two things must be laid down, which no good man (as long as he remains consistent in mind) will deny. The first is that, while opinions about this delimitation of the Church are heard and discussed, we ought to bear with one another, and not, as is customary in the best commonwealths and well-ordered courts, pronounce judgment before the case has been heard. The second is that, so that we may more easily agree on this question, we should also agree that there is need of certain middle principles, or rather principles confessed on both sides by the different parties; from these, gradually, with minds calmed and quarrels set aside, we may come to the determination of that delimitation and definition of the Church. Meanwhile, lest we seem in this work of ours to beat the air, without prejudice to the parties differing among themselves, we will lay down, with the good peace of all, a principle agreed upon by everyone. This is Holy Scripture, of which Augustine, dealing with the Donatists long ago, rightly said: "In the Scriptures we learned Christ; in the Scriptures we learned the Church. Why then do we not hold to the common Christ and Church in the Scriptures?" From these Scriptures, as from immediate, certain and unmoved principles given by God, we shall delineate the Church, not gathering here and there whatever seems to pertain to this argument; but, abiding in this very canticle, we shall follow the footsteps of the Prophet [illegible]. Thus we shall speak of the Church, which this very place will supply to us, and into which the Spirit of God will instruct us from it.

units.la: Hæc igitur informata est à Dauide Ecclesiæ ratio, quam ex ipsissimis verbis omnes (spero) mecū recognituri sunt. Ecclesiæ duplex est ratio: Interna, & Externa. Internam rationem Propheta explicat,hac vnà appellatione, quòd domus Iehoua est. Externam verò rationem in communione sanctorum positam demonstrat planè sequentibus. Id solum discrimen intervenit inter illam Ecclesiam & hanc nostram, quam Christus adunat Euangelij prædicatio-ne, ne, quòd illa cum re habuit vmbracula; hæc re cum illà eadem est, sed inuolucris exempta vmbraculorum typorumq; eiusmodi, vt facta à Christo fuit difparatio. Iam de ratione interna & essentiali Ecclesia videamus.
units.tr: The plan of the Church, then, as David has set it out, is one which I hope everyone will recognise with me from his very words. The plan of the Church is twofold: internal and external. The Prophet explains the internal plan by this single name, that it is the house of Jehovah. The external plan, set in the communion of the saints, he clearly shows in what follows. The only difference between that Church and this one of ours, which Christ gathers by the preaching of the Gospel, is that the former had shadows alongside the reality, whereas this one has the same reality with the same thing, but freed from the wrappings of such shadows and types, so that the separation made by Christ took place. Now let us see the internal and essential plan of the Church.

units.la: Describitur Ecclesia duabus suis partibus essentialibus (vt omnibus rebus fieri solet) cùm domus Jehoua appellatur. Nam quà domus, materia significatur: quà Jehoua domus, forma essentialis huic materiæ indita.
units.tr: The Church is described by its two essential parts (as is usual with all things) when it is called the house of Jehovah. For insofar as it is a house, matter is signified; insofar as it is the Jehovah's house, the essential form imposed on this matter is signified.

units.la: Materiæ quam in Ecclesiâ obseruamus, cognitio est euidens. Neque enim agere hoc loco statuimus de Ecclesia Dei in cælis versante atq; gloriosâ, ex angelis hominibusq. coagmentata fecundum electionem Dei in Christo Jesu: sed tantùm de Ecclesiâ Dei, quæ hic in terris verfatur, & in fide tantisper ambulat dum ad persectionem illam perducta fit. Materia igitur huius ecclesiæ ex hominibus est: nam ex his, tanquam ex lapidibus domus, ædificatur ecclesia Dei. Sed hi lapides viui sunt, vt à Petro appellantur, ex quibus coagmentatur Dei viuentis domus. Lapidum autem quibus structores in ædificationibus vtuntur, duplex est ratio, extra opus, & in opere. Nam primùm sparsi & jacentes in agro lapides videntur, qui ad structuram adhiberi possunt: post in ipso opere & ædificatione domus. Eâdem quoque ratione homines considerantur: tum secundùm naturam tanquam jacentes in via, qui adhiberi pofsunt ad structuram spiritalem Dei, tum fecundùm opus gratiæ, quum in structura diuina ex facto occupati sunt. .
units.tr: The knowledge of the matter we observe in the Church is evident. For we do not intend here to treat of the Church of God that dwells in heaven in glory, joined together from angels and men according to God's election in Christ Jesus; but only of the Church of God which dwells here on earth and walks in faith for as long as it is brought to that perfection. The matter of this Church, then, is from men: for from these, as from stones, the house of God is built. But these stones are living, as Peter calls them, out of which the house of the living God is put together. Now there is a twofold consideration of the stones which builders use in their constructions: outside the work, and within the work. For first they appear as stones scattered and lying in the field, which can be brought to the structure; afterwards, in the work itself and the building of the house. In the same way men are considered: both according to nature, as lying in the way, who can be brought to God's spiritual structure, and according to the work of grace, when they have been taken up into the divine structure and made part of it.

units.la: Secundùm naturam itaque sunt in potentia quodam modo, vt vocari possint tàuíper[?] dum hic in via sunt:quemadmodum idem Propheta cecinit Psal.2. dicens, Osculamini filium, vt non irascatur & pereatis in via, cùm exarserit vel minimùm ira eius. Ac proinde cùm Deus illos in via relinquat,sibi iudicium feruans de iis quos aut affumpturus ad opus suum,aut in via media reliEturus est otiosos, non est hominis cuiufquam iudicium de illis facere: nam Dei hoc iudicium est. nō est cuiufquam illos negligere:nam præceptum charitatis in omneis omnibus est datum. non est cuiufquam propter ofsensas in illos inuehi; fiue Deum offendant, nam ferui alieni sunt, non autem nostri; fiue nos ipsos ratione vlla,nam mea est vltio,ego rependam, dicit Dominus. Sed potiùs eædem nobis omnibus partes obseruandæ sunt , quas Deus exemplo suo mõftrat, faciens vt Sol suus exoriatur super malos ac bonos, & pluat super iustos & iniustos : & quas Christus reipfa præstitit erga nos ,cùm adhuc effemus peccatores atq. inimici ipsius,pro nobis mortuus. Deniq. illud ipsum præceptum quod Dauid illius verbis denunciauit eodem in psalmo , quàm diligentiffimè colendum est: vt singuli tanquam administri gratiæ & misericordiæ Dei, ipsos, dum in viâ sunt, fraternè appellemus, dicentes, Nunc animadvertite, eruditionem percipite, colite Iehovam cum reverentia, & exultate cum tremore: osculamini filium, &c. quæ paulò ante adduximus.
units.tr: According to nature, therefore, they are in a certain sense in potential, so that they may be called wayfarers while they are here on the way. As the same Prophet sang in Psalm 2, saying: "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish in the way, when his wrath is kindled even a little." Since God therefore leaves them in the way, reserving to himself the judgment about those whom he will take up for his work, or leave idle in the middle way, it is not for any man to make a judgment about them, for that judgment is God's. It is not for anyone to neglect them, for the command of charity has been given to all men. It is not for anyone to rail against them because of offences committed against them: whether they offend God, for they are other men's servants and not ours; or ourselves, for "vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." Rather, the same parts should be observed by all of us, which God shows by his example, causing his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and to rain on the just and the unjust; and which Christ actually performed toward us, when we were still sinners and his enemies, dying for us. Finally, that very command which David announced in the words of that psalm must be cultivated most diligently: that each of us, as ministers of God's grace and mercy, should call them brothers while they are on the way, saying: "Now take heed, receive instruction, serve Jehovah with reverence, and rejoice with trembling; kiss the Son," and so on, which we quoted a little before.

units.la: Quod autem ad opus gratiæ, & illos qui in ipso opere & ædificatione sunt per gratiam, quis neget religiosè illos agnosci oportere, tanquam materiam à Deo sanctificatam ad opus divinum ipsius? Etsi horum duo sunt genera: nam alij tanquam lapides rudes atque impoliti ad ecclesiam adducuntur verbo aceruatim: Alij in ecclesia sunt, & de substantia illius dicuntur esse, ut lapides in opere structuræ singulatim occupati. Nam perinde accidit in hac ædificatione spiritali, ut in structuris humanis videmus observari. Primùm adfertur materia promiscuè: Deinde verò speciatim hic lapis in opere occupatur, ille intactus relinquitur. Demonstrat illud Ioannes dicens, E nobis egressi sunt, sed non erant ex nobis: nam si fuissent ex nobis, permansissent utique nobiscum: sed ut patefieret non omneis esse ex nobis, egressi sunt. Quod si isti ipsi lapides qui in agro iacent, dum hic in terris viuimus, non sunt negligendi: profectò bonâ fide nemo homo hominem neglecturus est, qui aut sistetur coram ædificio Domini, aut in eo occupabitur singulari gratia illius. Nam quemcunque Deus sistit, qua auctoritate, quo iure homo depulsurus est, donec ipse Deus architectator suae domus depulerit? quemcunq. occupat Deus in opere,quis deturbaturus est ? pudeat ergo Christianos, qui inscientissimis suis praejudiciis aut impotentissimis studiis sic abripiuntur, ut quam Deus materiam domus suae advocat, ipsi negent, avertant, & omnibus viribus interturbent. Deus fert materiam tamdiu,quae ad domus suae structuram[?] adhiberi potest: & tu, homo miser, ne ad momentum quidem perferre potis? Deus advehit materia, & struem accumulat ad commoditatem aedificationis suae: & tu, homo demens, disperdas & dissicias protervè quae coa-. cervavit Deus? Ad summam, Deus aedificat de hac materia quoscunque tanto honore gratiae dignatus est in filio dilectionis suae:& tu,homo ingratissime, gratiam illam Dei,& opus gratiae, & Deum ipsum oppugnes iniquitate tua? absit à nobis longissimè istæc insania.Statuamus potius cum animis nostris, Nos omnes,quotquot Christiani sumus,operas Dei esse:ac propterea vocatione communi teneri ferre,quæcunq. fert Deus, & proximos omnes nostros secundum naturam, vocationem, & gratiam ad eandem communionem advocare.In primis autem quicunque operarij sunt·Domini ex vocatione singulari,aut in numero dignissimo operariorum eius ex ordine haberi volunt, quo amplius honoris à Domino donis,& vocatione adepti sunt,ij sic cogitent, se non ut præceant arbitratu suo, sed ut Dominum præeuntem sequantur omni religione ac fide vocatos esse: Itaque sui esse maximè officij, ut homines disiectos & exteros ab ædificio Domini miserentur animo, sermone vocent, & opere exemploque præeant diligentissimè: Quoscunq. vero aut verbo traxit ad domum suam, aut virtute spiritus applicat, iis omne officium pietatis & humanitatis per charitatè ἀνυπόκριτον [?] præstent in Domino. Nam commune hoc officium est omnibus imperatum, ut omnibus benefaciamus: sed cùm de illo numero omnium propiùs adiungantur nobis, qui vocantur verbo (nam mihi Christianus est quàm Turca propinquior) proximè autem qui vnitate spiritus continentur nobiscum in ecclesia Dei: nos his maximè omnium, velut domesticis fidei, oportet benefacere. Nulla materia, dum in via sumus, negligenda (nam quis nouit quo vtatur Deus?) sed hæc tamen illi anteponenda est, prout verbo & opere demonstrat Deus. Atque hæc de materia ad domum Dei pertinente satis.
units.tr: As for the work of grace, and those who are in the very work and building by grace, who would deny that they must be religiously acknowledged, as matter sanctified by God for his divine work? Although there are two kinds of these: for some are brought to the Church by the Word in a heap, like rough and unpolished stones; others are in the Church and are said to be of its substance, each set in place in the work of the building. For the same thing happens in this spiritual building as we see observed in human buildings. First the material is brought in promiscuously; then, individually, this stone is put to work, while that one is left untouched. John demonstrates this, saying: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us; but that it might be made plain that not all are of us, they went out." But if those very stones which lie in the field are not to be neglected while we live here on earth, surely no man in good faith will neglect a man who either is set before the building of the Lord or will be occupied in it by his singular grace. For whomever God sets there, by what authority or right will a man drive him away, until God himself, the architect of his house, has driven him away? Whomever God employs in the work, who will cast down? Let Christians then be ashamed, who through their most ignorant prejudices or most violent zeal are so carried away that they deny, reject, and with all their strength disturb the material which God calls into his house. God bears the material for as long as it can be used for the building of his house; and you, wretched man, cannot bear it even for a moment? God brings in the material and heaps up the structure for the convenience of his building; and you, foolish man, wilfully scatter and break down what God has heaped up? In sum, God builds from this material whomever he has deigned to honour with the grace of his beloved Son; and will you, most ungrateful man, attack that grace of God, and the work of grace, and God himself, with your iniquity? Far from us be such madness. Let us rather resolve in our hearts that we, all of us who are Christians, are workers of God; and therefore are bound by a common calling to bear whatever God bears, and to summon all our neighbours, according to nature, calling and grace, to the same communion. Especially those who are workers of the Lord by a singular calling, or wish to be counted in the most worthy number of his workers, let them think that they are called not to lead by their own judgment, but to follow the Lord going before them with all devotion and faith. Thus it is especially their duty to pity with their minds men scattered and foreign to the Lord's building, to call them by word, and to go before them diligently by work and example. But those whom he has drawn by word into his house, or whom the power of the Spirit joins to it, let them perform toward these every duty of piety and humanity in the Lord, with unfeigned [ἀνυπόκριτον] love. For this common duty is enjoined on all, that we do good to all; but since, of that whole number, those who are called by the Word are more closely joined to us (for a Christian is nearer to me than a Turk), and most closely those who are bound with us by the unity of the Spirit in the Church of God, we ought to do good especially to these, as to the domestics of the faith, above all. No material is to be neglected while we are on the way (for who knows what use God may make of it?), but yet this is to be placed before the rest, as God shows by word and work. And so much for the material pertaining to the house of God.

units.la: Forma autem essentialis huius domus in relatione, id est, ordinatione & applicatione ad ipsum posita est: cuius respectu domus Iehoua appellatur. Nam ut corpus unum ex omnibus hominibus constituatur, prout specie omnes sumus unum: non tamen continuò sumus domus una Iehoua. Sed alia quædam forma ab altero principio, quàm à natura est, secundum quam quàm ex hac communi materia vel corpore, id est ;*ex specie humani generis domus Iebova conficitur. Notum est autem in scholis, relationem, quam vocant, formam esse earum rerum quæ ad aliquid referuntur: ac proinde citra relationem ea quæ reipsa relata sunt, id ipsum quod sunt, non posse esse. Relationem autem, secundum quam hæc domus ex lapidibus vivis coagmentata veram suam formā & essentialem obtinet, demonstrat nomen Iebova: quia ecclesia domus Iebova appellatur, tanquam domini sui; & vicissim Dominus, huius domus, quam Ecclesiā vocamus, dominus. Est autem essentialis forma, per quam res est atque operatur. Quod si res relatiua est, eius forma essentialis vsq. adeò in respectu alterius & relatione posita est, ut citra illum respectum nec sit, nec agat quicquam. Sic Ecclesia, quicquid est, quicquid agit quà ecclesia est, id totum est & agit in Domino: & relatio eius ad Dominum, certissima & unica forma eius essentialis est. Formam autem dico inde à principio, & secundum esse, & secundum potentiam, & secundum actiones operationesque ipsius, & secundum finem: quia ex eo, & per eum & in eum quia ex eo, & per eum & in eum sunt omnia: Cui sit gloria in secula.
units.tr: The essential form of this house, however, lies in its relation, that is, its ordering and application to him, and it is from this relation that the house is called the house of Iebova. For although one body is made up of all human beings, since in species we are all one, we are not for that reason at once one house of Jehovah. There is rather another form, from a principle other than nature, by which the house of Jehovah is made out of this common matter or body, that is, out of the species of the human race. It is well known in the schools that relation, as they call it, is the form of those things which are referred to something, and that therefore apart from relation the things that are truly related cannot be what they are. The relation by which this house, joined together from living stones, obtains its true and essential form is shown by the name Jehovah: the Church is called the house of Jehovah as of its Lord, and conversely the Lord is the lord of this house, which we call the Church. An essential form is that through which a thing is and acts. If a thing is relative, its essential form lies so entirely in respect to another and in relation that without that respect it neither is nor does anything. Thus the Church, whatever it is and whatever it does insofar as it is the Church, all of it is and acts in the Lord, and its relation to the Lord is its most certain and only essential form. I speak of form from the beginning, both as to being and as to power, as to its actions and operations, and as to its end, because from him, through him and unto him are all things, to whom be glory forever.

units.la: Etenim Deus solus solum est principium supernaturale gratiæ, Deus, inquam, Pater in Christo Iesu per communicationem Spiritus. Quapropter tum ab eo omnis cognatio dicitur nominari in cælo & terrâ, tum verò Ecclesia & singula illius membra dicuntur esse Christi, & Christus Dei. Atque hic etiam locus eò pertinet (prout argumentum docet Apostoli) ut intelligamus hunc respectum siue relationem, ad essentiam totam Ecclesiæ, hoc est, non ad generationem solùm, verùm etiam ad constitutionem eius protendi oportere: quia ut ab eo, sic in eo subsistit Ecclesia: imò longè firmiùs ac gloriosiùs in eo subsistit, qui solus immortalis est & subsistit per se, quàm aliud quicquam.
units.tr: For God alone is the sole supernatural principle of grace: God, I say, the Father in Christ Jesus, through the communication of the Spirit. Therefore from him every family is named in heaven and on earth; and the Church and its individual members are said to be Christ's, and Christ is said to be God's. This passage also bears on this point, as the argument of the Apostle teaches: we should understand that this respect or relation extends to the whole essence of the Church, that is, not only to its generation but also to its constitution. For as the Church subsists from him, so it subsists in him; indeed it subsists far more firmly and gloriously in him, who alone is immortal and subsists through himself, than in anything else.

units.la: Quin etiam cùm omni essentiæ suæ sit à natura inclinatio & operatio, gratiâ verò naturam anteceat numeris omnibus; ex eo quoq. illud consequitur, quòd omnem suam potentiam Ecclesia à Deo obtinet gratiosè; qui omnia in omnibus vniuersè implere dicitur, & cuius vicissim complementum Ecclesia appellatur: quia Deus singulariter in ea collocat thesauros potentiæ suæ, & illa vicissim cum Apostolo agnoscit libentissimè & audenter prædicat, Omnia possumus in eo qui confirmat nos. Cùm autem illius potentiæ, quæ ad omnia etiam contraria subeunda instruitur virtute Dei, suæ sint actiones, in quibus potentia illa & virtus quasi determinatè occupatur, quemadmodum ex potentia habitu, & ex habitu actum generari tradunt scholastici: id quoque fateantur omnes etiam imperitissimi necesse est: Deum, qui principium est omnis potentiæ & operationis in rebus creatis universè & in tota natura rerū, multò magis fundamentū esse operationum omnium Ecclesiæ suæ per singularem assistentiam gratiæ, quam promisit dicens, Nam ero tecum, ut auctor Epistolæ ad Hebræos argumentatus est. Quòd si rerum istarum omnium ratio ita est cōparata, ut ecclesia sine relatione ad Deum nulla sit, omninò ex ea ipsa relatione & respectu finem quoque Ecclesiæ pendere statuimus. Nam, cùm domus sit propter dominum & habitatorem suum, Ecclesia vero sit Dei viuentis domus; quis usque adeò inter homines desipiat, ut domum luteam & ex necessitate misero homini fabrefactam, ad usum hominis velut finem suum spectare iudicet? Ecclesiam vero à Deo liberrimè, sine ulla necessitate ipsius, ex indignissimis & abiectissimis hominibus collectam, putet ad alium finem quàm ad eius gloriam, qui sine ullo defectu suo, sed mera gratia ædificauit, pertinere?
units.tr: Moreover, since every essence has its inclination and operation from nature, while grace precedes nature in every respect, it follows from this also that the Church obtains all its power from God by grace. He is said to fill all things in all, and the Church in turn is called his complement, because God places the treasures of his power in her in a singular way, and she in turn gladly and boldly acknowledges and proclaims with the Apostle: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me." Since the actions of that power, which is equipped by the power of God to undergo even all contrary things, are its own, and in them that power and virtue are as it were determinately occupied, just as the scholastics teach that from power as habit, and from habit, act is generated, even the most unskilled must necessarily concede this: God, who is the principle of all power and operation in created things and in the whole nature of things, is much more the foundation of all the operations of his Church, through the singular assistance of grace which he promised when he said, "For I will be with you," as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews argued. But if the reason of all these things is so arranged that the Church is nothing without relation to God, we hold that from that very relation and respect the end of the Church also depends. For since a house exists on account of its lord and its inhabitant, and the Church is the house of the living God, who among men is so foolish as to judge that a house of clay, made of necessity for wretched man, looks to human use as its end? Or who would think that the Church, gathered by God most freely and without any necessity on his part from the most unworthy and abject men, pertains to any end other than his glory, who built it without any defect of his own, but by pure grace?

units.la: His ita constitutis, optimè concludimus in relatione Ecclesiæ ad Deum formam essentialem Ecclesiæ constituī oportere: cuius relationis fundamentum Deus est, & principium omnis boni, ut in natura rerum naturaliter, sic in natura Ecclesiæ supernaturali gratia: ac proinde, sicut in natura nihil est quod ortū, essentiam, virtutem, operationem, finemque suum assequatur sine hoc principio atque fundamento; ita nihil plane in Ecclesia esse, nedum Ecclesiæ corpus, quod sine hoc principio gratiæ quidquam istorum fuerit habituram. Denique ut corpus sine anima nihil est, ita Ecclesia sine illa anima sua nihil futura est: Nam anima (inquit Augustinus) vita est corporis, animæ vita Deus.
units.tr: With these things thus established, we rightly conclude that the essential form of the Church must be constituted in her relation to God, whose foundation is God himself and the principle of all good: as in nature things naturally, so in the supernatural nature of the Church by grace. Accordingly, just as in nature nothing attains its origin, essence, power, operation and end without this principle and foundation, so nothing at all in the Church, let alone the body of the Church, would have any of these without this principle of grace. Finally, as a body without a soul is nothing, so the Church without that soul of hers will be nothing. For, as Augustine says, "the soul is the life of the body; God is the life of the soul."

units.la: Sed istius formæ essentialis quam Deus hæc beatissima relatione indit Ecclesiæ suæ, modus itidem divinus est. Est quidem naturalis relatio Lunæ ad Solem à quo fœneratur lucé, sed non est unio; non in relatione stabilitas. Est quidem relatio animæ ad corpus in homine constituendo: sed hæc unio naturalis est, ac proinde ut ortum habet, sic etiam fertur ad interitum naturali quodam impetu, prout res compositæ ad principia sua dissolutione continuitatis suæ reducuntur. In hac vero relatione, magnifica, gloriosa, divina omnia. Nam Deus pater sic mittit filium ad Ecclesiam suam, ut semper unum sint: filius à Patre missus sic ad eam venit, ut semper unum sit cum Patre, quod æternum est; & semper unum cum Ecclesia, quod beneficium suo tempore cœptum in æternum permansurum est; unum inquam cum Ecclesia sua, tum participatione naturæ & affectionum illius omnium, tum personæ suæ in unitate naturæ nostræ & spiritus sui bonorumque suorum omnium communicatione: Spiritus denique sanctus à patre & filio procedens in Ecclesia est præsentissimus illa ipsa præsentia gratiæ,secundum quam Ecclesia tota & singula ipsius membra templa Dei & Christi,quia Spiritus Dei habitat in ipsis, appellantur. Utcunque dissolvatur naturalis relatio,utcunq. folvatur unio, quæ in rebus creatis invenirí potest, hæc unio supra naturam est: ac proinde non tendit ad interitum,ut res naturales; sed supra omnem interitum omniaque interitus instrumenta quàm longissimè evecta est, cùm fundamentum suum habeat in Domino.
units.tr: But the mode of that essential form, which God impresses on his Church by this most blessed relation, is likewise divine. There is indeed a natural relation of the moon to the sun, from which it receives its light, but it is not a union; stability does not lie in that relation. There is indeed a relation of soul to body in constituting a human being, but this union is natural, and therefore, just as it has its origin, so it is also carried toward dissolution by a certain natural impulse, as composite things are reduced to their principles when their continuity is broken. In this relation, however, all things are magnificent, glorious and divine. For God the Father so sends the Son to his Church that they are always one; the Son, sent by the Father, so comes to her that he is always one with the Father, which is eternal, and always one with the Church, a benefit begun in its time that will remain forever: one, I say, with his Church, both by participation in her nature and all her affections, and by the communication of his person in the unity of our nature, of his Spirit and of all his goods. Finally, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is most present in the Church by that very presence of grace according to which the whole Church and its individual members are called temples of God and of Christ, because the Spirit of God dwells in them. However the natural relation may be dissolved, however the union that can be found in created things may be undone, this union is above nature; it does not tend toward ruin as natural things do, but is raised far beyond all ruin and all instruments of ruin, since it has its foundation in the Lord.

units.la: Usus verò relationis istius qualis,obsecro,suturus est,cùm omnia divina & suppeditata divinitus in hâc relatione videamus? Certè quid Ecclesia videt,audit,odoratur,gustat,tangitæ,sentit, imaginatur, appetit, intelligit, quidquid vivit,quidquid movetur, quidquid est,id totum divinum oportet esse: Et quidquid fidelia illius membra instituunt,similiter ab eodem principio, eodem motu, & modo àb illis institui convenit. Nam si Deus, si Christus vita nostra est (ut est) cur vitam alteram vivamus quàm Christi? cur aliud cogitemus, quàm cogitationes decentes membra Christi? cur aliis rebus studeamus, quàm iis quas docet Christus? cur denique in Christo dicamur esse, si non vivimus Christo? Ut forma rei cuiusque est, ita operatur. quisquis Christianus es, quà Christianus es, spiritum habes Christi, principium & formam Ecclesiæ Christi. In hac forma Christum, & proximum, & teipsum oportet[?] recognoscas, vt digne incedas vocatione tua. Id sibi olim voluit Apostolus, cum ad Corinthios scriberet, Charitas illa Christi constringit nos; vt qui hoc statuerimus, si vnus pro omnibus fuit mortuus, nempe omnes fuisse mortuos: illum autem pro omnibus mortuum esse, vt qui viuunt posthac non sibi viuant, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus & suscitatus est. Itaque nos posthac neminem nouimus secundum carnem: quod si etiam nouimus Christum secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius nouimus. si quis igitur est in Christo, noua creatura est: vetera praeterierunt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia. haec autem omnia ex Deo, qui reconciliauit nos sibi per Iesum Christum, &c.
units.tr: But what, I beg you, will be the use of this relation, since we see all things in it as divine and supplied divinely? Surely whatever the Church sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, feels, imagines, desires and understands, whatever lives, whatever moves, whatever is, all of it ought to be divine. And whatever the faithful members of the Church institute ought likewise to be instituted by them from the same principle, the same motion and in the same manner. For if God, if Christ is our life (as he is), why should we live another life than Christ's? Why should we think thoughts unbecoming to the members of Christ? Why should we be occupied with other things than those Christ teaches? Why, finally, should we be said to be in Christ if we do not live to Christ? As the form of each thing is, so it operates. Whoever you are as a Christian, insofar as you are a Christian, you have the Spirit of Christ, the principle and form of the Church of Christ. In this form you ought to recognize Christ, your neighbour and yourself, so that you may walk worthily in your calling. This is what the Apostle meant when he wrote to the Corinthians: "The love of Christ constrains us, since we judge this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them. Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh; and even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so. So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. And all these things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, etc."

units.la: O diuinam formam veritatis! formam scientiae, formae charitatis! quam Apostolus de se in Christo subsistente ita praedicauit, ita gloriatus est in Domino, vt eadem tum formam corporis Ecclesiae Catholicam exprimat, tum singularem membrorum illius in Christo Iesu. Nam videmus Paulum in Christo constrictum vinculo charitatis: cuius charitatis pignora effectaque certissima haec sunt, quod & Christus mortuus est, resurrexitque pro nobis, & nos in ipso mortui ac suscitati sumus, vt viuamus ipsi.
units.tr: O divine form of truth! Form of knowledge, form of love! The Apostle proclaimed it of himself as abiding in Christ, and boasted of it in the Lord, so that it expresses both the Catholic form of the body of the Church and the distinctive form of its members in Christ Jesus. For we see Paul bound in Christ by the bond of love. The pledges and most certain effects of this love are these: that Christ both died and rose again for us, and that we have died and been raised up in him, so that we might live for him.

units.la: Videmus Paulum in ista coniunctione charitatis, vera scientia formae illius Christianae ita praeditum diuinitus, vt eadem scientia, non autem diuersa, & Christum, & se, & fratres suos cognoscat simul,non fecundum carnem,id est, naturale corpus & speciem illam externam quam à primo homine etiâ citra rationem peccati habitantis in nobis accepimus, sed fecundum illam sanctissimam cõftitutionem fpiritalem quam Christus in sese à carnis infirmitatibus & morte vindicatus virtute suâ obtinet, ac communicauit, velut Ecclesiæ caput & primogenitus inter multos fratres, cum Ecclesiâ suâ & membris singulis illius. Quâ in conftitutione effectum est, vt Christus nos omnes, & vicissim nos Christum & fratres nostros in Christo fecundum renouationem illam ab eo factam cognoscamus. Videmus denique in his duabus rebus, charitate inquam & cognitione Christianâ nostrâ, certissimam veritatem ab omni mendacio, vanitate, & mutatione alienam:fecundum quam,quisquis in Christo est, noua creatura est: vetera præterierunt, quæ propè sunt vt intereant, & noua facta in credente sunt omnia nouitate æternùm duraturâ, cùm & auctorem habeat Deum patrem,& mediatorem effectoremque Christum, per quem reconciliati fumus Deo & patri nostro.
units.tr: We see Paul, endowed by God with the true knowledge of that Christian form, through this bond of love, so that by the same knowledge, and not by different ones, he knows Christ, himself and his brothers together. He knows them not according to the flesh, that is, the natural body and that outward appearance which we have received from the first man, dwelling in us even apart from the reason of sin, but according to that most holy spiritual constitution which Christ, vindicated from the infirmities and death of the flesh by his own power, possesses in himself and imparts, as the head of the Church and the firstborn among many brothers, together with his Church and each of its members. By this constitution it comes about that we all know Christ, and in turn know Christ, and our brothers in Christ, according to that renewal made by him. Finally, we see in these two things, I mean our love and our Christian knowledge, a most certain truth free from all falsehood, vanity and change. According to it, whoever is in Christ is a new creature: the old things have passed away, which are near to perishing, and in the believer all things are made new, with a newness that will last for ever, since God the Father is its author and Christ the mediator and effecter, through whom we have been reconciled to God our Father.
