units.la: Hæc radice charitatis, hoc succo veritatis, hac luce cognitionis atq; scientiæ, hac denique forma Christianitatis instructi[?],fi Christum nouimus,fi nos in Christo experimur,cur non & Ecclesiam,& membra illius, tum quæ iam ex facto vocata sunt per Dei gratiâ,tum quæ porrò vocanda misericorditer, cur non (inquam) hos omnes in eadē charitatis radice, & succo veritatis, eadem cognitionis luce, eademque Christianitatis forma cognoscamus? Hæc enim illa ratio est, quæ recreauit summaque lætitia Davidem affecit, & omnes bonos exemplo eius afsectura est: hæc illa forma cuius conscientia Apostolus non dubitabat dicere, Sive insanimus, insanimus Deo; sive sana mente sumus, vobis mente sana sumus: adeò poslidebat vera illa formā hominis Christiani Apostolum Christi, ut non ad se respiceret, sed ad Christum caput nostrum, & in Christo omnia membra corporis illius in veritate, scientiâ, & charitate Christiana amplexaretur studio & amore infuperabili. Horum exemplis si nos religiosè studebimus conformare, & mysterium pietatis in bona conscientia & fide αὐτοκέιτῳ[?] & charitate retinebimus; non dubium est quin eiusdem lætitiæ cùm in hoc, tum in futuro seculo confortes suturi simus per Dei misericordiam. Sed, cheu, si ad hæc tempora oculos & cogitationes nostras convertimus, quid aliud dicturi sumus, quàm quod olim dicebat Christus? Væ mundo propter scandala: væ homini per quem evenient scandala. Prospiciat gratiosè pater ille misericordiarum, & mundum ruentem gratia salutari retrahat. Omninò, ut res sunt, forma illa Christianitatis deperit, quâ Deus scripturis expressit, quam sancti vitâ adumbrárunt, quam denique Christique Christus quotidianis signis & documentis testatam facit. Veritas in profundo demergitur, lux scientiæ cognitionisque salutaris certatim oppugnatur atque extinguitur, Charitas fermè non comparet usquam. Et quis miretur, si lætitiæ illius spiritualis loco grassatur carnificina in mentibus manibusque plurimorum, quos hoc etiam tempore revocat Dominus auctoritate, rationibus, & exemplis ab impietate & iniustitia ipsorum?
units.tr: Equipped with this root of love, this sap of truth, this light of knowledge and learning, and finally this form of Christianity: if we know Christ, if we experience ourselves in Christ, why should we not also know the Church and its members, both those already called by the grace of God and those who are yet to be mercifully called, why should we not, I say, know all of them in the same root of love and sap of truth, in the same light of knowledge, and in the same form of Christianity? For this is the principle that refreshed David and filled him with the greatest joy, and that will affect all good people by his example. This is the form of which the Apostle, conscious of it, did not hesitate to say: "Whether we are beside ourselves, we are beside ourselves for God; or whether we are of sound mind, we are of sound mind for you." So thoroughly did the Apostle of Christ possess that true form of the Christian man that he looked not to himself but to Christ our head, and embraced in Christ all the members of his body in truth, knowledge and Christian love, with an unconquerable zeal and affection. If we diligently strive to conform to these examples, and hold the mystery of godliness in a good conscience, and in faith [αὐτοκέιτῳ] and love, there is no doubt that by God's mercy we shall share this same joy both in this age and in the age to come. But alas, if we turn our eyes and thoughts to these times, what else shall we say than what Christ once said: "Woe to the world because of offences; woe to the man through whom the offences come"? May that Father of mercies look graciously upon us, and draw back the falling world by saving grace. Clearly, as things stand, that form of Christianity is perishing, the form which God has expressed in the Scriptures, which the saints have shadowed forth in their lives, and which Christ himself makes attested by daily signs and teachings. Truth is plunged into the depths; the light of saving knowledge and understanding is fiercely assailed and extinguished; charity hardly appears anywhere. And who would be surprised if, in place of that spiritual joy, slaughter rages in the minds and hands of many, whom the Lord still recalls at this time by his authority, reasons and examples from their impiety and injustice?

units.la: Hactenus duo exposuimus ad hunc locum pertinentia : nam Iehouam finem esse oftendimus Ecclesiæ toti & piis in ea singulis propositum: deinde Ecclesiam relatione spirituali cum Deo coniunctam, tantisper dum coniuncta manet, quaque ipsum respicit, velut iter piæ cuiusque animæ esse demonstravimus, ubi inveniat Dominum. Restat locus tertius de actione piorum ad Deum in Ecclesia contendentium : Eamus, inquiunt, in domum Iehoue, &c. Duplex igitur est piorū actio in Ecclesia, & per Ecclesiam ad Deum verum & viuentem contendentium. Vna est, quòd eunt ad Dominum: altera, quòd in Ecclesia euntes permanent atque perseverant. Prioris actionis documentum habetur his verbis ; Domum Iehoue adeamus: posterioris autem illis : Consistentes fiunt pedes nostri intra portas vestras, ô Hierosolyma. Hic fides, hic patientia, hic perseverantia sanctorum paucissimis verbis à Propheta grauissimè demonstrata, cùm ite[?] dicuntur, & in iis finibus se euntes continere quos circumscripsit Deus, utcumque intus foris, dextrorsum & sinistrorsum lætitia & labor ipsorum oppugnetur.
units.tr: So far we have set out two points pertinent to this place. For we have shown that Jehovah is the end set before the whole Church and before each of the pious within it. Then we have shown that the Church, joined to God by a spiritual relation, while it remains joined and looks to him, is the way for every pious soul to find the Lord. The third point remains, concerning the action of the pious who strive toward God in the Church: "Let us go," they say, "into the house of Jehovah, etc." There is therefore a twofold action of the pious in the Church, and of those striving through the Church toward the true and living God. One is that they go to the Lord; the other is that, going in the Church, they remain and persevere. Evidence of the first action is given in these words: "Let us go up to the house of Jehovah"; of the second, in those: "Our feet shall stand within your gates, O Jerusalem." Here faith, patience and perseverance of the saints are most weightily demonstrated by the Prophet in very few words, when they are spoken of as going, and as keeping themselves, while going, within the bounds which God has marked out, however their joy and labour are assailed within and without, on the right hand and on the left.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem non temerè dicuntur ire quicunque ad Ecclesiam Dei vocati sunt, aut vocantur adhuc miseri cordia eius? Nam siue ad hominem, sedemque illius respexeris, siue ad Deum & sedem gloriosam eius, nihil est quod nos non doceat, iter (fi-sapimus) fieri à nobis oportere, ut egredientes è nobis ipsis & sede hac nostra, iusto itinere non autem iniusto, vero ac non fictitio, ad Deum transeamus, & sedem cælestem illius.
units.tr: And first, those who have been called to the Church of God, or who are still being called by its mercy, are not without reason said to "go." For whether you look to the man and his seat, or to God and his glorious seat, there is nothing that does not teach us that a journey must be made by us, so that, leaving ourselves and this seat of ours, we may pass over to God and his heavenly seat by a righteous journey, not an unrighteous one, a true one and not a fictitious one. (If we are wise.)

units.la: Nam quid est homo? totus miser, natus in miseria, in eadem[?] à natura agens, vivens, & moriens, denique miseria ipsa. Quid sedes hominis? miseriae campus, quem nemo homo (usque adeò miseri sumus) vel minima ex parte possit decurrere.
units.tr: For what is man? Wholly wretched, born in misery, acting, living and dying in misery by nature, in short, misery itself. What is the seat of man? A field of misery, which no man (so miserable are we) could run over even in the smallest part.

units.la: E diuerso autem quid est Deus, nisi pater ille miserationum & omnis bonae donationis autor, qui solus miserum hominem sola misericordia sua potest ut omnipotens est, vult ut optimus est atque misericors, scit ut est sapientissimus, è miseria ipsius & sede miseriae eripere? Quam rem, quia promisit & fidelis est ac verax, secundum illam potentiam suam, bonitatem, misericordiam, & sapientiam est effecturus.
units.tr: On the other hand, what is God, except that Father of mercies and author of every good gift, who alone, as he is almighty, can, as he is good and merciful, wills, and as he is most wise, knows how, to rescue wretched man from his misery and from his seat of misery by his mercy alone? Since he has promised this, and is faithful and true, he will accomplish it according to that power, goodness, mercy and wisdom of his.

units.la: Et quae huius sedes? iustitiae, vitae, gloriae, in quam omnino quisquis conscenderit, tutus ab omni impetu in Dei praesidio, ad æternitatem, conquieturus est. Quantum autem, obsecro, intervallum putandum est inter illum quem prædicamus Deum, & nos miseros homunciones, qui domos luteas incolimus? Quantum distat illa, æterna & cælestis sedes & immota civitas, ab hoc momentaneo & putri gurgustio quod nos incolimus? Est igitur faciendum iter, si ex hoc miserrimo domicilio nostro ad illud beatissimum aspiramus. Hoc iter nemo homo in terris, aut Angelus è cælo docere aut monstrare potuit. Deus idem docuit, & posuit. Docuit in scriptura; posuit in Ecclesia, deducit nos ac potius trahit virtute sua, id est, spiritus æterni sui communicatione.
units.tr: And what is this seat? It is that of righteousness, life and glory, into which whoever ascends, safe from every assault under God's protection, will at last rest in eternity. But how great, I pray, must we think the distance is between that God whom we proclaim and us wretched little men who dwell in houses of clay? How far is that eternal and heavenly seat and unmoving city from this momentary and rotting hovel that we inhabit? A journey must therefore be made, if we aspire from this most wretched dwelling of ours to that most blessed one. No man on earth, nor an angel from heaven, could teach or show this journey. God himself has taught it and appointed it. He taught it in Scripture; he appointed it in the Church; he leads us, or rather draws us, by his power, that is, by the communication of his eternal Spirit.

units.la: Primum itaque quod ex illo sanctorum sermone discimus, illud est; nos peregrè abesse à Domino; & ubicunque locorum simus, videndum esse, ut tu à nobis supra nos, tum à mundo supra totum hunc mundum fugiamus, nisi mala nostra, id est, peccata & miseriæ innumerabiles ex peccatis accumulatæ nobis plus æquo allubescant maximo malo nostro. Deinde, cùm homini cuiuis prudenti nō id tantum sit videndum, unde effugere ipsum oporteat, verumetiam quò & qua utiliter ipsum contendere; alterum illud Christianis opus est, ut, prout à se ipsis mundoque toto profugiunt, ita ad finem summum omnium & summum bonum suum transfugiant diligentissimè: præsertim cùm is ipse, qui principium & finis omnis boni, adeoque summum bonum, vel potiùs vnicum nostrû est, se tám gratiosè sistat in oculis omnium & exhibeat perfruendum. Quam ad rem si defixa oculorû acie toto animo & totâ mente adlaboraremus, profectò nec tam multis incommodis alij afficeremus alios, nec in singulis quæ obueniunt impedimentis, citò, trepidè, segniter, atque infirmè hæreremus. Accedit ad hæc sanctissimum illud Dei, qui nos vocauit, studium Ecclesiam suam in hoc terrarum orbe seculoque pangentis, velut ouili caulam, & familiæ domum: cuius claustra & repagula propterea à Deo fixa sunt, vt cùm nosmetipsos in Ecclesia Dei fratresque nostros agnoscamus, aditum ad Deum molientes, tum verò Deum ipsum sanctificationem Ecclesiæ suæ & membris eius adferentem præsentia sua & salutari gratia. Quorum omnium feria contemplatione sancti iam olim percitij inter se dixerunt; Dominum Iehoue adeamus, vt Propheta hoc loco narrat; id est, cùm ipsi sibi gratulantes addiderunt calcaria, vt Deum & sacratium eius accederent, tum alios sermone, exemplo, & omni pietatis officio, non imperio & violentia (quò plerique omnes videntur tuëri) non ostentoso metu, religiosissimè prouocarunt.
units.tr: First, therefore, what we learn from that holy speech is this: that we are far away from the Lord, and wherever we are we must take care to flee from ourselves above all, and from the world above all this world, unless our evils, that is, our sins and the countless miseries heaped up from sins, please us more than is right, to our greatest harm. Next, since it is not enough for any prudent man to see only whence he must flee, but also whither and by what way he must usefully strive, a second task is needed of Christians: that, as they flee from themselves and the whole world, so they diligently flee over to the highest end of all and their supreme good, especially since he who is the beginning and end of every good, and therefore the supreme good, or rather our only one, presents himself so graciously before the eyes of all and offers himself to be enjoyed. If with our gaze fixed on this we laboured with our whole soul and whole mind, we would surely not afflict others with so many troubles, nor, hindered by each obstacle that arises, hesitate hastily, timidly, sluggishly and weakly. Added to this is the most holy zeal of God, who called us, in building his Church in this world and age, as a sheepfold for the flock and a house for the household; its enclosures and bars have therefore been fixed by God, so that, recognising ourselves and our brothers in the Church of God as we strive toward access to God, God himself, bringing sanctification to his Church and its members by his presence and saving grace, may be known. The saints of old, moved by a full contemplation of all these things, said among themselves: "Let us go up to the Lord Jehovah," as the Prophet relates in this place. That is, while rejoicing in themselves they added spurs to go to God and his sanctuary, and then, not by command and violence (by which most people seem to maintain their position), nor by ostentatious fear, but by speech, example and every duty of piety, they most religiously stirred up others.

units.la: Quid ergo est, ô grex Christi, quod nos tantopere impediat ab his omnibus pietatis, iustitiæ, sanctimoniæ, & religionis veræ, officiis? Quid est, obsecro, quod miseram illam peregrinationem nostram, ac potius emānsionem quā emanemus à Domino, nobis tam suauem efficiat? Quid est siue in nobis, siue in hac misera statione & tota conuersatione nostra, quo alliciamur atque constringamur, ne possimus à nobis ipsis & nostra miseria fugere? Quòd siquid est suauitatis (vt quidem videtur nobis) in hac ipsa miserrima conditione nostra, quid est vsquè adeò suaue aut vtile, aut boni instructum specie, quod cum illo fine summo & bono vnico comparari possit? quid est quod non perrumpamus, vt tandem conatu iusto ad rapiendum fructum summi illius boni perducamur? quid est in hac abiectissima statione nostra factoque nostro contaminatissima, quod nos sic fascinet[?], vt mentes ad domum illam cæ-lestem, quam Iebùsa inhabitat, minimè attollamus? quid, quod oculos præstinguat, ne lucem illam à Deo in Ecclesia ipsius commodissimè expositam prosequamur, eaq. præluceñte mala fugienda, & bona prensanda, vtenda, fruenda, secundum Deum cognoscamus, & alij alios ad eandem cognitionem, apprehensionem, & fructum gratiæ excitemus? quid, quod nos iubeat saluti nostræ ipsorum obsistere, & metum, minas, artes, vim, gladios, ignes, laqueos, quærentibus salutem secus quàm nobis videtur, oppangere? Cogitemus potius per Deum immortalem, per salutem illam nostram, quam pretioso sanguine suo Christus comparauit, quantum malum nos circumsideat opprimatque, nisi ad Deum contendamus: quanta bonorum innumerabilium in Deo suauitas: quanta in Ecclesia claritas: quanta in communione sanctorum delectatio, mutuis celeusmatis inter se adhortantium: quanta vis maximæ illius nubis testium (vt Apostolus ad Hebræos vocat) nos velut circumsonantis clamore sanctissimo in cælo & terra, vt præeuntes sequamur & obsequamur Domino. Hæc cogitatione armati sugiamus nosipsos & mala nostra, ad Deum transfugiamus per Ecclesiam eius, & alij alios ad participationem admirabilis eiusdem lucis religione & charitate vera provocemus. Hæc illa est sanctorum actio, quam Deus imperat, quam Dauid prædicat, quam pius quisque diuinam iudicat, & quam nemo nisi impius, si viderit aut modo aliquo senserit, abdicaturus est.
units.tr: What then is it, O flock of Christ, that holds us back so greatly from all these duties of piety, justice, holiness and true religion? What is it, I beg you, that makes this wretched pilgrimage of ours, or rather this departure from the Lord by which we depart, so pleasant to us? What is it, either in us or in this wretched station and our whole way of life, that entices and binds us so that we cannot flee from ourselves and our misery? If there is any sweetness (as it seems to us) in this most miserable condition of ours, what is so very sweet, useful, or furnished with the appearance of good, that it can be compared with that supreme and only good end? What is there that we do not break through, so that at last by a just effort we may be brought to seize the fruit of that supreme good? What is there in this most abject station of ours, so polluted by our deeds, that so bewitches us that we do not lift our minds to that heavenly home which Jebus inhabits? What is it that blinds our eyes, so that we do not follow that light which God has most conveniently set forth in his Church, and so that by its shining we do not know to flee evils and to seize, use and enjoy goods according to God, and to stir one another up to the same knowledge, apprehension and fruit of grace? What is it that bids us resist our own salvation, and to oppose fear, threats, arts, force, swords, fires and snares to those who seek salvation otherwise than we think fit? Let us rather consider, by the immortal God and by that salvation of ours which Christ bought with his precious blood, how great the evil that surrounds and oppresses us unless we strive toward God; how great the sweetness of countless goods in God; how great the brightness in the Church; how great the delight in the communion of the saints, exhorting one another with mutual shouts; how great the power of that very great cloud of witnesses (as the Apostle calls it in the Letter to the Hebrews), which, as if with a most holy clamour sounding around us in heaven and on earth, bids us follow those who go before us and obey the Lord. Armed with this thought, let us flee from ourselves and our evils, let us desert to God through his Church, and let us provoke one another to share in that wonderful light with true religion and love. This is that action of the saints which God commands, which David proclaims, which every pious person judges divine, and which no one but the impious will renounce, if he has seen it or perceived it in any way.

units.la: Sed hanc actionem animus non corpus, mens non manus præstare potest; quandoquidem (vt docebat Christus) Deus est Spiritus, & eos qui ipsum adoraturi sunt, in spiritu & veritate præcipit adorare. Det nobis idem qui præcipit, vt corpore, & animo, & spiritu ita comparati, à nobis ad ipsum in Ecclesia fugiamus indefinenter, & alij alios secundum illam charitatem Christi adiuuemus in persequenda percipiendaque illa communicatione gratiæ, incredibilem lætitiam, fructum spiritus suauissimum, in nobis edicturam.
units.tr: But this action can be performed by the mind, not the body, and by the spirit, not the hands; since (as Christ taught) God is Spirit, and he commands those who are to worship him to worship in spirit and truth. May he who commands it grant us, made ready in body, soul and spirit, to flee continually to him in the Church, and may we help one another, according to that love of Christ, to pursue and receive that communication of grace, which will bring forth in us incredible joy and the sweetest fruit of the Spirit.

units.la: 2. Quod consistentes sunt pedes nostri in portis tuis, ô Hierosolyma.
units.tr: 2. That our feet stand in your gates, O Jerusalem.

units.la: ACTIONEM sanctorum omnium singulorumque diximus ante à Propheta circcumscriptam esse certissimis ac pernecessariis finibus, cùm illos accedere ad Deum Ecclesiam que illius, & permanere in ea prædicaret apud Dominum Deum suum. Jam vero exposita priore parte, qua pii se ad Deum in Ecclesia eius adeundum comparaverunt, hic altera subiicitur, qua sanctam perseverantiam suam profitentur in boni illius diuinitùs percepti communicatione. Huius ergò propositionis summa est, profiteri pii, & hoc tempore Christianos omnes, se in Catholica Dei Ecclesia & parte Catholicæ quæ hic in terris versatur, constanter mansuros esse, neque ab ea aut divinis institutis eius temerè discefluros. Atque hanc professionem singuli pii hoc loco ita dicuntur facere, ut sui religiosi studii non hunc solùm aut illum, sed totum Ecclesiæ corpus, Ecclesiam (inquam) ipsam testem advocent, spectatricem sancti consilii & voluntatis suæ. Quamobrem ut hoc argumentum commodiùs exponamus, & singuli melius intelligant, tria nobis ordine videnda sunt in hoc versu paucis comprehensa. Primùm, quam perseverantiam profiteantur pii: Secundò, quos fines statuant illius perseverantiæ: Postremò autem quos adhibeant testes conscientiæ ipsorum annuentes atque attestantes. Perseverantiam denotant hæc verba, Consistentes sunt pedes nostri. Fines illius perseverantiæ circumscribuntur ab illis, cùm inquiunt, in portis tuis. Testimonium verò Ecclesiæ ad hæc omnia appellatur, quia illius est testificari secundum Deū, tum de portis suis (vt cum Propheta loquamur) tum de membris intra portas eius agentibus.
units.tr: We said earlier that the action of all the saints, and of each one, is bounded by the Prophet with most certain and most necessary limits, since he proclaimed that they approach God and his Church, and remain in it before the Lord their God. Now that the first part has been set out, in which the pious prepared themselves to approach God in his Church, here the second part is added, in which they profess their holy perseverance in the sharing of that good which they received from God. The sum of this proposition, then, is that the pious, and at this time all Christians, profess that they will remain steadfast in the Catholic Church of God and in that part of the Catholic Church which dwells here on earth, and will not rashly depart from it or from its divine institutions. And each of the pious is said here to make this profession in such a way that, as witnesses of their religious zeal, they summon not merely this or that person but the whole body of the Church, the Church itself, as the watcher of their holy counsel and will. Therefore, so that we may expound this argument more conveniently and each may understand it better, three things must be considered in order, briefly comprehended in this verse. First, what perseverance the pious profess; second, what limits they set to that perseverance; last, which witnesses they call upon to nod assent and attest their conscience. The words Our feet stand denote the perseverance. The limits of that perseverance are marked out by them when they say in your gates. The testimony of the Church is invoked for all these things, because it belongs to the Church to bear witness before God, both concerning its gates (to speak with the Prophet) and concerning the members who act within its gates.

units.la: Ac primus quidem ille locus de perseverantia sanctorum nō temerè à piis adhibetur: quia omnes homines ad sanctitatem veram à Deo provocati & accensi in Ecclesia eius, adhuc ea cæcitate mentis & carnis infirmitate sunt, dum hic in terris vivunt & lubricū iter huius mundi premunt, vt nullo fermè negotio pedes eorum à viis quas Deus præscripsit avertantur. Probat Deus, excæcat mundus, debilitat caro, peccatum [illegible, ~2 letters]ngit, Satanas fallit, omnia denique pedibus piorum insidiari videntur quàm periculosissimè, nisi Dei manus, Ecclesiæ ars, & nostra ipsorum observatio diligentissima adversus tot mala, quæ nos infestant, concurrerint. Peregrinantes itaque pij à Domino & arduum huius vitæ iter cōtemplantes, quo ex se ipsis egredi, in Ecclesiam ingredi, & ad Deum transgredi ipsos necesse est, actionem illam spiritalem corporeis umbraculis significauerunt, cùm sibi pedes in hoc spiritali incessu & consistendi of-ficium tribuerunt. Hic enim sive incedamus, sive
units.tr: Now this first point, about the perseverance of the saints, is not rashly adduced by the pious, because all men, called by God to true holiness and kindled in his Church, are still in such blindness of mind and weakness of flesh while they live here on earth and tread the slippery road of this world, that their feet are turned aside from the ways God has prescribed with almost no effort. God tests, the world blinds, the flesh weakens, sin [illegible] pricks, Satan deceives; in short, everything seems to lie in wait for the feet of the pious most dangerously, unless the hand of God, the art of the Church and our own most diligent watchfulness come together against so many evils that assail us. Therefore the pious, as pilgrims from the Lord, contemplating the steep road of this life, along which they must go out from themselves, enter the Church and pass over to God, signified that spiritual action by bodily shadows when they ascribed to themselves feet and the office of standing in this spiritual journey. For here, whether we walk or stand, it is the work not of the foot but of the mind (as we said before), which exercises its power in spiritual things in a spiritual manner, without any operation of bodily instruments. Yet since we are carnal, and according to the flesh receive spiritual things through a certain analogy suited to our weakness, the Prophet shadows its actions with bodily instruments.

units.la: consistamus,non pedis,sed mentis opus est (vt antè diximus) quæ facultatem suam in rebus spiritualibus occupat spirituali modo, sine corporalium instrumentorum operatione vllá:sed tamen nobis, qui carnales sumus,& secundum carnem per analogiam quandam infirmo caprui nostro accommodam res spirituales accipimus , sdumbrat actiones suas corporalibus instrumentis. Pedes igitur nostri, inquiunt, sunt consistentes, id est, perstamus in Ecclesiâ Dei sad quam peruenimus , vt præcedente versu fuit expositum. Et quamuis subinde nostrâ ipsorum infirmitate & alienâ occasione factoque impellamur,& propemodum de beatâ illâ sede, quantum in nobis est, deiiciamur , tamen experimur subinde etiam nos in Deo & in Ecclesia eius cósirmari,quo nomine gloriamur etiam in mediis nostris asslictionibus.
units.tr: Therefore, they say, our feet are standing, that is, we persist in the Church of God to which we have come, as was explained in the preceding verse. And although we are sometimes pushed by our own weakness and by another's occasion and deed, and almost cast down, as far as in us lies, from that blessed seat, yet we experience at times that we too are strengthened in God and in his Church, and for this we also glory in the midst of our afflictions.

units.la: Itaque in locutione hâc, Pedes nostri suntsonsistentes,reuerâ plusinest, quàm si dictû stisset à piis simpliciter, Consistunt pedes nostri, quemadmodum Hebrææ linguæ vsu demonstratur passim . Nam primùm testantur pij factum suum,deinde tentationes suas,ac postremò studium quo tentationibus obsistunt in Domino. Factum suum hoc esse pronunciant,quòd freti virtute Iehouæ (qui formam essentialem ecclesiæ & membrisillius indit Spiritus sui communicatione) se in Ecclesia & domo Dei viuentis continent, ad quam singulari gratia illius vocati, adducti,& agglutinati sunt, vt immoti in ea hæreant, tanquam superstructi salutari,illi, petræ, cuius Christus Matthæi 16. & Paulus 1.Cor.10. meminerunt. Tentationes sunt non quidem disertis verbis expressæ, sed hac loquendi formulâ tacitè comprehensæ, quòd intus & foris in pios irruunt mille incommoda, quibus ab illâ statione deturbari possent in quam gratia Dei perducti sunt, absque Deo esset vindice ipsorum. Nam vt homini qui totus infirmus est, etiam infirmo pedibus, si aduersentur solum lubricum aut arena fluens atque instabilis, æstus Solis, imbres, procellæ, venti, omnia denique obstiterint, conditio eius in ipso est miserabilis: ita pios, dū hic sunt, versari coftat in Ecclesia Dei infestos grauissimis, innumerabilibus, ac diuersissimis calamitatibus; aduersus quas sibi ipsi nequeant prospicere, sed tantum fortiter fixo pede id sibi statuant laborandum, ne demoueantur de eo loco ubi fruuntur præsentia Dei ipsos confirmantis. Hoc enim sibi verba illa volunt, Pedes nostri sunt confistentes: perinde atque si dicerent; Impelli quidem multifariam grauissimè sæpissimèque ipsorum pedes, & singulis momentis propè esse vt dilabantur impedimentorum vehementia: verumtamen se adhuc pedibus firmis consistere, nec rebus aduersis, quæ infestant ipsos, vel ad momentum cedere. His denique rebus accedit studium illud, quod tertio loco posuimus: cuius studij documenta duo sunt, Phrasis quam ante diximus, & tota hæc enúciatio. Nam Phrasi vel locutione Hebræa constantiam suam in labore studioque consistendi apud Dominum prositentur: Enunciatio verò tota sermonem resipit hominum verè sanctorum, qui iustificati fide & pacem habentes cum Deo in Christo, etiam in suis oppressionibus & angustiis gloriantur, ut Apostolus prædicavit. Viderunt nempe sanctæ illæ animæ spiritu Dei actæ, id non esse suarum partium, ut alienos pedes observarent, aut iis offendicula insidiásue ponerent: non ut eos, contrà quàm pietas & charitas Christiana docet, proterue in lapsum impellerentgnon[?] ut miseros etiam non intelligentes, vel ad se non advertentes animum, persequerentur infesti: sed hoc sibi potiùs curandum esse, ut ad suos pedes, id est, institutum vitæ & administrationis suæ attenderent, eos circummunirent à rebus omnibus adversis, & se in omni bono secundum Deum & coram ipso in Ecclesia confirmarent.
units.tr: So in this expression, Our feet are standing, there is really more meaning than if the pious had simply said, Our feet stand, as is shown by frequent use of the Hebrew language. For first the pious testify to their own deed, then to their temptations, and last to the zeal with which they resist temptations in the Lord. They declare that this is their deed: trusting in the power of Jehovah (who gives the essential form of the Church and its members by the communication of his Spirit), they keep themselves in the Church and house of the living God, to which they have been called, brought and joined by his singular grace, so that they cleave to it immovably, like those built upon the saving rock, of which Christ speaks in Matthew 16 and Paul in 1 Corinthians 10. The temptations are not expressed in plain words, but are tacitly included in this manner of speaking, because a thousand inconveniences, both within and without, rush upon the pious, by which they could be thrown down from that station into which the grace of God has brought them, were God not their defender. For as a man who is wholly weak, even with weak feet, if the ground is slippery or shifting sand, if the heat of the sun, showers, storms, winds, in short everything opposes him, his condition is wretched; so the pious, while they are here, are bound to live in the Church of God, troubled by the gravest, countless and most diverse calamities, against which they cannot provide for themselves, but must resolve only to labour with a firmly fixed foot that they not be moved from the place where they enjoy the presence of God, who confirms them. For these words mean just this: Our feet are standing, as if they were saying: our feet are indeed pushed many ways, very grievously and very often, and at every moment they are nearly slipping away from the violence of the obstacles; yet they still stand on firm feet, and do not yield even for a moment to the adversities that assail them. To these things is added that zeal which we placed third: the evidences of this zeal are two, the phrase we mentioned before and this whole utterance. For by the Hebrew phrase or idiom they profess their steadfastness in the labour and zeal of standing before the Lord; while the whole utterance savours of the speech of men who are truly holy, who, justified by faith and having peace with God in Christ, glory even in their oppressions and distresses, as the Apostle proclaimed. Those holy souls, driven by the Spirit of God, saw that it was not their part to watch other people's feet, or to set stumbling-blocks or snares before them, nor (contrary to what Christian piety and charity teach) to drive them headlong into a fall, nor to persecute the wretched who do not understand or do not give heed, as enemies. Rather, they saw that this was what they had to attend to: to look to their own feet, that is, to the course of their life and conduct, to fortify themselves against all adversities, and to confirm themselves in every good thing according to God and before him in the Church.

units.la: Quem finem si actuosum hoc nostrū seculum ante oculos iamdiu proposuisset sibi, certè tot funestis malis iamdiu caruisset mundus, & feliciter Ecclesia increscens ægrè fecisset Satanæ & sceleratissimis administris eius. De perseverantia diximus; iam de altero illo quem proposuimus loco, de finibus, inquam, & terminis ad perseverantiam constitutis videamus.
units.tr: If this busy age of ours had long since kept this goal before its eyes, the world would surely have been spared so many deadly evils, and the Church, growing happily, would have been a great vexation to Satan and his most wicked ministers. We have spoken of perseverance. Now let us consider the other place we proposed, namely the ends and limits set for perseverance.

units.la: Fines quibus sese religiosissimè perseverantia sanctorum continet, proponuntur his vocibus, In portis tuis. Describuntur autem allegorice, vel potius typice, pro commoditate Ecclesiae, quae tum in gente Iudaeorum fuit. Quapropter antequam de argumento dicamus, aliquid deliberandum est de isto prisce Ecclesiae usu, secundum typos a Deo institutos Ecclesiam catholicam, & partes, & attributa illius in Scriptura adumbrantis. Quaecunque igitur hoc modo enunciantur de Hierosolymis, civitate Davidis, Sione, domo Iehovae, & similibus, pro ratione locorum variam habent interpretationem. Ea autem est triplex. Nam aut secundum rem naturae fit enunciatio, aut secundum aliquam figuram veritatis, aut secundum veritatem figuratae gratiae. Secundum rem naturae, sive (ut loquuntur vulgo) per naturalem modum intelliguntur Chananaea, Ierusalem, Sion, &c. quum intelliguntur prout fuerunt in natura rerum, citra divinae relationis per gratiam institutae contemplationem. Nam ex eo quod singulari instituto Deus haec sanctificaverat, non est mutata earum rerum natura, quin Chananaea regio esset, ut alias, & Ierusalem civitas, & Sion mons, ut ante fuerat, & post[?] etiam permansit in rerum natura; sed eandem naturam suam in se singula habuerunt. Atque hoc sensu interdum in sacra Scriptura nominantur. Secundum figuram aliquando in Scripturis usurpantur eadem nomina, propter symbolicam vel facramentalem ( vt vocant ) relationem ad res diuinas,quæ ipsis adumbrabantur,non ex natura ipsarum, sed institutione & ordinatione Dei : Quæ institutio non tollebat id quod naturâ erant, sed tantùm efficiebat, vt id ipsum quod in rerum natura exstabat,quendam velut colorem & lucém relationis ad res spirituales institutione Dei acciperet. Itaque factum est non raró,vt nomina eiusmodi figurątivam significationem in verbo Dei habuerint. Secundum veritatem gratiæ tertio modo (vt antè diximus) hæc eadem nomina vsurpâtur pro iis ipsis rebus spiritualibus quas instituto Dei figurabant : quemadmodùm hoc nostro tempore, vt iusta fiat harum enunciationum quæ in Testamento vetere sunt accommodatio, accipi eas à nobis necesse est. Nam Ierusalem, quæ in Testamento vetere dicitur, nunc Ecclesia est : eodemque modo portæ, quæ à Propheta hoc loco nominantur, fines seu termini Ecclesiæ non muris aut portis definiti,sed animo & cogitatione interpretandæ sunt. Alioquin etiam non raró vsu veniebat in prisca illâ Ecclesiâ, vt tria hæc interpretationum genera in comprehensione vnâ simul concurrerent: vt nomine Chananæ tum regio quâ erat in natura rerum, tum figura quæ ad veritatem gratiæ diuinæ Ecclesiæque significandam fuerat à Deo instituta , tum denique veritas ipsa qualis in Deo & apud Deum est, non autem in natura, turâ, aut figurâ solùm intelligeretur. Atque in hanc sententiam pij nomen portarum hoc loco in prisca Ecclesia acceperunt. Nam & ad portas urbis Hierosolymorum respiciebant, prout erant in natura rerum, & ad figuram relatiuam ipsarum, prout Dei ordinatione & verbo figurales credebant esse, & ad veritatem ipsam portis (ut ita dicam) temporalibus figuratiue & sacramentali modo adumbratam. quemadmodum & in Sacramentis nostris aquam, panem, vinum, tum materiam elementarem, tum relationem figuralem, tum figuratam ea veritatem appellamus. Nos verò ad quos plenitudo temporum peruenit, non refpiciliiis [?] ad materiales portas, quæ iam diu esse desierunt; non ad figurales proprie, cum id quod non est in natura rerum figura esse non possit alterius, prout vulgò dicitur non entis non esse accidentia; sed tantùm veritate spectamus gratiæ quam Deus portarum nomine figuravit.
units.tr: The ends within which the perseverance of the saints is most devoutly contained are set forth in these words: Within your gates. They are described allegorically, or rather typically, to suit the needs of the Church, which at that time existed in the nation of the Jews. Therefore, before we speak of the subject, something must be considered about the use of the ancient Church, in which God instituted types, and about the way Scripture pictures the catholic Church, its parts and its attributes. Whatever is stated in this way about Jerusalem, the city of David, Zion, the house of Jehovah, and similar things, has a varied interpretation according to the nature of the passage. This interpretation is threefold. For the statement is made either according to the natural reality of the thing, or according to some figure of the truth, or according to the truth of the grace that is figured. According to the natural reality, or, as people commonly say, in the natural sense, Canaan, Jerusalem, Zion and so on are understood when they are taken as they were in the nature of things, without regard to the relation to God established by grace. For from the fact that God had sanctified these places by a unique ordinance, the nature of those things was not changed. Canaan remained a region, as before, and Jerusalem a city and Zion a mountain, as they had been, and they continued so in the nature of things; each had its own nature in itself. It is in this sense that they are sometimes named in holy Scripture. According to a figure, the same names are sometimes used in the Scriptures, on account of their symbolic or sacramental (as they call it) relation to divine things which were prefigured by them. This relation comes not from their nature but from the institution and ordinance of God. This institution did not take away what they were by nature, but only made it so that what existed in the nature of things received, as it were, a certain colour and light of relation to spiritual things by the institution of God. Thus it has often happened that names of this kind have carried a figurative meaning in the word of God. According to the truth of grace, in the third way (as we said before), these same names are used for the very spiritual things which they prefigured by the institution of God. In the same way, in our own time, if the application of these statements of the Old Testament is to be correct, they must be taken by us in this way. For Jerusalem, which is spoken of in the Old Testament, is now the Church; and in the same way the gates named by the Prophet in this place, that is, the ends or limits of the Church, are not to be defined by walls or gates but are to be understood in mind and thought. Otherwise it also happened, not rarely, in that ancient Church, that these three kinds of interpretation came together at once in one comprehension: so that by the name of Canaan there was understood at once the region as it was in the nature of things, the figure which God had instituted to signify the truth of divine grace and the Church, and finally the truth itself as it is in God and before God, not only in nature or in figure. And the godly of the ancient Church took the name of the gates in this place in this sense. For they looked both to the gates of the city of Jerusalem, as they were in the nature of things, and to their figurative relation, as they believed them to be figures by the ordinance and word of God, and to the truth itself, which was shadowed forth figuratively and sacramentally by the gates, so to speak, which were temporal. Just as in our sacraments we call water, bread and wine both the elemental matter, and the figurative relation, and the truth figured by them. But we, to whom the fullness of time has come, do not look to the material gates, which long ago ceased to exist, nor properly to figurative gates, since what is not in the nature of things cannot be the figure of another thing, as it is commonly said that the accidents of a non-being are not. We look only to the truth of grace which God figured under the name of gates.

units.la: Utergo de veritate constet, id primùm ad hæc nobis tenendum est, has portas in scripturis synecdochicè appellari, tùm rei illius terminos quæ agitur, tum rem ipsam totam suis terminis circumseptam, tum denique ius, auctoritatem, dominium, administrationemque, & vsum illius. Nam etsi muri vrbis cuiusque portis iuncti constituunt terminos: tamen excellentiore quodam modo dicuntur portæ ciuitatum termini; quia intus & foris commoditate portarum efficiuntur omnia quæ ad usum opidorum utilitatem q; pertinent: muri autem termini cæci sunt (ut ita loquamur) non ad actiones quasuis ciuitati cōmodas, sed ad tegumentum & defensionem solummodò comparati. Quòd autem extremitatum appellatione id totum intelligatur quod illis comprehenditur, hominI insolens videri potest, qui in ore vulgi innumeras eiusmodi locutiones animadverterit, continens pro contento, ut vocant, usurpantis: ut crumenam petens pecuniam petit. Quòd autem postremò pro iure, auctoritate, potentia, administratione, & usu significando dicuntur portæ, id à communi more prisci illius, seculi profectū est. Nam ad portas munitiones erant; armamentaria, basilicæ, fora, & conuentus dicendi iuris, ut multis Scripturæ locis confirmatur: Unde mos ille obtinuit, ut iūs, auctoritas, consilium, potentia, & vires omnes portarum nomine notarentur. Quò sensu dicebat Christus, aduersus petram & superstructam Ecclesiam non esse prævalituras inferorum portas. Hic vero non agitur de portis Ecclesiæ fabrefactis & materialibus, non de corpore ciuitatis aspectabilis, non de ordine humano aut potentia ulla carnis; sed de corpore ipso Ecclesiæ: quod cùm spirituale sit quà Ecclesia est, portarum quoq; appellatione spirituali modo oportet intelligamus. Sunt igitur portæ Ecclesia ipsa, & sancti illius fines, & termini à Deo circumpositi Ecclesiæ atque constituti ad corporis vnius coagmentationem, & iustum ordinem gubernationemque illius.
units.tr: So that the truth may be established, the first thing we must hold to is this: these gates are called in the Scriptures by synecdoche, both the limits of the matter under discussion, and the thing itself enclosed within its limits, and finally the right, authority, lordship, administration and use of that thing. For although the walls of any city, together with its gates, form its boundaries, yet in a certain more excellent manner the gates of cities are called their limits. This is because by the convenience of the gates, everything that pertains to the use and advantage of towns is brought about, within and without, whereas walls are, so to speak, blind limits, made not for any action useful to the city but only for covering and defence. That the whole thing is understood by the name of its extremities may seem strange to a man who has noticed in common speech countless expressions of this kind, where the container is used for the contents, as when one who seeks a purse seeks money. Finally, that the gates are said to signify right, authority, power, administration and use comes from the common custom of that ancient age. For the gates were fortifications; the armouries, the basilicas, the marketplaces and the assemblies for pronouncing law were there, as is confirmed by many passages of Scripture. Hence the custom prevailed that right, authority, counsel, power and all strength should be marked by the name of gates. In this sense Christ said that the gates of hell would not prevail against the Church built upon the rock. Here, however, we are not dealing with the gates of the Church made by hands and material, nor with the body of the visible city, nor with human order or any power of the flesh; but with the body of the Church itself. Since this body is spiritual in so far as it is the Church, we must understand the name of gates also in a spiritual way. The gates, therefore, are the Church itself, and its holy ends and limits, placed around the Church by God and established for the joining together of one body and for its just order and government.

units.la: His portis à Deo positis, personæ, res, & actiones quæ coram Deo in Ecclesia sunt, continentur. Personæ, à Deo vocatæ; res à Deo datæ; actiones denique à Deo in Ecclesiam præstitæ, & in ea nobis imperatæ. Cùm itaque Sancti testantur palàm pedes suos esse consistentes in portis Hierosolymorum, ad tria illa respiciunt; Deoq;. & Ecclesiæ spondent, se tanquam personas à Deo electas atque vocatas gratiosè, perseueraturos apud se & inter se, coram Domino in Ecclesia eius vti rebus à Deo datis, se laborem confiqumptuiros in actionibus eius percipiendis, & in obseruandis colendisque operibus ab ipso imperatis occupatum iri. Cùm autem rerū & actionum, quarum aliæ in priuato & singulari visu, aliæ in publico ordine positæ sunt, modus deinceps sequentibus versibus exponatur, hæc omnia eò sumus reiecturi. Id vnum quàm diligentissimè recordari pios necesse est, perseucrantiam qua vtuntur homines extra Ecclesiam, aut etiam in Ecclesia, extra fines à Deo constitutos, damnabilem esse pertinaciam; omnes autem laborem suum, operam, atq; industriam eò conferre oportere, vt non solùm in Ecclesia sint, sed etiam ex Ecclesia sint, & tanquam germana membra illius in rebus & actionibus decentibus vocationem suam indesinenter sese exerceant.
units.tr: Through these gates set by God, the persons, things and actions which are before God in the Church are contained: persons called by God, things given by God, and finally actions performed by God in the Church and commanded to us in it. When therefore the saints openly testify that our feet are standing within the gates of Jerusalem, they look to those three things. They promise to God and to the Church that they, as persons graciously chosen and called by God, will persevere among themselves and with one another before the Lord in his Church; that they will use the things given by God; that they will take up their labour in receiving his actions; and that they will be kept busy in observing and cultivating the works commanded by him. But since the manner of the things and actions, some of which are placed in private and individual view, and others in public order, is set out in the following verses, we shall refer all of these to that place. This one thing the godly must remember most carefully: the perseverance which men use outside the Church, or even within the Church but beyond the ends set by God, is damnable obstinacy. All men ought to direct their labour, effort and diligence to this end, that they not only be in the Church but also be of the Church, and, like its true members, exercise their calling without ceasing in fitting things and actions.

units.la: Hierosolymorum] ... exerceant: atque etiam siquæ dubiæ sunt, siquæ incognitæ, de iis quærant, & consulant, quemadmodum in portis olim singuli functiones suas solebant cognoscere, & ab iis qui communi præerant mandata diligentissimè accipere, fidelissimeque exequi. Nam quæcunque Christianus sentit vocationi suæ tum communi omnium, tum etiam singulari atque (ut vocant) personali convenire, ea ultrò defungitur: de quibus verò nihil planè, aut non satis informatus videtur sibi in animo & conscientia, certam eorum rationem ex Dei verbo, aut certis administris illius fidelibus què dispensatoribus, antequam ad opus accingatur, religiosè cogniturus est.
units.tr: ...exercise their calling: and if there is anything doubtful or unknown in it, let them seek out and consult about it, just as in former times at the gates each man used to learn his duties and receive the orders of those who presided over the common life most diligently, and carry them out most faithfully. For whatever a Christian judges to belong to his calling, both the common calling of all and his particular and (as they say) personal calling, he discharges of his own accord. But where he seems to have no clear or sufficient understanding in his mind and conscience, he should, before he sets his hand to the work, carefully learn the proper account of it from the Word of God, or from its faithful ministers and stewards.

units.la: Hac: perseuerantia piorum hominum finibusque positis, de testibus videndum'est, qui à filiis Dei hoc loco appellantur. Ac testium quidem, ante quorum oculos decet nos obire vocationem nostram, multa sunt genera. Testem enim habemus universorum, & rerum etiam abditissimarum cognitorem, qui etiam iudex futurus est, Deum. Huius testimonium sanctè coram hominibus, ubi alia testimonia non prosunt, ex pietate, veritate, & charitate appellamus. Testes ité habemus angelos é caelo, communi Domino cum ecclesia obsequentes, & cives Hierusalem illius in caelis: qui& intuentur faciem patris nostri qui in caelis est, mandata illius accepturi, & minimorum etiam puerulorum curam gerunt, prout iubentur à Domino, & in Ecclesia hic observant studiosissimè multiformem illam sapientiam Dei: neq. id solùm in opere gratiosò spiritalium benedictionum eius, sed etiam in externo illo ordine, qui conuenienter cum interna illa Dei gratia in communione sanctorum coniunctus est: quò spectans dicit Apostolus, à muliere potestatem, id est, potestatis signum habere in capite propter angelos: denique etiam rebus piorum gestis & perpessionibus: de quibus dicitur eadem epistola Dei servos etiam angelis spectaculum factos esse. Testis praeterea mundus est, coram quo similiter sancti fiunt spectaculum, ut ibidem affirmat Apostolus: adeò ut non dubitauerit Episcopo ministranti in Ecclesia Dei legem hanc indicere, ut etiam ab extraneis bonum habeat testimonium, ne in probrum incidat & laqueum Diaboli. Testes deniq. habemus privatim sanctos quosque, nobiscum in Dei Ecclesia conversantes: quorum testimonia eo pluris fieri à nobis necesse est, quòd domestici sunt illius domus, cuius & nos. Ex his omnibus, & aliis quoque testimoniis unicum Propheta hoc loco adhibuit, & apud hunc testem cogitationem, studium, officia sua professus est: nimirum Ecclesiam Dei.Non quòd idem apud Ichouâ Deum suum fideles non profiterentur: nam quisquis in Ecclesia professionem hanc adhibet, apud Deum profitetur, qui indesinenter in Ecclesia habitat, eamque sanctificat lauacro regeneratiomis per verbum. Non etiam quòd angelorum testimonii Ecclesia prisca nesciuerit, cui Deus quamplurimis angelorum significationibus crebrò testatus est praesentiam suam. Non quòd mundi ipsius refugerit testimonium, coram quo nos omnes confiteri Deum & Christum necesse est, ac non negare beneficium eius. Sed testimonium Ecclesiae quoties adhibetur, & quoties apud eam quod partium nostrarum est ex animo profitemur, toties corā Deo & angelis eius eadem opera officium facimus: quod officium domestici foluum vident, non vident exteri. Videt ergo Deus officium hoc & probat, vt Dominus iustus domus: Vident angeli, vt conserui in eadem domo: Videt Ecclesia & membra illius nobiscum versantia, vt custos beneficiorum Dei & mater nostra omnium in Domino, ac proinde eodem iure custos professionis nostrae erga Dominum Deum nostrum. Hanc verò professionem non videt mundus, quia oculis carnis videt, sed optimè videt Ecclesia fecundum Deum, quia sanctos oculus fidei cernit in charitate & vnitate spiritus. Rectissimè itaque pij apud Ecclesiam profitentur sanctam professionem hanc, cum quia eadem opera Deum & angelos ipsos certissimos testes habent eorum omnium quae in Ecclesia faciunt, cum quia singulari quodam instituto & conuentione Ecclesia est communis depositaria Dei pariter ac nostri: nam in ea Dominus exposuit thesauros suos à piis singulis delibandos, & vicissim in ea pij exponunt vota sua & professiones quasque pietatis suæ, vt coram Domino acceptæ sint in vnitate corporis Christi. Hanc fidelem depositariam olim appellabant pij, cùm Hierosolyma nominarent: idque iisdem modis, quos proximè declarauimus cùm de portis Hierofolymorū ageremus. Vrbs enim Hierofolymorū aut secundum naturalem illam materiam, aut secundum figuram, aut secundùm veritatem à sanctis illis hominibus enunciata est. Hïc triplex modus simul concurrebat; cùm pij verbis Prophetæ istis vterentur: Nam & materiam Ierusalem videbant, & figuram cernebat qua vestiebatur materiata Ierusalem instituto Dei, & in veritate velut anima illius conquiescebant, quia Deus præsentiam suam gratiosam prolixè in ea confirmabat.
units.tr: Here, in the perseverance of godly men within the limits that have been set, we must consider the witnesses whom the sons of God are here called. There are many kinds of witnesses before whose eyes it is fitting for us to carry out our calling. For we have God as the witness of all things, the knower even of the most hidden things, who will also be the judge. We call on his testimony solemnly before men, where other testimonies do not avail, in piety, truth and charity. We also have as witnesses the angels from heaven, who serve the common Lord together with the Church, and the citizens of his Jerusalem in the heavens; they behold the face of our Father who is in heaven, ready to receive his commands, and they take care even of the least little ones, as they are bidden by the Lord, and here in the Church they diligently observe that manifold wisdom of God, not only in the work of his gracious spiritual blessings but also in that outward order which is joined in fitting manner with that inward grace of God in the communion of saints. Looking to this, the Apostle says that the woman should have power, that is a sign of power, on her head, because of the angels. Finally, they are also witnesses of the deeds and sufferings of the godly, of which the same epistle says that the servants of God have been made a spectacle even to the angels. Besides, the world is a witness, before which the saints likewise become a spectacle, as the Apostle affirms in the same place; so much so that he did not hesitate to lay down this rule for the bishop who ministers in the Church of God, that he should also have a good testimony from those outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. Lastly, we have as witnesses all the saints privately who live with us in the Church of God; and their testimonies must be held of greater worth by us, because they are members of that household of which we also are members. Out of all these, and other testimonies too, the Prophet in this place took up one alone, and before this witness he declared his thought, his zeal and his duties: namely, the Church of God. Not that the faithful did not likewise profess the same before Jehovah their God; for whoever makes this profession in the Church professes it before God, who dwells continually in the Church and sanctifies it by the washing of regeneration through the Word. Nor is it because the ancient Church did not know the testimony of angels, to whom God often attested his presence by very many messages of angels. Nor because it refused the testimony of the world itself, before which we must all confess God and Christ and not deny his benefits. But whenever the testimony of the Church is called upon, and whenever we profess from the heart before it what belongs to our part, we at the same time perform that duty before God and his angels: the household sees this duty, outsiders do not see it. God therefore sees this duty and approves it, as the just Lord of the house; the angels see it, as fellow servants in the same house; the Church and its members who live with us see it, as the guardian of God's benefits and our mother in the Lord in all things, and therefore by the same right the guardian of our profession towards the Lord our God. But the world does not see this profession, because it sees with the eyes of the flesh; yet the Church sees it excellently according to God, because the eye of faith discerns the saints in charity and the unity of the Spirit. Rightly, therefore, the godly profess this holy profession before the Church: both because by the same act they have God and the angels themselves as most certain witnesses of all that they do in the Church, and because by a special institution and agreement the Church is the common trustee of God and of us alike. For in it the Lord has set forth his treasures to be tasted by each of the godly, and in turn the godly in it set forth their vows and whatever professions of their piety, so that they may be accepted before the Lord in the unity of the body of Christ. The godly used to call this faithful trustee Jerusalem, when they named Jerusalem; and this in the same ways which we have just set out when we were treating of the gates of Jerusalem. For the city of Jerusalem has been named by those holy men either according to its natural material, or according to its figure, or according to its truth. Here all three modes came together at once, when the godly used these words of the Prophet: for they saw Jerusalem in its material form, and they perceived the figure in which Jerusalem was clothed in material form by the appointment of God, and in its truth they rested as in its soul, because God abundantly confirmed his gracious presence in it.

units.la: Prodest autem piis huiusmodi Ecclesiæ appellatio plurimum, facto, & exemplo. Facto prodest, quia singvli hoc facto officium suum erga Ecclesiam probant (quid enim piæ matri non debeant pij filij?) & quia Ecclesiam prouocant ad officia in prolem mortigeram & officiosam maiore cū fructu & alacritate maiore præstanda: Illi præstamus singvli personalia officia nostra; illa verò dispensat nobis tùm communia omnibus quæ habet, tam etiam singulis personalia ad ædificationem nostram. Atque hoc illud est quod ante diximus, Ecclesiæ partes esse has secundum Dominú, vt cum de portis suis exhibeat testimonium, tum de membris agentibus intra portas suas. Nam ex portis suis (vt ita loquamur) depromit iura Dei quæ in sinu habet; de membris verò testimonium edit, siue intus piorum singulorum mentes[?] instituendo, & cósolando,& recognoscendo ex verbo Dei & fide ipsorum obedientiaq.[?] fidei, siue foris in communione sanctorum fouendo atque educando: immò (quod amplius est) aberrantes castigando, & veluti salutari manu ad gremium suum reuocando indulgentissimé.
units.tr: Moreover, this kind of naming of the Church is of great benefit to the godly, both by deed and by example. It benefits by deed, because each one by this act proves his duty towards the Church (for what do godly sons not owe a pious mother?), and because they stir up the Church to render its duties to its offspring, who bring forth and serve, with greater fruit and greater readiness. To her we each render our personal duties; and she in turn dispenses to us both what she has in common for all, and also what is personal to each, for our building up. And this is what we said before, that the Church's functions, according to the Lord's appointment, are these: both to bear witness concerning its gates, and concerning the members who act within its gates. For from its gates (so to speak) it brings forth the rights of God which it keeps in its bosom; and it bears witness concerning the members, whether by instructing and comforting the minds of individual godly persons, and acknowledging them from the Word of God and their faith and the obedience of faith, or outside, by cherishing and training them in the communion of saints; indeed (what is more) by rebuking those who go astray, and by calling them back most kindly into its bosom, as with a healing hand.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem hæc facta singulis nobis utilitatem adferunt, sicetiam aliis exempla commodissimé offeruntur ad ædificationem filiorum Dei. Quapropter illi quoque ipsi qui in hunc modum instituunt vitam suam, in scripturis sacris fideles testes Iesu Christi & Ecclesiæ eius nominantur. Neque dubium est quin eódem pij respexerint, cum hoc loco non scorsim apud se singuli, sed coniunctis operis publicè in Ecclesia prædicaret, consistentes sunt pedes nostri. Poterat quidem separatim quisque dicere, Consistentes sunt pedes mei; Sed hæc communio sanctorum, hæc sanctimoniæ communicatio, ut suis actoribus ex facto prodest, ita spectatoribus exemplo, & auditoribus hortamento.
units.tr: Just as these deeds bring benefit to each of us, so also examples are most conveniently offered to others for the building up of the sons of God. Therefore those very persons who order their lives in this way are called in the holy Scriptures faithful witnesses of Jesus Christ and of his Church. Nor is there any doubt that the godly had this in mind, when in this place they proclaimed publicly, not each one apart to himself, but in common work in the Church: Our feet are standing. Each could indeed have said by himself, "My feet are standing"; but this communion of saints, this sharing of holiness, benefits its own actors by the deed, as it benefits spectators by example and hearers by exhortation.

units.la: Ecquis iam adeò demens aut furiosus est, ut non videat quantas utilitates piæ illæ animæ jucunda hac praedicatione & professione ossiciorum suorum fore animadverterint? Quod autem in illis videmus ; agite, demus operam ut ipsi quoque in nobis videamus. Si non videmus, ut profecto multi sunt oculis capti, quibus princeps huius mundi oculos mentis ipsorum excaecauit ne credant veritati, discant illi Deo auctori gratiae se committere, quem auctorem naturae sciunt: Discant praelucente Domino ex verbo ipsius, se hic in via esse, ac potius in bivio, quod Christus elegantissime nobis figurauit: Discant viam quae fert ad salutem Ecclesiam esse, cuius humilitas non debet quemquam avertere a via salutis ineunda: Nam iter angustum ad salutem est. Discant sibi pedes & commoditatem ad instituendum iter suppeditari gratiose a Domino, si verbo promissionum eius crediderint: Discant, ex quo in Ecclesia sunt, animum & vires sibi a Deo ingenerari & augeri, quo sint constantes eorum pedes, nec adversarum procellarum impetu deturbentur, prout Dominus in Ecclesia est praesentissimus: Discant denique Ecclesiam Dei muris & portis munitam esse quas Deus ante oculos pietas & manu inscriptas habet, quemadmodum per Isaiam pronunciavit, ut tum impetus omnes hostiles & tela adversantia frangant quiescentes sub umbra alarum Domini, tum ad omne officium in pietate, iustitia, veritate, & charitate adducantur: Nos vero qui jam Dei beneficio immerentes,inuiti,repugnantes, ad lucis illius admirabilis participationem vocati fumus,& qui hac luce freti videmus mysteria Dei in Ecclesia eius exposita, quæ non videt mundus, & spiritalem fructum ex eis communiter ac singulariter percipimus in Christo Iesu, quanto studio, quanta religione, quanta contentione pietatis ad hæc omnia recognofcenda in Domino, in ecclesia,in fratribus nostris, in nobis ipsis opus est accurrere?qui Ecclesiam nouimus Dei domum esse, qui salutem à Deo in Ecclesia quodammodo depositam, qui pedes nostros diuino duétu in ea collocatos, qui eadem virtute pedes ibidem consistentes omnium procellarum impetum proculcare, qui nos à Deo Ecclesiaque curari in portis illius quamfideliffimè, qui denique omni benedictioni spirituali in locis fupercæleftibus in Christo nos locupletatos esse, quo vsque tandem operibus nostris & conuersatione ementiemur lucem diuinæ veritatis in nostris mentibus & conscientiis radiantem? Quin potius Deo, Ecclesiæ, fratribus, & nobis ipsis tribuiuus singulis quod suum est ? Iam plus fatis à Deo auertimus mentes, animos, &officia pietatis omnia, quibus nos obstrictos esse iamdiu Deo auctore, restante verbo ,conscientia fodicante nouimus. Iam plus fatis eripiuntur ab Ecclefia Dei illa trophea[?],quæ adolescentes ingenui matribus natura duce solent refundere, ac potiùs ( vt vno verbo dicam ) deripiuntur de Ecclesiâ membra viuentia Domini, quæ prætiofo sanguine suo comparauit, impietate, iniustitia, & inhumanitate, addo etiâ imprudentia indignissima eorum qui velut columnæ Christianitatis dici & haberi volunt. Iam plus satis in fratres nostros iniqui fuimus, & grassantur in Ecclesia Dei pastores qui pascunt se ipsos, adipem comedentes, lanam induentes, quod optimum est mactantes, gregem non pascentes, ouem Christi morbo affectam non confirmantes, ægrotam non curantes, confractam non obligantes, depulsam non reducentes, pereuntem non requirentes, sed vi dominantes in gregem Christi & per sæuitiam, adeo vt dispersæ sint oues Christi destitutæ pastore, & sint cibo omnibus bestiis agri, dispersæ, & fraudi, violentiæ, atque tyrannidi impotentissimorum hominum expositæ. Iam plus satis ruimus præcipites in perniciem nostram ; & quamuis cum animis nostris veritatis diuinæ & gratiæ in Ecclesia conscij,tamen delicias facimus in ignoratione, infirmitate, & aberratione nostra. Videamus igitur deinceps,si vis facienda est,(est autem)vt nobis ipsis vim sanƈtè faciamus,memores illius quod olim dicebat Christus,rapi à violentis regnum Dei:qui in carne cæci sumus, videamus in Spiritu;qui infirmi, confirmemur ; qui dormientes,excitemur;qui segnes, animemur ;qui frigentes aut etiâ tepidi, inardescamus ad illa pietatis in Deum, veritatis in Ecclesiam, iustitiæ & charitatis in fratres, & sanctimoniæ in nobis officia, quæ Deus imperat. Deum nouimus, Ecclesiam nouimus: & nos igitur, & fratres in Ecclesia noscamus, obseruemus, & colamus studiosissimè; pedes nostros & ipsorum pariter confirmemus facto, sermone, & exemplo; consistamus in Ecclesia Dei, neque sinanus[?] nos ab ea quacunque specie dimoueri; in portis Ecclesiæ disciplinam Christi & Ecclesiæ, quàm maxima fide possumus, studeamus discere atq; retinere; & in testimonio Dei Ecclesiæq; ipsius piorumq; omnium Deo in Ecclesia obsequentium conquiescamus, vt fructum illum tranquillum iustitiæ & gloriæ superatis hostibus salutis nostræ Dei virtute reportemus in Christo Iesu. Faxit Dominus Deus salutis nostræ.
units.tr: Who then is so mad or frenzied as not to see what great benefits those pious souls noticed in this joyful proclamation and in the profession of their duties? But what we see in them, let us make the effort to see in ourselves as well. If we do not see it (as indeed many are blinded in their eyes, whose eyes the prince of this world has blinded in their minds so that they do not believe the truth), let them learn to commit themselves to God, the author of grace, whom they know as the author of nature. Let them learn, with the Lord shining before them from his Word, that they are here on the road, or rather at a crossroads, which Christ depicted most elegantly for us. Let them learn that the way that leads to salvation is the Church, whose lowliness ought not to turn anyone away from entering the way of salvation, for the road to salvation is narrow. Let them learn that feet and the means of making the journey are graciously supplied to them by the Lord, if they have believed his promises. Let them learn that, from the time they are in the Church, courage and strength are engendered and increased in them by God, so that their feet stand firm and are not overthrown by the force of adverse storms, since the Lord is most present in the Church. Let them learn, finally, that the Church of God is protected by walls and gates, which God has inscribed before his eyes and in his hand, as he declared through Isaiah, so that they may both break all hostile assaults and hostile weapons, resting in the shadow of the Lord's wings, and be brought to every duty in godliness, righteousness, truth and love. But we, who by God's kindness have been called, though undeserving, unwilling and resisting, to share in that wonderful light, and who, relying on this light, see the mysteries of God set forth in his Church, which the world does not see, and receive spiritual fruit from them in common and individually in Christ Jesus, with what eagerness, what reverence, what earnest striving of godliness must we hasten to acknowledge all these things in the Lord, in the Church, in our brothers and in ourselves? We who know that the Church is the house of God, that salvation has in some sense been deposited with God in the Church, that our feet have been placed in it by divine guidance, that by the same power our feet standing there can trample down the force of all storms, that we are most faithfully cared for by God and the Church at its gates, and that we have been enriched with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ: how long will we belie, by our works and our conduct, the light of divine truth shining in our minds and consciences? Why do we not rather render to God, to the Church, to our brothers and to ourselves, each what is their own? Already we have turned our minds, our souls and all the duties of godliness far enough away from God, though we have long known that we are bound to him as author, while the Word remains and conscience pricks us. Already those trophies, which noble young men are accustomed to bring back to their mothers under nature's guidance, are snatched far enough away from the Church of God; or rather (to say it in one word) the living members of the Lord, whom he bought with his precious blood, are torn away from the Church by impiety, injustice and inhumanity, and even by the most unworthy folly of those who wish to be called and considered the pillars of Christianity. Already we have been unjust enough toward our brothers, and in the Church of God there are shepherds who feed themselves, eating the fat, clothing themselves with wool, slaughtering what is best, not feeding the flock, not strengthening the sheep of Christ that is sick, not healing the diseased, not binding up the broken, not bringing back the driven away, not seeking the lost, but ruling over the flock of Christ with force and cruelty, so that the sheep of Christ are scattered without a shepherd and become food for all the beasts of the field, exposed, scattered, to the fraud, violence and tyranny of the most powerful men. Already we have rushed headlong to our own destruction; and although we are aware in our minds of divine truth and of grace in the Church, nevertheless we take our pleasure in our ignorance, weakness and wandering. Let us therefore see, from now on, if force must be used (and it must), that we use force upon ourselves, mindful of what Christ once said, that the kingdom of God is taken by the violent: we who are blind in the flesh, let us see in the Spirit; we who are weak, let us be strengthened; we who are sleeping, let us be roused; we who are sluggish, let us be encouraged; we who are cold or even lukewarm, let us burn with zeal for those duties of godliness toward God, of truth toward the Church, of righteousness and love toward the brothers, and of holiness in ourselves, which God commands. We know God, we know the Church: let us therefore also know and observe and cherish both ourselves and our brothers in the Church with the utmost care; let us equally strengthen their feet and ours by deed, word and example; let us stand firm in the Church of God, and let us not allow ourselves to be moved away from it in any form; at the gates of the Church let us strive, with the greatest faith we can, to learn and to hold fast the discipline of Christ and of the Church; and let us rest in the testimony of God, of the Church itself, and of all the godly who obey God in the Church, so that by the power of God we may win back in Christ Jesus that peaceful fruit of righteousness and glory, our enemies having been overcome. May the Lord God of our salvation grant it.

units.la: 3. Hierosolyma constructa, vt ciuitas quæ coagmentata est in se se pariter.
units.tr: 3. Jerusalem built, as a city that is knit together within itself.

units.la: ADHUC sequuti vestigia Prophetæ & prisciæ illius Ecclesiæ, de piorum lætitia diximus ex causis singularibus: nempe quòd pij singuli cùm sibi ipsis, tum suis fratribus sermone acclamant, & operibus suis adiumento sunt, vt Ecclesiam Christi ineant, &in ea perseuerent quam maxima fide ac religione possunt: Huius rei aspectu &cō scientia ingenerari mentibus ipsorum & inualescere spirituale gaudium, quo singuli in fide & obsequio Dei magis ac magis confirmentur. Deinceps videndum nobis est de causis communibus eiusdem gaudij, prout tribus versibus huius Cantici (quorum hic primus est) eas diximus contineri. Neque enim Christiano homini fatis esse debet, quòd fe & aliquot alios, qui proximè aderunt, facientes officium animaduerterit, nisi etiam vniuerfitatem Ecclesiæ animo contempletur, & communi gaudio de bono communi illius saturetur[?]. Quemadmodum enim nullum membrum in corpore humano ita est ἀντίνομον[?], vt se solum curet aut ea ipsa quibus proximè coniunctum est, sed naturæ instinctu quodam corporis integritatem suam integritatem putat; ita etiam pios in vnum corpus coalescentes Spiritus vnitate, cuius corporis caput est Christus, omninò decet cum membris non modò proximis & coniunctissimis, sed cum omnibus etiam quæ Spiritus adunat quàm longinquissimè communicatio. Etenim quod priuati hominis, vt fingularis membri, gaudium esse potest, fi commune corpus in quo agit male habuerit? aut quæ salus expectanda membro, fi cõtabescit corpus? contrà vero, quod gaudium singulari membro deesse potest, fi valere corpus animaduerterit? quòd fi ipsum singulari quodam modo afficiatur male, quod malum ipsi graviter damnosum esse potest, fi commune bonum corporis ipsi suturum est bono, & vires communes suas ad singularis membri commoditatem collaturum?In hunc modum Prophetæ sanctí & prisca Ecclesia Dei à singularium membrorū bono & boni conscientia,docuerunt nos omnes ad boni communis exploratiónem & sensum assurgendum esse,vt veram lætitiá assequamur ; quandoquidem nec diuturna est lætitia membri pereunte corpore,nec certa pernicies eius,si quo maloinfestabitur,valente corpore , & ad confirmationem laborantis membri accurrente. Nunc ergo secundum hoc causarum genus videamus,quibus recreantur pij,& in omnibus rerum difficultatibus consolationem certam adipiscuntur, gaudent, atque gloriantur.
units.tr: Still following the steps of the Prophet and of that ancient Church, we have spoken of the joy of the godly from particular causes: namely, that each of the godly, both by speaking to himself and to his brethren and by helping them with his works, urges them to enter the Church of Christ and to persevere in it with the greatest faith and devotion they can. From the sight and awareness of this, a spiritual joy is kindled in their minds and grows strong, by which each is more and more confirmed in faith and in obedience to God. Next we must consider the common causes of this same joy, as we have said that three verses of this Canticle (of which this is the first) contain them. For it is not enough for a Christian to notice that he and a few others who are near him are doing their duty; he must also contemplate the whole Church and be filled with the common joy of its common good. For just as no member of the human body is so separate that it cares only for itself or for those parts to which it is most closely joined, but by a certain natural instinct regards the wholeness of the body as its own wholeness, so the godly, growing together into one body by the unity of the Spirit, whose head is Christ, ought altogether to share, not only with their nearest and closest members, but with all whom the Spirit binds together, however far apart they may be. For what joy can a private man, as a single member, have if the common body in which he lives is in bad health? Or what safety can a member expect if the body wastes away? On the contrary, what joy can be lacking to a single member if it sees the body is well? And if the body is affected in some particular way by evil, how greatly can that evil harm the member, when the common good of the body will belong to the member and the body will bring its common strength to the advantage of the single member? In this way the holy Prophets and the ancient Church of God have taught us all that we must rise from the good of single members and the awareness of that good to the examination and feeling of the common good, so that we may attain true joy; since the joy of a member is not lasting when the body perishes, nor is its ruin certain if some evil attacks it while the body is healthy and runs to the support of the suffering member. Now, then, let us see according to this kind of cause what refreshes the godly, and what they obtain, rejoice in, and boast of as a sure consolation amid all the difficulties of things.

units.la: Positis antè priuatis & singularibus causis Christiani illius gaudij,cómunes iam tribus his versibus afferuntur, quarū hæc summa est:Pios priuato & singulari quidē respectu quem in superioribus exposuimus, sanctá lætitiam animis suis percipere ; sed longè maiori lætitia affici ex communis boni contemplatione, quod bonum in Ecclesia cernunt,& ab Ecclesia ad se sentiunt deriuari: tum quia hac recognitione bonorum in Ecclesia recognoscūt Ecclesiam , tum verò quia suam ipsorum conditionem in Ecclesia ipsa sentiunt,& sibi de ea gratulantur.Bonorum autem quæ ad Ecclesiæ cognitionē,& ad membrorum eius ædificationē faciunt, ratio duplex hoc loco ponitur. Nā primùm absolutissima Ecclesiæ in se coagmentatio proponitur,hoc versu ; deinde verò
units.tr: Having first set out the private and particular causes of that Christian joy, three verses now present the common causes, of which the sum is this: the godly, indeed with respect to the private and particular aspect we have set out above, perceive holy joy in their minds; but they are affected by a far greater joy from contemplating the common good, which they see in the Church and feel flowing from the Church to themselves. This is so, partly because by this recognition of the goods in the Church they recognise the Church itself, and partly because they feel their own condition within the Church and rejoice in it. Now a twofold account of the goods which serve the knowledge of the Church and the edification of its members is given at this point. For first the most complete binding together of the Church within itself is set forth in this verse; then, however,

units.la: vero officia omnia ad coagmentationem illam pertinentia atq. indesinenter in ea profluentia, duobus sequentibus.
