Atq. hæc duæ res omninò sunt opus ad piorum confirmationẽ: quemadmodum in symbolo Apostolorum, postquam professi sumus nos credere sanctam Ecclesiam catholicam, illico subiicimus, communionem sanctorum; cuius communionis modus in hoc versu, opera sequentibus duobus exponuntur.
units.tr: the duties of all kinds that pertain to that binding together, and that constantly flow forth within it, are set forth in the two following verses. And these two things are altogether necessary for the strengthening of the godly; just as in the Apostles' Creed, after we have professed that we believe in the holy catholic Church, we at once add "the communion of saints"; and the manner of this communion is set out in this verse and in the two following, which describe works.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem descriptio Ecclesiæ vel domus Iehovæ (vt ante fuit appellata) tum quidem erat necessaria, cùm locus Hierosolymorum ad symbolum sanctæ Ecclesiæ recens constitutus esset; prout principio ostendimus fuisse locum nuper à Deo designatum, & gratulante populo celebritate maximam fuisse indictam, vt cultus Dei semel eo in loco institutus Deo auctore permaneret. Sed si iam necessaria fuit hæc circumscriptio, certè multo magis necessaria videtur esse his miseris temporibus, quibus omnes certatim sibi Ecclesiam arrogant: nec præfidentiores vlli doctores aut duces ad demonstrandam Ecclesiam exstiterunt fermè, quàm ij ipsi qui nec Deum, nec Ecclesiam, nec proximum, nec seipsos norunt, aut etiam si norunt (proh dolor) non possunt ipsi à se discedere, & sibi renunciare, vt Deo, Ecclesiæ, proximoque cedant, & cōsulant salutì suæ. Quia igitur, si qui hæc lecturi sunt, statim obiicient: At quænam hæc Ecclesia est, quam Spiritus Dei hac magnificentia[?] verborum prædicauit? hoc illi à nobis responsum habeant: primùm sapientissimè à Spiritu Dei magnifica hæc verba ad commendationem Ecclesiæ adhiberi, quia parui vel potius minimi, addo etiam nullius pretij à plerisque omnibus censetur esse: qui nihil sibi, carni, & sensui suo non arrogant, vt quiduis de Ecclesia derogent: Deinde verò nos paratos esse, si viri boni esse volent, cum ipsis bene agere, & Ecclesiam quam sibi offendi volunt ex veritate & in simplicitate demonstrare. Ex veritate: nam verbum Dei sequemur ducem, & (ne abeamus longius) ex his ipsis Prophetarum & priscæ Ecclesiæ verbis exponemus: nam verbum Dei est veritas, & verbum vitæ æternæ. In simplicitate autem, quia sepositis omnibus argutiis & verbis humanæ sapientiæ, enuntiaturi sumus de hoc argumento quæcunque nos hîc docet veritas, vt omnes hac ratione (qui fructus est maximus, de quo antè diximus) tum Ecclesiam in Deo, tum nos in Ecclesia noscamus, & lætemur de hoc utroque bono lætitia illa spirituali, quam sancti olim professi sunt.
units.tr: This description of the Church, or house of Jehovah (as it was called before), was indeed necessary at the time when the place of Jerusalem had been newly established as the symbol of the holy Church; as we showed at the beginning, that place had recently been designated by God, and with the people rejoicing, the greatest solemnity had been proclaimed, so that the worship of God, once instituted in that place by God's authority, might remain. But if this circumscription was already necessary, it certainly seems much more necessary in these wretched times, when everyone eagerly claims the Church for himself. Scarcely any teachers or leaders have been more forward in displaying the Church than those who know neither God, nor the Church, nor their neighbour, nor themselves; or even if they know them (alas!), they cannot withdraw from themselves and renounce themselves, so as to yield to God, the Church and their neighbour, and to consult their own salvation. Therefore, if any who read these things will at once object, "But what is this Church, which the Spirit of God proclaimed with such a magnificence of words?", let them have this answer from us. First, that these magnificent words are most wisely used by the Spirit of God in commendation of the Church, because the small or rather the least, I add even of no worth, are esteemed by almost all, those who claim nothing for themselves, for their flesh and their own feeling, so that they may disparage the Church in any way they please. Second, that we are ready, if they wish to be good men, to deal honestly with them, and to demonstrate from the truth and in simplicity the Church which they wish to be shown to them. From the truth: for we shall follow the Word of God as our guide, and (not to wander too far) we shall expound it from these very words of the Prophets and of the ancient Church; for the Word of God is truth, and the word of eternal life. In simplicity, however, because, all cleverness and words of human wisdom set aside, we shall state about this subject whatever truth teaches us here, so that all of us in this way (which is the greatest fruit, of which we spoke above) may come to know both the Church in God and ourselves in the Church, and may rejoice in each of these goods with that spiritual joy which the saints of old professed.

units.la: Ecclesiam ergò, diuinum argumentum lætitiæ nostræ, Propheta hoc loco descripsit atque commendauit duobus nominibus, vt studium piorum adeundi eam & permanendi in eâ magis ac magis accenderet: quum ostendit primùm quid sit Ecclesia in se, deinde quæ officia & operationes in ipsa, ex quibus internosci pof-fit. sit. Nam quod plerique omnes hoc tempore conqueruntur, id certissimum est, Ecclesiam, ut in se est, non facilè ab hominibus cognosci posse, sed notas illius observari foris oportere. Habet quidem Ecclesia in sese notas, sed quas ij solùm vident, qui in Ecclesia sunt: Sed quæcunque foris existunt notæ, ex à domesticis optimè, ab exteris etiam aliquo pacto, etsi non optimè, videri possunt. Hunc igitur ordinem Propheta servans, Ecclesiam, prout in se est, hoc versu describit, dicens: Hierosolyma constructa, ut civitas quæ coagmentata est inter se pariter. Meminisse autem velimus lectores eotum[?] quæ antè diximus, de Hierosolymorum interpretatione. Fuerunt materialia (ut ita dicamus) Hierosolyma in natura rerum: Fuerunt figuratiua & sacramentalia instituto: Fuit veritas figura sacramentali adumbrata: Vidit prisca illa Ecclesia materiatam urbem Hierosolymorum: accepit à Deo figuræ institutum & coluit: Credidit veritatem, & prehendit fide, quam nos eadem fide percipimus, postquâ materiata Hierofolyma perierunt, & figuræ sunt à Christo antiquatæ. Est ergo in hoc loco nomen Hierosolymorum sic accipiendum atque si perscriptum à Propheta esset, Ecclesia constructa, &c. de qua Ecclesia cùm tantopere hoc nostro seculo laboretur, audiamus quid Propheta dicat, & insequamur vestigia illius ad peruestigandam in veritate Ecclesiam Dei. Dicit ergo; constructa ut civitas qua coagm. &c. Quibus verbis ostendit Ecclesiam in se ipsa aedificium esse, deinde ostendit aedificationis modum. Nam aedificium esse pronunciat discens, Optime constructam: Modum vero aedificationis sequentibus declarat, dicens; ut civitas qua coagmentata est inter se pariter. Sed quemadmodum Hierosolyma in typo & figura dicta sunt, pro eo quod est Ecclesia; sic etiam attributa haec secundum modum illius figurae & typi conscripta sunt: Et quod tum in opere materiatum fuit, nunc in opere citra materiam illam intelligendum est, quia Ecclesia opus spirituale est. Nam etsi homines (ut ante diximus) materia sunt Ecclesiae, tamen non sunt materiati secundum animam, quod est praecipuum ipsorum: deinde Ecclesiam forma, non materia facit: ac proinde homines in Ecclesia & de Ecclesia sunt, quà is qui forma Ecclesiae, in eis est: quam formam in versum primum declarauimus, cum de domo Iehouae diceremus. Postquam igitur formam illam essentialem & internam ex Prophetae verbis cognouimus, iustissimum est & ordini conuenientissimum (quemadmodum Propheta fecit) ut quaecumque huic formae adiuncta sunt necessaria cognoscamus: Cumque res omnes à forma habeant suum esse & operationes suas, ut ex eodem auctore; quid illa forma in materia efficiat, & quid per materiam, doceamur. Efficit ergo forma illa quàm supra diximus, vt Ecclesia sit ædificium spirituale, & vt sit ædificium omnibus modis vnum. Etsi non temerè à Propheta dicitur, Hierosolyma ædificata, proeo[?] quod nos dicimus, Ecclesia ædificium. Nam hac ratione duo voluit Propheta à nobis observari, quid sit, & à quo fit effecta ac potiùs efficiatur id quod est. Est enim ædificium, & quidem ædificatum ab eo qui solus divinitus divinam ædificationè potuit instruere, & quod in dies ædificatur per gratiam illius: quemadmodum etiam Apostolus ad Hebræos hanc domum à Christo Iesu constructam prædicat, & subesse illius vt filij imperio ac gubernationi.
units.tr: Therefore the Prophet, the divine subject of our joy, described and commended the Church in this place by two marks, so that the zeal of the godly to enter it and to remain in it might be kindled more and more: first he shows what the Church is in itself, and then what duties and operations there are in it, by which it can be recognised. For what almost everyone complains about in this age is most certainly true: the Church, as it is in itself, cannot easily be known by men, but its marks must be observed from outside. The Church does indeed have its marks within itself, but only those who are in the Church see them; yet whatever marks exist outside can be seen best by those within, and by outsiders in some way, though not so well. Keeping this order, therefore, the Prophet describes the Church, as it is in itself, in this verse, saying: Jerusalem built, as a city that is knit together within itself. Now let us, the readers, remember what we said before about the interpretation of Jerusalem. Jerusalem existed in the nature of things as material (so to speak); it existed as figurative and sacramental by institution; the truth was foreshadowed by the sacramental figure. That ancient Church saw the material city of Jerusalem; it received from God the institution of the figure and worshipped it; it believed the truth and laid hold of it by faith, which we also grasp by the same faith, after material Jerusalem perished and the figures were abolished by Christ. Therefore in this place the name Jerusalem is to be understood as if the Prophet had written "the Church built," etc. Since the Church is so greatly troubled in our own age, let us hear what the Prophet says, and follow his footsteps in order to search out the Church of God in truth. He says, therefore: "built as a city which is compacted together," etc. By these words he shows that the Church is in itself a building, and then he shows the manner of building. For he declares that it is a building by saying "well built"; and he explains the manner of building in what follows, saying: "as a city that is knit together within itself alike." But just as Jerusalem was spoken of in type and figure, standing for what the Church is, so these attributes too have been written according to the manner of that figure and type; and what was then a building of material must now be understood as a work without that material, because the Church is a spiritual work. For although men (as we said before) are the material of the Church, yet they are not formed according to the soul, which is their principal part; moreover, it is the form, not the matter, that makes the Church; and therefore men are in the Church and belong to the Church insofar as he who is the form of the Church is in them; this form we explained in the first verse, when we spoke of the house of Jehovah. Having therefore learned that essential and internal form from the words of the Prophet, it is most just and most fitting to the order (as the Prophet did) that we should learn what necessary things are joined to this form; and since all things have their being and their operations from their form, as from the same author, we should be taught what that form effects in matter, and what it effects through matter. That form, then, which we spoke of above, makes the Church a spiritual building, and makes it a building one in every way. Nor does the Prophet say "Jerusalem built" without reason, in regard to what we call the Church a building. For in this way the Prophet wished us to observe two things: what it is, and by whom it has been made, and rather, what it is being made into. For it is a building, and indeed one built by him who alone could arrange the divine building in a divine way, and which is built day by day through his grace; just as the Apostle also proclaims to the Hebrews that this house has been built by Christ Jesus, and is subject to his rule and governance as a son's.

units.la: Hoc fundamento universè posito, Ecclesiam esse ædificium Dei, Propheta transfit ad declarationem modi vel conditionis divinæ, quàm in Ecclesia vident[?] soli ij quibus Deus illuminauit mentis oculos vt videre possint. Dicit enim, ut civitas coagmentata inter se pariter, & semper eodem simili, tria de conditione communi Ecclesiæ Dei prædicat: Primùm quidem civitatem vel quasi civitatem esse; tum civitatem optimè inter se coagmentatis partibus; postremò dignitatem maximam & civitati inesse, & singulis partibus illius, eo quòd inter se pariter coagmentata sint omnia.
units.tr: With this foundation laid down in general, that the Church is the building of God, the Prophet moves on to explain the manner or condition of God's work, which only those see in the Church to whom God has illuminated the eyes of the mind so that they can see. For he says that the city is compacted together, and he states three things about the common condition of God's Church: first, that it is a city, or something like a city; second, that it is a city whose parts are fitted together very well; and third, that the city and each of its parts have the greatest dignity, because all things are joined together in harmony.

units.la: Quod itaque primùm civitatem esse dicit, simile alterum est ab eo, quod primo versu positum est, cùm domum Iehouæ appellaret: sed tamen utrumque Ecclesiæ catholicæ optimè cōvenit. Nam eadé est una domus, si ad Deum inhabitantem in ea respexeris: & una civitas, si respexeris ad incolas eius uni Deo, & uni Domino una fide, uno baptismate servientes, & adhaerentes in unitate spiritus. Quemadmodum etiam (quod est augustius ) unum corpus appellatur,quà subest uni capiti & vivit de vita illius in spiritus illius unitate. Ac proinde ut corpus unum ex membris compluribus,domus una ex lapidibus , civitas una ex domibus coagmentata & constituta est,ita etiam Ecclesia ex variis velut membris, lapidibus vivis , ædibusque constare dicitur.
units.tr: The first point, that he calls it a city, is a different image from the one in the first verse, where he calls it the house of Jehovah. Yet both fit the catholic Church very well. It is one house if you consider God dwelling in it, and one city if you consider its inhabitants, who serve the one God, the one Lord, by one faith and one baptism, and who cleave together in the unity of the Spirit. In the same way (and this is a more august title) it is called one body, inasmuch as it is subject to one head and lives by his life in the unity of his Spirit. Therefore, just as one body is made up and constituted of many members, one house of stones, and one city of houses, so too the Church is said to consist of various members, as it were, of living stones and buildings.

units.la: Ad hanc autem constitutionem sive corporis,sive domus , sive etiam civitatis , necessaria sunt multâ,communia pleraque,pauca singularia. Communia sunt hæc: principium,quod à Deo ( ut Apostolus ad Hebræos loquitur) constructa est, & adhuc construitur continetúrque & est virtute illius: finis,quòd ad Dei gloriam inhabitantis ipsam; materia, quod ex hominibus,ut membris lapidibusq. vivis,ad hanc spiritualem structurâ pertinentibus: forma, quòd çatenus[?] corpus,domus, civitas Christi est,quatenus suam relationem ad ipsum habet,& vicissim[?] Deo optimo maximo visum est relationem ad ipsam habere per gratiam & εὐδοκίαν[?] ipsius: tum etiam actionis modus, quòd ædificatur adhuc & colligitur per verbum Euangelij,& illa verbum accipit quo adiungatur Christo, & maneat in ipso, prout Evangelicis promissionibus declaravit Christus : postremò efsectus multiplex,quē Ecclesia in genere agnoscit,cùm à se prædicat credi sanctorum communionem,prout est cōmunio membrorum isi[?] corpore, partiū in domo,& in ciuitate ædium. Ex quibus omnibus illud conficitur, Ecclesiam Dei tum reipsa unà esse, prout corpus, domus, ciuitas suntaliquid unum: tum etiam iure uno esse,prout corpus,domus, ciuitas iuri uni subsunt, & ex eo administrari solent, ·
units.tr: For this constitution, whether of a body, a house, or a city, many things are necessary: most of them common, a few peculiar. These common things are these. The origin: that it was built by God (as the Apostle says to the Hebrews), and is still being built, and is held together and sustained by his power. The end: that it is for the glory of God, who dwells in it. The matter: that it is made up of men, as members and living stones, belonging to this spiritual structure. The form: that it is the body, house, and city of Christ, inasmuch as it has its relation to him, and in turn it has seemed good to almighty God to have its relation to him through his grace and good pleasure [εὐδοκία]. Then there is the mode of action: that it is still being built and gathered together through the word of the gospel, and that it receives that word by which it is joined to Christ and remains in him, as Christ has declared in the evangelical promises. Finally, there is the manifold effect which the Church acknowledges in general when it professes belief in the communion of saints, as it is the communion of members in one body, of parts in one house, and of buildings in one city. From all these things it follows that the Church of God is one in fact, since body, house, and city are something one, and also one in law, since body, house, and city are subject to one law and are usually governed by it.

units.la: Veruntamen in hac communione & rei & iuris,quædà inveniuntur singularia , prout singulis in corpore membris,in domo partibus,in ciuitate domibus suus ordo,suæque functiones attributæ sunt. Nam primùm in ipsa velut ma-teria domus , corporis, aut ciuitatis, partesália ab aliis inter se differunt proprietatibus singularibus , quas in Ecclesia personales possumus appellare: cū nec omnia membra idem sint,sed eiusdem corporis membra ;nec eodem ordine sint, sed eodem corpore : similiterq. nec omnes lapides domus,nec ædes ciuitatis singulæ. Deinde habitu & officiis inter se differunt , prout à Deo distinguuntur donis & vocationibus: quas vocationes rursum Apostolus distinguendas docet duobus modis ; cùm respectu operæ sive actionis , administrationum meminit; respectu verò operis sive effectus ostendit diver-
units.tr: Yet within this communion of fact and of law there are certain particular things, since each member in the body, each part in the house, and each building in the city has been assigned its own order and its own functions. For first, in the very matter, as it were, of the house, body, or city, the parts differ from one another by particular properties, which we may call personal in the Church. For not all the members are the same, but they are members of the same body; nor are they in the same order, but in the same body. Likewise not all the stones of the house, nor all the buildings of the city, are alike. Then they differ in their state and offices, as they are distinguished by God through gifts and callings. The Apostle teaches that these callings are to be distinguished in two ways: with respect to the work or action he mentions administrations, while with respect to the product or effect he shows that there are various operations.

units.la: fas esse operationes : fecundum quæ, quamuis inter fe plurimum differentia , membra singula Ecclesiæ ita occupantur in iis muneribus quæ præscribit Deus , vt vnus & idem Spiritus omnia efficiat in omnibus pro demenso donationis Christi. Quapropter expendant Christiani, quantopere indignum fit vocatione ipsorum & honore quem Deus ipsis habere dignatus est in filio dilectionis suæ , si aut membra corporis, aut lapides domus , aut ciuitatis partes, quas Deus adunat gratiosè , animo ingratissimo diuulserint atque disperserint : Et quia hoc tempore Deus in colligendo sanctissimo illo corpore,templo,& ciuitate operam suorum occupat , quantopere ab iis alienum qui Christiani audiunt , si membra quæ Deus aduocat deterruerint,quę adducit depulerint,& in eos sint iniurij quibus gratiam facit Deus, aut spes oftenditur facturum esse.
units.tr: According to these, although they differ greatly from one another, the individual members of the Church are so employed in those offices which God prescribes, that one and the same Spirit works all things in all, according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Therefore let Christians consider how unworthy it is, in regard to their calling and the honour which God has deigned to give them in the Son of his love, if they tear apart and scatter, in the most ungrateful spirit, the members of the body, or the stones of the house, or the parts of the city, which God graciously gathers together. And since at this time God occupies his labour in gathering that most holy body, temple, and city, how far removed from the name of Christian are those who, if they frighten off the members whom God calls, drive away those whom he brings in, and wrong those on whom God bestows grace, or on whom hope is shown that he will bestow it.

units.la: Quòd si hæc omnia vel hac vna ciuitatis appellatione nobis ostenduntur; quanto magis, si ad modum ciuitatis illius venerimus,veritatem istorum omnium sentiemus , & officium charitatis animaduertemus præstari à nobis oportere? Nam Ecclesia non quoduis ædificium aut vulgare appellatur, sed reipsa præstantissimum (vt sequentibus verbis exponitur ) & dignitate nulli in cœloaut terra postponendum.Hanc dignitatem ( vt anté perstrinximus) duobus modis Propheta ostendit : quod est vt ciuitas coagmentata inter se membris ipsius, & quòd pariter coagmentata est: quibus duabus in rebus interna illa sanctorum communio versatur, quam ante diximus. Nam quòd pariter coagmentati sunt qui in Ecclesia sunt, illud est à communione Dei & Christi sanctificantis ipsos: quòd autem inter se coagmentati sunt in ea, illud communionis est, quam colunt inter se sancti & vocationis sanctæ in Christo participes. Hanc ergo communionem, quam sancti inter se habent intùs, & quam mundus videre nō potest, sed oculus fide purgatus à Domino in corpore ipsius, declarant hæc verba; ut civitas quæ coagmentata est inter se, nimirum membris suis, ex quibus coagmentata est. Quod item de corpore & domo enuntiari debet: tanquâ si dixeris Ecclesiam esse corpus, quod firmè coagmentatis est inter se membris, vel domum coagmentatis optimè partibus.
units.tr: But if all these things are shown to us by this one name of city, how much more shall we perceive the truth of all of them, and notice that we ought to render the duty of charity, if we come to the character of that city? For the Church is not called any ordinary or common building, but is in truth most excellent (as is explained in the following words), and not to be placed below anything in heaven or on earth in dignity. The Prophet indicates this dignity (as we have touched on before) in two ways: that the city is compacted together in its members, and that it is compacted together as a whole. In these two matters that inner communion of the saints, which we spoke of before, is found. For that those who are in the Church are joined together as one comes from the communion of God and of Christ, who sanctifies them; but that they are joined together among themselves in it belongs to the communion which the saints cultivate among themselves, as sharers in the holy calling in Christ. So these words declare this communion, which the saints have among themselves inwardly and which the world cannot see, but which the eye cleansed by faith sees in the Lord's body: a city which is compacted together, namely by its own members, of which it is compacted. The same must be said of the body and the house: as if you were to say that the Church is a body firmly fitted together in its members, or a house whose parts are very well joined.

units.la: Huius autem coagmētationis respectus duplex est. Nam est coagmentatio membrorum cum suo capite, partium domus cum fundamento, & regionum cum arce civitatis sanctæ; & est eorundem inter se coagmetatio [?]. Ad priorem respectu coagmentationis illa fermè omnia pertinent quæ in versum primum de domo Ichouæ dicebamus: ex quibus constat Deum ipsum essentialem formam esse Ecclesiæ, suæ relatione gratiosa. Sed quia non poterat fieri, ut formæ illius capaces efficerentur homines propter materiæ ineptitudinem (nam potiùs conuenirét igni cum aqua,id est, creaturæ vni cum altera, quàm conueniat creaturæ cum creatore suo,finitæ cum infinito) propterea Deus ille &
units.tr: Now there is a twofold aspect to this coagmentation. For there is the coagmentation of the members with their head, of the parts of the house with the foundation, and of the regions with the citadel of the holy city; and there is the coagmentation of these same things with one another. With regard to the first aspect of coagmentation, almost all those things pertain which we said about the first verse, the house of Jehovah. From these it is clear that God himself is the essential form of the Church, by his gracious relation to it. But since men could not be made capable of that form, because of the unfitness of their matter (for fire would sooner agree with water, that is, one creature with another, than a creature agrees with its creator, the finite with the infinite), therefore God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, by a singular dispensation of grace,

units.la: pater domini nostri Iesu Christi singulari difpensatione gratiæ misit filium suum, qui materiâ naturæ nostræ sibi assumeret, vt in ea ipsa caput esset istius corporis, & λόγος ἐκφοντικός istius ædificij,denique arx & fundamentum ciuitatis huius , quam Deus exstruxit ac non homo.Hic ergo primus locus coagmētationis est: nimirum quòd Christus se adiunxit nobis,& nos item sibi,vt essemus cum ipso vnum , os ex ossibus eius,& caro ex carne eius,denique vt ex eo totū corpus congruenter coagmentatum & compactum per omnes suppeditatas cōmissuras ex vi intus agente pro mensura vnius cuiusquè membri incrementum capiat corpori conueniens ad extructionem sui ipsius per charitatem.Cumque huius capitis, quod dedit Ecclesiæ pater,sit summa perfectio in se,summa virtus in alias res,& summus ordo ad omnia;ex eo sequitur quod dicit Apostolus, prout in eo inhabitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter, ita nos in eo completos esse , & nostram societatem cum filio Dei Iesu Christo , & cumpatre in ipso.
units.tr: sent his Son, who took our nature as his own matter, so that in that very nature he might be the head of this body, and the expressive Word [λόγος ἐκφαντορικός] of this building, and finally the citadel and foundation of this city, which God built and not man. This, then, is the first place of coagmentation: namely, that Christ joined himself to us, and we likewise to him, so that we might be one with him, bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh; and finally, that from him the whole body, fitly joined and compacted through every supplying joint, by the working of power within, according to the measure of each single member, makes increase suitable to the body for building itself up in love. And since the summit of perfection of this head, whom the Father gave to the Church, is in himself, the summit of power over other things, and the highest order over all things, it follows from this what the Apostle says: that just as in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, so we are made complete in him, and have our fellowship with the Son of God Jesus Christ, and with the Father in him.

units.la: Ex illa autem societate & communione quam sancti cum Christo habent, omnino se- quitur altera hæc consociatio atq. communio, qua membra inter se consociata & coagmentata sunt, siue (vt Paulus loquitur) constricta charitate Christi. Nam idem qui nos adunauit sibi, eoipso quod diversa membra adunat sibi, eadé inter se adunauit. Unio cum Christo primas tenet, & Christi nobiscum virtute Spiritus; ex hac unione consequitur unio sanctorum inter se, & coagmentatio siue compages inviolabilis, quam nulla res potest dissoluere aut labefactare, quia nullus eorū quem Christo dedit pater de manu eius periturus est.
units.tr: Yet from that fellowship and communion which the saints have with Christ there necessarily follows this other association and communion, by which the members are joined and fitted together with one another, or, as Paul puts it, bound together by the love of Christ. For he who has joined us to himself, by the very fact that he joins diverse members to himself, has joined them to one another as well. Union with Christ holds the first place, and Christ's union with us by the power of the Spirit comes first. From this union follows the union of the saints with one another, and a fitting together or joining that is inviolable, which no thing can dissolve or weaken, because none of those whom the Father has given to Christ will perish out of his hand.

units.la: Quæ cùm ita sint, facilè Christianus quili-bet nobis assensurus est, si imperturbato animo ad hæc legenda & expendenda venerit: non posse quenquam Christianum[?] bona fide renunciare communioni alterius, quem Christus aut adiunxit sibi, aut se adiunctum spem fecit. Nam qui fratrem suum, seruum dei, membrum Christi proterue abdicat, persequitur, infestat, aut vlla denique iniuria afficit, is eo ipso facto Christum auctorem communionis salutaris nostræ abdicat, qui nos sibi, & alios æquè ac nos sic adunauit & adiunxit virtute spiritus, ut nos unum esse inter nos voluerit, qui unum cum ipso sumus. Nam ubi est Christus, obsecro, nisi ubi Spiritus illius? & ubi Spiritus, nisi ubi vita Christi? & ubi vita Christi, nisi ubi vivit, id est, in corpore eius? & ubi corpus unum, nisi ubi consensus inter membra corporis de uno capite, uno spiritu, & vnâ vitâ communiter viventia. Quòd si unum sumus, quomodo in funestam divisionem effemus ruituri? quod unum est, id plane indivisum fit necesse est; quidquid est, eo ipso est, quòd unum est. Divisi cùm sumus, non sumus unum: divisi cùm sumus, non sumus. Quis ergo obducta nominis Christiani specie mihi persuadeat se Christianum esse, cùm te divisus est,& animo divisionem spirat atque interitum? O miseram Christianitatem, quæ in sua divisione unitatem, in renunciatione Christi Christianitatem, in interitu suo certissimo vitam sibi spondet imaginatúrque,& de eâ nō secus exultat quàm qui phrenesi abreptus dat se in mare præcipitem, videturque sibi in suavissimo cubili suorum membra sua ad quietem componere.
units.tr: Since these things are so, any Christian will readily agree with us, if he comes to read and weigh these matters with an undisturbed mind: no Christian can in good faith renounce fellowship with another whom Christ has either joined to himself or made a promise to join. For whoever wantonly rejects his brother, the servant of God and member of Christ, or persecutes him, harasses him, or in any way wrongs him, by that very act renounces Christ, the author of our saving communion, who has joined us to himself and likewise others, just as he has joined us, by the power of the Spirit, and who has willed that we be one among ourselves, since we are one with him. For where is Christ, I ask you, unless where his Spirit is? And where the Spirit is, unless where the life of Christ is? And where the life of Christ is, unless where he lives, that is, in his body? And where there is one body, unless where the members of the body, living together from one head, by one Spirit and one life, are in agreement? But if we are one, how shall we be about to fall into deadly division? What is one must necessarily be undivided; whatever it is, it is so by the very fact that it is one. When we are divided, we are not one; when we are divided, we are not. Who, then, under the cloak of the Christian name, will persuade me that he is a Christian, when he is divided and breathes division and destruction in his mind? O wretched Christianity, which in its division promises itself and imagines unity, in renouncing Christ promises itself Christianity, and in its certain ruin promises itself life, and exults in this no less than one who, carried away by frenzy, throws himself headlong into the sea, and seems to himself to be laying his limbs to rest on the sweetest of beds.

units.la: Auertat hanc labem Dominus pro sua misericordia; quam video, & horreo magis an lugeo? horreo casum incuntem, Christianitatem lugeo pereuntem: nec habeo quod dicam, nisi ex Prophetæ verbis: Propter contritionem filiæ populi mei conteror, attratus [?] incedo, stupor corripit me. an opobalsami nihil est in Galaade? an nullus medicus ibi est? Nam cur non reualescit filia populi mei? cur magis ac magis in fiam infirmitatem relabitur? Sed ad rem venio.
units.tr: May the Lord in his mercy turn away this stain. I see it, and do I shudder at it or mourn it? I shudder at the fall that is beginning; I mourn Christianity that is perishing. I have nothing to say but the words of the prophet: "For the breach of the daughter of my people am I broken; I go about mourning; astonishment has seized me. Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? For why does the daughter of my people not recover? Why does she sink more and more into a lasting weakness?" But I come to the matter.

units.la: Secundus locus, quem in modo coagmentationis voluit Prophèta observari, est quòd Ecclesiæ membra, aut domus, & civitatis huius partes coagmentatæ sunt pariter. Pariter? dixerit quispiam. & quomodo pariter coagmétati sint qui sunt impares, qui donis differentes, qui vocationibus distincti? Agnosco lubens non omnia esse paria in omnibus ciuitatis istius partibus, & corporis huius membris: sed de coagmentatione, non de personis agimus. Ergo vt demus aliquid impar esse, aut (si ita placet) imparia plurima; tamen quod reicapureft, id in omnibus par esse res ipsa demonstratura est.
units.tr: The second point which the prophet wished to be observed in the manner of their joining is that the members of the Church, or the houses and parts of this city, are joined together alike. "Alike?" someone may say. "And how can those be joined alike who are unequal, who differ in gifts, who are distinguished by callings?" I gladly acknowledge that not all parts of this city and members of this body are equal in all respects; but we are speaking of the joining together, not of the persons. So, even if we grant that some or (if you like) many things are unequal, the matter itself will show that what remains is equal in all.

units.la: Nam sunt quidem Christiani inter se impares donis, quae admittitur Christus vnicuiq. prout vult; sunt item impares vocationibus, communibus, & singularibus, in quarum officiis dona à Deo accepta occupari atque consumi necesse est. In his rebus si qui pares Christianos statuunt, morbo animi, non autem scientia iudicioque in eam sententiam adducuntur. Neque obscurus est ille insignis locus Apostoli, vbi differentiam donorum, administrationum, operationumque agnoscit in Ecclesiae membris, & illustrat copiose membrorum quae in corpore humano sunt similitudine. Sed etsi in his rebus, tum quas Deus agit, tum quas nos secundum Deum agimus, non mediocris videtur diuersitas; tamen in capite rei (vt ante diximus) pares sumus, pariter consociati Christo, pariter Spiritum eius participantes, Spiritum vitae & sanctificationis verae, & pariter vitae radicem habentes in Christo & Spiritu eius, quamuis non pariter vitae accessiones & processus ab illo habeamus, & actiones operationesque præstemus : quemadmodum & taleis furculisque in trunco vita vna est ,licet nec eadem omnino à trunco accedant omnibus, nec itidem procedant singuli, nec folia, flores, fructus edant illi pariter. Est autem caput rei & fundamentum Christus, Spiritus, & vita illius. Qui alias res in seipsis non perinde habent,neque Christi & Spiritus & vitæ fructus pariter explicatos sentiunt in fe,aut corā aliis proferunt,hi non continuò extrudi possunt ex regno Christi, aut frangi eorum animi odiosis comparationibus. Nam si ramos & fructus eosdem non habent;at idem principium,eandem radicem habent:ac proinde cùm in principio & radice & vita sint pares, pariter coagmentati à nobis censendi sunt. quò respiciebat Apostolus dicens , nullum per Spiritum Dei loquentem dicere Jesum anathema, & neminem posse Jesum dicere Dominum,nisi per Spiritum sanctum. Est enim relata,etiam minimi cuiusque in regno cælorum cum Christo capite nostro coagmentatio,qua omnes manemus in illo, & ille in nobis manet : ac propterea prout anima in omnibus corporis membris viuit,& omnia vicissim in illa , & viuit indiscreta vita, quæ omnium & singulorum communis est: ita etiam in nobis Christus. Par itaque omnium est unio , & communio par: sed impar à Christo quidem;donorū, vocationum, & operationū ex communione hac in nos proficiscentium módus: à membris verò, ordo, functiones,& operationes impares.
units.tr: For indeed Christians are unequal in gifts, which Christ bestows on each one as he wills; they are likewise unequal in callings, both common and particular, in whose duties the gifts received from God must necessarily be employed and used up. If some set Christians as equal in these things, they are brought to that opinion by a sickness of mind, not by knowledge and sound judgment. Nor is that notable passage of the Apostle obscure, where he recognises a difference of gifts, of ministries and of operations among the members of the Church, and illustrates at length by the likeness of the members which are in the human body. But although in these things, both those which God does and those which we do in accordance with God, a considerable diversity appears, nevertheless in the head of the matter (as we said before) we are equal: equally joined to Christ, equally sharing his Spirit, the Spirit of life and true sanctification, and equally having the root of life in Christ and his Spirit, although we do not equally receive from him the additions and growth of life, nor perform the same actions and works; just as, on a trunk, the grafts and shoots have one life, although the same things do not wholly come from the trunk to all of them, nor do the individual shoots grow alike, nor do they put forth leaves, flowers and fruit alike. Now the head and foundation of the matter is Christ, his Spirit, and his life. Those who do not have the other things in themselves in the same way, and do not feel the fruits of Christ, of the Spirit and of life unfolded equally in themselves, or display them equally before others, cannot therefore be straightway thrust out of the kingdom of Christ, nor have their spirits broken by hateful comparisons. For if they do not have the same branches and fruit, yet they have the same beginning and the same root; and therefore, since they are equal in beginning, root and life, they are to be judged by us as equally joined together. To this the Apostle looked when he said that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says "Jesus is anathema," and no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit. For there is also a joining, reaching even to the least of each one in the kingdom of heaven, with Christ our head, by which we all abide in him and he abides in us; and therefore, just as the soul lives in all the members of the body and all in turn in it, and lives a life undivided, which is common to all and to each, so Christ is in us. Equal, therefore, is the union of all, and equal the communion; but the manner in which gifts, callings and operations proceed from Christ into us through this communion is unequal; and on the part of the members, the order, functions and operations are unequal.

units.la: Est igitur Christiani cuiusque officium, vt quam diligentissimè secum ipse reputet, quantam gratiam honoremq. à Deo acceperit, quòd in spirituale illud ædificiū accitus, & coagmentatione firmissima compactus cum Christo & membris illius, parem cum reliquis suis fratribus sortem hæreditatis & gloriæ in communione Christi adeptus est: Ac proinde quemadmodum interno illo Seruatoris nostri testimonio in fide credit, & suo testimonio in charitate credi defiderat se esse membrum Christi Ecclesiæque catholicæ eius, ita etiam de aliis pro sua in Christum fide & charitate in fratres statuat, eos secum in compagem sanctissimam hanc adducendos curet, adductos cum Christo & Ecclesia eius coaluisse sentiat, honoremque eis tribuat prout honorem à Deo ipsis habéri videt. Non hīc opiniones hominum quæ fidei Christianæ repugnant, non aduersantes charitati suspiciones, offensiones, odia, aut eiusmodi alia adducenda sunt, vt iudiciis nostris ; quæ de aliis temerè facimus, supérciliosè indulgeamus.
units.tr: It is therefore the duty of every Christian to consider as carefully as possible how great the grace and honour is that he has received from God, in that he has been called into that spiritual building and, compacted together by the firmest joining with Christ and his members, has obtained an equal lot of inheritance and glory with his other brothers in the communion of Christ. Accordingly, just as he believes by faith in the inward testimony of our Saviour, and desires to be believed by his own testimony in love, that he is a member of Christ and of his catholic Church, so too he should judge of others according to his faith in Christ and his love towards the brethren; he should take care to bring them into this most holy joining, and when they have been brought in, he should perceive that they have grown together with Christ and his Church, and should give them the honour which he sees is to be held by them from God. Here, suspicions, offences, hatreds, or any such things that are not consistent with love, and which oppose the opinions of men that are contrary to the Christian faith, are not to be brought into our judgments, nor are we to indulge in haughty opinions about others that we form rashly.

units.la: Fides in Christum, qui alterum vocat vt me, & charitas in proximum, quæ me æquè erga illum obligat atque alios erga me, hæc illa sunt quibus nos agi in hac vita decet: vt deinceps neminem secundum carnem cognoscamus, quemadmodum profitetur de se Apostolus, sed siquis est in Christo, cum novam creaturam esse statuamus, & patris nobiscum vitæ dignitatisque consortem. Non sum nescius Hebræam vocem aliter exponi vulgò, & ad solam quantitatem (ut vocant) discretam referri plurimùm, cuius ratione cöftat nos omnes, qui diuisi fumus alij ab aliis, vocati in corporis illius vnitatem. Veruntamen cùm rem introspicio diligentiùs, non possum quin ad quantitatem quoque (ut vocant) continuam hanc vocem referam, & hoc in loco intelligam conuenientissimam æqualitatem nostra omnium, in summo illo beneficio Christi participando hac voce declarari, ut in structura iusta omnes partes ad dignitatem & fitmitatē operis sunt suo modo æquabiles. Quæ doctrina plurimum momenti ad cōfensionem & pacem inter eos quos Christus Ecclesiæ suæ accensuit, & porrò vocaturus est, alendam & continendam adiicit. Atque hæc causa est, cur pariter potiùs quàm ut[?] visum fuerit Hebræam vocem reddere.
units.tr: Faith in Christ, who calls another as he calls me, and love towards the neighbour, which binds me to him just as others are bound to me, these are the things by which it is fitting that we be governed in this life, so that henceforth we know no one according to the flesh, as the Apostle professes of himself, but if anyone is in Christ, we hold him to be a new creature, and a partner with us in the life and dignity of the Father. I am not unaware that the Hebrew word is commonly explained otherwise and referred chiefly to discrete quantity, by which reckoning we are all, who are divided from one another, called into the unity of that body. Nevertheless, when I look into the matter more carefully, I cannot help referring this word also to what is called continuous quantity, and understanding that in this place the most fitting equality of us all in participating in that great benefit of Christ is declared by this word, just as in a right structure all the parts are in their own way equal to the dignity and firmness of the work. This doctrine adds great weight to fostering and preserving agreement and peace among those whom Christ has counted in his Church, and will yet call. And this is the reason why I have preferred to render the Hebrew word "together" rather than otherwise.

units.la: 4. Nam illuc ascendunt tribus, tribus Iah, ad testimonium Israeli datum, ut celebrent nomen Iehoua.
units.tr: 4. For thither the tribes go up, the tribes of Jah, as a testimony given to Israel, to give thanks to the name of Jehovah.

units.la: POSTQVAM de forma essentiali Ecclesiæ diximus, & communione interna sanctorum, quam illa relatio Ecclesiæ ad Deum, ut formae essentialis efficit; nunc pro eo ordine quem sapientissimè obseruauit Psaltes, de cõmunione externa videndū est, quam interna illa communio perpetuam sibi & inter homines plane necessariam adiungit comitem. Nam si illud verum est quod Philosophi omnes natura teste docuerunt, formæ internæ in re quaque externam à natura respondere, & suam inter utramque esse conuenientiam; non potuit certè gratia (quæ modis omnibus naturam superat) non prouidere atq. efficere, vt formæ internæ quam Deus Ecclesiæ indidit, adhiberetur externa propria, & cum illa tanquam matre conuenientissima. Rem sic habere à natura demonstrat hominis cum animante bruta comparatio. Hominis enim forma essentialis à natura quantum (Deus bone) anteit formam pecudis? quanto præstantior anima illa est, quam Deus ad imaginem suam secundum suam similitudinem fecit, & qua hoc figmentum terræ animauit, sentiente illa anima quæ agit pecudes? propterea homini forma longè præstantior, & animæ illi principatum habenti in his rebus creatis & ad res superas euocandæ conuenientior, foris est indita. Sic in rebus cæteris, quæ ordine naturæ progignuntur. Quòd si in natura Deus ordinem sapientiæ suæ hoc pacto demonstrauit, natura autem, si cum gratia comparabitur, tanto inferior est quanto vestigium alicuius est inferius imagine expressa, & ipsa imago homine: non posset sine grauissima in Deum contumelia Iiâ statui contra id quod anté diximus, Deum formam externam rei cuiufq. in natura accommodauiffe internæ, in gratia veró operibusque gratiæ illam huic minimè contéperauiffe: præsertim cùm gratia naturam superet, s imperfecēam perficiat, & instaurat perditam. Stat igitur certum & indubitatum axioma illud, Deum formæ illius internæ in Ecclesia auctoré, etiam externam formam illi indidiffe pro ratione internæ illius formæ accommodam: Iam verò alterum quoque axioma certum est, nec ab vllo homine controuerti potest, qui mente sibi constituerit: externam rei cuiusque formam esse internæ indicem, & notam cuiuis ante oculos expositam: ac propterea si quis de forma interna ratiocinari voluerit, eamque comprobare, optimè argumenta duci ab externa forma, tanquam à ligno necessario quo res certò internosci postest. In hunc modum à forma externa hominis quem videmus, quamuis dormientem, rationale animal esse concludimus: sic de pecude, itemque de arbore, & consimilibus eadem via post omnem hominum memoriam in recognoscenda Dei gratia & Ecclesia, tanquam obiecto gratiæ, sapientes homines argumentati fuĭt,& obseruatis externis Ecclesiæ notis de veritate interna iudicarunt: quemadmodum etiam hoc in loco. Psalmus explicata essentiali forma & interna sspecis, eius, probationem illius ipsius veritatis, quæ à Deo fuit Ecclesiæ indita, instituit à forma & ratione externa illius,dicés : Nam illuc, &c. Sic enim statuit, cùm forma externa summam semper habeat à natura cum interna convenientiam, & illa fit huius index apud eos qui tantùm ex indiciis & signis iudicare possunt; se propterea hoc argumento naturali vti, & in recognoscenda veritate gratiæ Dei & Ecclesiæ in veritate regenitæ per verbum formam externam illius adhibere testem. Atque hic quidem modus cùm omni tempore fuit necessarius ad veritatem & simplicitatem Christi Ecclesiæque à mendacio, hypocrisi, & simulatione Satanæ administrorum q. illius secernendam; tum verò hoc nostro sæculo vt cùm maximè est observandus: in quo maxima animorum dissensio doctrinarumque varietas extitit iamdiu, & tamen singulorum est constans & pertinax in suis dissensionibus, an erroribus? de Christo,& de veritate,& de Ecclesia gloriatio. Quod itaq.antè recepimus , idem hoc loco facturi sumus, & κατὰ σάρκας[?] (vt loquuntur) sequentes Prophetæ nostri & priscæ illius Ecclesiæ vestigia , notas formamque externam illius Ecclesiæ,ac proinde etiam Christianæ secundum Prophetæ verba demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Having spoken of the essential form of the Church and of the inward communion of the saints, which that relation of the Church to God brings about as its essential form, we must now, in the order the Psalmist observed so wisely, consider the outward communion. The inward communion necessarily brings with it, as its constant companion among men, this outward communion. For if it is true, as all the philosophers have taught from the testimony of nature, that in every thing the outward form answers to the inward and there is agreement between the two, then grace (which surpasses nature in every way) could not fail to provide and bring it about that the inward form which God has given the Church should have its own outward form, and one most fitting to it, as to its mother. That this is so in nature is shown by the comparison of man with the brute beast. How far, good God, does the essential form of man surpass the form of a beast? How much more excellent is that soul, which God made in his own image and according to his own likeness, and which breathed life into this clay, than the soul that sentient beasts have? Therefore the human form, far more excellent, and more suited to that soul which holds the sovereignty over these created things and is to be raised to things above, is set outwardly. So it is with the other things that are produced by the order of nature. But if God has shown the order of his wisdom in this way in nature, and nature, when compared with grace, is as far inferior as a footprint is inferior to the image it expresses, and the image itself is inferior to the man, then it could not be maintained, without the gravest insult to God, that God has fitted the outward form of each thing in nature to its inward form, but has in no way matched it to the inward form in grace and the works of grace; especially since grace surpasses nature, perfects what is imperfect, and restores what is lost. It stands, therefore, as a certain and undoubted axiom that God, the author of that inward form in the Church, has also given it an outward form suited to the nature of that inward form. Moreover, there is another axiom that is certain and cannot be disputed by anyone who has thought about it: the outward form of each thing is the index of its inward form, and a sign set plainly before everyone's eyes. Therefore, if anyone wishes to reason about the inward form and to prove it, he may well draw his arguments from the outward form, as from a sure sign by which the thing can be known with certainty. In this way we conclude from the outward form of man, which we see even when he is asleep, that he is a rational animal; in the same way, wise men have always, since the memory of man began, reasoned about the animal, and about a tree and similar things, and in recognising the grace of God and the Church as the object of grace, they have observed the outward marks of the Church and judged its inward truth by them. So also in this place: the Psalm, having set out the essential form and inward character of the Church, establishes the proof of that very truth which God has implanted in the Church by its outward form and manner, saying: "For thither, etc." For he holds that, since the outward form always has the highest agreement by nature with the inward form, and is its index for those who can judge only from indications and signs, he therefore uses this natural argument, and in recognising the truth of God's grace and of the Church, regenerated in truth through the Word, he calls its outward form as a witness. This method has always been necessary for distinguishing the truth and simplicity of Christ and his Church from lying, hypocrisy and the pretence of Satan and his servants; and in our own age it is to be observed above all, since for a long time there has been the greatest division of minds and variety of doctrines, and yet each party boasts, constantly and stubbornly in its dissensions, of Christ, of truth and of the Church, whether these are errors or not. Therefore we shall do here what we did before: following our Prophet and the footsteps of that ancient Church, as they say, "according to the flesh" [κατὰ σάρκας], we shall demonstrate, according to the Prophet's words, the marks and outward form of that Church, and therefore also of the Christian Church.

units.la: Postquam igitur Propheta statuit illam' veram & germanam Dei Ecclesiam esse, quam ex forma essentiali & proprietatibus internis eius describserat, probationem dicti illius suiinstituit à forma externa eius & proprietatibus . externæ formæ, tanquam signis euidentiffimis & simpliciter necessariis, ex quibus interna veritas cognoscatur. Huius formæ summa est, Externa communio sanctorum, habens suam cum interna communione analogiam. Cùm autem internæ communionis, quam anté exposuimus, sint partes duæ: vnà, à Deo respiciente ad Deum suum per fidem: ciente Ecclesiam suam per gratiam ; altera, ab. Ecclesia respiciente ad Deum suum per fidem:. Iusta analogia inter vtramque formam poftulabat, vt duæ quoq; partes assignarentur externæ formæ Ecclesiam hominibus, qui foris vident, indicaturæ. Hanc rationem Propheta seruauit, cùm argumentis à forma externa ductis interna veritatem Ecclesiæ probare statuisset. Itaque vtrasque partes in descriptione formæ externæ circumscribit diligentissimè : tum partes Ecclesiæ tendentis ad Deum salutis suæ, verf.4. tum verò partes Dei Ecclesiam regentis & ducentis præfentia gratiæ, verf.5.
units.tr: Since, therefore, the Prophet has established that the true and genuine Church of God is the one he described by its essential form and inward properties, he sets up the proof of his statement from its outward form and the properties of that outward form, as from the most evident and simply necessary signs by which the inward truth is known. The chief element of this form is the outward communion of the saints, which has its analogy with the inward communion. Now the inward communion, which we set out earlier, has two parts: one, of God regarding his own through faith, when he calls his Church by grace; the other, of the Church regarding its God through faith. The right analogy between the two forms required that two parts also be assigned to the outward form, which would show the Church to men who see from outside. The Prophet kept this principle when he determined to prove the inward truth of the Church by arguments drawn from its outward form. Accordingly, he most carefully describes both parts in his description of the outward form: first the part of the Church tending to God for its salvation (verse 4), and then the part of the presence of grace of God, who rules and leads his Church (verse 5).

units.la: In hoc igitur versu prior communionis fanctorum locus in cultu positus exponitur, fiue in externa cultus ex pio & religioso sensu animi obseruatione. Quia autem hic cultus, de quo iam dictum fumus, quædam habet communia, & quædam singularia ad priscam illam Ecclefiam (quam Deus variis rudimentis inftituit) proprie pertinentia; videndum nobis est, vt primùm verba ipsa Prophetæ, prout ad Ecclefiam illam respiciebant, exponamus: deinde verò veró ex figuris illis atque umbraculis recognoscamus veritatem communem Ecclesiæ illius & nostræ.
units.tr: In this verse, then, the first place of the communion of the saints is set out, as it is placed in worship, that is, in the outward observance of worship that comes from a pious and religious sense of mind. Since, however, this worship of which we have now spoken has some features in common with us and some that belong particularly to that ancient Church (which God established with various rudiments), we must first explain the Prophet's words as they bore on that Church, and then, from those figures and shadows, recognise the truth common to that Church and to ours.

units.la: In ratione Ecclesiæ illius,quod ad formā externam attinet , quatuor sunt capita ex verbis Prophetæ observandā, quibus forma externa Ecclesiæ circumscribitur : nimirum res, persona, actiones, & circumstantiæ : quæ omnia in iusta Ecclesiæ Dei constitutione,prout effici inter homines potest, necessarium est obseruari. Ac rerum quidem ad formam externam Ecclesiæ pertinentium veritas non ab hominibus,sed à forma interna Ecclesiæ pendet; id est, à reali illa relatione , qua homines res verè diuinas sibi à Deo oblatas suscipiunt tanquā de manu illius, ut earum,tanquam externarum (ut cum Tertulliano loquar ) conteserationem [?] argumento sentiant, profiteanturque, se in præsentia gratiosa Dei , & relatione siue ordinatione Ecclesiæ ad ipsum symbolis externis contestata, salutem suam agnoscere. In his autem rebus quid est boni,quod homo adferre possit? qui & ipse ab omni bono & salute alienus est totus, & res omnes ita labefactavit vitiositate sua, ut omnia , etiam si tentaret millies ingrata Deo, ut pote peccato suo ingratus , esset præstiturus. Quam rem optimè Michæas exprimebat dicens, Quare instructus veniam ante Iehovam, & incurvabo me adorans Deum excelsum? an veniam ante eum cum holocaustis,cum vitulis anniculis? an accepta haberet Iehoua millia arietum? myriadas torrentium olei? an darem primogenitum meum pro defectione mea? stum ventris mei pro peccato animæ meæ? indicauit tibi, ô homo, quid sit bonum. Ecquid Iehoua requisiuit abs te, nisi vt exerceas ius,& ames benignitatem, & modeste ambules cum Deo tuo? Cùm itaque in Ecclesia Dei ad iustam rationem formæ externæ illius sanctas res eas quæ formam externam constituunt,necesse sit adhiberi; quæ res nunquam ab homine,sed à Deo solùm omnia in omnibus operante in Ecclesia sua prÆstari possunt, vt idem formæ externæ sit auctor qui internæ est: propterea priscam illam Ecclesiam & cultum eius externum Propheta describens, omissa planè mentione illarum rerum quas sibi homines conferre posse viderentur, ad eas solùm vel potiùs ad eam solum pios reuocauit, quam Deus in Ecclefia sua testem salutaris præsentiæ suæ pofuerat. Hanc rem Propheta exprimit testimonij appellatione, cùm dicit: Ascendere tribu [?] Iehowæ ad testimonium datum Israeli. Testimonium autem in vulgo quid appelletur, omnibus notum est; in rebus sacris quid appellatur, videndum est. Est igitur testimonium in Ecclesia Dei, à Deo proficiscens, aut intùs, aut foris. Intùs est testimonium Spiritus Dei, viuificantis & excitantis testimonium spiritus nostri & conscientiæ inspiratione sua. Foris est testimonij verbi, & symbolorum quæ verbo coniunxit Deus. Prius testimonium ad formam internam pertinet. Est enim lux illa, qua Ecclesia Christi illustratur & singula membra eius. Sed de hoc testimonio ante satis dixi mus pro consilio nostro, neque est huius loci. Quod autem foris est in Ecclesia testimonium, aut in sermone positum est (nam sermo vitæ atque salutis est à Deo) aut in symbolis & sacramentis eius. Quapropter in Scripturis Deuter. 4. & 5. & in libro Psalmorum passim, verbum Dei nomen testificationis vel testificationis obtinet: Arca verò foederis, in quâ nihil nisi lapides legis tabulæ continebantur, & ex qua Deus testabatur præsentiam suam, consulentibus, respondebat, cõsimiliter testimonium fuit appellata. His duobus capitibus continetur, quidquid ad formam exteriorem Ecclesiæ in rebus positam proprie instituit Deus. Quinetiam hæ duæ res ipsæ (ut modo diximus) uno aspectu in Ecclesia videbantur: quia teucra unum sunt secundum substantiam, sed in specie materiaq. externa differunt. Nam quid fuit testimonium illud materiale arcæ; quàm capsa & loculus verbi & quid aliud verbum in tabulis exaratum fuit, quàm anima quædam corporis materialis illius? tantum eo discrimen est, quòd ut anima nunquam interit, sed permanet in natura (ut corporis autem figura transit; ita verbum (quod anima est) in Ecclesia permanet; ut nota constans & perpetua. Ecclesiæ Dei; corpus vero transmeat & antiquatur instituto Dei. Rectissimè ergo Psaltes, cùm rerum diuinarū (quæ formam externā Ecclesiæ ostendunt) mentionem factūrus esset, testimonium hoc loco pronunciauit synecdochicè ( vt loquuntur )& verbum testimonij diuini & thecam illius comprehendens.
units.tr: Concerning that Church, as far as its outward form is concerned, four heads are to be noted in the Prophet's words by which the outward form of the Church is defined: namely, the things, the persons, the actions, and the circumstances. All of these must be observed in the right constitution of the Church of God, as far as it can be brought about among men. Now the truth of the things pertaining to the outward form of the Church does not depend on men, but on the inward form of the Church; that is, on that real relation by which men receive the things truly divine offered to them by God, as from his hand, so that, as Tertullian says, they perceive them as outward things, and by the outward signs of the covenant they profess that they acknowledge their salvation in the gracious presence of God and in the relation or ordering of the Church to him. But in these matters, what good can man bring? He is himself wholly alien to all good and salvation, and by his wickedness has so weakened all things that, even if he were to try a thousand times, everything he did would be displeasing to God, since it would be tainted by his sin. Micah expressed this very well when he said: "Wherewith shall I come before Jehovah, and bow myself before the high God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? Will Jehovah be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousand rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does Jehovah require of you, but that you do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God?" Therefore, since in the Church of God the holy things which constitute the outward form must necessarily be employed if that form is to be rightly ordered, and since these things can never be furnished by man, but only by God, who alone works all in all in his Church, so that the author of the outward form is the same as the author of the inward form, the Prophet, describing that ancient Church and its outward worship, passed over entirely any mention of those things which men might seem able to contribute themselves, and called the godly back only to those things, or rather to that one thing, which God had placed in his Church as the witness of his saving presence. The Prophet expresses this by the term "testimony," when he says: "The tribes go up, the tribes of Jehovah, to the testimony given to Israel." Now what is commonly called a testimony is known to everyone; what it is called in sacred matters must be considered. A testimony in the Church of God, then, proceeds from God, either inwardly or outwardly. The inward testimony is the testimony of the Spirit of God, who by his inspiration quickens and rouses the testimony of our spirit and conscience. The outward testimony is that of the Word, and of the signs which God has joined to the Word. The former testimony belongs to the inward form; for it is that light by which the Church of Christ and its individual members are illumined. But I have said enough about this testimony earlier, according to my plan, and it is not the place for it here. The outward testimony in the Church is either the spoken word (for the word of life and salvation comes from God) or the signs and sacraments of it. Therefore in Deuteronomy 4 and 5, and throughout the book of Psalms, the Word of God bears the name of testimony or witness; and the ark of the covenant, which contained nothing but the stones of the tablets of the law, and from which God bore witness to his presence when men consulted him and he answered, was likewise called the testimony. These two heads contain whatever God properly appointed concerning the outward form of the Church as it is set in things. Indeed, these two things (as we have just said) were seen in the Church as one, because they are one in substance, though they differ in species and in outward matter. For what was the material testimony of the ark but the case and chest of the Word; and what else was the Word written on the tablets but a kind of soul of that material body? There is only this difference: as the soul never perishes but remains in nature, while the bodily shape passes away, so the Word, which is the soul, remains in the Church as the constant and perpetual mark of the Church of God; but the body passes and grows old by the appointment of God. Rightly, then, when the Psalmist was about to mention the divine things which show the outward form of the Church, he spoke here of the testimony, by synecdoche, as they say, comprehending both the word of the divine testimony and its case.

units.la: Cùm autem theca facilè pereat, corrumpatur, mutetúrque, thesaurus verò in ea conditus (vt modò dicebamus) sit per prouidentiā Dei durabilis in Ecclesia eius: sic statuendum est, in forma externa Ecclesiæ quæcunque res ad hanc formam constituendam pertinent, eas in duos ordines distribui posse, permanentium & pereuntium: quas etiam commodè antiquorum vocibus nominaueris illas statas, & hasambulatorias. Itaque ante legem fuit Ecclesia Dei, cùm nondum esset Arca testimonij: & inde quoque à deportatione in Babyloniam Ecclesia fuit sine arca, quemadmodū in suis Commentariis passim Iudæi agnoscunt, & ex libris Ezræ ac Nehemiæ non obscurè colligitur. sed sine verbo Dei nunquam Ecclesia Dei extitit, nunquam extitura est: Deus in domo sua mutus es-se non potest. Ac proinde cùm aliæ res omnes natura sua adesse & abesse possint sine corruptione tei quæ agitur, & variam (vt ita loquiámur) faciem induant ex dispositione Dei fapientissima; nō dubium est quin Propheta hoc loco maximè ad rem permanentem respexerit; ex qua, velut specifica (ut vocant) differentia, species vera Ecclesiæ. Dei secundùm formam externam illius dignoscatur. Nam etiàm (ut diximus) in illa ipsa Arca inerat verbum Dei digito eius exaratum. Restat igitur ut dicamus, non ex arca, aut aliis eiusmodi accessionibus cognitā fuisse Ecclesiam, sed ex verbo quod continebatur arca, & quod Ecclesia in ea seruabat: ac proinde verbum Dei externū forma externa est Ecclesiæ, ad quā respicere oportet omnes qui certò ex necessariis & indubitatis indiciis Ecclesiam nosse foris voluerint: & quemadmodū per illud tempus hoc indicio cognita est, ita etiam memoria nostra Ecclesiā Dei cognosci oportet e.
units.tr: Since the case (theca) can easily perish, be damaged or be changed, while the treasure kept inside it (as we have just said) endures in the Church through God's providence, we must hold that among the things that make up the external form of the Church, they can be divided into two classes: those that remain and those that pass away. These may conveniently be called, in the old terms, the fixed and the movable. So the Church of God existed before the Law, when there was not yet an Ark of the Testimony, and likewise the Church existed without the Ark after the deportation to Babylon, as the Jews acknowledge throughout their commentaries and as is not obscurely gathered from the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. But the Church of God has never existed, and never will exist, without the Word of God, for God cannot be silent in his own house. Since all other things can be present or absent by their nature without harm to the business in hand, and take on a varied face (so to speak) through God's most wise disposition, there is no doubt that the Prophet in this place looked chiefly to the enduring thing, from which, as from its specific difference (as they say), the true appearance of the Church of God is recognised according to its external form. For, as we have said, the Word of God written by his finger was contained in that very Ark. It remains, then, to say that the Church was known not from the Ark or other such additions, but from the Word that the Ark contained and that the Church kept within it. Therefore the external Word of God is the external form of the Church, to which all must look who wish to know the Church with certainty from necessary and indubitable signs. And just as in that period the Church was known by this sign, so in our own time the Church of God ought to be known in the same way.

units.la: Duo hic obstare videntur, ad quæ ordine paucis respòdebimus: Prius est, Ecclesiam prisc-am ante Legem nō habuisse verbum Dei scriptis exaratum, quod videri posset: ac propterea hanc formam non esse ad iustam cognitionem Ecclesiæ necessariam. Posterius, legem fuisse in arca, non Euangelium: Quòd si Lex fuit Ecclesiæ index, & index perpetuus ac permanens, apud Iudæos potiùs quàm apud Christianos. Ecclesiam esse, quia lex forma sit Ecclesiæ aspectabilis, non autem Euangelium Christi: Ad hæc, soluenda (ut rem ordine persequamur) intelligendum est verbum Dei formam sensilem Ecclesiæ esse, primùm quà enunciatur & auditur, deinde verò quà scribitur legiturque enunciatum: nam verbum est mentis index, scriptura, verbi.Cumque sensilia omnia externa sint,certè ipsam verbū quà fuit enunciatum , ante quàm commendaretur scriptis , ratione habuit extérnæ formæ in Ecclesia Dei: fiue Deus per fe, fiue per alios enûciauerit ipsum. Et (quod amplius est) vt demus libros apud priscos illos patres ante legem minimè extitisse , tamen sanctos illos patres ( prout centurias aliquot annorum viuebant prouidétiá Dei ) libros loquêtes fuisse in sanctis suis familiis cum libris mutis comparandos;vt qui Dei Prophetæ effent ordinarij; quorum fides atque áuctoritas in dubium vocari non posset : præsertim cùm ordinariaillis . effet cum Deo communicatio,& Deo cum illis. Quapropter cùm verbum sensile habuerint, id est,á Deo pronunciatū , & quotiescunque opus fuit , testatum amplissimis significationibus illius ante ora & oculos omnium;non est cur desideremus verbum scriptum in Ecclesia illa, quemadmodum post illud tempus datum est. tum enim primùm scriptum dari cœptum est, (etsi iam anté in carne Abrahami & feminiseius fuerat scripta quodammodo Dei reuelatio) cùm Dei populus numerosissimus effectus effet, & grauissimæ corruptiones ingressæ ex Ægyptiorum aliorumque impiorum conuersatione , postquam ducentos amplius annos in Ægypto , immemores diuinæ promissionis & fœderis cum Abrahamo initi, in peccatis miferè cónsenuissent, vt Apostolus ad Galatas fcribens confirmauit. Nam ex eo demum tempore Deus populum suum, tum à præsente corruptione, tum à futura gratiosissimè vindicauit, cùm doctrinâ veritatis & salutis scriptis commendaffet. Sic verbum enunciatù & auditum perpetua est nota Ecclesiæ Dei: verbum scrip-tum, ex quo est, perpetuum symbolum enunciati & enunciandi: idem verbum, sed tradendi solùm ratione differens. Quò respiciebat Apostolus, cùm auctore Spiritu Dei scriberet in hunc modum: Quomodo credent ei de quo non audierint? quomodo autem audient absq; prædicante? & paulo post: Non omnes auscultarunt Euangelio. Esaias enim dicit, Domine, quis credidit sermoni nostro? Ergo fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per verbum Dei. Hæc ad primam obiectionem satis.
units.tr: Two objections seem to stand in the way, and we shall answer them briefly, in order. The first is that the ancient Church before the Law did not have the Word of God written down in books, which could seem to show that this form is not necessary for a sure knowledge of the Church. The second is that it was the Law, not the Gospel, that was in the Ark; so if the Law was the sign of the Church, and a perpetual and enduring sign, it belongs rather to the Jews than to Christians, and the Church is recognised because the Law, not the Gospel of Christ, is its visible form. To resolve these, and to take up the matter in order, we must understand that the Word of God is the perceptible form of the Church, first insofar as it is uttered and heard, and then insofar as it is written down and read when uttered. For speech is the sign of the mind, and writing the sign of speech. Since all perceptible things are external, the Word itself, insofar as it was spoken before it was committed to writing, already had the character of an external form in the Church of God, whether God uttered it himself or through others. And (what is more) even if we grant that books did not exist at all among those ancient fathers before the Law, nevertheless those holy fathers (who lived for some centuries by the providence of God) were, in their holy households, speaking books, to be compared with mute books, as being the ordinary prophets of God, whose faith and authority could not be called into doubt, especially since they had ordinary communication with God and God with them. Therefore, since they had the perceptible Word, that is, the Word uttered by God, and bore witness to it with the fullest signs whenever need arose, in the sight and hearing of all, there is no reason for us to miss a written Word in that Church, as was given after that time. For then, for the first time, the writing of God's word began to be given (although even before, in the flesh of Abraham and in his seed, a revelation of God had in some measure been written). This happened when the people of God had grown very numerous, and the most serious corruptions had entered from their association with the Egyptians and other impious peoples, after they had grown old in sins through more than two hundred years in Egypt, forgetful of the divine promise and of the covenant made with Abraham, as the Apostle confirmed in writing to the Galatians. For it was from that time that God most graciously delivered his people, both from the present corruption and from the future one, when he had committed the doctrine of truth and salvation to writing. Thus the Word uttered and heard is the perpetual mark of the Church of God, and the written Word, from which it comes, is the perpetual token of what is uttered and what is to be uttered: the same Word, differing only in the mode of transmission. This is what the Apostle had in view when, writing under the inspiration of the Spirit of God, he said: "How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?" And a little later: "Not all have obeyed the gospel. For Esaias says, Lord, who has believed our report? So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God." This is enough for the first objection.

units.la: Altera, quòd verbum Legis, ac nō Euangelij, in prisca illa Ecclesia fuerit scriptum, falsa propositio est, & in sanctam illam Ecclesiam contumeliosa. Nam habuit Ecclesia eandem fidem quam pater Abraham olim habuerat: Abraham autem promissiones, fœdus ex promissionibus, & veritatem promissionum fœderisque in Christo perceperat; quibus rebus Lex ne minimum quidem derogauit. Nam, inquit Apostolus, Pactionem priorē ratam factam à Deo, respicientem in Christum, Lex (quæ post annos quadringentos & triginta coepit) non fecit irritam, ut vanam promissionem redderet. Sed, inquient; Agitur de testimonio quod fuit in arca foederis; illud autem testimonium solummodo decem praecepta Legis tabulis inscripta continebat. Agnoscimus id quidem, si recte intelligatur, sed non dicimus primùm nihil fuisse de testimonio scripto, nisi quod arca includum erat, et fetinàm [?] & illam ipsam scripturam & reliquum Legis divinae cationem [?] Deus per Mosen conscribi, sacerdotibus & Ecclesiæ tradi, religiosèque coram eodem testimonio seruari mandauerat. Fuit ergo testimonium, hoc in arca, illud ante arcam: In arca, velut depositum seruandum: Ante arcam, velut beneficium vtendum: Sed utrumque idem substantia, quamuis qui in arca erat Canon, esset canonis illius quem sacerdotes manibus terebant, Epitome. Posteà, nequid glorientur qui hoc argumentorum genere insidiati cupiunt imperitiorum mentibus; addendum est, quod illi fortasse non videant, ipsa decem praecepta (quae vocat) tabulas illas, non Legis solùm mentionem facere, sed & Euangelij. Nam nonne à promissionibus Euangelicis, & à recordatione illarum & à recente typo, nempe liberationis ex Ægypto, Deus initium facit, dicens: Audi Israel, Ego sum Iehova Deus tuus qui eduxi te è terra Ægypti? Nonne eas docuit Apostolus nō fuisse abolitas superueniente Lege? Omninò igitur pias mentes statuere illud necesse est, verbum Dei enunciatum & scriptum formā externam esse, quàm Deus in Ecclesia positam voluit; vt cùm se & suos ipsa internosceret, tum eam alij, prout Deum confitetur, hac forma externa obseruare possent.
units.tr: The second, that it was the Word of the Law and not of the Gospel that was written in that ancient Church, is a false proposition and an insult to that holy Church. For the Church had the same faith that the father Abraham had once had, and Abraham had received the promises, the covenant founded on the promises, and the truth of the promises and of the covenant in Christ; the Law took away not even the smallest part of these things. For, says the Apostle, "The covenant previously ratified by God, looking to Christ, the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, did not make void, so as to render the promise vain." But, they will say, the matter concerns the testimony that was in the Ark of the covenant, and that testimony contained only the ten precepts of the Law inscribed on the tables. We acknowledge this, if it is rightly understood, but we do not say that at first there was nothing written in the testimony except what was enclosed in the Ark. Rather, we say that God, through Moses, had commanded that the writing itself, and the remainder of the divine ordinance of the Law, be set down in writing, delivered to the priests and the Church, and faithfully kept before that same testimony. So there was a testimony in the Ark and a testimony before the Ark: in the Ark, as a deposit to be kept; before the Ark, as a benefit to be used. Yet both were the same in substance, although the canon that was in the Ark was the canon of which the priests handled the abridgement with their hands. Furthermore, lest those who wish to ensnare the minds of the unlearned with this kind of argument should boast, we must add something that they perhaps do not see: the ten precepts, as they are called, those tables, make mention not only of the Law but also of the Gospel. For does not God begin from the Gospel promises, and from the remembrance of them, and from the recent type, namely the deliverance from Egypt, saying: "Hear, Israel, I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt"? Did not the Apostle teach that these promises were not abolished when the Law came in?
