It is altogether necessary, therefore, for devout minds to hold that the Word of God, uttered and written, is the external form which God willed to be set in the Church, so that the Church might recognise itself and its own, and so that others, insofar as they confess God, might observe the Church by this external form.

units.la: Atque hoc quidem testimonium quo fit argumento, nolumus hoc loco exponere, quia id est loci alterius. In præsentia id satis futurum esse iudicamus, si testimonium hoc intelligendum esse Dei moneamus, quo tum Deus de seipso, rebusque diuinis tantum nobis testatur quantum expedit gloriæ ipsius & saluti nostræ, tum nostrum singuli illustrati patentissimo illo Dei testimonio adducimur, vt de nobis ipsis vicissim testimonium exhibeamus Deo; in nobis habeamus, & in oculis mundi sancta prosessione Dei & salutis nostræ præbeamus. Quæ causa est, cur Prophetæ visum est testimonium non simpliciter nuncupare, sed nominatim addere, fuisse Israeli datum, & Ecclesiæ indefinitè esse expositum. Sed quia hoc quod iam attingimus, ad locum secundum pertinet, quem de personis esse diximus, tempus est vt ad eum locum veniamus explicandum.
units.tr: We do not wish to set out in this place the argument by which this testimony is proved, because that belongs to another place. For the present we judge it will be enough to remind the reader that this testimony must be understood as the testimony of God, by which God bears witness about himself and about divine things only so far as is expedient for his own glory and our salvation; and by which each of us, enlightened by that most manifest testimony of God, is led in turn to bear witness to God about ourselves, to have it in ourselves, and to present it, in the sight of the world, as a holy profession of God and of our salvation. This is why the Prophet thought fit not simply to name the testimony but to add expressly that it was given to Israel, and was set forth to the Church without restriction. But since what we are now touching upon belongs to the second point, which we said concerns persons, it is time to come to that point and explain it.

units.la: Personarum igitur quas Deus intus informat testimonio suo, & palàm testatas facit in oculis omnium, prout verbum Dei internum percipiunt atque externum profitentur, ratio à Propheta duobus modis ostenditur, vniuersè, & particulatim. Vniuersè Ecclesia ostenditur Israël siue Israelitarum nomine; particulatim verò, prout singulares Ecclesiæ à Deo distributæ sunt, demonstratur tribuum & quidem tribuum Iah siue Iehouæ appellatione. Quemadmodum autem in explicatione rerum docuimus, res typicas & particulares à substantia & veritate earum in nominibus istis discerni oportere, hîc eodem modo fieri necesse est. Nam typicæ sunt appellationes; & angustiores; quarum veritas diffusa est latissime[?]. Typica illa duo sunt, quòd Israel vel Israelitæ, & quòd tribus appellantur. Nam cùm populus Iudæorum pars fuerit Ecclesiæ Dei per illud tempus præstantissima, & Ecclesiam Catholicam Christi certo quodam modo adumbrauerit, primùm de ratione illius Ecclesiæ proprie, tum de ratione Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, quod ad personas attinet, per analogiam videndum est. Cùm ergo Israelem Propheta nominat, totum corpus Ecclesiæ quam Deus tum vocabat verbo, intelligit: cùm autem tribus nominatim inter se distinctas (nam id sibi vulgo ex Hebræorum vsu repetitio illa nominis tribus, tribus Iah) partes illius Ecclesiæ, quam totam dixerat Israelis nomine, designauit; & ita quidem designauit, vt ordo membrorum in corpore voce tribuum comprehenderetur. Tria sunt igitur ex Prophetæ verbis ad rationem personarum, quas Deus informat in Christo, pertinentia: vniuersitas velut corpus, partes vt membra corporis iusto ordine inter se conftituta, & applicatio formæ illius quam antè ex posuimus: Ecclesiæ universitas in illo ipso typo quem Propheta hoc loco nominat, tribus modis spectari potest: primùm secundùm rationem externam eius; deinde secundùm internam, postremò autem secundùm utramque fimul. Secundùm rationem externam solùm Israel dicebatur, qui erat in propatulo Iudæus, & cui erat in carne circumcisio, ut Pauli utamur verbis: Secundùm internam solùm Israelis nomine dicebantur, qui in occulto Iùdæi erant, & circumcisione cordis in spiritu ac non litera præditi, quorum laus non ex hominibus est, sed ex Deo ipso. Secundùm utramque dicebantur, in quibus ratio interna & externa formæ divinitus impressæ respondebat. Ad quæ omnia respexit Apostolus, cùm diceret: Non omnes qui sunt ex Israele, sunt Israel, neque qui sunt semē Abrahami, omnes sunt filij. Secundùm externam formâ fuerunt Israelitæ, quos Deus profligavit in deserto, & quicumque auditis promissionibus nō perceperunt sermonem fide contemperatum in se ipsis, ut Apostolus ad Hebræos loquitur, id est, Israelitæ carnales & impij. Secundùm internam nos Israelitæ sumus, & semen Abrahæ, ut scribit Apostolus ad Galatas: nos qui à litera & observationibus corporalibus liberati sumus in Christo Iesu. Secundùm utramque dicti fuerunt Israel in Ecclesia illi, qui secundùm carnem ex Israele descendentes vestigia fidei illius secuti sunt. In hunc modum Propheta loquutus est, cùm vniuerfitatem Ecclesiæ, Israelis nomine designatet; cui vniuersitati datù est à Deo illud testimonium. Nam vniuersitati illi promiscuè credita sunt eloquia Dei, quæ singulis illis hominum generibus testimonio essent: iis quidem qui solùm fecundùm carnem fuerùt Israelitæ, ad euictionem & iudicium ipsorum: reliquis vero ad informationem & salutem ipsorum Deo gloriosam.
units.tr: Therefore, of the persons whom God inwardly shapes by his testimony and makes openly attested in the sight of all, as they receive the inward Word of God and profess the outward one, the prophet sets out the matter in two ways, in general and in particular. In general, the Church is designated by the name Israel or Israelites; in particular, as God has distributed the individual congregations, it is shown by the name of the tribes, and specifically the tribes of Jah, or Jehovah. Now, as we taught in explaining the things, typical and particular things must be distinguished from their substance and truth in these names, and the same must be done here. For these names are typical and narrower, while their truth has spread most widely. There are two typical features: that Israel or the Israelites are named, and that they are called tribes. For since the Jewish people was for that time the most outstanding part of the Church of God, and in a certain way foreshadowed the Catholic Church of Christ, we must consider by analogy, first, the nature of that Church properly speaking, and then the nature of the Catholic Church as far as persons are concerned. So when the prophet names Israel, he means the whole body of the Church which God then called by his Word; but when he names the tribes, distinct from one another (for that repetition, "the tribes, the tribes of Jah," is commonly taken by him from Hebrew usage), he designates the parts of that Church which he had called in general by the name of Israel. And he designates them in such a way that the order of the members in the body is comprehended in the word "tribes." There are therefore three things in the prophet's words that pertain to the account of the persons whom God shapes in Christ: the whole, like a body; the parts, as members of the body arranged among themselves in right order; and the application of that form which we set out earlier. The totality of the Church, in that very type which the prophet names in this place, can be viewed in three ways: first according to its external aspect, then according to its internal aspect, and lastly according to both together. According to the external aspect alone they were called Israel who were visibly Jews, and to whom circumcision in the flesh belonged, to use Paul's words. According to the internal aspect alone were they called Israelites who were Jews in secret, and endowed with circumcision of the heart in the Spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not from men but from God himself. According to both were they called who in them the inward and outward aspects of the form divinely imprinted corresponded. The Apostle had all these things in view when he said: "Not all who are of Israel are Israel, nor are they all children because they are the seed of Abraham." According to the outward form there were Israelites whom God overthrew in the wilderness, and all who, having heard the promises, did not receive the word mingled with faith in themselves, as the Apostle speaks to the Hebrews; that is, carnal and ungodly Israelites. According to the inward aspect we are Israelites and the seed of Abraham, as the Apostle writes to the Galatians: we who in Christ Jesus have been freed from the letter and from bodily observances. According to both were they called Israel in the Church who, being descended from Israel according to the flesh, followed the footsteps of that faith. In this way the prophet speaks when he designates the totality of the Church by the name of Israel; and to this totality God gave that testimony. For the words of God, which were to be a testimony to each of those classes of men, were entrusted without distinction to that whole body: to those who were Israelites only according to the flesh, for their conviction and judgement; but to the rest, for their instruction and salvation, to the glory of God.

units.la: Quòd autem illa Israelitarum vniuersitas in tribus distincta fuit, id partim ciuilis exnaturæ principiis petita, partimque cetemonialis fuit obseruationis ex institutis gratiæ. Principium naturæ est, quòd fecundùm ortum familiarum distinguuntur tribus: eo principio leges ciuiles, de tribuum distinctione in Israele obseruanda, à Deo profectæ sunt; quæ leges fecundùm rationem tum beneficij à Deo collati, tum Israelitarum tanquam emphyteutarum fiue perpetuorum (vt vocant) colonorum Dei, tum denique regionis ipsius latæ sunt, cùm in eius possessionem à Deo mittebantur. Gratiæ verò, quam Deus fecundùm typum & veritatem Israeli contulit, præcepta sic fuerunt lege temperata, vt ceremonialibus quibusdam ritibus ac distinctionibus instruxerit populum illum veterem ad gratiæ suæ commendationem. Sic omnibus rebus istis per singularem Dei prouidentiam in Iudæorum populo adunatis, suus ordo singulis fuit attributus: Ordo autem partim à natura, partimque ab instituto, vt in optimis rebus publicis solet obseruari. Nam fuit ordo in illa vniuersitate, primùm quidem Ecclesiæ ipsius ad Deum, deinde membrorum partiumque ipsius inter se, tum communium, quas vulgò Ecclesias particulares appellamus, tum verò singulariū. In vniuersitate id fuit ordinis, quòd tota Ecclesia & respublica sequebantur Dei, hærebantque Deo secundum institutionem Dei, qui locum Hierosolymorum elegerat in quo habitaret, suamque præsentiam testatam faceret, & ad illud velut consilium summum, cui certissimè præerat Dominus, & ad responsa extraordinaria ipsius, in rebus Ecclesiasticis æquè ac politicis (si quæ graviores forte obtingebant) solita est accutrere. In partibus vniuersitatis illius consimiliter ad ordinem pertinebat, quòd alia tribus ad res sacras & Ecclesiasticas, alia ad humanas atque politicas cum auctoritate curandas à Deo erat distributa, dum aliæ subessent illarum administrationi. In personis verò singularibus id quoque fuit ordinis, quòd præter communem vocationem omnium, quæ charitatem in omnes spectat promiscuè, (hanc enim cuique debemus semper, etiam tum cùm præstantius maximè) aliæ peculiari quadam obstrictæ fuerunt vocatione ad rerum, hæ diuinarum, illæ humanarum procurationem, aut etiam vtrarumque simul, quà priuata opera, quà publica, cùm ciuili, tum Ecclesiastica. Atq; hic quidem ordo totus à summa illa & essentiali forma Ecclesiæ Dei profectus est: qui dominis & nis & vocationibus singulos instruebat, ut in rebus sibi ab eo. mandatis ponerent operam. Sed quia totius ordinis vsus in actione versabatur, restat ut ad locum tertium, qui de actionibus est in Ecclesia Dei, transeamus.
units.tr: Now, that this whole body of Israelites was divided into tribes was partly derived from the principles of civil nature, and partly was a matter of ceremonial observance drawn from the institutions of grace. The principle of nature is that the tribes are distinguished according to the descent of families; by this principle the civil laws concerning the observance of the distinction of tribes in Israel proceeded from God. These laws were enacted with respect to the benefit conferred by God, to the Israelites as his tenant-farmers, or perpetual (as they are called) colonists, and finally to the land itself, when they were sent by God into its possession. The precepts of grace, which God bestowed on Israel according to type and truth, were so tempered by the law that he instructed that ancient people with certain ceremonial rites and distinctions, to commend his grace. Thus, with all these things gathered together in the Jewish people by the singular providence of God, a due order was assigned to each: an order partly from nature and partly from institution, as is usually observed in the best commonwealths. For there was an order in that whole body: first, of the Church itself towards God; then, of its members and parts among themselves, both the common ones, which we commonly call particular churches, and the individual ones. In the whole body the order was this: the entire Church and commonwealth followed God and adhered to God according to God's own institution, who had chosen the place of Jerusalem in which he would dwell and make his presence known, and to which, as to a supreme council over which the Lord most certainly presided, they were accustomed to resort, both for extraordinary answers from him in ecclesiastical matters as well as civil ones, if any weightier matters chanced to arise. In the parts of that whole body the order was likewise that some tribes were appointed by God to handle sacred and ecclesiastical matters, others human and civil matters with authority, while the rest were subject to their administration. Among individual persons too there was this order: that apart from the common calling of all, which looks to love towards everyone without distinction (for we always owe this to each person, even when we are at our most excellent), some were bound by a particular calling to the care of divine things, others of human things, or of both together, whether by private work or public work, in civil or ecclesiastical affairs. Now this whole order proceeded from that supreme and essential form of the Church of God, which equipped each person with gifts and callings, so that they might labour in the tasks committed to them by him. But since the practice of the whole order was carried on in action, it remains for us to pass to the third head, which concerns the actions in the Church of God.

units.la: Actiones igitur Ecclesiae & membrorum eius duobus modis circumscribuntur hoc loco. Nam primùm dicuntur omnes ire ad teftimo-nium, deinde verò in Dei laudibus occupari. De priore Propheta inquit, Ascendunt tribus ad testimonium datum Israeli: de posteriore verò dicuntur hæc verba: ut celebrent nomen Iehovae. Hæ autem occupationes duæ sanctissimæ in prisca illa Iudæorum Ecclesia suas quasdam externas ceremonias habuerunt: quarum aliæ communes sunt omnium ætatum, puta quæ ad honestatem & iustum ordinem in sacris rebus agendis pertinent: Aliæ singulares illius temporis ad vmbram futurarum rerum pertinentes, quemadmodum scitè distinxerunt Apostoli in celebri illo conuentu Hierosolymis habito, & Paulus ad Galatas & Colossenses demonstrat euidentissimè. Omninò tamen perpetuum illud est, quòd omnes pij in communione sanctorum compárent coràm facie Domini ad testimonium ipsius, & quòd celebrant nomen ipsius. Est igitur iam olim piorum in communione sanctorum officium duplex: unum, ut percipiant à Deo verbum salutare eius, & loquentem audiant: Alterum, ut suis orationibus appellent ipsum, & gratiarum actione omnique profeffione sancta[?] agnoscant beneficium eius. Atque hæc quidem duo officia singuli apud fe & intra priuatos parietes tenentur præstare Domino; sed cùm hîc agatur ex professo de ordine publico in prisca Ecclesia ad communionem sanctorum instituto atque obseruato, commodè Propheta vsurpauit a/fcendendi verbum: vt eo significaret officium publicè à piis præstitum, qui ex suis domibus, sedibus[?] & tribubus etiam longinquissimis prodibant vltrò, vt ad hæc duo officia coram Domino præstanda castè & religiosè accederent.
units.tr: The actions of the Church and of its members are therefore described in this place in two ways. For first all are said to go up to the testimony, and then to be busied in praising God. Of the former the prophet says: "The tribes go up, to the testimony given to Israel"; of the latter these words are said: "to give thanks to the name of Jehovah." Now these two most holy occupations had, in that ancient Church of the Jews, certain external ceremonies of their own: some of them common to all ages, namely those that pertain to decency and right order in performing sacred duties; others peculiar to that time, pertaining to the shadow of things to come, as the Apostles wisely distinguished in that famous assembly held at Jerusalem, and as Paul demonstrates most plainly to the Galatians and Colossians. Yet this is wholly perpetual: that all the godly in the communion of the saints appear before the face of the Lord for his testimony, and that they give thanks to his name. Therefore the duty of the godly in the communion of the saints has long been twofold: one, that they receive from God his saving Word and hear him as he speaks; the other, that they call upon him with their prayers, and acknowledge his benefit with thanksgiving and every holy profession. Now these two duties each person is bound to perform to the Lord privately and within his own walls; but since the matter here is expressly about the public order in the ancient Church, instituted and observed for the communion of the saints, the prophet fitly used the verb "go up," so as to signify the duty publicly performed by the godly, who of their own accord went out from their homes, seats, and even the most distant tribes, to present themselves chastely and devoutly before the Lord for these two duties.

units.la: His officiis adiungendum est quartum illud caput quod ante diximus, nimirum circumstantiarum, quæ in rebus omnibus agendis folent occurrere, alia perpetuæ, alia verò prooccafione variantes. Perpetuas appellamus eas, quæ nequibus nec personæ agentes, nec actiones illarum constare possunt: cuiusmodi sunt temporis,& loci. Variantes autem eas, quæ modò sese offeruntin nostris actionibus, modò absunt ab illis: & cùm adsunt, aliàs hoc modo adsunt, aliàs illo modo: quia vt adsint in agendis rebus, nec per ipsas, nec per nos terta est necessitas atque perpetua. Quinetiam illæ ipsæ duæ, quas diximus necessarias, suis quoque ceremoniis non simpliciter, sed propter significationem ipsarum necessariis olim fuerunt quasi[?].
units.tr: To these duties must be added the fourth head we mentioned earlier, namely the circumstances that usually attend all actions: some are perpetual and others vary with the occasion. We call perpetual those without which neither the persons acting nor their actions can exist, such as time and place. Varying circumstances are those that sometimes present themselves in our actions and sometimes are absent from them, and when they are present, they are present sometimes in one way and sometimes in another, since there is neither a necessity nor a constant requirement that they be present in the performance of things, either through themselves or through us. Indeed, those two which we called necessary once had their own ceremonies, and these were necessary not simply in themselves but because of what they signified.

units.la: vestitæ mandato Dei: vt cùm (exempli causa) dicrum[?] dierum distinctio lege imperata est, & feriae anniversariae constitutae: Similiterque in ratione loci, cùm locus Hierosolymorum est consentientibus sacris destinatus, & quaecunque eiusmodi lege indixit Deus, ut typi rerum futurarum essent. Ad hanc ambulatoriam (ut ante appellavimus) ceremoniam Propheta respexit, cùm diceret, Nam illuc ascendunt, ad urbem puta Hierosolymorum; cuius duobus praecedentibus versibus proximè meminerat.
units.tr: They were clothed with the command of God, as when (for example) the distinction of days is enjoined by law and yearly feasts are appointed. So too with regard to place, when Jerusalem was designated by common consent as the place for the sacred rites, and whatever else of this kind God ordained by law so that they would be types of things to come. It was to this walking ceremony (as we called it above) that the Prophet looked when he said, "For thither they go up," namely to the city of Jerusalem, which he had mentioned in the two preceding verses.

units.la: Ex his autem omnibus quae de prisca Iudaeorum Ecclesia proprie hoc loco enuntiata sunt, cùm Spiritui sancto visum fuerit haec ipsa cantica ad Catholicam Ecclesiam & Christianam transmittere; ita colligimus: eandem quoque rationem in forma externa, personis, actionibus, & circumstantiis, quae quidem per se aut respectu alterius necessariae sunt, observari à piis oportere. Forma externa si fuit illis testimonium à Deo datum Israeli: Ergo formam externam Ecclesiae catholicae hoc etiam tempore in testimonio Scripturae sacrae, quam Prophetae & Apostoli diuinitus inspirati cōsignarunt scriptis & Ecclesiae tradiderunt, recognosci oportere. Personarum si fuit distinctio ex donis & vocationibus à Deo institutis, ad commoditatem: etiam externae formae atque internae veritatem, Ergo in eadem Ecclesia catholica ex donis & vocationibus à Deo testatis distinguì personas oportere. Si actiones, officiaque tum Ecclesiae ipsius, per opus est obseruantiae propterea circumstantiarum quoque non negligenda ratio, quæ ad harum rerum obseruationem sine vanitate aut superstitione commodare possunt.
units.tr: From all these things that have been said here properly about the ancient Church of the Jews, since it has pleased the Holy Spirit to hand these very songs on to the Catholic and Christian Church, we conclude as follows: the same principle should be observed by the godly in external form, persons, actions and circumstances, which are necessary either in themselves or in relation to something else. If the external form was a testimony given by God to Israel, then the external form of the Catholic Church should likewise be acknowledged today, in the testimony of holy Scripture, which the Prophets and Apostles, divinely inspired, committed to writing and handed down to the Church. If the distinction of persons was based on gifts and callings instituted by God for the sake of good order, then, since the external form serves the inner truth, persons in the same Catholic Church ought likewise to be distinguished by the gifts and callings attested by God. If actions and offices, both of the Church itself, are to be observed through necessity, then the consideration of circumstances must not be neglected either, since these can serve the observance of such things without vanity or superstition.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem omnia ubicunque esse animadvertimus, ibi cogitandum est Deum Ecclesiam suam statuisse; id est, & præsentem esse singulari præsentia gratiæ,& formam internam atque essentialem Ecclesiæ illi ac membris illius indere ex beneplacito voluntatis suæ.
units.tr: Wherever we see all these things, we must think that God has established his Church there: that is, that he is present with a singular presence of grace, and that by his good pleasure he imparts the inner and essential form of the Church to that assembly and to its members.

units.la: Quòd si hæc omnia non compárent simul in eo cœtu ad quem respicimus, tamen non existimanus temerè sententiam adversus ullum ferri oportere, tanquam si à Deo abesset planè qui abest à iudicio nostro. Serui alieni sunt, il-lius lius Domini, qui & nos & alios & illos ipsos redemit sanguine pretiosò suo: siue stent, siue cadant, stant & cadunt Domino. suo. Ac propterecà[?] fugienda nobis sunt quàm diligētissimè præpropera illa iudicia, quibus alij alios plus fatis, irritante Satana & mundo applaudente, infestamús atque offendimus. Quid enim? an continuò siquid formæ illius externæ deest, quàm circumscripsit Propheta his verbis, legitimum futurum est, alienos ab interna Ecclesiæ forma conuentus illos aut fratres illos iudicare? & tamen (proh Deum immortalem) quotus quisque hoc tempore est, qui ferìò cogitet de impediendis aut inhibendis iudiciis eius modi? quotusquisque non effunditur in acerbissima severissimaque iudicia, cogitatione, animo, sermone, scriptis; siquè non solùm privatim communicatis, sed etiam publicè in lucem datis maximo Ecclesiæ malo?
units.tr: But if all these things do not come together in the assembly to which we are looking, we should not rashly pass judgment against anyone, as though he who is absent from our judgment were altogether absent from God. They are another's servants, of that one Lord who redeemed us, them, and all others with his precious blood; whether they stand or fall, they stand or fall to their own Lord. Therefore we must flee, as diligently as possible, those hasty judgments by which some, with Satan urging and the world applauding, harass and offend others beyond what is fitting. For what? Shall we immediately declare that, if anything is lacking in that external form which the Prophet described in these words, those assemblies or those brothers are alien to the inner form of the Church? And yet, (good God!) how few people nowadays seriously think of preventing or restraining judgments of this kind? How few do not pour out the most bitter and severe judgments in thought, in feeling, in speech, and in writings, and not only in private communications but also in public publications, to the very great harm of the Church?

units.la: Si forte in vna aliqua circumstantia, aut etiam altera, pluribúsue, priuatus aliquis dissenserit, si etiam publica auctoritate instructus, si Ecclesia vna, si plures, in circumstantiis, ritibus, ceremoniis, non planè iudicio nostro, aut moribus conformantur; plerique omnes clamant de pietate, de Christianitate actum; atque vtinam clamarent solùm. Etsi hi clamores totidem sunt infesta tela, quibus imperitorum mentes obfirmantur, & labefactantur infirmorum. Sed cùm accedunt cætumeliæ, proscriptiones, condemnationes & alia id genus, putásne[?], mi homo, illud institutum à Christo esse, aut à Christiano sui compote probari posse? non vides dum ordinem externum propugnas verbo, eundem ordinem à te ipso ante omneis oppugnāti? destruis quod ais exstruendum?
units.tr: If perhaps some private individual disagrees in one circumstance, or even in another, or in several, or if even one Church, or several, publicly authorized, do not wholly conform to our judgment or customs in circumstances, rites and ceremonies, nearly everyone cries out that piety and Christianity are finished; and would that they only cried out! Yet these outcries are so many deadly weapons by which the minds of the unlearned are hardened and the weak are shaken. But when insults, proscriptions, condemnations and things of that kind are added, do you think, my friend, that such a practice was instituted by Christ, or that it can be approved by a Christian in his right mind? Do you not see that, while you defend external order with words, you yourself are assailing that same order before everyone? You tear down what you say should be built up.

units.la: Sed quid si res gravior sit, quàm quae his circumstantiis debeat accenseri? nam circumstantiarum locus postremus est. ergo quid si in actionibus, aut in ratione personarum vocationum, numqueaut[?] in ipsa externa forma non sit consuenientia, quam oporteat esse? Etiam hîc suspendi cupio & inhiberi iudicium nostrum. Nam ad actiones quod attinet, quas æquum est pluris fieri quàm circumstantias, eas sic oportet in personis Ecclesiisq; expendi, ut non propterea oppugnentur Ecclesiæ Dei quia Ecclesiæ sunt & aliquid in Christo obtinent; quamuis actionibus malis, impietatem & iniustitiam plane redolentibus circumfluant. Erit quidem hic, illè[?] erunt plerique (si ita videtur) impij: sed tamen tantisper dum ordo aliquis est, & forma illa externa permanet, quam primo loco posuimus; cave Ecclesiæ nomen huic conuentui abijudices. Si secetis, non fecit Christus, non Prophetæ in prisca Judæorum Ecclesia (nam & Eliam iudicio suo facientem revocavit Deus) non Apostoli in tam multis Ecclesiis Christi, quarum ulcera gravissima animadvertebant, curantes malum (quoad eius fieri poterat) prudentia charitate sua, non abiicientes Ecclesiam importunitate atque confidentia imprudentissima.
units.tr: But what if the matter is more serious than can be counted among these circumstances? For the place of circumstances is last. So what if there is a lack of agreement in actions, or in the reckoning of persons and callings, or even in the external form itself, such as ought to exist? Here too I wish our judgment to be held back and restrained. For as regards actions, which rightly count for more than circumstances, they must be weighed in persons and Churches in such a way that the Churches of God are not attacked merely because they are Churches and obtain something in Christ, even though they are surrounded by evil actions that plainly reek of impiety and injustice. Indeed, there will be here, and there will be many (if it so seems) who are ungodly; but for as long as some order exists and that external form which we placed first remains, take care not to deny the name of Church to that assembly. If you do otherwise, Christ did not do so, nor did the Prophets in the ancient Church of the Jews (for God also called back Elijah, who was acting on his own judgment), nor did the Apostles in the many Churches of Christ, whose most grievous sores they saw; they tended the wound with their prudence and charity, as far as it could be done, and did not cast off the Church through impatience and most imprudent self-confidence.

units.la: Sed. quid si etiam in personis agnoscendis conuentus errēt? seruos Dei in Ecclesia legitimè ordinatos non agnoscat? illegitimè ordinatos habeat pro legitimis? denique Ecclesiam vnam contra alteram ædificet, siue hæretico studio, siue feruore chismatis[?] ardescente? pergraue quidem hoc malum: sed tamen ne hos quidem maximo publico malo ex morbo animi laborātes ita præfractè à nobis oportet iudicari, vt si iam planè abdicati essent à Domino, qui ordinem illius hoc modo abdicant: non ita feruet iudicio Deus. Nā primùm etsi ordinem Christi reiiciunt iniquitate sua, tamen non totum ordinem reiiciunt, sed hunc ordinem, huius aut illius Ecclesiæ, aut etiam plurium: non enim planè ordinem ab ipsis reiici ex facto ostendunt, cùm ipsi ordinem in suo corpore & conuentibus suis obseruent quodammodo. Deinde (quod est rei caput) formam illam exteriorem Ecclesiæ seruant, id est; verbum Dei, Scripturam sacram: quæ cùm integra apud illos est, colituràque, non possunt iure sic damnari, vt si ab omni Ecclesia planè discessissent. Quam ob causam orthodoxi Patres fidelissimè quidem aduersus hæreticorum Ecclesias pugnauerunt gladio spiritali Dei; sed tamen nec Ecclesias esse planè negauerunt eorum qui ita sentirent, nec ministerium illarum funditus deleuerunt, nec factasacramentum baptismatis in eis perceptum, si eius substantia integra servata esset, iterari censuerunt in Ecclesiis orthodoxis suis oportere. Iudicabant enim sapie[illegible, ~2 letters]tiffimè ista infirmitate hominum, quamuis gravissima, irritam fieri non posse veritatem Dei.
units.tr: But what if assemblies even err in acknowledging persons? If they do not recognize God's servants lawfully ordained in the Church? If they regard those ordained unlawfully as lawful? Finally, if they build one Church against another, whether from a heretical zeal or from a fervor of schism burning hot? This is indeed a very grave evil; yet we ought not to judge even these, who labor under a disease of the mind and bring about the greatest public harm, so harshly, as though they had already been wholly cut off from the Lord, since they cut off his order in this way. God is not so fiercely angry in judgment. For first, although by their wickedness they reject Christ's order, they do not reject the whole order, but this order of this or that Church, or even of several; for by their deeds they do not show that they have wholly rejected order, since in some measure they keep order in their own body and assemblies. Next (and this is the heart of the matter), they keep that external form of the Church, that is, the Word of God and holy Scripture. Since this is whole among them and is worshipped, they cannot rightly be condemned as though they had wholly departed from every Church. For this reason the orthodox Fathers fought most faithfully against the Churches of the heretics with the spiritual sword of God; yet they did not deny that these were Churches of those who thought thus, nor did they utterly destroy their ministry, nor did they judge that baptism received among them, if its substance had been kept whole, must be repeated in their own orthodox Churches. For they wisely judged that the truth of God cannot be made void by the weakness of men, however grave it may be.

units.la: Sed quid si ergo Scriptura S. quæ forma externa est Ecclesiæ à Deo impressa, accipiant quidem & habeant pro certissimo principio, sed tamen non satis accipiant bene? Nam de illis qui Scripturam nō accipiunt plane, quæstio hic nulla est: cùm id pro certo habeamus omnes, quibuscunque forma externa à Deo subministrata non inest, iis internam inesse non posse: ac proinde infidelibus non competere nomen Ecclesiæ, ac ne Iudæis quidem, quamuis recipiant partem scripturæ, tum quia publica testificatione renunciauit illis Deus, tum quia potissimam partem non accipiunt. Quamuis enim præsignificatione, quam in Testamento vetere habemus, colant;complementum tamen, quod in novo doceri credimus, protulerunt pedibus. Deillis ergo qui Scripturam agnoscunt & colunt, abest vt iudicium præceps feramus arbitratu nostro: suspendi iudicia potiùs necesse est, quàm in eos quibus gratiam suam Deus testatam facit incurrere. Quod malù quot & quanta mala Christiano orbi hæc nostra memoria attulerit, nemo homo est qui non videat, & (si quidem verè homo est) horreat. In hoc igitur hominum genere duo velim observari, quae piis (spero) satisfactura sunt, & quibus temeraria audaciaq. esse eorum iudicia demonstrari potest, qui momento[?] perrumpi omnia statuunt oportere, & damnari quoscunque non probaverint. Primum igitur quod in hoc genere pervelim observari, hoc est, utrum Scripturam teneant & habeant pro divino principio regulaque fidei & conversationis nostrae: Alterum est, si quide Scripturam tenent, utrum rem scripturae teneant, id est, ea accipiant quae Scripturis sacris exponuntur. Nam primùm Scripturam si tenuerint, retinent formam datam divinitus: quam formam externam tanti voluit haberi Deus, ut Ecclesia Dei vocatione habenda sit quaecunque hanc formam retinet. Atque hoc illud est, quod sibi voluit Apostolus cùm ad Romanos scriberet: Quae est igitur praestantia Iudaei? aut quae utilitas circumcisionis? Multa per omnem modum. primarium enim illud est, quod eis credita sunt eloquia Dei. Ex his enim evidentissime docemur, quibus credita sunt Dei eloquia, eos (utcunque homines infidi sint plerique) tamen adhuc praerogariuam illam retinere, non per se, sed per illam Dei fidem quam ipsorum infidelitas non potest inanem reddere, dum ipsi in tolerantia expectare eos placuerit. Formam externam ipsam imprimit Dominus traditione verbi sui: quod verbū qui retinent, tantisper dum retinent, principium formæ à Deo impressæ iudicandi sunt retinere: quemadmodū nummo tritissimo, tantisper dum vestigia signatæ formæ permanent, promiscuè vtimur, eumq. iustum agnoscimus. Et certè maximus est piis hominibus aditus ad miseros illos, qui Scripturam retinent, infor-mandos in via Christi; si in spiritu charitatis lenitatisq́ue cum illis egerint, cùm principium commune vtrimq́ue agnoscitur, ex quo de religionis nostræ veritate conferre possimus, & instrumento communi alij alios instruere.
units.tr: But what if, although they receive holy Scripture, which is the external form impressed on the Church by God, and hold it as a most certain principle, they nevertheless do not receive it aright? For there is no question here about those who do not receive Scripture at all, since we all hold it for certain that those in whom the external form given by God is not present cannot have the internal form; and therefore the name of Church does not belong to unbelievers, nor even to Jews, although they receive part of Scripture, both because God has renounced them by a public testimony and because they do not receive the chief part. For although they worship by the foreshadowing which we have in the Old Testament, they have trampled underfoot the fulfillment which we believe is taught in the New. Therefore, toward those who acknowledge and worship Scripture, we are far from making a headlong judgment according to our own opinion; we must rather withhold judgment than fall upon those to whom God has made known his grace. How many and how great evils this our own age has brought upon the Christian world, no one is there who does not see, and (if he is truly a man) shudder at. In this class of men, then, I should like two points to be observed, which (I hope) will satisfy the godly, and by which it can be shown that the judgments of those are rash and reckless who decide that everything must be broken through at once, and that whoever does not approve them must be condemned. The first point I should especially like observed in this class is whether they hold Scripture and regard it as the divine principle and rule of our faith and conduct. The second is, if indeed they hold Scripture, whether they hold the matter of Scripture, that is, whether they accept those things which are expounded in the holy Scriptures. For if they hold Scripture, they keep the form given by God; God so wished this external form to be valued that whatever Church keeps this form is to be regarded as a Church of God by calling. This is what the Apostle meant when he wrote to the Romans: "What advantage then has the Jew? Or what is the profit of circumcision? Much in every way. For first of all, they were entrusted with the oracles of God." For from these words we are very clearly taught that those to whom the oracles of God were entrusted (however unfaithful most of them may be) still retain that privilege, not through themselves, but through that faith of God which their unbelief cannot make empty, while God has been pleased to wait for them in patience. The Lord himself impresses the external form by the handing down of his Word; those who keep this Word, so long as they keep it, are to be judged to keep the principle of the form impressed by God, just as we use a much-worn coin, and acknowledge it as genuine, so long as the marks of the stamped form remain. And certainly there is a very great opening for godly men to instruct those miserable people who hold Scripture in the way of Christ, if they deal with them in a spirit of charity and gentleness, since a common principle is acknowledged on both sides, from which we can confer about the truth of our religion, and instruct one another by a common instrument.

units.la: Sed tamen fieri non potest, ut qui Scripturam tenent,iidem nō teneant rem Scripturæ,saltem aliqua ex parte ipsius: Nam si qui ut Iudæi tenuerint eam, ij ne Scripturam quidem retinent, cùm nihil retineat eius. Ut ergo de iis dicamus qui Scripturam cum rebus scriptura expositis retinent, gradus horum sunt innumeri. Nam quantum interuallum est à perfectione huius officij, vsque ad extimum imperfectionis gradum,qui vniuersæ alienationi à Deo est proximus, tantus numerus graduum constitui potest in iis siue hominibus, siue Ecclesiis, à quibus Scriptura cum re scripturæ retinetur. Sunt autem hi gradus planè innumerabiles,cùm hoc ab his,illud ab illis, plùs, minus,explicitè,confusè, purè,impurè teneatur. Sed quia non est consilij nostri, vt gradus illos peruestigemus, duo summa genera solùm destringemus ad institutum hoc pertinentia; quandoquidem hîc de illis tantùm laboratur qui propter defectum aliquem non videntur habendi in Ecclesiæ numero. Nam alioquin constat neminem hominem aut Ecclesiam esse in terris, quæ perfectè perfectionem Scripturæ cum rerum Scriptura comprehensarum perfectione teneat; sed aliquam tolerabilem inter homines constitutionem Ecclesiæ perfectionem humano sermone appellari, & eos dici ab Apostolo perfectos, qui ad aliquem vsque gradum per Dei gratiam ascenderint. Eorum igitur quorum imperfectio facit vt Ecclesiam Dei habere penes se minimè videantur, respectu illius formæ externæ quam Scripturæ sacram appellamus, duo sunt genera: Nam alij Scripturam & rem scripturæ in fundamento tenent; alij Scripturam sic tenent, vt à fundamento discedant longissimè. Fundamentum appellamus, siue (vt loquuntur vulgò) articulos fundamentales fidei, eos sine quibus fides Christiana constare non potest; cuiusmodi sunt articuli de Deo, qui fundamentum est salutis nostræ obiectum fidei immutabile. Qui ergo Scripturam & fundamentum illud salutare tenent, quamuis in rebus singulis non æquè sit explicata illorum fides, tamen ex forma externa quam impressit Deus, in Ecclesia Dei habendi sunt. Nam quæ ratio est in membro, eandem in corpore quoque Ecclesiæ oportet observari. Membri in fide infirmi miseremur, recte: quid ni etiam corporis ex infirmi-tate tate laborantis? Dum anima est in eo, vivit: dum aliquid est vitæ; anima est in eo. Qui verò à fundamento absunt, & de litera Scripturæ in carne gloriantur, ij certè Ecclesia Christi haberi non possunt. Sed rursum in illo genere multa veniunt observanda. Verbi gratia: Si ij qui fundamentum retinent, ipsum purum aut impuratum retinent: si impuratum, quanta impuritate impuretur: Si impuritate summa, utrum apertè impuretur ab ipsis, an verò ab iis qui contradicunt reuincatur ex consequente impuritas. Nam in his rebus magno judicio in hominibus, magna religione opus est; ne illud ipsum beneficium, quantulumcumque est quod à Christo Jesu perceperunt, importunitate & acerbitate nostra intereat.
units.tr: But it is not possible that those who hold Scripture should not also fail to hold the matter of Scripture, at least in some part of it. For if those who hold it do so as the Jews do, they do not even hold Scripture, since they hold nothing of its substance. So, to speak of those who hold Scripture together with the things Scripture sets out, there are countless degrees among them. For as wide as the gap is between the perfection of this office and the furthest degree of imperfection, which lies closest to total alienation from God, so great a number of degrees can be set among those, whether men or churches, by whom Scripture is held together with the matter of Scripture. Indeed these degrees are plainly innumerable, since one holds this more, another that less, one explicitly, another confusedly, one purely, another impurely. But since it is not our purpose to trace out those degrees, we shall touch only on the two highest kinds that pertain to this undertaking, since here we are concerned only with those who, on account of some defect, do not seem to be counted among the Church. For it is agreed that there is no man or church on earth that holds the perfection of Scripture perfectly together with the perfection of the things comprehended in Scripture; rather, a tolerable constitution of the Church among men is called its perfection in human speech, and those are called perfect by the Apostle who have ascended to some degree by the grace of God. Of those, then, whose imperfection makes it seem that they do not have the Church of God among them, with respect to that external form which we call the sacred Scripture, there are two kinds. For some hold Scripture and the matter of Scripture on the foundation; others hold Scripture in such a way that they depart far from the foundation. By the foundation we mean the fundamental articles of faith, as they are commonly called, those without which the Christian faith cannot stand; such are the articles concerning God, which is the foundation of our salvation, the unchangeable object of faith. Those, then, who hold Scripture and that saving foundation, although their faith is not equally explained in every particular, are nonetheless to be regarded as in the Church of God, on account of the external form which God has impressed. For whatever reason holds in a member, the same ought to be observed in the body of the Church too. We rightly pity a member weak in faith; why not also the body labouring under weakness? While the soul is in it, it lives; while there is any life, the soul is in it. But those who are far from the foundation and boast in the letter of Scripture in the flesh cannot certainly be regarded as the Church of Christ. Yet again, many things must be observed within that kind. For example: if those who hold the foundation hold it pure or defiled; if defiled, how greatly it is defiled; if with the greatest defilement, whether the defilement is plainly made by themselves, or whether it is rather refuted by those who contradict them, and the defilement follows as a consequence. For in these matters there is need of great judgement and great piety in men, lest that very benefit, however small it is, which they have received from Jesus Christ, be lost through our harshness and bitterness.

units.la: Atque utinam hic modus charitatis veritatisque inter Christianos his calamitosis temporibus observari posset: utinam sententiæ importunæ, animi infesti, sermones aculeati, actiones asperæ atque vehementes à Christianis hominibus toties abessent longissimè, quoties cum iis qui aliud sentiunt, conferre cogitant. Nam quid agimus? quid cogitamus, obsecro, cùm sermonum ejusmodi habendorum necessaria occasio offertur? pleriq; omnes in eo fumus, ut ostendamus nihil nobis placere posse, quàm quod à nobis cogitatur, dicitur, præstatur, in communicationibus ejusmodi: adeò suaviter nos ipsos nobis admetimur. Itaque præiudicia nobiscum afferimus de iis hominibus quibuscum agendum est, de sermonibus ipsorum detrahimus, indignitatem augemus quibuscunque modis possumus, absurda accumulamus, quibus magis deterreamus ipsos, quàm adducamus ad veritatem Christi, pro eo quod manus erigendis & fulcra firmandis iis admoueri oporteret, & faces illustrandis. Nam his absurdis quæ ne per somnium quidé ipsis in mentem venerunt, iniuriam sibi fieri clamitant.itaque clamores vltrò citroque audiuntur, conuicia, contumeliæ, maledicta, scripta etiam profunduntur his rebus omnibus instructissima, quibus animi quo iure, qua iniuria obfirmantur: sed nihil de penu charitatis, pauca de fonte veritatis, ex quo in præiudicata de personis, mentibus, sermonibus, actionibus ipsorum traducimur. Imò (quod longè grauissimum) si qui veritate victi cogitent sine ignominia transire ad veritatem, inuidemus Christo laudem, volumus vicisse, & tropæa illorum nobis, non Christo cupimus: quo obfirmantur miseri, ne per nos dicantur pudefieri. Quousque tandem, ô fratres in Christo dilectissimi, quousque abutemur patientia Dei nos studiossimè ad veritatem suam in charitate & humilitate reuocantis & ad vnitatem Ecclesiæ suæ? quousque perturbationibus animorum nostrorum sinemus nos, quà prudentes, quà imprudentes abripi? quousque dabimus operam vt alij aliis extorqueamus formam illam externam,quam Deus nobiscum gratiosè & cū fratribus nostris communicat? Jam plus satis aliena bona minuimus, mala amplificauimus, & noua insuper accumulauimus,vt deiiciamus quos ex mādato Dei opera nostra oportuit erigi. Quin potiùs agnoscimus testimonium Iehouæ apud hos & illos esse,in quos infesti ruimus ? Quin videmus Israelem esse, quemcunque Deus informat in sui illius testimonij communicatione? Quin cernimus eòdem alios contendere atq. nos facimus, ac de amplectendo Iehouæ testimonio retinendoque laborare ? Quin animaduertimus illos, absque nobis esset qui importunè inter nos obstrepimus,ad celebrandū nomen Domini concurrere? Iinamus[?] potius illos, per Deū immortalem,in sanctis his studiis occupari,& bonum illorum studium Christiana prudentia duce omni studio industriaque adiuuemus: neque committamus,vt facto nostro à bonis institutis auocentur,atque ad mala inardescant, prout in cōtentionibus humanis plurimùm euenit. Cur de circumstantiis rerum magnopere laboremus,& Ecclesias imprudentia grauissima inter se committamus ? Cur etiam propter actiones varias, si quas improbamus, & reipsa improbandæ sunt,perinde censores agamus in fratres nostros, ac si momento apud illos tota Ecclesia concidisset? An ergo existimamus actiones hominum formam Ecclesiæ esse ? Effecta sunt confequétia illius; ex quibus homines quidem possumus cognoscere singulos: sed si Ecclesiam iudicamus, mox ad eorū castra nos transfugere (quod absit) oporteret, qui nullam Ecclesiam in hac vita iudicant existere. Cur etiam de personis & earū dignitate, ordine, auctoritate tuenda,ita contendimus, vt si extra hurt[?] aut illum Ecclesiæ modum non esset Ecclesia? Equidem non probo ab illis Ecclesias seindi: sed ne hoc quidem probo, vt qui scindunt inscientia & infirmitate sua, ij scientia & auctoritate tua ac potius tyrannide (quisquis es) ita refcindantur. Si enim Ecclesiam, in qua versor per Dei gratiam illi non agnouerint: at mihi tamen hoc tempore satis futurum est, si videro aliquam Christi Ecclesiam ab illis agnosci: vt me, vt hanc, aut illam Ecclesiam agnoscant, non magnopere laborabo, modo agnoscant Christum: pro certo habens, si in Christo paulatim confirmentur, fore vt confirmato mentis oculo me & alios viuere in Christo videat, & ampliùs cum coetu piorū coalescant. Quòd si nitidissimum illum Scripturæ fonte suarum inuentionum & traditionū cœno coinquinant, vtrùm nos meliores veritatis illius vindices putamus fore, quàm Deus ipse sit? Conquiescamus igitur in voluntate illius, neque anteuertamus opera mifericordiæ, aut iudicia eius nostris iudiciis: quos expectat, expectemus sequentes ipsum: quos vocat, si per nos vocare placuerit, vocemus in fide & spiritu lenitatis: si per alios, ne interuertamus; sed gloriam ipsi tribuamus, quòd & alia, & plura, atque haud scio an commodiora instrumenta quàm nos sumus, ad opus suum dignetur adhibere. Ipsius est praestare omnia: nostrum verò ad perpauca & tenuissima ministeria, ad quae nos vocauerit, fidem & obsequium nostrum ei sanctificare ex voluntate eius: & de eo laetari sanctissima laetitia spiritus, si quos nobiscum à Deo videbimus adhiberi qui dicant, Domum Iehouae adeamus.
units.tr: And would that this measure of charity and truth could be observed among Christians in these calamitous times! Would that unfriendly opinions, hostile minds, stinging words and harsh and violent actions were kept far away by Christians whenever they think of conferring with those who think otherwise! For what are we doing? What are we thinking, I beg you, when the necessary occasion of holding such discussions is offered? Almost all of us are intent on showing that nothing can please us except what we ourselves think, say and do in such dealings; so sweetly do we flatter ourselves. And so we bring prejudices with us concerning those men with whom we must deal, we detract from their words, we magnify their unworthiness by every means we can, we pile up absurdities with which to frighten them away rather than lead them to the truth of Christ, when we ought to be raising their hands, strengthening their supports, and kindling their torches. For they cry out that wrong is done to them by these absurdities, which never even entered their minds in a dream. So shouts are heard back and forth, reproaches, insults, curses; writings too are poured out, fully equipped with these things, by which minds are hardened, rightly or wrongly; but nothing of the store of charity, little of the fountain of truth, from which we are led into prejudgements about their persons, minds, words and actions. Indeed (and this is by far the most serious) if any, conquered by the truth, think of passing over to the truth without disgrace, we begrudge Christ the praise, we want to have conquered, and we desire their trophies for ourselves, not for Christ; so the wretched men are hardened, lest they be said to be put to shame through us. How long, O brothers most dearly beloved in Christ, how long shall we abuse the patience of God, who most earnestly calls us back to his truth in charity and humility and to the unity of his Church? How long shall we allow ourselves to be carried away by the disturbances of our minds, some of us prudently, some imprudently? How long shall we labour to wrench from one another that external form which God graciously shares with us and with our brothers? Already we have diminished the goods of others far too much, magnified their evils, and piled new ones upon them, so that we cast down those whom, by God's command, our work ought to have raised up. Why do we not rather acknowledge that the testimony of Jehovah is among those whom, and against whom, we rush in hostility? Why do we not see that whoever God forms in the sharing of that his testimony is Israel? Why do we not perceive that others strive as we do, and labour to embrace and keep the testimony of Jehovah? Why do we not notice that those whom we loudly disturb among us would, were it not for us, be gathering to celebrate the name of the Lord? Let us rather go on, by the immortal God, and let us see them occupied in these holy pursuits, and with all zeal and diligence, under the guidance of Christian prudence, let us help their good endeavour; and let us not allow them, through our conduct, to be drawn away from good purposes and inflamed toward evil, as very often happens in human contentions. Why should we labour so greatly over the circumstances of things, and set churches against one another with the gravest imprudence? Why also, on account of various actions, if any we disapprove, and which indeed deserve disapproval, should we so censure our brothers as if the whole Church had fallen in a moment among them? Do we then think that the actions of men are the form of the Church? They are consequences of it, from which indeed we can know individuals; but if we judge the Church, we would have to flee, which God forbid, to the camp of those who hold that no Church exists in this life. Why do we also contend so about persons and the defence of their dignity, order and authority, as if there were no Church apart from this or that manner of ours? Indeed I do not approve of churches being torn apart by them; but neither do I approve that those who tear apart through their ignorance and weakness should be torn down by your knowledge and authority, or rather tyranny, whoever you are. For if they do not acknowledge the Church in which I dwell by the grace of God, yet for me at this time it will be enough, if I see that some Church of Christ is acknowledged by them; I shall not labour greatly that they acknowledge me, or this or that Church, provided they acknowledge Christ, being sure that if they are gradually confirmed in Christ, the time will come when, with their mind's eye strengthened, they will see me and others living in Christ, and they will unite more fully with the company of the godly. But if they defile that purest fountain of Scripture with the mire of their own inventions and traditions, do we think we will be better defenders of that truth than God himself is? Let us therefore rest in his will, and not anticipate his works of mercy, or put his judgements before our own: those whom he awaits, let us await, following him; those whom he calls, if it pleases him to call them through us, let us call in faith and in the spirit of gentleness; if through others, let us not overturn them, but give glory to him, because he deigns to use other and more numerous, and perhaps more suitable, instruments than we are for his work. It belongs to him to accomplish all things; but ours is to sanctify, by his will, our faith and obedience to him in the few and slightest ministries to which he has called us; and to rejoice in that with the holiest joy of the Spirit, if we see him employ with us others who say: Let us go up to the house of Jehovah.

units.la: §. Quia ibi confident throni iuri, throni domui Dauidis.
units.tr: §. Because there the thrones of judgment are set, the thrones of the house of David.

units.la: IN explicatione proximè praecedentis versus ostendimus Prophetã formae internae, quam Deus indidit Ecclesiae suae, externam formam subiecisse ordine commodissimo: vt omnes Ecclesiae partes intus & foris iustã proportionem & [?] habere videamus. Illius autem externae formae substantiam esse docuimus in canone verbi Dei, quod verbum per Prophetas & Apostolos à Deo inspiratos literis consignatum est, & in Ecclesia depositum: hoc charactere signatam esse Ecclesiam Christi, ex cuius auctoritate & praescripto duplex opus in communione sanctorum obseruari possit: vnum , à piis erga Deum & verbum ipsius: alterum à Deo erga pios, & omnes eos qui in Ecclesiam aspectabilem [?]tabilem verbi diuini signo colliguntur. Operis nostri erga Deum duas esse partes: Unam, ut indesinenter ascendamus ad testimonium Domini, et contendamus ad perfectionem illius: Alteram, ut omnia conferamus ad eius gloriam, consilia, instituta, sermones, & facta nostra. Nunc vero locu alteru qui ad cõmunionē sanctorū pertinet, Propheta hoc versu aggreditur, nequis se in incertū currere aut aērem cædere existimet, dum opera dat Ecclesię in cõmunione sanctorum; sed potius ita statuat cum animo suo, nō debere se, ut seruum Domini, in officio suo segnescere; præsertim cũ sciat Dominum in ea communione præsentem esse, & nunquā ab actionibus suis salutaribus desinere.
units.tr: In explaining the verse immediately before this one, we showed that the Prophet, having given the Church of God its inner form, went on to set out its outer form in a most fitting order, so that we may see all the parts of the Church have a due proportion inside and out, and [?] order. We taught that the substance of that outer form lies in the canon of the Word of God, which, inspired by God through the Prophets and Apostles, has been committed to writing and deposited in the Church. By this mark the Church of Christ is sealed, and by its authority and prescription a twofold work can be observed in the communion of the saints: one, of the godly towards God and his Word; the other, of God towards the godly and all who are gathered into the visible Church by the sign of the divine Word. Our work towards God has two parts. The first is that we ceaselessly ascend to the testimony of the Lord and strive towards its perfection. The second is that we direct all our counsels, institutions, speeches and deeds to his glory. Now the Prophet, in this verse, takes up the other part, which belongs to the communion of the saints, lest anyone think he runs at random or beats the air while he labours for the Church in the communion of the saints. Rather, let him resolve in his own mind that he must not grow slack in his office, like a servant of the Lord. This is especially so since he knows that the Lord is present in that communion and never ceases from his saving works.

units.la: Summa igitur est huius versus, nunquam Dei partes desinere, aut otiari Deum in communione sanctorum: Deum semper esse accedentibus & consulentibus se præsentissimum, qui exaudiat, curet, præster quicquid opus est ad suorum bonum, ut rex iustissimus, gratiosisimus, ac potentissimus, sanctificans Ecclesiam suam, idq. nō solùm spiritu (hoc enim ad formam internam pertinet, de qua antè diximus) verùm etiam ordine aspectabili coniuncto cum verbo, atque ex verbo ipsius. Ad hunc enim ordinem aspectabilem Propheta respexit, dicens: Quia ibi [?]confident throni iuri, &c. Sensus igitur est; pios omnes lætari cum animis suis, accurrere, & sigere pedes suos in Ecclesia visibili, tum propter formá internam quam Deus exhibet Spiritu , tum propter formam externam inditam traditione verbi , & officia vltrò citroque ex verbo consequentia; id est, non so- lùm propter officia piorum ad testimonia Dei confluentium & celebrantium nomen illius, sed ante omnia propter officia, quæ Deus exercet in Ecclesia aspectabili, eam regens sceptro potente verbi, & iusto-ordine ad sceptri illius exercitium(vt vulgò loquuntur)pertinente. Et certè neminem puto ita desipere, vt domi suæ ordinem habendum putet, in domo Dei non putet; cùm Deus sit ordinis,non autem consusionis & status incompositi,vt dicit Apostolus.
units.tr: The sum of this verse, then, is that God never ceases from his part, nor is he idle in the communion of the saints. God is always most present to those who come to him and consult him: he hears them, takes care of them, and provides whatever is needed for their good, as a most just, most gracious and most powerful king who sanctifies his Church. He does this not only by the Spirit (for that belongs to the inner form, of which we spoke above), but also by an outward order joined to the Word and arising from the Word itself. For it is to this visible order that the Prophet looks when he says: "For there the thrones of judgment are set," and so on. The sense, therefore, is that all the godly rejoice in their hearts, hasten, and set their feet in the visible Church. They do so both because of the inner form which God gives by the Spirit, and because of the outer form that is bestowed by the handing down of the Word and by the mutual duties that follow from the Word. That is, they come not only for the duties of the godly who gather to the testimonies of God and celebrate his name, but above all for the duties which God performs in the visible Church, ruling it with the mighty sceptre of the Word and by a just order that belongs (as people commonly say) to the exercise of that sceptre. And indeed I do not think anyone is so foolish as to think that order must be kept in his own house but need not be kept in the house of God, since God is a God of order and not of confusion or disorder, as the Apostle says.

units.la: Quòd si quis ordinem illum diuinum in spiritu solùm,ac non in rebus externis esse contenderit , profectò cum hominem aut plane spiritualem,aut nulla ex parte spiritualem esse oportebit.Nam si omnis ordo à recta ratione est , & recta ratio à Deo velut principio omnis boni in natura rerum,quisquis ita sentit aut puré naturalis est & ψυχικὸς[?] (vt Scriptura loquitur) qui ordinem in domo Dei nò videt,aut (quod amplius est)ipsum naturæ sensum amiserit: spiritu- alem enim hominis perfectionem , dum in hac vita est,imaginari ridiculum. Si ergo mundus naturæ domicilium est , & hoc domicilium ordinem suum habet; quid de Ecclesia, quæ domicilium est gratiæ, dicturi fumu[?] Scilicet gratia naturam corruptam instaurabit, & perficiet imperfectam: domum verò suam fine ordine abire sinet auctor ille gratiæ.
units.tr: But if anyone should maintain that this divine order exists in the Spirit only, and not in external things, then he must surely be either wholly spiritual or not spiritual in any part. For if all order comes from right reason, and right reason comes from God as the source of all good in the nature of things, then whoever thinks this way is either purely natural and soulish [ψυχικὸς] (as Scripture speaks), who does not see order in the house of God, or else (what is worse) has lost the very sense of nature. For to imagine a spiritual perfection of man while he is in this life is ridiculous. If, then, the world is the dwelling of nature, and this dwelling has its own order, what will they say about the Church, which is the dwelling of grace? Surely grace will restore corrupt nature and perfect what is imperfect, and yet that author of grace will allow his own house to go on without order!

units.la: Huius autem ordinis quem Deus in domicilio suo constituit, duplex est ratio: Vna, simplex, propria, & necessaria; altera, composita figuris & ceremoniis, atque ambulatoria. Quam utramque rationem distinctè Deus posuit in prisca ecclesia Iudæorum. Partes verò pro ratione obiecti duæ: Vna Ciuilis, ad rerum humanarum administrationem spectans; altera Ecclesiastica, ad rerum sacrarum procurationem. Has duas partes secundum modum quem ante perstrinximus, Propheta attingit, dicens primùm quidem de rebus sacris & diuinis, Vt confidere thronos tui; deinde verò de humanis, Ibidem esse thronos domui Danidis. Quapropter vt singulæ huius versûs partes melius intelligantur, primùm administrationes illæ ex Prophetæ verbis distinguendæ sunt; post videndum quid fit quod de illis administrationibus prædicatur.
units.tr: Now of this order which God has established in his house there are two kinds: one simple, proper and necessary; the other composed of figures and ceremonies, and changeable. God set out both kinds distinctly in the ancient Church of the Jews. The parts, according to the nature of their object, are also two: one civil, concerned with the administration of human affairs; the other ecclesiastical, concerned with the management of sacred things. The Prophet touches on these two parts in the manner we have just outlined. First, he speaks of sacred and divine things, saying that thrones are set of yours; then he speaks of human things, saying that there are thrones for the house of David. Therefore, so that each part of this verse may be better understood, we must first distinguish those administrations from the Prophet's words, and afterwards see what is said of those administrations.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem id necesse est obseruari, administrationes metonymicè thronorum vel foliorum [?] appellatione designari. Notum est eos qui iuri dicundo præsunt, & alios qui auctoritate præualent, ex foliis [?] responsa dare consulentibus: & folia [?] esse iuris, auctoritatis, & potestatis signa. Cum itaque Propheta non vnius throni aut folia, sed complurium meminerit, eo significatum voluit à Deo esse potestates, vt Apostolus ad Romanos scribit, & ordinem inter poteftates ipsas constitutum, quarum sola sunt, ac postremo ordinem ipsarum ad eos quibus præsectæ sunt. Potestates autem cùm dicimus, secundùm rationem administrationis illius quæ ipsis commissa est, volumus accipi. Nam cùm potestas nulla sit nisi à Deo, id pro certo nobis habendum est, solam Dei potestatem, quæ sine principio est, sine sine esse, & non solùm tempore, verumetiam re ipsa (ut loquuntur) indeterminatam: Et diuerso autem cùm reliquæ potestates principium à Deo habeant, etiam finibus suis circumscriptas esse, & limitatum (ut vocant) earum modum.
units.tr: And first of all we must note that the administrations are designated by metonymy through the name of thrones or seats. It is known that those who preside over giving judgment, and others who hold sway by authority, give answers to those who consult them from their seats, and that seats are signs of right, authority and power. Since the Prophet speaks not of one throne or seat but of several, he meant to signify that powers are from God, as the Apostle writes to the Romans, and that an order has been established among the powers themselves, whose these powers are, and finally an order of these powers toward those to whom they are set over. When we say "powers," we wish them to be understood according to the nature of the administration committed to them. For since no power exists except from God, we must hold this as certain: God's power alone, which has no beginning, has no end, and is unlimited not only in time but also in its very nature (as people say). The other powers, on the contrary, have their beginning from God, and are also bounded by their ends, and their measure is limited (as they call it).

units.la: Est autem inter homines potestatum in hac uita modus (si bene obseruaui) triplex.Primus est, quem Philosophi dictione Græca [?]δεσποτικὸν appellauerunt: Secundus, quem πολιτικὸν; Tertius, quem ὑπηρετικὸν vocant. Despoticam siue dominicam (ut cum iureconsultis loquar) potestatem eam appellamus, quæ sic absoluta est, ut tota illius ratio ex voluntate illius pendeat qui dominus est, citra ullam iuris illius cum subditis communicationem. Atque hæc in Tyrannicam transfit facillimè, cùm dominus plenitudine potestatis suæ (ut cum vulgo loquar) abutitur. Politicam potestatem eam appellamus, quæ temperatum habet dominium cum eorum qui subsunt voluntate, & consensu. Tertij verò generis potestatem, quam ministratoriam dicere possumus, intelligimus eam quæ voluntati alienæ tota obsequitur: ac proinde partim ex superioris, à quo instituta est, voluntate leges accipit, partimq. voluntati eorum qui subsunt accommodatur interdum, & contemperatur quodammodo ad utilitatem ipsorum. Primum genus à solius dominantis pendet arbitrio; qui ad se respicit & utilitatem suam. Secundū pendet à consilio præcipuè dominantis, subditosrumque secundarió; & respicit ad utilitatem publicam. Tertium ab utrisque pendet, voluntatemque horum & illorum spectat legitimè ad utilitatem omnium. Atque hæc quidem potesstatum genera si cum potestate Dei comparentur, plane subsunt voluntati illius: sed Deo, qui est per se (vt ita dicam) sufficientissimus, adeoque ipsa in se sufficientia, nullam utilitatem adferunt. Sin autem secundum se, vt inter homines sunt, considerari eas placuerit, Primum genus, vt apud homines vsurpatur, plerumque nimis est αὐτοκράτωρ[?], & brutū nescio quid aduersus naturā sapit: Cætera tam in societate humana ordini publico conuenientiora videntur esse, tum etiā à Deo in regendo populo ipsius; tanquā æquiora & naturæ humanæ magis consentanea fuerūt instituta: cùm illa potestas impetio mentis tespondeat, hæc sensuum & corporis ministerio. Sic autem instituta sunt, vt politicus ordo vtrumque genus potestatis in se habuerit; Ecclesiasticus verò contentus fuerit solo ministratorio, quia in ratione Ecclesiæ Dominus summum ius imperiumque semper & constantissimè sibi vindicauit. Itaque in Politico fuit ordo potestatum inter se, cum summæ quæ regia dicebatur, cum vero inferiorum ex ordine : quem ordinem potestates illæ omnes, & inter se ipsæ, & erga eos qui ipsis suberant & commissi erant administrationi ipsorum, obseruabant. In Ecclesiastico vero erant omnia ministratoria, à solo Dei imperio pendentia, & ad vniuersi vtilitatem solùm pertendentia: adeò vt ne ipsi quidem sacerdoti summo liceret in re incognita quidquam, nisi consulto ore Domini, statuere : quemadmodum aliquot exemplis in libris Mosis ostenditur.
units.tr: Now there is, among men in this life, a threefold mode of powers (if I have observed rightly). The first is what the philosophers called despotic [δεσποτικὸν]. The second is political [πολιτικὸν]. The third they call ministerial [ὑπηρετικὸν]. We call that power despotic or lordly (to speak with the jurists) which is so absolute that its whole nature depends on the will of him who is lord, without any sharing of that right with the subjects. This power very easily turns into tyranny, when the lord abuses the fullness of his power (to speak with the common people). We call that power political which holds its dominion in moderation, with the will and consent of those who are subject to it. We understand the third kind of power, which we may call ministerial, to be that which wholly obeys the will of another. Accordingly, it receives its laws partly from the will of the superior by whom it was instituted, and partly is adapted to the will of those who are subject, and sometimes tempered in some measure for their benefit. The first kind depends on the will of the ruler alone, who looks to himself and his own advantage. The second depends chiefly on the counsel of the ruler, and secondarily on that of the subjects, and looks to the public good. The third depends on both, and legitimately regards the will of both the one and the other for the good of all. Now if these kinds of power are compared with the power of God, they are wholly subject to his will; but they bring no advantage to God, who is in himself (so to speak) most sufficient, and so entirely sufficient in himself. If, however, it pleases us to consider them in themselves, as they are among men, then the first kind, as it is used among men, is for the most part too self-ruling [αὐτοκράτωρ] and savours of some brutish thing contrary to nature. The others seem more fitting to public order in human society, and also to God's own governing of his people. They were established as fairer and more agreeable to human nature, since the former kind answers to the impulse of the mind, while these answer to the ministry of the senses and the body. And these were so instituted that the political order would have both kinds of power within itself, while the ecclesiastical order would be content with the ministerial alone, because in the nature of the Church the Lord has always and most constantly claimed for himself the supreme right and command. Thus in the political order there was an ordering of powers among themselves, with the highest, called royal, and the lower in their order; and all these powers, both among themselves and toward those who were subject to them and committed to their administration, observed this order. In the ecclesiastical order, however, everything was ministerial, depending on the command of God alone and reaching only to the common good. So much so that not even the high priest himself was permitted to decide anything in an unknown matter without first consulting the mouth of the Lord, as is shown by several examples in the books of Moses.

units.la: De his ergo potestatibus tria sunt quæ Propheta hoc versu distinctè prædicat: Primum, quod nam fit officium harum potestatum : Secundum, qui custodes officij : Tertium denique qualis earum constitutio à Domino. Ossicium demonstrat Psaltes[?], cum thronos appellat iuri : custodes & ϱομοφύλακας[?] exprimit, dicendo, thronos domui Dauidis institutos : Constitutionem verò pauculis verbis declarauit dicens: illic confidere: id autem est, Hierosolymis. Ius autè officiumq. ad potestates pertinent pro conditione earum, & conditione temporum, varié circumscriptum est. Nam cùm potestatum aliæ humanæ & politicæ sint, aliæ diuinæ & Ecclesiasticæ; similiter rationem iuris necesse est duplicem obseruari : unam, civilem & humanam, secundùm quam hominem inter homines necesse est inculpatè & fine crimine ciuiliter viuere : alterà spiritualem & diuinam, secundùm quam necesse est hominem quemque coram Domino ambulare inculpatè, & esse integrum, vt cōtinetur verbis fœderis quod Deus olim cum Abrahamo pepigit. Iuris humani præcepta tria prudentes tradiderunt: honestè viuere, alterum non lædere, & suum cuique tribuere. Etsi hæc duo, si quis accuratiùs volet expendere, ad vnum & idem vidētur pertinere. Nam qui suum cuique tribuit, non lædit alterum: & contrà qui lædit alterum, suum cuique minimè tribuit. Iuris autem diuini præcepta si quis in pauca volet contrahere, commodè verbis Pauli vsurus est, ad Titum scribentis hoc modo, Illuxit gratia illa Dei salutifera quibusquis hominibus, erudiens nos, vt abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatibus, sobriè, & iustè, & piè viuamus in præsenti sæculo, expectantes beatā illam spem & illustrem aduentum illum gloriæ magni illius Dei ac servatoris Iesu Christi. Nam proeo quòd humanæ iustitiæ fundamentum est natura; & lux, sconscientia naturæ corruptissimæ : hic fundamentum supernaturale diuini iuris ponitur gratia Dei salutaris; & lux gratiæ, sides in conscientia domesticorum Dei & piorum illucefcens. Proeo quòd opera humanæ iustitiæ illius ponuntur ea quæ paulo ante diximus; diuini iuris religiosissima opera nobis præfcribuntur duo: unam, ut opera infructuosa naturæ corruptæ, adeoque ipsa corruptio quæ inhæret nobis, & arma quæuis illius depellantur: alterum, ut opera lucis vel fructus spiritus progignamus. horum modus triplex; Primus, respectu nostri, prudens & peruigil sobrietas, ne circumueniamur ab extrinsecis impedimentis, aut intrinsecis perturbationibus nostris: Secundus erga alios, iustitia, qua damus operam mente, animo, sermone, facto, nequem lædamus, sed suum cuique tribuamus coram Domino, à quo vocati sumus in unitaté spiritus: Tertius erga Deum, pietas, qua Deum religiosè cognoscimus, colimusque, & in ipso recognoscimus quoscunque vocat ad participationem eiusdem gratiæ. Postremò autem pro eo quòd humana illa atque, ciuilis iustitia, in terminis miseræ huius naturæ conquiescens, nihil certò habet quò ulterius præter hanc vitam respiciat, salutaria illa præcepta Dei nos ad spem gloriæ & gratiæ excitant, quæ hominem vel miserrimum & desperatissimum supra hanc naturam possit ad boni summi expectationem erigere.
units.tr: There are therefore three things that the Prophet distinctly sets out in this verse concerning these powers. First, what the office of these powers is. Second, who are the guardians of the office. Third, and finally, how they are constituted by the Lord. The Psalmist shows the office when he calls the thrones "judgment" [iuri], and he expresses the guardians, the fellow-guardians [ὁμοφύλακας], by saying that the thrones were set up for the house of David. He declares the constitution in a few words when he says: "There to sit; that is, at Jerusalem." Right and office belong to the powers, and they are defined in various ways according to their condition and the condition of the times. For since some powers are human and political, and others divine and ecclesiastical, it is necessary that a twofold rule of right be observed in the same way. One is civil and human, according to which a man must live blamelessly and without crime among men as a citizen. The other is spiritual and divine, according to which every man must walk blameless before the Lord and be upright, as is contained in the words of the covenant that God once made with Abraham. The jurists handed down three precepts of human right: to live honourably, not to harm another, and to give each his own. Although these two, if anyone wishes to weigh them more carefully, seem to pertain to one and the same thing. For he who gives each his own does not harm another, and conversely he who harms another does not give each his own at all. If anyone wishes to gather the precepts of divine right into a few words, he will use fittingly the words of Paul writing to Titus in this way: "The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live soberly, righteously and godly in the present age, looking for that blessed hope and the glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ." For in the one case nature is the foundation of human justice, and light is the conscience of corrupt nature. Here the supernatural foundation of divine right is laid down: the saving grace of God, and the light of grace, faith shining in the conscience of the household of God and of the godly. In the one case the works of that human justice are set down as those we have just mentioned; in the other, two most religious works of divine right are prescribed to us. One is that the unfruitful works of corrupt nature, and indeed that corruption which clings to us, and all its weapons, be driven away. The other is that we bring forth the works of light, or the fruit of the Spirit. The manner of these is threefold. The first, with respect to ourselves, is a prudent and watchful sobriety, lest we be overcome by external hindrances or by our own inner disturbances.
