The second, toward others, is justice, by which we take pains in mind, heart, speech and deed not to harm anyone, but to give each his own before the Lord, by whom we have been called into the unity of the Spirit. The third, toward God, is piety, by which we know and worship God in a religious manner, and in him acknowledge all whom he calls to participation in the same grace. Lastly, since that human and civil justice, resting within the limits of this wretched nature, has nothing certain to look to beyond this life, those saving precepts of God rouse us to the hope of glory and of grace, which can lift up even the most wretched and despairing man above this nature to the expectation of the highest good.

units.la: Ad hæc duo iuris, corporalis inquam & spiritualis, humani & diuini, genera, thronos, id est, administrationes olim in populo suo instituit Deus. quarum administrationum tanta est necessitas, ut neq. ordo naturæ sine ordine humano in rebus creatis constare possit, neque in hominibus ordo gratiæ fine ordine diuino & Ecclesiastico. Suus naturæ ordo à Deo datus est,& suus gratiæ, suumque ius ordini vtrique inditum : quod ius à singulis hominibus prudenter coli,à custodibus verò quàm religiofifsime diligentissimèque vrgeri necesse est.
units.tr: By these two kinds of right, I mean the bodily and the spiritual, the human and the divine, God once established thrones, that is, administrations, among his people. So great is the necessity of these administrations that neither the order of nature can stand among created things without human order, nor the order of grace among men without divine and ecclesiastical order. The order of nature is given by God, and so is the order of grace, and a right is implanted in each order. This right ought to be cultivated prudently by individual men, and urged most religiously and diligently by its guardians.

units.la: Nihil de singularibus istius iuris partibus dicturi fumus, pramus [?] Deum,iuris diuini ex gratia, & humani ex natura auctorem fanctiffimum,vt mentes hominum plus fatis hoc funesto tempore à iure aberrantes afficiat vero ftudio quaerendi vtriusque iuris: quia frustrà ius docebitur, nisi adest animus noscendi illius & retinendi studiosus ; quem animū tum ipsi nobis,tum aliis omnibus magisac magis indi optamus à Domino. Id vnū dicturi fumus, quod ex multis Scripturæ locis apud Mosem constat: quemadmodum populares,inter quos de iure non fatis conueniebat , superiores suos consulebant,vt quid iuris effet ex eis cognoscerent ; ita etiam eos qui iuri dicendo praerant, fi ius non tenerent,aut non fatis sibi tenere viderentur, non temere & pro imperio consulentibus refpondiffe ; sed potestatem summam, summum iuris potestatumque auctorem, consuluisse, ex cuius ore ( vt Scriptura loquitur ) responsa darent. Atque hanc rem non solùm pij reges & principes diligenter obferuarunt in rebus-humanis,verumetiam rerum sacrarum administri eo religiosius ad confulendū Dominū adiucrunt; quo grauiús in rebus sacris & diuinis quàm in profanis atque humanis peccari animaduerterunt: præsertim cùm sibi cōfcij essent longè angustiorem ipsis esse potestatem à Deo attributam, id est, non auctoritate politica, sed administratoria solùm se esse praeditos, suprà quem administrationis modum si quid arrogarent sibi, impium fore in Deum, & Ecclesiam eius sacrilegium.
units.tr: We are not going to say anything about the particular parts of this right. We pray God, the most holy author of divine right through grace and of human right through nature, that he may move the minds of men, which in this baneful time stray from right more than enough, to a true zeal for seeking both rights. For right will be taught in vain unless there is a mind eager to know and retain it, and this mind we wish for ourselves and for all others more and more from the Lord. We will say only this one thing, which is clear from many passages of Scripture in Moses: just as the common people, among whom there was not enough agreement about right, consulted their superiors so that they might learn from them what the right was, so too those who presided over judging, if they did not hold the right or seemed not to hold it sufficiently, did not rashly answer those who consulted them on their own authority. Rather they consulted the supreme power, the supreme author of right and of powers, from whose mouth (as Scripture speaks) they gave their answers. This matter was not only diligently observed in human affairs by pious kings and princes, but also the ministers of sacred things approached the consultation of the Lord all the more religiously, the more they perceived that sin is more serious in sacred and divine matters than in profane and human ones. Especially since they were aware that the power given them by God was much narrower, that is, that they were endowed not with political authority but only with administrative authority, and that if they claimed anything for themselves beyond this measure of administration, it would be impiety against God and sacrilege against his Church.

units.la: Atque hoc illud est, ad quod nominatim Propheta respiciebat, cùm faceret mentionem iuris. Nam Deus inter veltes sacras λόγον[?] instītuerat, quod vulgò ex translatione vetere Pectorale iuris appellatur: ex quo pectorali Deus per Vrim & Tummim respondebat extra ordinem consulentibus, siquid grauius, aut quod scientiam excederet ipsorum, oriretur. Hinc reges; hinc sacerdotes, hinc iudices responsa exorabant; & certi aliquid cognoscebant de rebus incertis. Quae cum ita sint, omninò videmus quàm verum sit illud quod antè dicebamus; hīc agi potissimum de ordine Ecclesiastico, quo Deus sanctis olim voluit consulere & testificari praesentiam suam. sed ex eo sequitur alia esse perpetua in ordine Ecclesiastico, alia tran-feuntia. Perpetuū habuit Ecclesia λόγον[?] inde à principio, & habitura est ad consummationē vsque seculi: temporarium verò habuit prisca Ecclesia Iudaeorum & ceremoniale praeter alia pluri-ma;
units.tr: This is precisely what the Prophet had in mind by name when he made mention of right. For God had placed among the sacred vestments the oracle [λόγιον], which is commonly called in the old translation the breastplate of right. Through this breastplate God answered by Urim and Thummim those who consulted him outside the ordinary course, whenever something more serious arose, or something that exceeded their knowledge. Hence kings, hence priests, hence judges sought answers, and they learned something certain about uncertain matters. Since these things are so, we see entirely how true is what we said before: that here the ecclesiastical order is treated chiefly, by which God once willed to give counsel to his saints and to bear witness to his presence. But from this it follows that some things in the ecclesiastical order are perpetual and others transitory. The Church has had the oracle [λόγιον] perpetually from the beginning, and will have it until the consummation of the age. But the earlier Church of the Jews had a temporary ceremonial, along with many other things.

units.la: Note: the nine-line sentence above ends "pluri-" at the page foot; the line "ma;" is the catchword. ma, λόγος. Transiit ceremonia & antiquata est; λόγῳ in seculum permanet, quem nos cōsuluimus, & omnes administros Dei æquissimum est sepositis aliis omnibus studiis & occupationibus, quibus plus æquo inconsiderati & imprudentes quam plurimi immerguntur, studiosissimè consulere. Atque hæc quidem de potestate Ecclesiastica, quam Deus in Iudæorum Ecclesia auctoritate sua sanciverat.
units.tr: The ceremony passed away and was abolished; but the word [λόγος] remains into the age, and we, and all the ministers of God, ought most diligently to consult it, most fairly setting aside all other pursuits and occupations, in which very many, inconsiderate and imprudent beyond what is right, are immersed. These things indeed concern the ecclesiastical power, which God in the Church of the Jews had sanctioned by his authority.

units.la: Illius autem potestatis & ordinis, sicut etiam humani, custodes instituit Deus Reges & Princi-pes, quorum solia in pietate iustitiaque constabiliuntur à Domino. Propterea Pfalres[?] ab his potestatibus, quas Ecclesiasticas appellauimus, ad civilem potestatem transit; subjiciens ibidem thronos ad domum Davidis in urbe Hierosolymorum constituere: tanquam si diceret Deum auctorem esse naturæ pariter ac gratiæ; ac proinde ut gratia administras potestates ordinat; ita etiam naturæ & humani ordinis potestates esse ab ordinatione eius: Cumque naturæ bona perficiat gratia ac nō aboleat, sapientissime Deum prospexisse, ut quæ bona in ordine humano sunt, eadem in Ecclesia observentur: non enim reiicienda esse, quia humana sunt; sed quia bona, retinenda & excolenda cultura salutaris gratiæ. Sunt ergo Reges, & Principes, & potestates humanæ in Ecclesia, & sunt deEcclesia, cùm ejusdē capitis & corporis in unitate Spiritus una fide sunt effecti participes. Quapropter etiam hortabatur Apostolus; vt deprecationes, preces, postulationes, gratiarum actiones pro Regibus, & quibusuis in eminentia constitutis.
units.tr: Yet God also established kings and princes as guardians of that power, as of the human order as well, and their thrones are established in piety and justice by the Lord. Therefore the Psalmist passes from these powers, which we have called ecclesiastical, to the civil power, placing in the same place thrones for the house of David in the city of Jerusalem. It is as if he were saying that God is the author of nature no less than of grace, and that accordingly, just as grace ordains the ecclesiastical powers, so too the powers of nature and of the human order come from his ordinance. And since grace perfects the goods of nature and does not abolish them, it was most wisely provided by God that what goods exist in the human order should be observed also in the Church. For they are not to be rejected because they are human, but because they are good they are to be retained and cultivated by the care of saving grace. Therefore there are kings, and princes, and human powers in the Church, and they belong to the Church, since by being made partakers of the same head and body, in the unity of the Spirit and one faith, they are of it. For this reason also the Apostle exhorted that supplications, prayers, petitions and thanksgivings be made for kings and for all who are set in high places.

units.la: Sed tamen cùm domus Dauidis throni differtis verbis hoc loco appellantur, tria illa capita in memoriam opus est revocari, quæ ante distinximus, cùm de domo Iehouæ & Hierofolymis ageremus: Domum Dauidis nempe fecundùm naturæ modum, fecundùm figuram, & fecundùm veritatem intelligi pro ratione locorum oportere: Secundùm naturam significari homines qui suo ordine extiterunt ex ea familia in rerum natura: Secundùm figuram eandem familiam intelligi, quia regnum spirituale Christi figuravit: Secundùm veritatem esse illud ipsum Spirituale regnum, quod Christus Dauidis filius æternùm possidet, quemadmodum angelus dixerat: Hic erit magnus, & filius altissimi vocabitur, dabitq. ei Dominus Deus sedem Dauidis patris ipsius. Est autem regnum temporale, quodcunquein Ecclesia & inter homines humano ordine instituit Deus, ad custodiam omnis boni ita constitutum, vt he illud quidem ipsum bonum spirituale, quod in Ecclesia disposuit Deus, alienum à cura Regum habere oporteat. Nam si humano ordine & instituto obligantur ad procurationem communis boni; certè ex quo illi in eo ipso humano ordine à Deo præsente sanctificati sunt; reipsa obligantur humano & diuino iure etiam ad bonorum spiritualium procurationem. non dico administrationem: nam distincta sunt dona, administrationes, & operationes singulari prouidentia Dei. Quapropter nec reges in administrationes Ecclesiasticas inuolare possunt, nec administri Ecclesiastici in regias & ciuiles humanasque, singulis tantum est oneris, vt surore, non sapientia agi videantur, qui alia insuper onera sibi imponi petunt, aut etiam facile patiuntur, quacunque occasione aut specie id fieri posse putauerint. De cura solùm & custodia loquor, quam piis regibus principibusque Deus semper demandauit: non vt leges ferant Ecclesiis quà Ecclesiæ sunt, id est, regno spirituali Christi, qui vnus animarum nostrarum legislator est; sed vt leges à Deo latas per administros eius obseruari curét, instent, & vrgeant, nequid de cultu Dei decedat, vnde ira ipsius in administros, regemque siue principes, & populares omnes accendatur. Hoc igitur commune est omnium temporum in Ecclesia Dei: singulare autem illius temporis fuit institutum illius regni, qua typus à Deo institutus est, quo spirituale regnum Christi fuit in rudi populo ante plenitudinem temporum adumbratum. Nam huius typi, veritatisque contemplatione Ecclesiam illam confirmare in omnibus rerū difficultatibus & consolari voluerat inde à principio Deus, Abrahamo de ea dicens, In semine tuo. benedicetur omnibus gentibus: Dauidi verò longè gloriosiùs multa; ut cùm plurimis Scripturæ locis,tum Psal.89.demonstratur luculentissimè.Etenim cùm prisca illa ætas quibusdam veluti fulmentis opus habuerit, ut in expectatione Christi Iesu firma cosisteret,sapientissimè Deus prouiderat, ut quemadmodū sacerdotij, sic etiam regni æterni illius umbraculū aliquod & vestigium in rebus humanis existeret: quam ad rem tribus Iehudæ, & in ea nominatim domus Davidis electa est. Quapropter etsi ordinem politicum in Ecclesia Dei planè oportet existere, aut Ecclesiam sese in eo ordine continere, denique alterum ordinem alteri coniunctum esse: id tamen ex hoc loco intelligendum est, ciuilis huius ordinis non tam propter necessitatem ipsius mentionem hoc loco factam (quæ tamen summa est necessitas) quàm propter typum à Deo institutum, ut promissionum suarum de regno spirituali æternoque Christi veritatem aliquo pacto ante oculos priscæ illius Ecclesiæ repræsentaret.
units.tr: But since the words "the house of David's throne" are used in this passage, we must recall the three points we set out earlier, when we were discussing the house of Jehovah and Jerusalem. The house of David is to be understood according to the manner of nature, according to figure, and according to truth, as the places require. According to nature, it signifies the men who in their proper order came into existence from that family. According to figure, the same family is understood, because it prefigured the spiritual kingdom of Christ. According to truth, it is that very spiritual kingdom which Christ, the son of David, possesses for ever, as the angel had said: "He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father" (Luke 1). But there is also a temporal kingdom, whatever God has established in the Church and among men by human order, constituted for the safeguarding of every good. Yet this must be so arranged that the spiritual good itself, which God has ordained in the Church, is not to be placed outside the care of kings. For if they are bound by human order and institution to promote the common good, then, since they have been sanctified in that same human order by the presence of God, they are truly bound by both human and divine right to the promotion of spiritual goods as well. I do not say to the administration of them, for "there are distinct gifts, administrations and operations" by the singular providence of God (1 Cor. 12). Therefore kings cannot break into ecclesiastical administrations, nor ecclesiastical ministers into royal, civil and human affairs. Each has his own burden only, so that those who seek to have other burdens laid upon them, or who readily allow it whenever they think it can be done on some occasion or pretext, seem to act from fury rather than wisdom. I speak only of care and protection, which God has always committed to pious kings and princes: not that they should make laws for the Churches as Churches, that is, for the spiritual kingdom of Christ, who alone is the lawgiver of our souls; but that they should see to it, press and urge that the laws given by God be observed through his ministers, lest anything be lost from the worship of God, by which his wrath would be kindled against the ministers, the king or princes, and all the people. This, then, is common to all times in the Church of God. But that kingdom had a peculiar institution in that time, in which God established a type, by which the spiritual kingdom of Christ was foreshadowed among a rude people before the fullness of time. For from the contemplation of this type and of the truth, God had willed from the beginning to strengthen and console that Church in all the difficulties of things, saying to Abraham of it, "In your seed all the nations will be blessed"; but to David he promised much more gloriously, as is most clearly shown in many places of Scripture, and especially in Psalm 89. For since that ancient age needed certain supports, as it were, so that it might stand firm in expectation of Jesus Christ, God in his wisdom had provided that, just as there was a priesthood, so also some shadow and trace of that eternal kingdom should exist among human affairs. To this end the tribe of Judah was chosen, and within it the house of David by name. Therefore, although a political order must certainly exist in the Church of God, or the Church must keep itself within that order, and one order must be joined to another, yet this is to be understood from this passage: the mention of civil order made here is not so much because of its necessity (which is nonetheless supreme), as because of the type instituted by God, so that it might in some way set before the eyes of that ancient Church the truth of his promises concerning the spiritual and eternal kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Atque hæ quidem administrationes in ea Ecclesia à Deo constitutæ sunt, ut forma externa Ecclesiæ conveniente ordine servaretur: qua forma singuli ad conscientiam & probationem internæ illius formæ, quam principio dicebamus,quasi ducerentur manu. Sed quia (ut olim dicebat Iurisconsultus quidam) parum est si ius in ciuitate sit, nisi sint qui dicere possint; ita etiam res fein Ecclesia habet; age de custodibus & curatoribus iuris istius videamus.
units.tr: Indeed these administrations were established by God in that Church so that the external form of the Church might be kept in a fitting order; by this form individuals were, as it were, led by the hand to the conscience and proof of that inward form which we spoke of at the beginning. But because (as a certain jurist once said) it is of little use for there to be law in a state unless there are men who can speak it, so it is also with the matter in the Church. Let us therefore see who are the guardians and curators of that law.

units.la: Custodes igitur iuris & ordinis sancti,quem hoc loco Ecclesia prædicauit, communi appellatione significati sunt domus vel familiæ Dauidis: quemadmodum apud Prophetas passim videmus eo nomine hanc domum celebrari,& contrà præ cæteris familiis in populo Dei reprehendi,fi quando iusta ratio ordinis à Deo imperati publicè negligeretur . Huius autem cuftodiæ ac procurationis modus in his Prophetæ verbis duplex intelligendus est. Nam quà Dauid fecundùm humanú ordinem fuit potestate præditus,modus custodiæ humanus est;quà autem fuit typus Christi ex diuina institutione, diuinus modus ; cuius in Christo & à Christo cõfummabatur veritas:Humani illius modi caput fuit Dauid;& quicunq. ad familiã eius pertinuerunt, ij quæda velut membra extiterunt; cum summo illo capite ad corporis totius & ordinis in corpore conseruationem conspirantia fecundùm Deum. Diuini autem modi caput vnicum & immutabile Christus est : qui minifterio non solùm sacerdotis summi ,aut seniorum ex sacerdotibus, aut sacerdotum ipsorum atque Leuitarum ex ordine , verumetiam Prophetarum extra ordinem,quotiescunque visum effet,vtebatur ad hoc suum opus in Ecclesia sua promouendum . ex quo fiebat , vt hi quidem singulari sua vocatione in ministerio[?] suo ope- râm ram consumerent ;illi veró , Dauid inquam & qui ex familia eius,vrgerent ministerium illud, & ordinem humanum suum in procurando rerum sacrarum ordine religiosè occuparent. Sic videmus Pfalres à Dauide fuisse Ecclesiæ datos;& ordines ministeriį sacri, adhibito Prophetarum & fanctorū Dei virorum consilio,distributos : vt disertis verbis auctor libri Chronicorum aliquoties confirmauit.
units.tr: The guardians, then, of the holy law and order which the Church proclaimed in this place are designated by the common name of the house or family of David. Just as among the Prophets we see this house celebrated everywhere under that name, and, on the contrary, rebuked before the other families of the people whenever the just order commanded by God was publicly neglected. The manner of this guardianship and care is to be understood in a twofold way in these words of the Prophet. For insofar as David was endowed with power according to human order, the manner of guardianship is human; but insofar as he was a type of Christ by divine institution, the manner is divine, and its truth was fulfilled in Christ and by Christ. The head of that human manner was David, and those who belonged to his family were, as it were, certain members, agreeing with that supreme head, according to God, for the preservation of the whole body and of order in the body. The one and unchanging head of the divine manner is Christ, who used for this work of promoting his Church not only the ministry of the high priest, or of the elders from among the priests, or of the priests themselves and the Levites from the order, but also prophets outside the order, whenever it seemed good to him. From this it followed that the latter spent their labour in the ministry by their singular calling, while the former, David I mean and those of his family, pressed on with that ministry and religiously occupied themselves with their human order in the proper arrangement of holy things. Thus we see that the psalmists were given to the Church by David, and that the orders of the sacred ministry were distributed with the counsel of the Prophets and holy men of God, as the author of the Books of Chronicles has several times confirmed in plain words.

units.la: Restat locus tertius,de stabilimento istius ordinis: quod Prophera innuit perpaucis verbis, dicens hæc folia illic confidere. priùs quidem, vbi de fidelibus Ecclesiæ membrisactum est , dixit tribus ascendere illuc ad testimonium Iehouæ: nunc verò agens de diuino ordine , aut rebus diuinis ministrante ; qui Dei auctoritate inftitutus est in Ecclesia eius , dicit Prophetaillo in loco confidere. Id autem significare videtur Psalres confidendi verbo, Deu auctorem istius ordinis in Ecclesia sua , tum stabiliuisse ordinem illu, tum verò actiones illius ordinis præsentia sua direxisse & firmauisse ad gloriam suam.Confidentenim,qui in pace sunt,aut qui immoti sunt ab aduersis rebus:Confident prætereà,qui maturé coufilia ineunt, vt benè rebus gerendis præsint[?] ac salutariter. Cùm itaque hi throni dicuntur confidere , partim de pace & firmamento illorum prouisum esse à Deo intelligimus,partimque res iusto ordine consilio: que prouisas,curatas,gestas,tanquam à sapientibus administris diuinæ voluntatis,in quorum consessu cósilioque (ut alibi dicit Psaltes) Deus præsuerit. Enimuerò quidni sedíssent sedente Domino? quidni substitissent, Deo suam sedem ac domicilium in eo loco statuente? Nam vbi tutiùs sedeat Ecclesia piorum, quàm in side & habitatione Domini, sanctificantis præsentia sua & cósirmantis electos omnes; ac præsertim administros suos? Quòd si illic, nō alibi sedent, quid nobis cum illa ἀνθρωποτεχνία[?], quæ tam multorum infestat mentes? Hanc Spartam curemus singuli quam nacti sumus, & sequamur vestigia dicétis Pauli, Quid mea interest etiam de extraneis iudicare? nónne de iis qui intús sunt vos iudicatis? de extraneis verò Deus iudicat.
units.tr: There remains a third point, concerning the establishment of this order, which the Prophet indicates in very few words, saying, "These thrones are settled there." Earlier, when he spoke of the faithful members of the Church, he said that the tribes went up there to the testimony of Jehovah; but now, speaking of the divine order, or of those who minister in divine things, which was instituted by the authority of God in his Church, he says that the thrones are settled in that place. The Psalmist seems by the word "settled" to signify that God, the author of this order in his Church, both established that order and, by his presence, directed and strengthened the actions of that order to his own glory. For those are "settled" who are at peace, or who are unmoved by adverse things; and those are "settled" who take counsel maturely, so that they preside well and wholesomely over the affairs they manage. Therefore, when these thrones are said to be settled, we understand partly that their peace and stability were provided for by God, and partly that matters were provided, cared for and carried out in right order by counsel, as by wise ministers of the divine will, in whose assembly and counsel (as the Psalmist says elsewhere) God presides. Indeed, how could they not have sat, the Lord sitting there? How could they not have stood, God setting his seat and dwelling in that place? For where would the Church of the pious sit more securely than in the faith and dwelling of the Lord, who sanctifies by his presence and strengthens all the elect, and especially his ministers? But if they sit there and nowhere else, what have we to do with that human craftiness [ἀνθρωποτεχνία], which infests the minds of so many? Let each of us look after this Sparta which he has been allotted, and let us follow the steps of Paul's words: "What is it to me to judge even those outside? Do you not judge those who are within? But God judges those outside" (1 Cor. 5).

units.la: O verè beatos illos, qui hac præsentia Domini apud suos versantis in animis suis confirmati ordinem illum diuinum agnoscunt; tum Ecclesiasticum, quo docentur diuina iura, & in fide ac obsequio sancto continentur pij; tum verò Ciuilem, quo intercedente atq. adiuuante ad studiū diuini ordinis excitantur! Nam prosectò, ut Deus unus est, ita unus ordo quem instituit Deus: si non unus, ne ordo quidem est: Nam eo ipso quòd ordo est, unitas eius statutur. Quòd si ordo unus est, quomodo unū esse omnes inter nos ordine, & pugnantes item animis inter nos possimus? Atqui unum ordine diuinitus imperato sumus: throni ordinis à Deo instituti in Ecclesia, & in republica: in Ecclesia,
units.tr: Blessed indeed are those who, confirmed in their souls by the presence of the Lord dwelling among his own, acknowledge that divine order: the ecclesiastical order, by which the godly are taught the divine laws and held in faith and holy obedience, and also the civil order, by which, through his intercession and help, they are stirred to zeal for the divine order. For surely, as God is one, so the order that God has established is one. If it is not one, it is not an order at all, since its very being an order implies its unity. If the order is one, how can we, who are bound together in one order, be at odds with one another in our minds? Yet we are placed under one order, commanded by God: there are two thrones of order established by God, one in the Church and one in the commonwealth. In the Church there is the divine order of Christ, which no one can oppose without impiety; in the commonwealth there is the human order, which no one can resist without grievous insult to nature itself.

units.la: diuinus ordo Christi , quem nemo fine impietate oppugnare potest : in republica, humanus ordo,cui nemo obsistit fine atroce in naturam ipsam contumelia.In Ecclesia,ius ab ordine diuino cognoscimus, ius conftantiffimů ab xterna illa ratione proficiscens, & immutabile : In republica , iuris illius diuini habemus adiumentů, & potestates administras propter hunc ipsum finem à Deo datas. Atque hæc omnia in fede quadam firma & immota, id est,in Ecclefia,sunt à Deo cóftituta: vnde administros suos iubet ordini publico & singulis membris ad hunc ordinem. pertinentibus in sua quemque vocatione consulere, & omnes sanctificat præfentia sua.
units.tr: In the Church we learn of a right that springs from the divine order, a most constant right that proceeds from that eternal reason and is unchangeable. In the commonwealth we have the aid of that divine right, and the powers of administration, which God has given for this very end. All these things have been set up by God in a certain firm and immovable seat, that is, in the Church. Hence he bids his ministers attend to the public order, and to each member belonging to that order in his own calling, and he sanctifies all by his presence.

units.la: Absit igitur à nobis, fi Christiani fumus, fi ordinem Ecclesiæ & reipublicæ omnisque focietatis humanæ diligimus , fi ius à Deo & naturæ ordine imperatů,colimus; fi stabile quoddam veræ pacis & tranquillitatis domicilium appetimus : absit , vt_discidiis & contentionibus ordinem illum sanctissimum cóturbemus, quem Deus in Ecclesia sua obsignauit , & quo obsignat Ecclesiam suam. Absit,vt diuisi & diuulsi aribus violentiaq. Satanæ malimus esse, quàm in Deo vnitatis & pacis, & in catholica Ecclesia eius,vnitate spiritus,& vnitate ordinis contineri. Quòd fi non omnes idem sentimus per omnia , absit , vt continuò statuamus nos vnum ampliùs non esse, qui rebus tam multis & principalibus vnú fúmus. Qui vnum Deum habemus patrem, á quo omnia, vnú Christum in quo omnia,& vnum Spiritum per quě omnia, vnum corpus in vnitate Spiritus,vnam fidem in præcipuis his capitibus,quamuis fecundùm plus & minus (vt loquuntur vulgo) differentem,an propterea nos vnú esse negabimus, & discidia inter nos faciemus, quia vnum per omnia sententiis non fúmus? Quid? nónne in vno & eodem homine videmus voluntatem sibi ipsi repugnantem, quæ tamen vna est? voluntas naturalis appetet quod refugiet intelligens, sensus voluntatem hominis contra intellectus iudicium excitabit: volet ægrotus vna voluntate sanitatem & rem aducrfam sanitati, hoc sensus, illud naturæ facultate: volet pius sæpenumeró quod nó vult Dominus,& tamen religio simul ipsi futura est velle quod non vult Dominus: quemadmodum similitudine filij vitá petentis prorogari patri contrà quàm vult Deus, Augustinus olim demonstrabat, an propterea duo homines fiunt, aut seipsum homo lacerat & manus affert violentas sibi? Quod in vno homine fit, miraris fieri in tanto corpore? & quod in vno corpore fers, humano tamen; non feres in corporeChrifti diuinitus adunato? nec eo ipso tempore feres,quo inchoata est corporis illius coagmentatio, cùm in perfecto homuncionis[?] corpore, id est, ad perfectam staturam vel constitutione suam eucto feras? Deus meliora. Contendamus potiùs omnes vno animo, vt quamuis diuersum sentientes in rebus particularibus, vnum in communi fimus : Erigamus oculos ad cótemplationem throni illius gratiæ in cælo positi, vbi non solùm diffentientes, sed (quod grauius est) inimicantes Deo sunt reconciliati Deo per sanguinem Christi. Si me offendit alter in re humana dissentiens, condonare iubeor auctoritate Domini: qui autem ā me dissentit in causa fidei, fi errat, non me offendit, sed Dominum suum. Dominus autem condonat; ego non condonem? Deinde fi errat, non reuelauit Dominus ipsi ; ferendus est errans; expectandus Dominus qui errantem doceat ; & manus nostræ non ad depellendum errantem, sed ad viam monstrandam potiùs adhibendæ, fi Deus operam nostram ad falutem & institutionem eius volet occupari. Nam quis nescit propterea Euangelium & vniuerfam doctrinam salutis mysterium appellari, quòd sola reuelatione gratiæ homini innotefcat? aut, prout Christus ipse dicebat Nicodemo, quis ignorat nullum ascendisse in cælum, & res cœlestes perinde nouisse ac fi peruefti-gafset coràm,nisi eum qui descendit è cœlo,filium hominis qui est in cælo? Quis non audiat Iesum Christum clara voce inclamantem patri, & dicente , Gloriam tibi tribuo, pater domine cœli & terræ,quòd hæc occultaueris à sapientibus & intelligentibus , & ea retexeris infantibus? Quis in sese reflectens oculorum aciem non a[?]cat, & sentiat illud, quod optimè docet Apostolus de ministerio diuini verbi, sapientiam, [?]e non seculi huius, neque principum pu[?]seculi huius qui abolentur, sed sapientiam in mysterio positam? occulta sapientiam, quam praefinierat Deus ante saecula ad gloriam nostram? quam nemo principum seculi huius cognouit? sapientiam rerum quas oculus non vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in mentem hominis venerunt, quas parauit Deus iis à quibus diligitur? quam sapientiam Deus solus retegit per spiritum suum, prout spiritus scrutatur omnia, etiam profunditates Dei: Nam vt nemo hominum nouit ea quae sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis qui est in eo; ita etiam ea quae sunt Dei, neminem nouisse nisi Spiritum Dei, & quicunque Spiritum ex Deo acceperint: animalem hominem non esse capacem eorum quae sunt Spiritus Dei: Nam ea illi stultitiam esse, nec posse ab illo cognosci, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. Et tu, homo, non feras hominem in naturae tenebris errantem? quem Deus fert ante oculos tuos tolerantia sua, & vocat gratia? abscit à nobis isthaec insania.
units.tr: Far be it therefore from us, if we are Christians, if we love the order of the Church, of the commonwealth and of all human society, if we honour the right commanded by God and by the order of nature, if we desire that stable home of true peace and tranquillity, far be it from us to throw that most holy order into confusion by divisions and quarrels, the order that God has sealed in his Church and by which he seals his Church. Far be it from us to prefer being divided and torn apart, and the pleasure of Satan, to being held together in the unity of God, in his catholic Church, in the unity of the Spirit and the unity of order. And if we do not all think the same in every point, let us not suppose at once that we are no longer one, we who are one in so many and such important matters. We have one God the Father, from whom are all things; one Christ, in whom are all things; and one Spirit, through whom are all things; one body in the unity of the Spirit; one faith in these chief articles, although it differs in degrees, as people say. Shall we therefore deny that we are one, and make divisions among ourselves, because we are not one in all opinions? What then? Do we not see in one and the same man a will that opposes itself, and yet is one will? The natural will seeks what the reason will shun; the senses will stir up the will of a man against the judgement of the intellect. A sick man wills with one will both health and the thing opposed to health: the one by the power of sense, the other by the power of nature. The godly man often wills what the Lord does not will, and yet at the same time religion will make him will what the Lord does not will. Augustine once showed how, in the likeness of a son asking that his father's life be prolonged against God's will, this does not make two men, nor does a man tear himself apart and lay violent hands on himself. Do you marvel that what happens in one man happens in so great a body? And will you not bear in the body of Christ, joined together by God, what you bear in one human body? Will you not bear it at the very time when the framing of that body was begun, since you bear it in the body of a perfect man, that is, one grown to full stature and to its own constitution? God forbid. Let us rather strive, all of us with one mind, so that, though we think differently in particular matters, we may be one in what is common. Let us lift our eyes to the contemplation of that throne of grace set in heaven, where we who not only disagreed but, what is worse, were enemies of God, have been reconciled to God through the blood of Christ. If another man who differs from me in a human matter offends me, I am bidden by the Lord's authority to forgive him. But whoever differs from me in the cause of faith, if he errs, does not offend me but his Lord. The Lord forgives him; shall I not forgive? Furthermore, if he errs, and the Lord has not revealed it to him, the one who errs must be borne with, and the Lord must be waited for, who will teach the one who errs. Our hands are to be applied not to beating down the one who errs, but rather to showing him the way, if God wills to employ our labour for his salvation and instruction. For who does not know that the Gospel and the whole doctrine of salvation are called a mystery precisely because it is made known to man by the revelation of grace alone? Or, as Christ himself said to Nicodemus, who does not know that no one has ascended into heaven and known heavenly things as if he had seen them with his own eyes, except the Son of Man who came down from heaven and is in heaven? Who does not hear Jesus Christ crying out with a loud voice to the Father, saying, "I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the understanding and revealed them to babes"? Who, turning the eye of his mind upon himself, does not perceive what the Apostle teaches so well about the ministry of the divine word: wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are brought to nothing, but wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom that God foreordained before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew; the wisdom of the things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor which have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him; the wisdom which God alone reveals through his Spirit, since the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For as no man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him, so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, and those who have received the Spirit from God; the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned. And you, man, will you not bear with a man who wanders in the darkness of nature, whom God bears before your eyes in his patience and calls by his grace? Far be such madness from us.

units.la: Quòd sine illa quidem ipsa auctoritate Diuini verbi ab ista praesumptione iudiciorum nostrorum deducimur: pudeat saltem Christianos, pudeat eos omnes qui Christiani audire volunt, intolerandae istius audaciae, cum hominem naturalem & scientiæ humanæ inanisque philosophiæ opinione inflatum, plus humanitatis in suis iudiciis habuisse audient. Themiftium illum philosophum in historia Ecclesiaftica legimus longè mitiorem & æquiorem erga Christianos, fuisse quàm ipsi Christiani sint.
units.tr: Even apart from the authority of the divine word, which leads us away from this presumption of our own judgements, let Christians at least be ashamed, let all who wish to be called Christians be ashamed, of this intolerable audacity, when they hear that a natural man, puffed up with human learning and the opinion of empty philosophy, showed more humanity in his judgements. We read in ecclesiastical history that the philosopher Themistius was far milder and fairer towards Christians than Christians themselves were.

units.la: Narrat enim Socrates, cùm Imperator Valens Antiochiæ degeret, & quiescens à bellis exteris incursionibus quæ barbaricis grauiter infestaret orthodoxos, & quotidie maiora supplicia in eos excogitaret; tandem opera Themiftij illius Philofophi acerbissimam illam fuitiam hominis fractam, & ipsum ad maiorem æquitatem & moderationem reuocatum esse: nam libellum de ea causa, Valenti inferipsisse, quo nominatim ipsum Imperatorem appellabat, docebatque non esse cur mirum ipsi videretur, fi forte, Christianorum dogmata interdum dissiderent, nec inter fe conuenirent plane. Etenim reuerà perexiguam esse illorum differentiam, fi cum multitudine & confusione dogmatum comparentur, quæ apud Græcos obtinebant, illorum enim esse amplius trecenta dogmata. In rebus autem quæ sola opinione percipi possunt, prout ex necessitate, fi quid homo in rebus diuinis percipit, opinione percipit, (nam fidem nescieat carnalis Philosophus) plurimum fieri, vt dissideant valdè sententiæ: & Deû ipsum velle gloriam ita sibi conciliare diffidentibus hominum sententiis, vt eo magis quisque reuereatur maiestatem eius , quandoquidem cognitio eius non est illi exposita ad voluntatem animi. His sermonibus & consimilibus argumentis appellatus à Themiftio Imperator Valens lenior in orthodoxos effectus est. Quòd fi natura duce humaniter cogitandum in causa religionis de hominibus esse iudicauit Philosophus ignarus veritatis, vtens axiomate quòd Sapiens confirmauit, gloriam Dei esse celare verbum : fi Philofophi illius monitis fractus est quodammodo Valentis Imperatoris animus, qui fanguinem & cædes Christianorum tanta ferocitate spirauerat; quid nos Christianos, obsecro, nescire est facere erga ignorantes aut errantes quosque? quibus sermonibus reuocare in viam? qua commiseratione animi dies & noctes de miserorum errantium institutione & salute laborare? Hoc nos omnes docet, hucducit natura ipsa, & humanus ordo, & diuinus ordo, & communis Ecclesiæ, & priuata singulorum de gratia salutari Dei experientia, & constantissimè Dei ex verbo ipsius testificatione quibus omnibus nos præstat cedere, quàm particulari corruptioni naturæ nostræ in nostrath[?] ipsorum & aliorum perniciem obsequi[?] [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: For Socrates relates that when the emperor Valens was staying at Antioch, and was at rest from foreign wars, he was grievously harassing the orthodox with barbarous cruelty, and was devising greater punishments for them every day. At last, through the efforts of that philosopher Themistius, that most savage fierceness of the man was broken and he was called back to greater fairness and moderation. For Themistius wrote a little book on this cause and addressed it to Valens, naming the emperor himself, and he taught that it should not seem strange to him if Christians sometimes disagreed among themselves in their doctrines and did not wholly agree. Indeed, their difference was very small, if compared with the multitude and confusion of the doctrines that prevailed among the Greeks, for of these there were more than three hundred. In matters that can be grasped only by opinion, since whatever man grasps of divine things he grasps by opinion (for the carnal philosopher knows nothing of faith), it is very likely that opinions will sharply differ; and God himself wills to win glory for himself from the diverse opinions of men, so that each one reverences his majesty the more, since his knowledge is not laid open to the will of the mind. By these arguments and similar considerations, the emperor Valens, moved by Themistius, became gentler towards the orthodox. If the philosopher, ignorant of the truth, thought that in the cause of religion men should be judged humanely by the guidance of nature, using the saying that the wise man confirmed, that it is the glory of God to conceal a matter, and if the mind of the emperor Valens, who breathed out blood and slaughter of Christians with such ferocity, was in some measure broken by the admonitions of that philosopher, what, I beg you, is it for us Christians not to know how to act towards the ignorant or the erring? By what words are we to call them back to the way? With what compassion of mind are we to labour day and night for the instruction and salvation of the wretched wanderers? This nature itself teaches us, this human order leads us, and the divine order, and the common experience of the Church, and the private experience of each of us of God's saving grace, and above all the most constant testimony of God in his own Word; and it is better for us to yield to all of these than to give way to the particular corruption of our nature, to the ruin of ourselves and of others [illegible, ~20 letters].

units.la: 6. Expetite pacem Hierosolymorum dicentes, Tranquilli sint amantes tui:
units.tr: 6. Seek the peace of Jerusalem: may those who love you be at peace.

units.la: 7. Sit pax in præmunitione tua, tranquillitas in palatiis tuis.
units.tr: 7. Let there be peace within your walls, and tranquillity in your palaces.

units.la: QUAM multis circumsideantur bonis à Domino in Ecclesiâ eius, & quantam lætitiam in animis nostris ex eo percipiamus, hactenus satis, iudicio meo, ex verbis Prophetæ audiuimus. Nam cùm & priuatis singulorum membrorum officiis, & communibus Dei in corpus totum Ecclesiæ summisque beneficiis intus & foris demonstratis, potentissimè Propheta sè & Ecclesiam prisca suis temporibus ad hanc lætitiam excitauerit: nos, qui Deum esse nouimus constantissimum in promissionibus gratiæ, & salutari beneficentia in Ecclesiam suam, iisdem argumentis vti necesse est, vt confirmemur ipsi, & alios in cognitione ac cōscientia eiusdem boni, quo ad eius per nos fieri potest, confirmemus.
units.tr: How many good things the Lord bestows on the Church, and how great the joy we feel in our hearts because of it, we have heard enough, in my judgement, from the words of the Prophet. For when the Prophet, both by the particular duties of the individual members and by the common benefits of God to the whole body of the Church, shown both inwardly and outwardly, and by his supreme gifts, roused himself and the Church of his own time to this joy, we, who know that God is most constant in the promises of grace and in his saving kindness toward his Church, must use the same arguments, so that we ourselves may be strengthened and may strengthen others, as far as we can through our efforts, in the knowledge and awareness of the same good.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem Christianæ lætitiæ in nobis eiusmodi est, vt omnem metum omnemque dolorem eximere ex mentibus nostris & fugate possit, si eam animo verè concepimus. Sed quia illius gratiæ virtutisque diuinæ (quæ in se est absolutissima perfectissimaque) sensus est in nobis imperfectissimus: propterea visum est Spiritui sancto;expositá per Prophetam lætitia spirituali nostra, certissimisque illius argumentis, effectum lætitiæ illius coniunctissimum reliquo Psalmo exponere; nimirum publicam denunciationem lætitiæ illius ex studio Christiano, procurationemque diligentissimam illius lætitiæ propagandæ in vniuersitatem Ecclesiæ; ex quo ingeneratum est in nobis spirituale gaudium, de quo antè diximus. Id enim naturale est, vt lætitia hominem quasi fundat & dilatet modis omnibus; vt contrà, tristitia contrahit hominem, & quodammodo in angustum cogit: qui lætatur, diffunditur in se, & extra se, nec potest quin erumpat apud alios in testificationem lætitiæ suæ: quam rem sensus naturæ docet, & parabolis euidentissimis expressit Christus, viri qui ouem perdiderat, fœminæ quæ drachmam, & patrisfamilias qui filium.
units.tr: Now this Christian joy, if we have truly conceived it in our minds, is of such a kind that it can remove and drive out every fear and every sorrow from our hearts. But because our sense of that grace and divine power (which in itself is most complete and perfect) is very imperfect, it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, having set out through the Prophet our spiritual joy and its most certain proofs, also to set out in the rest of the Psalm the effect most closely bound up with that joy: namely, the public proclamation of that joy from Christian zeal, and the most diligent promotion of spreading that joy throughout the whole Church; from which the spiritual gladness we spoke of before is engendered in us. For it is natural that joy should, as it were, expand and widen a person in every way; whereas sorrow contracts a person and in a manner drives him into a narrow place. The one who rejoices pours himself out, both within himself and outside himself, and cannot help breaking out before others in witness to his joy. Nature's own feeling teaches this, and Christ expressed it in the most evident parables: of the man who had lost a sheep, the woman who had lost a drachma, and the father of the family who had lost a son.

units.la: Secundum hanc igitur rationem Propheta suam ipsius & communem Ecclesiæ lætitiam cùm describeret verbis antecedentibus, iam venit ad illam inclinationem naturalem lætitiæ, nimirum ad publicam denunciationem illius, & salüberrimam[?] adhortationem ad pacem, quā lætitia alituratque continetur ad Dei gloriam.
units.tr: Accordingly, when the Prophet had described his own joy and the common joy of the Church in the preceding words, he now comes to that natural inclination of joy, namely its public proclamation, and to the most wholesome exhortation to peace, in which joy is nourished and maintained to the glory of God.

units.la: Doctúrus autem Propheta illud officium pacis ad lætitiæ conseruationem pernecessarium, duobus modis credentes instruit de hac Christiana pace. Nam primum hortatione vtitur vehementissima, tanquam præco religiosissimus voluntatis Dei versu sexto & septimo, quos ante exscripsimus: Deinde verò suum ipsius exemplum spondet, & ante oculos piorum exhibet, sese velut ducem futurũ ex facto ad ista pietatis officia, non autem vocalem solùm præconem, spectatorem; hortatoremque otiosum, duobus versibus ultimis. Cùm autem sermone instituit docere alios Christianam pacem; tanquam doctor fidelissimus in schola Domini, primùm rem ipsam imperat, deinde præcit verba singulis ad rem quam imperauit pertinentia. Rem enim ipsam imperat summatim, dicens: Expetite pacem Hierosolymorum: Verba autem præcit credétibus quibus hoc imperat, cùm subiicit, tranquilli sint amantes tui &c. oratione conuersa ad Hierosolyma.
units.tr: Now the Prophet, intending to teach the believers about this Christian peace, instructs them in two ways. First, in verses six and seven, which we have already copied out, he uses a most urgent exhortation, like a most devout herald of the will of God. Then he offers his own example, and sets it before the eyes of the godly, showing himself as a future leader by deed to these duties of piety, and not merely as a vocal herald, an onlooker and an idle exhorter, in the last two verses. Now when he undertakes by his speech to teach others about Christian peace, he, like a most faithful teacher in the school of the Lord, first states the matter itself and then sets out the words that pertain to the matter he has enjoined. He enjoins the matter itself in summary, saying: Seek the peace of Jerusalem. He sets out the words for the believers by whom he enjoins this, when he adds, may those who love you be at peace, his speech being turned toward Jerusalem.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem quid sibi velit Psaltes[?] Hierosolymorum appellatione, satis (opinor) constat ex præcedentibus. Nam versu 2. & 3. rem totã copiosè explicauimus. Pax verò quid significet, nobis videndum est; ut singuli suum officium, ad quod excitantur his verbis, tenere possint. Ut itaque paucis absoluamus, cùm desiderium pacis universè hoc loco præcipiatur, & huius ipsius pacis sequentibus verbis tradatur enarratio, ne longiùs abeamus, Pacis nomine intelligimus constitutionem vacuam ab omni malo, & in omni bonorum genere intus & foris quiescentem. Ac proinde, quia pax certa homini esse non potest, qui nō solùm intus abundat malis & bonis vacuus est, sed etiam soris omnibus malis appetitur, & ab omni bono quasi refugitur: ita è diverso pacem homini illi esse statuimus, quem bona certatim appetunt & fugiunt mala. Eademque ratione de Ecclesia dicimus, quam urbs Hierosolymorum olim adumbravit; hanc dici pacem illius, cùm ipsi bene est ac non malè. Quomodo autem Ecclesiæ bene esse possit, superiora docuerunt. Bene est Ecclesiæ; quæ lætatur de filiis suis; ad quam filii adeunt & adhærent; cuius forma interna, est Deus; externa, communio sanctorum, cum Deo verbo salutis & precibus, & piorum inter se iusto ordine quem Deus instituerit ad coagmentationem sanctorū, ad ædificationem corporis Christi. His rebus vera pax Ecclesiæ continetur; quemadmodum vera pax & iusta corporis constitutio in optima formæ internæ, atque externæ, & actionum omnium, accidentiumque commoditate versatur. De hac pace quam pij cum Deo habent, cum animis suis, cum Ecclesia tota, & cum membris singulis eius, & cum omnibus hominibus, Propheta nunc demùm loquitur, & omnia antegressa bona comprehendit hac una pacis appellatione, dicens: Expetite pacem Hierosolymorum.
units.tr: First, what the Psalmist means by the name of Jerusalem is, I think, sufficiently clear from what has gone before, for in verses two and three we have fully explained the whole matter. But we must see what peace means, so that each person may hold to his duty, to which he is roused by these words. To finish briefly: since the desire for peace is here commanded in general, and the explanation of this very peace is given in the following words, so as not to wander too far, by peace we understand a condition free from all evil and resting, both inwardly and outwardly, in every kind of good. Accordingly, since a man cannot have peace who not only abounds inwardly with evils and is empty of good, but is also outwardly assailed by all evils and as it were shunned by every good, we hold on the contrary that a man has peace when good things eagerly seek him and evils flee from him. And by the same reasoning we say of the Church, which the city of Jerusalem once foreshadowed, that she has peace when it goes well with her and not badly. How it can go well with the Church, the earlier verses have taught. It goes well with the Church, which rejoices in her children, to which the children come and cling, whose inner form is God, and whose outer form is the communion of the saints, with God, with the word of salvation and with prayers, and with the godly among themselves, in the just order that God has instituted for the joining together of the saints and for the building up of the body of Christ. In these things the true peace of the Church consists, just as the true peace and right constitution of a body lies in the best arrangement of its inner and outer form, and in the convenience of all its actions and conditions. Of this peace, which the godly have with God, with their own souls, with the whole Church, with its individual members, and with all men, the Prophet now at last speaks, and he embraces all the good things that went before under this single name of peace, saying: Seek the peace of Jerusalem.

units.la: Hierosolyma, id est, Ecclesiam Dei bonam esse confitemur omnes, tanquam Dei viventis domum: tum pacem illius domus bonam & iucundam esse. Unum à nobis desideratur; ut cùm bonam esse Ecclesiam, & bonam Ecclesiæ pacem sentiamus omnes in nostra cóscientia, nos quoque bonum officium erga Ecclesiam, quam prædicamus bonam, & ad pacem, quam natura bonam esse docet, faciamus. Huc nos hortatur & vocat Propheta dicens; Experite pacem Hierosolymorum: tanquam si diceret; Ita estis singuli à natura comparati, ut neque bonum privatum vestrum, neque commune noritis; ac ne illud quidem expetatis, aut etiam procuretis, si quando nouisse datum est; adeò magnæ sunt in vobis tenebræ. Quòd si in ipsis humanis rebus non videtis, quid vobis, quid publico utile esse possit; multo magis aberraturi esletis [?] à bono spirituali vestro, & Ecclesiæ Dei, quarum rerum notitia nemini nisi ex reuelatione Dei poterit obtingere. Nunc verò cū per Dei gratiam ex præcedentibus constet, Deum, Ecclesiam, & fratres germanos vestros à Deo in Ecclesia genitos, & vos denique ipsos à vobis cognoscí prælucente face diuini verbi: videte, ne in malo naturæ vestræ torpentes hæreatis, néve à bono prosequendo, cuius notitiam impertiuit Deus, abstineatis impiè; sed bonum publicum Ecclesiæ, & priuatum spirituale vestrum in Ecclesia procurare, quibuscunque modis pote est. Quod si plura nō potestis (quemadmodú reuera non sumus idonei per nos ipsos ad cogitandum quidquam velut ex nobis ipsis; sed quòd idonei sumus, illud ex Deo est, ) saltem date operam, vt votis ardentibus ex animo, religiosissimisq. precibus coram Domino contendatis, & intus studia vestra quam diligentissime accendatis ad pacem, id est, bonum publicum Ecclesiæ, & in ea priuatum vestrum procurandum. Hoc igitur summum præceptum est, ad quod pios hortatur Psaltes [?] ex antecedentis lætitiæ causarumque lætitiæ argumento.
units.tr: We all confess that Jerusalem, that is, the Church of God, is good, as the house of the living God; and that the peace of that house is good and pleasant. One thing is required of us: that, since we all perceive in our conscience that the Church is good and that the Church's peace is good, we also do a good duty toward the Church, which we proclaim good, and toward the peace which nature teaches is good. The Prophet urges and calls us to this, saying: Seek the peace of Jerusalem, as if he were saying: "You are each so made by nature that you know neither your private good nor the common good, nor do you seek or even take care of it when it has been granted you to know it; so great is the darkness in you. But if you do not see in human affairs what can be useful to you and to the public, you will be much more likely to go astray from your spiritual good and that of the Church of God, the knowledge of which can come to no one except through the revelation of God. But now, since by the grace of God it is clear from what has gone before that God, the Church, and your brothers born of God in the Church, and finally yourselves, are known to you by the light of the divine word, see that you do not cling sluggishly to the evil of your nature, nor impiously abstain from pursuing the good whose knowledge God has imparted to you; but procure the public good of the Church and your own spiritual good in the Church, by whatever means are possible. And if you cannot do more (as indeed we are not fit by ourselves to think anything as if from ourselves; but that we are fit, that is from God), at least take care to strive before the Lord with ardent wishes from the heart and most devout prayers, and kindle your zeal within as diligently as possible for peace, that is, for the public good of the Church and for the procuring of your own good within it." This, then, is the highest precept to which the Psalmist urges the godly, from the argument of the joy that has gone before and the causes of that joy.

units.la: Cum autem præceptorum diuinorum omnium eiusmodi sit auctoritas, vt quibuscunque præcepta dantur, iis præceptis illius obsequi teneantur sine exceptione vllâ; profecto nos, qui singulari Dei beneficio in Ecclesiam ad percep- tionem voluntatis eius vocati sumus, necesse est de obsequio fidei cogitare, vt pacem Ecclesiæ petamus, quemadmodum nobis præcepit Deus. Ac propterea, ne forte in petendo incerti simus, tanquam si nesciremus quid à quo peti oporteat, indidit Propheta piis velut in os sanctissimam petitionis formulam, cum dicit: tranquilli sint amantes tui, sit pax in præmunitione tua, &c. Huius enim petitionis loci duo sunt à Propheta indicati, incremento conuenientissimo, cum pacem Ecclesiæ docet peti à nobis oportere & foris & intus, communiter & singulariter: Foris quidem etiam iis qui amant Ecclesiam communiter, quamuis nondum se cum illi adiunxerint; intus vero singulariter, domesticis fidei & Ecclesiæ catholicæ. Nam quemadmodum si quis pacem habitationis suæ desideraverit, circumspiciat opus est foris, quæ impedimenta arcenda, quæ adiumenta retinenda; deinde verò dispiciat intus quid ipsæ partes habitationis postulent; ita etiam pios omnes post omnem hominum memoriam Deus informavit, ut in hoc domicilio mundi omnibus benè cupiant, & pacem colant cum omnibus, quoad eius fieri potest, ut Romanis scribebat Apostolus; deinde ut ipsi Ecclesiæ ante omnia benè cup[?]ant secundùm Deum. Quinetiam hunc ipsum ordinem, quem nobis præscribit Psaltes, Deus in suis promissionibus quas enunciauit Abrahamo, distinctè servavit, ne quemquam Christianum tædeat illud postulare, quod in promissionum numero recensuit Deus. Dicebat enim primùm de omnibus etiā exteris; Benedicam iis qui benedicent tibi: postea verò de Ecclesiæ Christianæ membris subiecit illud alterum; Benedictæ erunt in te omnes familiæ terræ. De omnibus ergo promiscuè, etiam exteris, ab Ecclesia Dei pronunciantur hæc verba, tranquilli sintamantes tui; de ipsis verò domesticis sequentia enunciata sunt.
units.tr: Now since all divine precepts have such authority that those to whom they are given are bound to obey them without any exception, we who have been called by a singular benefit of God into the Church to perceive his will must surely consider, in the obedience of faith, how to seek the peace of the Church, as God has commanded us. And therefore, lest we be uncertain in our asking, as if we did not know what we ought to ask of whom, the Prophet has put into the mouths of the godly, as it were, a most holy form of petition, when he says: May those who love you be at peace; let there be peace within your walls, and so on. Two things are indicated by the Prophet in this place of petition, arranged in a most fitting sequence, since he teaches that the peace of the Church ought to be sought by us both outwardly and inwardly, in common and individually: outwardly, indeed, also for those who love the Church in general, though they have not yet joined themselves to her; inwardly, individually, for the household of faith and of the catholic Church. For just as, if someone desires peace for his dwelling, he must look around outside to see which hindrances are to be kept off and which aids retained, and then look within to see what the very parts of the dwelling require, so God has also shaped all the godly, from the beginning of human memory, so that in this dwelling of the world they wish well to all and cultivate peace with all, as far as it can be done, as the Apostle wrote to the Romans; and then that they wish well above all to the Church itself, according to God. Indeed, God in his promises, which he announced to Abraham, has kept this very order that the Psalmist prescribes to us, distinctly, so that no Christian should be weary of asking for what God has counted among his promises. For he said first, of all, even outsiders: I will bless those who bless you; afterwards, however, he added that other promise concerning the members of the Christian Church: In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed. So these words, may those who love you be at peace, are pronounced by the Church of God on all people in common, even outsiders; but what follows has been spoken concerning the members of the household themselves.

units.la: Ac prius quidè per se est evidens: si tantùm illud observemus, amantium[?] Ecclesiæ duo esse genera, prout distinctè à Psalte enumerantur paulo post octauo versu, dicendo;propter fratres meos;& amicos meos, &c. Sunt enim hi fratres, id est, germana Ecclesiæ membra, & iamiam ex facto ad eam pertinentia in Christo Iesu, aut etiam in ea degentia secundùm formam externam & ordinem aspectabilem illius; illi verò amici, quamuis extra Ecclesiam positi, qui nec oderunt Ecclesiam animo, nec sermone aut facto obsunt; sed aut bene cupiunt ipsi ex animo, quamuis ipsi sibi id non cupiant boni, aut certè amicè ferunt, vt Ecclesia sit, atq. tranquilla sit: de quo genere dicebat Christus, Qui non est aduersum nos, pro nobis est. Pro his ergo omnibus Ecclesia postulat, vt ipsis bene sit, & tranquillitate fruantur, denique communibus se-cum beneficiis magis ac magis cumulentur à Domino.
units.tr: Now, first of all, it is plain enough if we notice that the lovers of the Church are of two kinds, as the Psalmist distinctly lists them a little later in verse 8: for my brethren and my companions, and so on. The brethren are the true members of the Church, who already belong to her in fact, in Christ Jesus, or who dwell within her in her outward form and visible order. The companions, though standing outside the Church, do not hate her in their hearts, and they do her no harm by word or deed. Rather, they either wish her well from their hearts, though they do not wish it for themselves as good men, or at least they bear with her kindly, so that she may exist and be at peace. Of this kind Christ said, "He who is not against us is for us." For all these the Church asks that they may fare well, enjoy tranquillity, and be ever more and more heaped with the common blessings of the Lord.

units.la: Alterum verò optatum in versu 7. quod ad domesticos Ecclesiæ pertinet, duas partes illas pacis evidenter notat, de quibus antè dicebamus in definienda pace. Ad iustam enim & veram pacem desiderantur duo: defensio à malo, & bonorum pacis perceptio. De utroque preces concipiendas ostendit Psaltes verbis paucissimis; & seruata typi illius, qui tum ad figurandam Ecclesiam fuerat datus, allegoria. Ierusalem typus erat Ecclesiæ: ad tranquillitatem vrbis illius duo hæc fuerunt opus, tum vt aduersus mala foris minantia & irruentia circummunita esset vrbs, tum vt intus abundaret bonis. Defensionem à malo Propheta his verbis docuit expetendam; Sit pax in præmunitione tua: Constitutionem verò stabilem in bono ac florentissimam postulare docuit illis; Sit tranquillitas in palatiis tuis. Etsi ne hoc quidem prætereundum videtur silentio, quòd in hoc utroque genere prǽstantiam summam bonorum ad pacem pertinentium amplissimis vocibus denotauit.
units.tr: The second wish, in verse 7, which concerns the Church's household members, clearly marks out those two parts of peace that we spoke of earlier in defining peace. For true and righteous peace requires two things: defence from evil, and the enjoyment of good things. The Psalmist teaches us, in very few words, that prayers should be offered for both, and he keeps to the allegory of that type which was given at that time to figure the Church. Jerusalem was a type of the Church, and two things were needed for the tranquillity of that city: that it should be fortified all round against the evils that threatened and attacked from outside, and that it should abound in good things within. The Prophet taught that defence from evil is to be sought with these words: Let there be peace within your ramparts. He taught that a stable and most flourishing condition in good things is to be asked for with these words: Let there be tranquillity in your palaces. Yet this too should not be passed over in silence, that in each of these kinds he has expressed, in the most ample terms, the supreme excellence of the good things belonging to peace.

units.la: Nam de illa defensione à malo acturus, non simpliciter murum, fossam, vallum, aut aliquid simile appellauit; sed voce amplissima vsus est, quoduis munimentum, idque potentissimum & commodissimum ad defensionem significante. De interna verò bonorum copia tam magnificè loquitur, vt dignitatem Ecclesiæ non possit quisquam ampliùs extollere, cùm palatia nominaret. Videbat enim Prophetā omnes pios in Christum & Ecclesiam insitos, reges & sacerdotes apud Deum patrem in Christo factos, regale sacerdotium, vt appellat Petrus; sive, vt Moses, regnum sacerdotale. Huic dignitati piorum dignas stationes voluit demonstrare à Deo attributas, ac velut prætoria & regales domos, cùm tranquillitatem inesse palatiis eius expeteret: De rebus videlicet spiritualibus tam magnificè in fide sentiens, vt sibi ipse non posset satisfacere, nisi res illas in spiritu magnificas vocibus magnificis secundùm corpus exprimeret.
units.tr: For when he was about to speak of defence from evil, he did not simply name a wall, a ditch, a rampart, or something of the kind, but used a most ample word, signifying any fortification whatever, and that the most powerful and most serviceable for defence. And of the inner abundance of good things he speaks so magnificently that no one could raise the dignity of the Church higher than by naming her palaces. For the Prophet saw that all the godly are grafted into Christ and the Church, and are made kings and priests before God the Father in Christ: a royal priesthood, as Peter calls it, or, as Moses says, a kingdom of priests. He wished to show that God has assigned to this dignity of the godly fitting dwelling places, like princely halls and royal houses, when he asked that tranquillity should dwell in her palaces. He thought so highly, in faith, of spiritual things, that he could not satisfy himself unless he expressed those things, magnificent in the spirit, in magnificent words drawn from the body.

units.la: - Videmus ergo ex Prophetæ verbis, quidnam illud sit quod expeti à nobis omni tempore necesse est. Sed à quo expetamus, nisi à Deo, qui potest explere petitionem nostram? Deus igitur, Deus ille noster, auctor Ecclesiæ, custos & hospes constantissimus illius, ad quem Ecclesia respiciens nihil non habet boni, a quo respiciens aliorsum nihil non sentit mali: is ergo ipse est, qui hæc curare potest Ecclesiæ efficacissimè, & à quo nos indesinenter opus est petere quæcumque ad pacem & tranquillitatem illius pertinent. neque dubium est, si ex animo fidem & misericordiam illius imploremus his ipsis ferreis & luctuosissimis temporibus, quin oculi ipsius super iustos invigilaturi sint, & aures ipsius attentæ futuræ ad pias preces & suspiria illorum.
units.tr: We see, then, from the Prophet's words, what it is that we must always seek. But from whom shall we seek it, if not from God, who can fulfil our petition? God, then, our God, the author of the Church, her guardian and most constant host, looking to whom the Church has nothing of good lacking, and looking away from whom she feels nothing but evil: he is the very one who can most effectually take care of these things for the Church, and from him we must ceaselessly ask whatever pertains to her peace and tranquillity. Nor is there any doubt that if we implore his faithfulness and mercy from our hearts, even in these iron and most sorrowful times, his eyes will watch over the righteous, and his ears will be attentive to the pious prayers and sighs of his people.

units.la: Sed quia Deus pacem & tranquillitatem Ecclesiæ suæ non solùm procurat immediatè (ut loquuntur) arbitratu suo, verumetiam quibuscunque visum est mediis utitur ad præstandam pacem & tranquillitatem illius; videamus, ne singuli nostri deficiamus ab officio nostro, si forte Deus nobis, tanquam instrumentis indignis quidem, sed sanctificatis ab ipso per-gratiam, ad tantum opus dignetur uti. Nam quid nobis miseris futurum est, si quod ore petimus, illud manibus pedibusque obnixè oppugnemus? aut si nec manum nec pedem admoveamus, cùm honorem istum Deus nobis habuerit, & ad opus immerentes gratiosissimè vocaverit? quod ergo petimus sermone, petamus animo; quod animo & sermone petimus, idem etiam modis omnibus appetamus; & studium, operam, laborem, industriamq. nostram eò conferamus, ut idipsum quod petimus, tandem beneficio Dei, ut benedicturi officio ministerioque nostro, assequamur. Hoc autem ut faciamus sanctè, meminerimus ab eo qui omnia dat, expeti omnia; ab iis verò qui possunt aliquid ministrare secundùm voluntatē Dei donatoris omnium, aliqua postulari secundùm Deum oportere. Itaque omnia omninò à Deo petimus; ab aliis, aliqua secundùm Deum. Cùm autem ab aliis dicimus; quis adeò desipit, ut aliorum officium merito desiderari putet, & dissimulari nostrum? Quæcunq. creaturæ sunt, tenentur secundùm Deum ministrare voluntati eius. quid ergo exigamus ab aliis, quod nosipsi præstare minimè cogitamus? Utrumq. opus est in expetenda pace & tranquillitate Ecclesiæ: tum ut ipsi summo desiderio procuremus & colamus eam, tū ut proximos ad idem officium religiosè excitemus. Proximos autem omnes vniuersè provocari ad hoc officium ergà Ecclesiam Dei oportere docemur natura, & auctoritate Scripturæ: quemadmodum Christum legimus præcepisse, Diligite etiam inimicos vestros, benedicite iis qui devouent vos &c. & Paulum præcipientem, si fieri potest, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace viuite. Sed quia varia est proximorum (ut in Scriptura vocantur) ratio, & ipse quoque Propheta in hoc loco aliquam distinctionem adfert; paucis de ordine eorum dicendum est, vt melius constet ; quid quibus peti & præstari oporteat. Proximi omnes alij aliis fecundùm speciem à natura sumus:Sed Proximorum duo genera statuimus, nos quidem qui in Ecclesiæ sumus.Nam alij in Ecclesia sunt nobiscum, alij absunt abea: Quorum illos Apostolus vocat domesticos fidei, ad Galatas scribens ;hos ad Timotheum, exteros vel extraneos appellauit.
units.tr: But since God procures the peace and tranquillity of his Church not only immediately (as people say), at his own discretion, but also uses whatever means seem good to him to bring about that peace and tranquillity, let us see that we, each one of us, do not fail in our duty, in case God should deign, by grace, to use us for so great a work, as unworthy instruments, indeed, but sanctified by himself. For what will become of us wretched people, if we strive with hands and feet against what we ask for with our mouths? Or if we do not lift a hand or a foot, when God has given us this honour and has most graciously called us, though undeserving, to the work? Therefore let us seek with our hearts what we seek with our words; and what we seek with heart and words, let us also seek in every way; and let us bring our zeal, effort, labour and diligence to this end, that we may at last, by God's favour, attain what we ask for, being made blessers by our office and ministry. To do this rightly, let us remember that everything is sought from him who gives all things, and that from those who can supply something, according to the will of God the giver of all, some things ought to be asked in a godly manner. So we ask everything absolutely from God; from others, some things according to God. But when we say "from others", who is so foolish as to think that the duty of others is rightly demanded while our own is passed over? Whatever creatures there are are bound, according to God, to serve his will. Why, then, should we require of others what we ourselves do not think of performing? Both are needful in seeking the peace and tranquillity of the Church: that we ourselves, with the greatest desire, procure and cherish her, and that we stir up our neighbours to the same duty in a godly way. We are taught, by nature and by the authority of Scripture, that all our neighbours in general ought to be called to this duty towards the Church of God; as we read that Christ commanded, "Love your enemies also, bless those who curse you," and so on; and Paul, who enjoins, "If it be possible, as much as lies in you, live at peace with all men." But since the range of our neighbours (as they are called in Scripture) is various, and the Psalmist himself here draws a certain distinction, something must be said briefly about their order, so that it may be clearer what ought to be sought and granted to whom. All our neighbours are, by nature, of one kind, each to the other; but we distinguish two kinds of neighbours, namely those who are within the Church and those who are outside it. Of these, the former the Apostle calls the household of faith, writing to the Galatians; the latter he called outsiders or strangers, writing to Timothy.

units.la: Exterorum verò rursum duo sunt genera. Nam alij sunt amici Ecclesiæ Dei ; alij inimici. Qui amici sunt, aut ita sunt amici, vt bonum curent Ecclesiæ humano animo ; aut saltem amici eatenus ; vt malum illius non expectant ; sed simpliciter in eo acquiescant, vt & potest bene esse Ecclesiæ, bene sit. Inimicorum verò qui Ecclesiam oderunt atque persequuntur, alij ignoratione sunt inimici ; alij perturbatione & studiis particularibus ; alij denique malitiosa voluntate. Quid faciamus eum istis omnibus, quicunque ad expetendam pacem Ecclesiæ vocati sumus? Argumentum graue atque odiosum: sed tamen tam necessarium in hoc tempore quàm quod maximè. Quapropter de eo disturi sumus quàm breuissimè poterimus, vt rationem pacis expetendæ procurandæque in tot tantisque impedimentis, certam teneamus : Et dicemus diuerso ordine, vt ita paulatim ad singulorum gradum explorationem veniamus.
units.tr: Again, there are two kinds of outsiders. For some are friends of the Church of God, others enemies. Those who are friends are either so friendly that they care for the good of the Church with a human heart, or at least are friends to this extent, that they do not look for her harm, but simply rest content that, as far as possible, it may go well with the Church, and so it goes well. Of those enemies who hate and persecute the Church, some are enemies through ignorance, some through agitation and private partisanship, and some finally through malicious will. What shall we do with all these, we who have been called to seek the peace of the Church? It is a weighty and hateful subject, yet in this time as necessary as any. Therefore we shall treat of it as briefly as we can, so that we may hold a sure account of how peace is to be sought and procured amid so many and so great hindrances; and we shall proceed in a different order, so that we may thus gradually come to an examination of each rank.

units.la: Prifmum[?] igitur est, quid facto opus ad pacem Ecclesiæ,si res nobis cum iis futura est qui voluntarie certaque malitia inimici sunt illius? Stat sententia, pacem Ecclesiae procurari à nobis oportere: Cumq. pax fitin vacatione à malo & fructu boni posita, non esse cum iis aut apud eos de pace Ecclesiae agendum, qui maliciosè procurant malum ipsius. Quapropter si pacem Ecclesiae vere procuremus, & instrumenta eiusmodi nobis oblata videamus quae pacem impeditura sunt, non sunt commouerenda:[?] Sic enim praecepit Christus dicens; Ne date quod sanctum est canibus, nec proiicite margaritas vestras coram porcis, nequando conculcent ea pedibus suis, & conuersi lacerent vos. Nam tu qui pacem expetis, quorsum eos commoueas, qui nihil nisi oppugnent Ecclesiae pacem? Sed hic tamen duplicem à Christiano homine cautionem defidero; ne quando prudentiae opinione veniat contra charitatem, quam omnibus debemus, teste Apostolo. Vna est, ne temere iudicii feramus de vllo homine, quod certa malitia & deliberata, siue (vt Moses loquitur) elata manu oppugnet Deum, & veritatem, & Ecclesiam eius. Altera, si iudicandum est, ne ex fructu vno aut altero putemus nos arbores illas malas cognoscere; sed potius ex fructibus plurimis & grauissimis discamus cognoscere quod satis est ad cautionem nostram, non autem ad illorum condemnationem. Hunc ordinem nos docuit Christus diligentissimè, dicendo: Primùm quidem, ex fructibus eorum agnofcc[?] agnoscetis eos.; postea verò subiiciendo cautionem illam pernecessariam, ut iudicium Deo permittamus, cùm inquit, Non quisquis dicit mihi, Domine Domine; introibit in regnum cælorum; sed qui facit quod vult pater meus qui in cælis est. Multi dicent mihi die illo, Domine, Domine, nónne pér nomen tuum prophetauimus? & in nomine tuo dæmonia eiccimus? & per nomen tuum multas virtutes edidimus? Tunc autem profitebor eis, Certè nunquam noui vos; discedite à me qui operam datis transgressioni legis.
units.tr: First, then, what must be done for the Church's peace, if we have to deal with people who are voluntarily and with settled malice its enemies? The principle stands that we must work for the Church's peace. Since peace consists in freedom from evil and in enjoying good, we must not deal about the Church's peace with those who maliciously work its harm. So if we truly seek the Church's peace, and see instruments offered to us that would hinder it, we must not stir them up. For so Christ commanded: "Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you" (Matt. 7). For you who seek peace, why would you stir up those who do nothing but attack the Church's peace?
