Yet here a Christian needs a twofold caution, lest a show of prudence bring him against the charity we owe to all, as the Apostle bears witness. The first is not to pass judgment rashly on any man, as if he were acting with settled and deliberate malice, or, as Moses puts it, "with a high hand," against God, the truth and his Church. The second: if judgment must be made, let us not think we can know those bad trees from one or two fruits. Rather, let us learn from very many and very grave fruits what is enough for our caution, though not for their condemnation. Christ taught this order most carefully, saying first: "By their fruits you will know them" (Matt. 7). Then he added the most necessary caution, that we leave judgment to God: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? Then I will declare to them, I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness" (Matt. 7).

units.la: Quòd si res nobis cum eo futura est, qui singulari perturbatione victus, & cedens infirmitati suæ, Ecclesiæ aduersabitur, eadem planè ratio à nobis obseruanda est, dum homo ita est, tantùm differimen illud adhibendum, quòd Christianum hóminem perturbationi præsenti oportet ad tempus cedere, & dare operam ut prudenter ac commodè miser homo iámiam ex perturbatione animi sui reuocetur, aut expectetur dum fidat quodammodò illa animi perturbatio, prout homini ebrio fieri à nobis solet. Id enim natura docet, salubrius remedia ægroto adhiberi, cùm acres illæ morborum ἐχμαὶ[?] & perturbationum impetus quasi refracti sunt: & notum est illud dictum Cleostrati, qui cùm ebrius esset grauiter, cuidam sibi dicenti; Non te pudet quòd ebrius factus es? respondit illicò, Et te non pudet, quòd mones ebrium? Hic enim verè dictum illud est à Salomone adhibendum, Velut mala aurea cum figuris argenteis est verbum dictum cómodè, vt monile aureum, & ornamentum ex insigni auro est reprehensor [?] sapiens apud aurem auscultantém.
units.tr: But if we have to deal with a man who, overcome by some particular disturbance and yielding to his own weakness, sets himself against the Church, the same method must be observed by us, since he is still a man. The only difference to apply is this: a Christian must yield to the present disturbance for a time, and take care that the poor man is recalled from the agitation of his mind, prudently and fittingly, or else wait until that disturbance of his mind has somewhat spent itself, as we commonly do with a drunk man. For nature teaches that remedies are applied more healthfully to the sick once the sharp fits of their diseases and the onslaughts of their passions have, as it were, been broken. And the saying of Cleostratus is well known: when he was grossly drunk and someone said to him, "Are you not ashamed that you got drunk?", he answered at once, "And are you not ashamed that you lecture a drunk man?" Here indeed that saying of Solomon is truly to be applied: "Like golden apples in silver settings is a word spoken fittingly; like a golden ring and an ornament of fine gold is a wise reprover to an attentive ear" (Prov. 25).

units.la: Quòd si ignorantia veritatis hominem videbimus Deo, Ecclesiæ, & veritati Dei in Ecclesia aduersari; omninò videndum nobis est, vt in charitate expetamus institutionem hominis illius; nitendum vt præbeamus, quàm prudentissimè modestissimèque poterimus, lucem veritatis, qua tenebras mentis illius depellamus. Sed cum his omnibus vniuersè, qui inimici sunt, id semper nobis videndum est vt pacem Ecclesiæ præoptemus, & ante omnia expetamus. Quòd si cum bona Ecclesiæ pace hís prodesse possumus, faciamus sanctissimo studio salutisipforum: sin autem pax Ecclesiæ aut meritorum eius periclitabitur propter voluntatem; perturbationem, aut inscientiam istorum, abstineamus potius ab eis commouendis, quàm vt pacem dimoueamus Ecclesiæ, dorec miseri-cors ille Dominus, qui nostri misertus est, cùm sibi inimici essémus, viam patefecerit illis misericordiæ. Ad summam, quod veteres monuerunt olim non esse mouendum, id quod bene positum est, id in hoc hominum genere obseruatio opus est accuratissimè. Videndum vt ab iis qui semper mali sunt, certo quoque consilio dant expetamalo [?]; ne bonum quidem expetamus, aut commoveamus magno siue Ecclesiæ, siue nostro ipsorum, aut aliorum malo: Ab iis vero qui infirmitate aut ignoratione rapiuntur in malum, monendis tantisper caueamus, dum ita se habent: sed potius studeamus eis benefacere, cum erit commodum, quàm malum ipsorum accendere; ne spe beneficiorum nobis accerfamus importune malum.
units.tr: If we see a man, through ignorance of the truth, opposing God, the Church and the truth of God in the Church, we must certainly see to it that we seek his instruction in love. We must strive to offer, as wisely and modestly as we can, the light of truth by which we may drive out the darkness of his mind. But with all who are enemies in general, we must always see to it that we prefer the peace of the Church and, above all, seek it. If we can benefit these men without loss to the Church's good peace, let us do so with the holiest zeal for their salvation. But if the peace of the Church or its good standing would be endangered on account of their will, disturbance or ignorance, let us rather abstain from stirring them up than dislodge the Church's peace, until that merciful Lord, who had mercy on us when we were his enemies, opens to them the way of mercy. In sum, what the ancients long ago advised, that what is well settled should not be moved, needs the most careful observance with this class of men. We must take care not to give them counsel that seeks evil with settled purpose; nor should we even seek a good, or stir things up, to the great harm of the Church, of ourselves or of others. But with those who are carried into evil by weakness or ignorance, let us for the time being be cautious about admonishing them, as long as they remain in that state. Rather let us strive to do them good when it is convenient, than to kindle their evil, lest by hoping for their benefits we unseasonably bring evil upon ourselves.

units.la: Sed quid si homines erunt non inimico erga Ecclesiam & pios animo? horum duo genera, quæ ante dicebamus, semper distingui necesse est: Nam alij sunt non inimici, alij vero amici reipsa, & bono animo in Ecclesia Dei ac membra illius. Cum iis autem qui non inimici sunt, hic modus ad procurationem pacis in Ecclesia tenendus est, ut potius vincas animos ipsorum & amicitiam concilies bonis sermonibus, ossiciis, exemplis, & rebus consimilibus, quàm ut importune ab illis exigas benefacta: Animum istorum adduci priusquàm manus necesse est. qui secus fecerit, is præpostere de officio iudicat illorum, & suo: quod magnæ est imprudentiæ.
units.tr: But what if the men are not hostile to the Church, but well-disposed and pious? As we said before, these two kinds must always be distinguished: some are not hostile, while others are truly friends, of good mind toward the Church of God and its members. With those who are not hostile, the method for promoting peace in the Church is this: you should rather win over their minds and gain their friendship by kind words, services, examples and similar means, than unseasonably demand good deeds from them. Their mind must be brought round before their hand is needed. Whoever does otherwise misjudges both their duty and his own, which is a great imprudence.

units.la: Sin autem homines amici sunt, qui animum vltrò adiecturi sint ad benefaciendum Ecclesiæ, hic vtrumque, fieri pro commoditate potest, nonftra officia in illos exercere, & vicissim illorum ergâ Ecclesiam occupari: vt tum nostris beneficiis lucrifiant Christo, præsertim fiducia nostra de ipsis explorata, tum etiam suis ipsorum factis quodammodo obstringantur ad costantiam illius fui in benefaciendo studij. Nam cur hoc modo non certemus benefaciendo cum illis hominibus? quibus Deus fecit promissiones causa Ecclesiæ suæ, & amplissimam quandam earum partem cum piis assignauit : quos Chri. stus pro nobis dixit esse, quandoquidem non sunt aduersus nos : quibus promisit mercedem Prophetæ, si vas frigidæ in nomine Prophetæ ministrauerint: quorum societatem Abraham, Dauid,& pij omnes in Testamento vtroq. conciliare sibi nō dubitauerunt,cùm & cómunitate naturæ, & promissionum diuinarum consociatione hos sibi cõiunctos esse boni animaduerterint. Temeraria de his iudicia interdum audiui plus satis:à quibus Christiani abstineant oro & obsecro,ne in veritatem diuinam communemque charitatem impingant periculosissimè.
units.tr: But if men are friends who will of their own accord be ready to do good to the Church, then both can be done as opportunity allows: we may perform our own duties toward them, and in turn they may be engaged in their goodwill toward the Church. Thus on the one hand they are won to Christ through our kindnesses, especially since our trust in them has been tested; and on the other hand their own deeds bind them, in some measure, to constancy in their zeal for doing good. For why should we not in this way vie with such men in doing good? God made promises to them for the sake of his Church, and assigned a very large part of them to the pious. Christ said they are for us, since they are not against us. He promised a prophet's reward to those who give a cup of cold water in the name of a prophet. Abraham, David and all the pious in both Testaments did not hesitate to win their fellowship, since they perceived that these men were joined to them by the common bond of nature and by the partnership of divine promises. I have heard rash judgments about such men more than enough at times; I beg and beseech Christians to abstain from them, lest they dangerously strike against divine truth and common charity.

units.la: Quòd si his benefieri à nobis oportere, & (quantum quidem per eos fieri potest) pacem Ecclesiæ ab his secundùm Deum conuenirexpeti; quanto magis & maiore etiam fiducia hoc ipsum expetiabiis necesse est, qui éénsentur in numero domesticorum Ecclesiæ? Atque hæc causa est,cur nos passim Apostolus ad Christiana erga fratres nostros germanos Dei in Ecclesia filios officia accendit monitis saluberrimis, & hortationibus vehementissimis: modumq. officiorum istorum præscribit diligentissimè,vt cum omni modestia ac mãsuetudine, cum animi lenitate tolerantes alij alios per charitatem, studeamus feruare vnitatem Spiritus per vinculum pacis, & fundamenta principiaque bonorum officiorum quàm accuratissimè adscribit, dicens: Vnum est corpus, & vnus Spiritus, sicut & vocati estis in vnam spem vocationis vestræ: vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma, vnus Deus & pater omnium, qui est super omnes, & per omnes, & in omnibus nobis.
units.tr: But if we ought to do good to these men, and (as far as it can be done through them) the peace of the Church ought to be sought from them according to God, how much more, and with even greater confidence, must it be sought from those who are counted among the household members of the Church? This is why the Apostle everywhere urges us, with most wholesome admonitions and most vehement exhortations, to Christian duties toward our brothers, the true sons of God in the Church. He prescribes the manner of these duties most carefully: that with all modesty and gentleness, with meekness of spirit, bearing with one another in love, we strive to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. He sets out the foundations and principles of good duties most precisely, saying: "There is one body and one Spirit, as you were also called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in us all" (Eph. 4).

units.la: Atque his quidem omnibus officiis omnes promiscuè tenemur alij erga alios in Domino: sed tamen cùm ad eos respicio quos Deus singulari vocatione instruxit in Ecclesia sua, vt faciant & doceant quæcunq; sibi à Domino præcepta sunt, quo grauiorem esse video obligationem illorum, eo grauiorem quoque video & horreo condemnationem, si ab his officiis, quæ Deus docet, docendis & faciendis abscefferint[?]. Quid enim? qui Angeli sunt Domini, ministri Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, qui non sumus nostri iuris, sed Domini nostri Iesu Christi sumus, qui per ipsum mancipati Deo & Patri, & immissi ad colendam sanctam vineam illius, putamúsne licere nobis quod vulgo non licet? aut quod in aliis culpamus, in nobis vacare culpa? non cogitamus vnquam exemplum illius instrumenti electi à Domino, dicentis: Quisquis certat, in omnibus est continens; illi quidem qui instadio currunt, vt periturum coronam accipiant; nos autem, vt incorruptam. ego igitur ita: curro, vt non in incertū;ita pugilem ago,vt aérem non cædam; sed contundo corpus meum & in seruitutem redigo, neque modo cùm aliis prædicatim,ipse fiam reiectaneus?
units.tr: Indeed, we are all bound to these duties toward one another in the Lord. But when I consider those whom God has equipped by a special calling in his Church, to do and teach whatever the Lord has commanded them, I see that the greater their obligation, the greater also I see and dread their condemnation, if they have withdrawn from teaching and doing these duties that God prescribes. For what of it? We who are the Lord's angels, Christ's ministers and stewards of the mysteries of God, who are not our own but belong to our Lord Jesus Christ, who through him have been bound over to God the Father and sent in to cultivate his holy vineyard: do we think it lawful for us what is not lawful for others? Or that we are free of the fault we find in others? Do we never consider the example of that chosen vessel of the Lord, who says: "Whoever competes exercises self-control in all things; they indeed do it to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one. So I run, not aimlessly; I box, not beating the air; but I punish my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become a castaway" (1 Cor. 9.25–27)?

units.la: Quapropter mea núc ad vos, ô fratres charissimi & symmystæ obseruandi, sese conuertit oratio, qui præfecti estis ouili Domini, vt agatis & pascatis greges qui vobis commissi sunt ex auctoritate illius, & qui rationem illi Episcopo animarum nostrarum & summo pastori ouium estis reddituri, non solùm de vita, verùm etiam de administratione vestra.
units.tr: Therefore my address now turns to you, most beloved brothers and fellow-initiates, who are set over the Lord's flock, that you may tend and feed the flocks committed to you by his authority, and who are to render account to him, the Bishop of our souls and the chief shepherd of the sheep, not only for your life but also for your administration.

units.la: Nam quòd omnes in populo Dei siue in Ecclesia debent, id & vos debetis; ac proinde cum aliis omnibus pacem Ecclesiæ debetis postulare, & omnibus viribus, vt oues Christi, propugnate.
units.tr: For what everyone in the people of God, that is, in the Church, owes, you too owe; and therefore, together with all others, you ought to seek the peace of the Church and defend it with all your strength, as Christ's sheep.

units.la: Sed quia amplius quàm aliæ oues Christi accepistis, siue dono, prout varie sua dona admetitut [?] spiritus illius; siue vocatione, qua singulis imperata & commendata est sua administratio: propterea nobis supra quàm aliis necessaria est accuratio in gerendis rebus, quas fidei nostræ commisit Dominus.
units.tr: But because you have received more than the other sheep of Christ, whether by gift, as his Spirit distributes its various gifts, or by calling, by which each man's administration has been enjoined and committed to him, therefore greater care in carrying out the things the Lord has entrusted to our faith is necessary for us than for others.

units.la: Sermonem suum commisit nobis: in Ecclesia sua mandauit eloquii, & pascere oues suas: præire iussit exemplo fidei: probari voluit exitum conuersationis nostræ; propterea nos id semper ante oculos habere, vt typi [?] firmus boni operum, quæ grex Christi sequens consideret atque imitetur.
units.tr: He has committed his word to us; in his Church he has charged us to dispense the message and to feed his sheep; he has bidden us go before them by the example of faith; he has wished the outcome of our conduct to be tested. Therefore we must always keep this before our eyes, that we be a firm type of good works, which the flock of Christ may observe and imitate.

units.la: Sal terræ, lux mundi fuerunt Apostoli: hac dignitate officij omnes communicant qui sermonem illum Domini, quem tradiderūt Apostoli, prout à Christo accepērant, præferunt in ouili eius. Ambulent sanè alij in vocatione sua sibi ipsis,id est, suo & paucorum, quibus sunt coniuncti, commodo: at nos quibus dispensatio bonorum istorum suit concredita, siue stamus, siue cadimus,non solùm Domino nostro & nobis(vt alij)stamus, aut cadimus ;sed aliis quàm plurimis, qui nobis labentibus collabuntur & consistunt stantibus. Optima quæque de omnibus concipio, & opto ex animo : cùm tamen ex prisHcis recentibusque exemplis incommoda plurima Ecclesiis allata videam imprudente multorum administratione , qui nec dignitatem sermonis diuini, nec veritatem vocationis suæ , nec pacem Ecclesiæ satis prudenter expenderunt, dabitis veniant pro vestra in Deum Ecclesiamque pietate , si postquā de omnibus Ecclesiæ membris in communedixi, aliquid etiam speciatim de iis dixero,qui communi corpori Ecclesiæ ex vocatione Dei tenentur consulere; vt pastores in ea dati, ad coagmentationem sanctorum,ad opus ministerij , & ad ædificationem corporis Christi.
units.tr: The apostles were the salt of the earth and the light of the world. All who bear that word of the Lord, which the apostles handed down as they had received it from Christ, share in this dignity of office in his fold. Others, indeed, may walk in their calling for themselves, that is, for their own advantage and that of the few associated with them; but we, to whom the stewardship of these goods has been entrusted, whether we stand or fall, do not stand or fall only for our Lord and for ourselves, as others do, but for very many others, who fall with us when we fall and stand when we stand. I conceive the best of everyone and wish it from my heart. Yet since I see from ancient and recent examples that many disadvantages have been brought upon the churches through the imprudent administration of men who have not weighed sufficiently the dignity of God's word, the truth of their calling, or the peace of the Church, you will, for your piety toward God and the Church, pardon me if, having spoken generally of all the members of the Church, I say something also specifically of those who by God's calling are bound to care for the common body of the Church: the pastors given in it "for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, and for the building up of the body of Christ" (Eph. 4.12).

units.la: Est igitur munus commune omnium, vt communionem sanctorum colant, & pacem expetant, illius: nostrum verò singulare est, vt eandem communione colamus singulari modo, qui singulari vocationis lege à Deo prœfinitus est. Ad hanc communionem ante ostendimus; primùm formam internam, quàcum Deo coalescimus, pertinere: deinde externam, qua colligimur ad verbum ipsius percipiendum, preces exhibendas, praestandum obsequium, & ordinem honestatemq; in his omnibus rebus procurandam. Nostrum est, ut in his ipsis rebus summa religione ac studio aliis omnibus praeeamus sermone, & factis. Quid hic excusationis vel in speciem adferre possunt, qui aut sermone aut factis non ita procurant aedificationem illius corporis, quod Deus suo sanguine comparauit? Equidem perhorresco totus, nec sine dolore acerbissimo recolere possum cum animo meo, quantam Ecclesiae labem, quantam sibi ipsis ruinam accersiuerint, qui sive prudentes, sive imprudentes ab hoc officio suo desciuerunt. Faxit Dominus; ne quis porro desciscat, & se machinationibus Satanae ab hoc sanctissimo instituto vocationis suae abripi patiatur. Grauissima sane vulnera non nobis solum infligimus; sed ipsi Ecclesiae Christi, quam curae nostrae Dominus commendauit; cum dictis aut factis ab illo sine quem Deus imperat, aberramus, obliuiscentes illius pacis quam in Ecclesia Dei nos constantissimè oportet expetere. Nam cur non expendamus, quandoquidem administri sumus Christi & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei; cur (inquam) non expendamus diligentissimè dicta factaque nostra, quae
units.tr: It is therefore the common duty of all to cultivate the communion of the saints and to seek its peace. Ours, however, is a peculiar task: to cultivate that same communion in a peculiar way, which God has marked out under a peculiar law of calling. We have shown before that this communion pertains first to the inner form, by which we cohere with God; then to the outer, by which we are gathered to receive his word, to offer prayers, to render obedience, and to secure order and decency in all these things. It is our task to go before all others in these very matters, in word and deed, with the highest devotion and zeal. What excuse can even be pretended by those who, in word or deed, do not so promote the building up of that body which God purchased with his blood? Indeed I shudder all over, and cannot recall without the bitterest grief how great a stain on the Church, how great a ruin they have brought upon themselves, who, whether wisely or unwisely, have departed from this duty. May the Lord grant that no one depart from it henceforth, and that no one suffer himself to be snatched by the machinations of Satan from this most holy institution of his calling. Indeed we inflict very grievous wounds not only on ourselves but on the Church of Christ itself, which the Lord has commended to our care, when by word or deed we stray from the one whom God has enjoined, forgetting the peace which we must most steadfastly seek in the Church of God. For why should we not weigh, since we are ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, why (I say) should we not most diligently weigh our words and deeds, which

units.la: [The last word of the page is cut off by the lower edge of the scan; left as printed.] ab aliis diligentissimè nouimus obseruari? Nos laboro, vtrum ea sic obseruent alij iure, an iniuria: ex officio, an præter officium. etsi, cùm lux aliis iubemur esse, vt videant; & sal[?] esse vt veritate doctrinæ ab omni corruptione homines vindicentur; non possunt dici ex officio non facere, qui ad nos respiciunt. Omnino ita nos oportet cum animis nostris statuere: si religiosè dicta factaq; nostra ipsi cogitemus circumspiciamusq;e, id nos ex officio facturos esse: sin minùs, audaciam præsidentiamq;e inconsidecatam[?] nostram fore contra officium nostrum.
units.tr: [The last word of the page is cut off by the lower edge of the scan; left as printed.] we know are most diligently observed by others. I do not trouble myself whether they observe them rightly or wrongly, from duty or beyond duty. Yet since we are bidden to be light to others, that they may see, and salt, so that men may be delivered from all corruption by the truth of doctrine, those who look to us cannot be said to fail in their duty by not doing so. We must certainly resolve in our minds thus: if we religiously consider and examine our words and deeds, we shall be acting from duty; but if not, our rash boldness and presumption will be contrary to our office.

units.la: Quid ergo, dixerit quispiam, in dictis factisque nostris attendi a nobis necesse est? Exponam paucis. ad Deum, Ecclesiam, mundum, & ad nos ipsos oportet attendamus. Ad Deum, vt semper ab ipso pendeamus, & ad ipsum omnia referamus: ad Ecclesiam, vt ipsi ad Deum ituræ præcamus: ad mundum, vt inculpati extra ipsum fugiamus, & alios nobiscum euocemus: ad nos ipsos denique, vt in his omnibus officiis nos occupemus constantissimè, ad Deum, secundùm Deum, per Ecclesiam, & cum Ecclesia contendentes, & aduersus mundum armis iustitiæ dimicantes ad nostram salutem, & eorum qui nos audiunt. Hic verò, Deus bone, quàm multis modis peccatur ignorantiâ, imprudentia, & infirmitate nostra! Non libet, neque expedit omnia pertexere, quibus omnes grauiter offendimus. Non libet ea, in quibus commu-ni-[?] ter cum aliis peccamus, colligere. Id satis futurum arbitror, si de iis peccatis dixero, in quæ contra singularem vocationem nostram plus satis (eheu) incidimus; immemores gratiæ Dei, pacis Ecclesiæ, & vocationis nostræ : etsi fit plurimùm, ut huius ipsius vocationis nostræ præsexu & specie peccata nostra contegamus. Tacebo de internis peccatis, quæ videt Deus, & singulorum sentiunt apud se conscientiæ : de externis dicam.
units.tr: What then, someone may say, must we attend to in our words and deeds? I shall explain briefly. We ought to attend to God, to the Church, to the world, and to ourselves. To God, that we always depend on him and refer all things to him. To the Church, that we pray for it as those who are going to God. To the world, that we flee from it blameless and call others out with us. And finally to ourselves, that we occupy ourselves most steadfastly in all these duties: toward God, according to God, through the Church and with the Church striving, and fighting against the world with the weapons of righteousness, for our own salvation and that of those who hear us. But here, good God, how many ways we sin through ignorance, imprudence and our weakness! It is neither my wish nor expedient to go through all the ways by which we all grievously offend. I do not wish to gather those in which we sin together with others. I think it will suffice if I speak of those sins into which we have fallen, alas, more than enough, against our particular calling, forgetful of God's grace, the Church's peace and our own calling; though very often we cover our sins under the pretext and appearance of this very calling. I shall pass over the inward sins, which God sees and which individual consciences feel within themselves; I shall speak of the outward ones.

units.la: Qui debemus ex vocatione, sanctimoniæ & paci Ecclesiæ dictis & factis consulere, plerumque dictis & factis officimus : tum eas res quæ non sunt vocationis nostræ assumendo, tum eas quæ omnino ex vocatione sunt omittendo, tum contra ius vocationis alia committendo. Acdictis[?] quidem offendimus, quà privatim aliqua Ecclesiæ membra, quà publicè corpus ipsius, prout sese res nobis obtulerit. De privatis offensionibus quid dicam? aut unde incipiam? Alios offendit levitas sermonum qui nihil ad nos, alios silentium, alios importunitas. Præsertim si qui doctrina, reprehensione, aut consolatione opus habuerint, incredibile est quàm facilè imprudentia nostra offendantur animæ, quæ privatum Dei servorum officium desiderant in suis angustiis & perturbationibus gravissimis. Non solet enim illa cogitatio animos nostros insicessere[?], quà ab exemplo Christi Domini & præceptoris nostri singulis momentis
units.tr: We who ought, by virtue of our calling, to care for the holiness and peace of the Church by our words and deeds, for the most part hinder it by words and deeds: partly by taking up matters that are not part of our calling, partly by omitting those that are wholly within our calling, and partly by committing other acts contrary to the rights of our calling. We offend indeed by words, both toward individual members of the Church in private and toward its body in public, as occasion presents itself. What shall I say of private offences? Or where shall I begin? The levity of words that have nothing to do with us offends some, silence offends others, importunity others. Especially when certain people need teaching, rebuke or consolation, it is incredible how easily souls are offended by our imprudence, souls which in their distress and very grave perturbations look for the private office of God's servants. For that thought does not usually steal into our minds, by which we ought to recall at every moment the example of Christ the Lord, our teacher,

units.la: nos oportebat recolere ; non litigabit, neq. clamitabit, neque audiet quisquam in plateis vocem eius : arundinem quassatam non confringet,& linum fumigans non extinguet:quæ omnia Christus fecit opere , & in ministerio fieri imperat. Nec valde , nec sæpe animos nostros afficiunt illius verba,qui zelo sanctissimo dixit, Quis affligitur,quin ego affligar? Quis offenditur,quin ego vrar?
units.tr: We ought to remember these things: he will not wrangle or cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed, nor quench a smoking flax. Christ did all of these things by his work, and he commands that they be done in the ministry. Nor do the words of the man who said with the most holy zeal, "Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" move our minds strongly or often.

units.la: Quid? quòd in hæc mala, grauiora certè quàm putemus,in conscientias infirmorum & indignissima vocatione nostra , non solùm rusmus apud eos qui in grege nostro sunt; verumetiam,tanquam si domi nihil esset in quo occupemur, agimus εὐλογισμόν (summa licentia,&in rebus alienis sumus oculatissimi?Onos miseros, qui amplissimos fines vocationis nostræ , quibus capiendis nunquam satis idonea aut sufficiens esse potest ingenij nostri tenuitas, dilatari putamus oportere vanitate nostra: neq. in sermone,quem Deus imperat legi ; neque in grege, quem Deus imperat pasci , conquiscimus ex officio nostro. Sed leuiora sunt hæc priuata vulnera iis quæ publico sæpe imponuntur,partim fidentia,partimq.imprudentia nostra. Nā siue ad sermones in cōcionibus publicè habitos,siue ad reliquam administrationem oculos conuerteris, incidunt sæpe quàm plurima; quibus , nisi probè ad nos attendamus,nocemus publico,& auctoritatem vocationis illius nostræ, quam Deus contemni facto nostro noluit,ipsi minuimus. Quàm multa interdum pro concione funduntur,quæ nihil ad nos pertinent aut vocationem nostram? quæ nihil ad Ecclesiam? aut quæ alienæ cognitioni sunt credita? Testes sunt Ecclesiæ multæ apud omnes gentes,testes magistratus,testes historiæ, testes libri estã de iure diuino & humano scripti,plurimos eorum, qui finibus Ecclesiasticæ vocationis suæ continere sese debuerant, quà se ipsos, quà ministerium suum sanctissimamque auctoritatem illius, quà multas animas, quà respublicas, quà Ecclesias funditus perdidisse, dum ex angustia sui iudicij (quod putabant amplissimum) omnia agi & ferri statucrunt oportere.
units.tr: What of this? Do we not, in these evils (certainly graver than we think), act upon the consciences of the weak, and in our most unworthy calling, not only meddle among those who are in our own flock, but also, as if there were nothing at home to occupy us, play the reckoner [εὐλογισμόν] with the greatest licence and become most sharp-eyed in other men's affairs? Wretched us, who in our vanity think it fitting to stretch the wide bounds of our calling, which the narrowness of our wit can never be sufficient or adequate to take in! We do not settle down to the preaching that God commands to be read, nor to the flock that God commands to be fed, as our office requires. But these private wounds are lighter than those which are often inflicted on the public, partly through our boldness and partly through our thoughtlessness. For whether you look to the sermons delivered in public assemblies or to the rest of our administration, very many faults often occur, and unless we attend to ourselves carefully, we harm the public and diminish the authority of that calling of ours, which God did not want to be despised through our conduct. How many things are sometimes poured out from the pulpit that have nothing to do with us or our calling? Nothing to do with the Church? Or things entrusted to the knowledge of others? The many churches among all nations bear witness, the magistrates bear witness, history bears witness, and the books written on divine and human law bear witness, that many men, who ought to have kept themselves within the limits of their ecclesiastical calling, have utterly ruined both themselves and their ministry and its most holy authority, and many souls, commonwealths and churches, while they have decided that everything must be done and carried out according to the narrowness of their own judgement (which they thought very broad).

units.la: Librum sacrum,fratres dilectissimi,Librum scedéris siue Testamenti veteris & Noui versandum habemus nocturna & diurna manu, vt dicebat Satyricus; non libros huius mundi sorenses atque politicos : conscientias habemus curandas, ac non facultates : Ecclesias, ac non respublicas. Putámúsne igitur Deum malè prospexisse mundo, cùm res ciuiles ab Ecclesiasticis dispesceret? putamúsne nobis factam à Deo iniuriam, qui has res nobis, illas aliis curandas instituerit? putamúsne sufficere mentes cognoscendis & iudicandis, corpora faciendis tam multis rebus,quas Deus distribuit in multos propter earum infinitatem grauitatemquæ, &
units.tr: Brethren most beloved, we have the holy Book of the covenant, that is, of the Old and New Testament, to be turned over by night and by day, as the satirist said; we do not have the worldly and political books of this age. We have consciences to care for, not property; churches, not commonwealths. Do we then think that God looked poorly upon the world when he separated civil affairs from ecclesiastical ones? Do we think that he did us an injustice, when he appointed these matters to us and those to others? Do we think that our minds are sufficient for knowing and judging, and our bodies for doing, so many things, which God has distributed among many because of their infinite number and weight, and [our] weakness?

units.la: [?] The reading "dilectissimi" and "scedéris" is uncertain. que,& infirmitatem nostram ? Nempe hoc illud est,miseret Deum nostri, & nos ipsos nostri non miseret. Videamus potius , obsecro, vt tenuitatem nostram ferió coram Domino deinceps recordemur, grauitatem muneris nostri ex veritate cogitemus , & nobis ante oculos ponamus magnū illum Dei seruum & Christi Apostolum,dicenté : Fiduciam habemus per Christum ( non autem per nos ) apud Deum ( non autem apud nos ) non quòd idonei sumus per nos ipsos ad cogitandū quidquam velut ex nobis ipsis:sed quòd idonei sumus, id ex Deo est, qui etiam facit vt idonei simus ministri sanctiffimi illius fœderis , ex quo uiuificamur in Spiritu. Hic,hic pes figendus est , in ministerio ad quod uocati sumus : non est cur alió tranfuolemus,qui in opere nostro (si recté iudicabimus) longè plus laboris sensuri sumus , quàm vt nobis liceat animi nostri explendi causa in alienas curas irruere.
units.tr: Indeed, this is the case: God pities us, and we do not pity ourselves. Let us rather, I beg you, see to it that we henceforth remember our littleness before the Lord, and think in truth about the weight of our office, and set before our eyes that great servant of God and apostle of Christ, who says: "We have such trust through Christ toward God; not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is of God, who also has made us able ministers of the new covenant, of the Spirit, through which we are made alive." Here, here is where we must plant our foot, in the ministry to which we are called. There is no reason for us to fly to other places, for in our own work (if we judge rightly) we shall feel far more labour than we are allowed, for the sake of satisfying our minds, to rush into other men's cares.

units.la: Neque uerò hoc malum unum est in nostrâ administratione , quòd alienis rebus plus satis attendimus: sed ex eo alterum malum cōtinuò nascitur,quòd alienis implicati occupationibus eas plerumque omittimus, quas etiam flagitat inexcusabilis uocationis nostræ necessitas. siqui in Ecclesia sunt, quos doceri à nobis oporteat; ne per somnium quidem nobis in mentem uenit nostri officij : si qui redarguendi à veritate doctrinæ abludentes ; si qui ad probitatem & sanctifisanctimoniâ vitæ cohortandi ; fi qui à viis malis & distortis suis reuocandi; si qui verbi diuini consolationibus, vbi malis prostrati iacent,erigendi : siqui denique vllo modo verbis vitæ æternæ in Christo animandi (hîc enim Rhodus, hîc saltus), siue priuatim, vt lex charitatis iubet; siue publicè, vt ratio publica interdum postulat; tum verò nos. hîc non adsumus, & veré aliud agimus, quos hoc agere oportuit (vt in rebus sactis olim clamabat præco) & τόδ᾽ ἔργον ὡς [?] πράσσειν [?] transilimus. Nimirum hic fructus illius πανουργοσύνης [?], hoc opus illius architectonis aduersarij salutis nostræ, qui mille-opifex rerum & mille-artifex pro vno cogitato ad vocationem nostram pertinente infundit mille,ex quo nos ad mille potius alia quàm ad hoc ferri animaduertit ingenij nostri vanitate.
units.tr: Nor indeed is this the only evil in our administration, that we attend too much to other men's affairs; from this a second evil arises at once, that, entangled in other men's occupations, we often neglect those things which even the necessity of our inexcusable calling demands. If there are people in the Church whom we ought to teach, we do not so much as dream of our duty; if there are those who must be refuted because they stray from the truth of doctrine; if there are those to be exhorted to uprightness and holiness of life; if there are those to be called back from their evil and crooked ways; if there are those to be raised up with the consolations of the divine word, where they lie cast down by evils; if, finally, there are those to be encouraged in any way with the words of eternal life in Christ (for here is Rhodes, here is the leap), whether privately, as the law of charity bids, or publicly, as public reason sometimes requires, then indeed we are not present here, and we truly do something else, we who ought to have been doing this (as the herald cried in sacred matters of old), and we pass over the doing of this task [τόδ᾽ ἔργον ὡς πράσσειν]. Surely this is the fruit of that knavery [πανουργοσύνης], this the work of that architect of our salvation's adversary, who, the maker of a thousand things and the artificer of a thousand things, pours a thousand thoughts into the place of one thought that pertains to our calling, by which he turns us, through the vanity of our wit, to a thousand other things rather than to this one.

units.la: Atque vtinam in his finibus mali hoc nostrum malum subsideret, ne vlterius abriperemur à vocatione nostra. Grauissimum enim & indignissimum omnium ex perdito illo inftituto id cõsequi solet maximo Ecclesiæ damno, quòd ij qui aliena curant & ad sua sibi imperata minimè attendunt, eò tandem veniunt dementiæ, vt obliti planè vocationis suæ non dubitent ea facere quæ in totum vocationi ipsorum aduersantur. Quid enim, obsecro, facias, mi homo, qui forensia cum Ecclesiasticis, prophana cum sacris, humana cum diuinis conturbas præsidentissimè, nisi vt inescatus mellito veneno fastidioque huius mundi, exuas rerum sanctarum studium ex prophanarum cõfuetudine? Ita accidet tibi, quod olim prouerbio dicebatur, vt modò togatus, modò palliatus ambules,& vtramque paginam vir ἐπεφανῶς[?] corrumpas vocationis tuæ, dum vtramque paginam mundi tibi videris facere. Deus bonus, quantum delirium mentes istorum hominum occupat, qui rerum adeò multarum fe posse confidunt satagere! Non ita delirabant veteres illi poëtæ in ratione Deorum suorum, quos tamé hominibus longè potentiores efle fatebantur. huic cælum, illi æthera, huic inferiorem aërem, illi mare, vni terram, alteri inferos tribuebant procurandos: denique ordinem aliquem videbant in Diis suis cõmentitiis,quem tu, homo,in te ipso videre non potes:ac proinde vbi ordinem non vides,in contraria studia, sententias,actionesque prore nata,vt plumain diuærfos ventos,quàm facilimè abriperis. Nec verò aliter potest contingere:cùm tibi in rebus non cõftes, omninò necefle est eò delabaris,vt nec sermone, nec actionibus tuis perdiu idem esse possis.
units.tr: Would that this evil of ours might settle down within these bounds, and that we were not further carried off from our calling! For the most grievous and most unworthy result of that ruinous practice is wont to follow, to the greatest harm of the Church: those who attend to other men's cares and pay little attention to what is commanded them, come at last to such madness that, quite forgetting their calling, they do not hesitate to do things that are wholly opposed to it. For what, I ask you, will you do, my friend, who so presumptuously mix worldly affairs with ecclesiastical, profane with sacred, and human with divine, unless, enticed by the honeyed poison and weariness of this world, you strip off zeal for holy things through the habit of profane ones? So it will happen to you what was once said in a proverb: that you walk now in a toga, now in a cloak, and manifestly [ἐπεφανῶς] corrupt both pages of your calling, while you seem to make both pages of the world. Good God, what a delirium occupies the minds of those men who trust that they can manage so many things! The ancient poets were not so deluded in their account of their gods, whom nevertheless they confessed to be far more powerful than men. To one they assigned the heavens, to another the upper air, to another the lower air, to another the sea, to one alone the earth, to another the underworld, to be looked after: in short, they saw some order among their invented gods, which you, my friend, cannot see in yourself. And so, where you do not see order, you are most easily carried off, like a feather, by the winds into contrary pursuits, opinions and actions that have arisen by chance. Nor can it be otherwise: when you are not consistent in your affairs, you must necessarily slide to such a point that you cannot remain the same for long in either your speech or your actions.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem in rebus error est procliuis, vbi tam multiplicem capturam vnica ingenij nostri lineola & vnico iactu nos affecuturos cõfidimus,ita etiam alterum malum huic adnafcitur necessàrió;quòd iustum modum retum peregquè ac res ipsàs perdimus. Nam quæ priuatim ad salutem animarum curari opus est, ea publicè funditamus ; quæ in aurem infufurrari, ea super tecta pronunciamus ; quæ sedato animo, ea cum feruore; quæ cum vehementia, ea remisso animo; quæ cum sale,ea insulsè; quæ cum auctoritate, ea inepte ad Scribarü & Pharifæorum exemplum prædi cantur. Nempe auctoritatem nostram,nō Christi quærimus plerique,& opinione freti auctoritatis nostræ vtramque perdimus miseri. Et miramur, rebus ita stantibus, fi verbum Dei parum fructus edit in Ecclesiis Christianis hoc nostro tempore? cùm tam parum[?] in iis, per quos efferri ipsum oportet, plerumque radicetur; & radicatum adeò multis spinis & fentibus præfocetur, quas nos ipsi plerumque facto nostro imprudentiaque in aruo Domini conferimus?
units.tr: Now, just as in affairs the error is prone to arise when we trust that by a single thread of our wit and a single cast we shall obtain so many-sided a catch, so also another evil necessarily grows from this: that we lose the due measure of things and the things themselves together. For what ought to be cared for privately for the salvation of souls, that we publish in public; what should be whispered in the ear, that we proclaim from the housetops; what calls for a calm spirit, that we handle with fervour; what calls for gentleness, that we handle with vehemence; what needs salt, that we handle without savour; what needs authority, that we preach foolishly, after the example of the Scribes and Pharisees. Indeed, most of us seek our own authority, not Christ's, and, trusting in the reputation of our own authority, we wretchedly lose both. And are we surprised, things standing thus, if the word of God produces little fruit in Christian churches in our time, when it is so seldom rooted in those through whom it ought to be carried forth; and when what has taken root is choked by so many thorns and briars, which we ourselves very often sow in the Lord's field by our deeds and our thoughtlessness?

units.la: Equidem non possum quin vehementissimè cómoueat, quoties hæc mala apud me réputo: neque mihi voluptatis quidquam esse potest in iis perscribendis, quorum perhorresco cogitatione; & quæ fi qui indigné ferant à me confignari[?] scriptis ; pero[?] ex animo, vt ferant indigniùs ea fieri ab aliis quæ à nobis perfcribuntur. Deum oro, det nobis omnibus iustum argumentum tollendi è medio has querimonias,& mihi ipsi delendi scripturam meam.
units.tr: Indeed I cannot help being deeply moved whenever I call these evils to mind. I take no pleasure in setting down the things I shudder to think of. If some people take it badly that I have committed these matters to writing, I wish, from my heart, that they would take it even worse when others write them down. I pray God will give us all a just reason to remove these complaints from the world, and give me a reason to erase my own writing.

units.la: Sed quid agam ? taceámne in tanta perturbatione publica, tantoque incendio, quod plerifque custodibus dormientibus, aliud agentibus, aut variè in studia abreptis Satanas excitauit? certè incendium est in orbe Christiano, nisi Deus è cælo prospexerit, omnia cōfumpturum: animi humani foci sunt, in quibus peccatum flagrat; linguæ hæ folles sunt, illæ fomites, quibus incendium magis ac magis inardescit; linguis succedunt Chartarum virulentissimarum plaustra, quibus tamquam malleolis, perrumpit incendium in omnes partes, quæcumque lingua perflari non possunt: denique bona pars Christiani orbis hoc tempore bustum potius videtur esse peruadente & furente incendio, quàm Christiani gregis domicilium. An ergo hi pastores? hæ oues Christi quas in suo miserabili busto miserè video contabescere? Sunt certè pastores adhuc, sunt oues Christi, & Christi sunt: sed multi in hoc tetro & lethali incendio nec se Christi esse, nec oues esse, nec esse pastores meminerunt: usqueadeò Christus salutarisque gratia illius grauitate istius incendij, & studiorum nostrorum in publico hoc malo vanitate, animorumque tenebris, & mundi fluctuantis fumo obscurantur. Quin igitur dicam, quod ille Elihu apud Iobum? plenus sum sermonibus, coartat me spiritus ventris mei: ecce venter meus ut vinum cui non aperitur, sicut noui utres, findetur: eloquar, ut respiratio sit mihi: aperiens labia mea, enunciabo: ne, quæso, accipiam personam ullius, & apud quemquam non utar præfatione. non enim noui præfationibus uti: paululum si dissimularem, tolleret me qui fecit me. Ac multos quidem viros bonos, Dei & Ecclesiæ amantissimos, scio eadem verba mecum reputare sanctissimo religiosissimoque studio; cùm ad mala tám multa respiciunt, quæ hoc nostro seculo in Christiano orbe grassantur licentiosissimè. Sed quia illi tacent coram hominibus, effundentes suos gemitus apud Dominum solum cogitorem omnium; spero me illis rem gratam facturum, si communes ipsis ac mihi dolores hoc scripto expresso, & Christianos omnes tan-dem testes appellauero tum doloris acerbissimi illius nostri, tum etiā officij, quòd testatum facimus & spondemus in Domino, si forte ad restinguendum incendiū commoda Christianitati per voluntatem Dei opera nostra futura est.
units.tr: But what am I to do? Should I keep silent in such a public disturbance and such a great fire, which Satan has kindled while most of the watchmen sleep, or are busy with other things, or have been variously carried off into their own pursuits? Certainly there is a fire in the Christian world which, unless God looks down from heaven, will consume everything. Human hearts are its hearths, in which sin blazes. Tongues are its bellows, and pens are its kindling, by which the fire grows fiercer and fiercer. To the tongues succeed carts loaded with the most virulent writings, and with these, as with mallets, the fire breaks out into every part that tongues cannot reach. In short, at this time a large part of the Christian world looks more like a pyre, as the fire rages and rushes through it, than like a home for the Christian flock. Are these the ministers? Are these the sheep of Christ, whom I see wretchedly wasting away in their miserable pyre? Certainly they are still ministers, and still sheep of Christ, and belong to Christ. But many in this foul and deadly fire do not remember that they are Christ's, or sheep, or ministers. So far are Christ and his saving grace obscured by the heaviness of this fire, by the emptiness of our own studies in this public evil, by the darkness of minds, and by the smoke of a surging world. Why, then, should I not say what Elihu says to Job: "I am full of words; the spirit within my belly constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins it will burst. I will speak, that I may have relief; I will open my lips and answer. Let me not, I beg you, take on anyone's person, nor use flattery with anyone. For I do not know how to use flattery; if I were to keep quiet for a little, He who made me would take me away" (Job 32). Indeed, I know that many good men, who love God and the Church most dearly, weigh these same words with me, in a most holy and devout zeal, when they look upon the many evils that rage so unrestrainedly in the Christian world in our age. But since they keep silent before men, pouring out their groans before the Lord alone, who searches all hearts, I hope I will do them a favour if I set forth in writing our common sorrows, and if I call all Christians to witness both of that most bitter grief of ours and of the duty that we declare and promise before the Lord: that, if by God's will our work should be of any use in quenching the fire, it may serve Christianity.

units.la: Quid ergo agimus, ô fratres & peculiū[?] Christi? quid, grex Christi? quid, pastores gregis? quousque tandem in Christum, in membra ipsius, nostraque ipsorum viscera iniiciemus violentas manus? alij alios conterimus? dentibus, unguibus lacerabimus? pedibus proculcabimus? & sæviemus omni conatu nostro, ut immanes[?] ferae? quousque linguae gladij acuti futuri sunt? quousque veloces pedes ad effundendum sanguinem procurrentes? quousque manus ad horrendam lanienam & carnificinam adiicientur? Sunt enim quorum linguae priuatim ac publicè nihil nisi tubæ sunt ad canen-
units.tr: What then are we doing, brothers and Christ's own people? What are we doing, flock of Christ? What are we doing, shepherds of the flock? How long will we lay violent hands on Christ, on his members, and on our own bowels? Will we wear down one another? Will we tear each other with teeth and claws? Will we trample each other underfoot, and rage with all our strength like savage beasts? How long will our tongues be sharp swords? How long will our swift feet run to shed blood? How long will hands be applied to dreadful slaughter and butchery? For there are some whose tongues, in private and in public, are nothing but trumpets, most ready to sound for war,

units.la: dum bellicū paratiflimæ ; inflammantes rotam geniturę nostræ, & inflámatæ à gehenna. Sunt quorum manus calamo & atramento armata perfundit Ghriftianum orbem telis plané lethalibus quibus non corpora, sed corda hominum ad mortem sibi & aliis consciscendam furiosè adducuntur. Sunt quorum pedes ad excursiones & panegyres expeditissimi miniftrant diabolicis furiis in Christianum gregem irruentibus, sceleratissimè. Hæc tela iam in omnes partes Christiani orbis volitant adeò confertim, vt quemadmodum nimbo vehementiffimo lux'cæli, ita lux spiritualis denso telorum istorum numero multis Christianis mentibus minimè malis adimatur. An ergo tantum eftin scribendo voluptatis, vt propter eam Christi,Ecclesiæ, & animarum tam multarum expungatur ratio ? an voluptatem illam nostram quam in scribendo capimus, tanti audemus emere? Quin potiùs cogitamus quod olim dicebat ille Satyricus, teneri multos fcribendi cacoêthe insanabili?Scripta non ex morboanimi, sed ex iudicio certo exaranda atque edenda sunt. Alioquin taceri præstat : cùm doceat Salomon 'etiam stultum, quando tacet, yideri sapientem. Quòd fi certo iudicio fiant, profectò ad veritatem, & pacem, charitatemque spectare oportet omnia. Ac morbo quidem animi potiùs quàm iudicio scripta quàm plurima hoc tempore in vul- gus
units.tr: inflaming the wheel of our existence, and themselves set on fire by hell. There are some whose hands, armed with pen and ink, flood the Christian world with truly deadly weapons, by which not bodies but hearts of men are furiously led to bring death upon themselves and upon others. There are some whose feet, most nimble for raids and public gatherings, serve most wickedly the diabolical furies rushing upon the Christian flock. These weapons now fly in every direction across the Christian world, so thickly that, just as the light of heaven is taken away by a violent storm cloud, so the spiritual light is taken from many Christian minds, though they are in no way bad, by the dense number of these missiles. Is there so much pleasure in writing that for its sake the reckoning of Christ, of the Church, and of so many souls is to be wiped out? Or do we dare to buy that pleasure, which we take in writing, at such a price? Should we not rather consider what that satirist once said, that many are held by the incurable itch of writing (cacoethes scribendi)? Writings must be composed and published not from a sickness of the mind, but from a sure judgement. Otherwise it is better to be silent, since Solomon teaches that "even a fool, when he keeps silent, is thought wise" (Prov. 17:28). If writings are produced with sound judgement, then surely all things ought to aim at truth, peace and charity. Yet that many writings are scattered among the common people at this time, out of a sickness of mind rather than of judgement, can be proved by many arguments.

units.la: *Prov.17. gus dissipari, multis argumentis probari potest. Verumtamen, ne longiores simus, paucula quædam adferemus, ex quibus plurimorum scriptorum, quæ hoc tempore circumvolitant in manus omnium, conditionem ostendemus: ut singuli videant, quàm impune grassetur hoc malum maximo Ecclesiæ malo. De iis autem, perinde ac de actionibus internis & externis hominum, non ex genere materiaque (agimus enim de scriptis solùm ad res sacras pertinentibus) sed ex specie, ac circumstantiis, & sine ipsorum fieri iudicium necesse est. Primùm enim scripta edúntur, ac potiùs vomuntur quàm plurima ab ingeniis perturbatissimis; quæ pietati, veritati, charitati, & paci publicæ reipsa adversantur, & quæ in æternum præstàret supprimi quàm prodire in vulgi manus: adeò à bono principio absunt, & obiecto bono, quæ speciem factorum constituunt bonam. Deinde ut demus scripta multa existere, quæ non ita adversentur his bonis quæ modò diximus; sed ipsa (ut cum vulgo loquar) in substantia bona sint, tamen huic bonæ substantiæ multum veneni sæpe infunditur, cùm loco doctrinæ & dogmatum (ut vocant) veritatis iustæ circumstantiæ negliguntur, & res personales iniiciuntur, criminationes, convicia, contumeliæ, quamplurima denique acerbissima iudicia: quæ licet essent verissima, non iubet veritas dici, sed iubet reticeri charitas. Nam quid hoc ad veritatem propugnandam, aut mendacium expugnandum facit, si forte hominem suis coloribus (vt mihi quidem videtur) depinxero? neque enim veritatem suam per homines Deus ita probari voluit, vt ex bono aut prauo huius, illius, aut cuiusquam hominis instituto vitæ, de veritate diuina iudicent. Transcendit veritas omnem hominum captum: neque per homines illa iudicatur, sed homines per illam. Quapropter non dicebat Christus, ex fructibus hominum, aut ex hominibus cognoscetis veritatem; sed ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos. Et optimè inquit Apostolus: Quid si infidi fuerunt quidam? Num ipsorum infidelitas fidem Dei inanem reddet? absit, imò esto Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax: sicut scriptum est; vt iustificeris in sermonibus tuis, & vincas quando tu iudicas. Postremò si ad finem, quem sibi in scriptis proponunt multi, aut ad euentum etiam respicimus, omninò cõperturi sumus, aut finem multorum qui scribunt iniquum esse, aut si quidem minimè malus est, plurimum à fine discrepare scriptionis modum: ipsum denique euentum ab utroque abesse quàm longissimè. Cur autem? nisi quia in scribendo nec finis, nec modus servatur plurimùm: & res tacendæ diuulgantur in publicum; & incompetentes iudices in rebus etiam gravissimis malitiâ hominum appellantur, competentes verò multitudine oppressi in tanta rerum conturbatione silent.
units.tr: Prov. 17. Nevertheless, so as not to be too long, we will set down a few points by which we may show the condition of many writings that now fly about in everyone's hands, so that each may see how freely this evil, the greatest evil of the Church, rages with impunity. Concerning these writings, just as concerning the internal and external actions of men, we must judge them not by their kind and matter (for we are speaking only of writings that pertain to sacred things), but by their species and circumstances, and without regard to their authors. First, many writings are published, or rather vomited out, by very disturbed minds; they actually oppose piety, truth, charity and public peace, and it would be better for them to be suppressed forever than to go out into the hands of the common people. So far do they depart from a good beginning and a good object, which together constitute the good character of an act. Next, granting that there are many writings which do not oppose the good things just mentioned, but are (to speak with the common people) good in substance, still a great deal of poison is often poured into this good substance, when the circumstances of true teaching and doctrine (as they call it) are neglected, and personal matters are introduced: accusations, reproaches, insults, and in short very many bitter judgements. Even if these were perfectly true, truth does not command that they be spoken, but charity commands that they be passed over in silence. For what does it contribute to defending the truth or overthrowing a lie, if perhaps I paint a man in his own colours (as it seems to me)? God did not will his truth to be proved through men in such a way that men should judge the divine truth from the good or bad conduct of this or that person's life. Truth transcends all human understanding; it is not judged by men, but men are judged by it. Therefore Christ did not say, "You will know the truth from the fruits of men, or from men," but "from their fruits you will know them" (Matt. 7:16, 20). And the Apostle rightly says: "What if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness make the faith of God void? Certainly not! Let God be true, though every man be a liar; as it is written, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged" (Rom. 3:3–4). Finally, if we look at the end that many propose to themselves in writing, or even at the outcome, we shall surely find either that the end of many who write is wicked, or, if it is not wicked at all, that the manner of writing differs greatly from the end, and that the outcome itself is as far from both as possible. Why is this? Because in writing neither end nor manner is for the most part observed: things that ought to be kept quiet are made public, and incompetent judges are called upon, through the malice of men, even in the most serious matters, while the competent are overwhelmed by the great confusion of affairs and keep silent.

units.la: Certè hæc mala, quæ modò à me adducta sunt, si quis accuratè sine perturbatione animi expenderit; mirabitur mecum summam illam Dei misericordiam, qui corpus illud lacerum Christianitatis, & in suam ipsius salutem coniuratum hactenus adeò gratiosè à meritissima ruina & pestè conseruauerit. Nam vt nihil de fine & modo scriptionum dicam, quia iam antè perstrinximus, quotusquisque est qui à rebus fundendis abstineat, quas taceri præstitisset? si ad dogmata respexeris, hîc multa incommodè, multa improprie, multa falsò deblaterantur ab his & ab illis, quæ vbi semel euolauerint, neque ex scriptis reuocari possunt, neque ex animis scribentium; qui se cupiunt victores esse, ac non victricem veritatem: neque ipsis in mentem venit sanctissimi illius dicti, quo Paulus utebatur, nihil posse nos contra veritatem, sed pro veritate. Sin ad actiones hominum, quæ perscribuntur, animum & cogitationem converteris, de quibus dicimus eo liberiùs, quo magis studiis in hanc aut illam partem impellimur; quis nescit multa etiam benefacta nō nisi tempestiuè enunciari oportere? malefacta verò nunquam, nisi ex necessitate? Atque hic ille campus est, in quo plerique delicias agunt hoc ipso tempore; quo ad charitatem non solùm auctoritate diuini verbi, sed etiam grauitate iudiciorum eius, euentorumque lamentabilium, quæ (proh dolor) videmus quamplurima, nos omnes vno animo necesse habemus cōtendere.
units.tr: Certainly, if anyone weighs these evils, which I have just brought forward, carefully and without agitation of mind, he will wonder with me at the great mercy of God, who has so graciously preserved that mangled body of Christendom, which has so far conspired against its own salvation, from its most deserved ruin and plague. To say nothing more of the aim and manner of writings, since we have already touched on this, how few there are who refrain from pouring out things they would have done better to keep silent! If you look at doctrines, here many things are blurted out unfittingly, many improperly, many falsely, by these people and those, and once they have flown out they cannot be recalled, either from the writings or from the minds of the writers, who wish to be victors rather than the victorious truth. Nor does it come to their minds that saying of the most holy Paul, that we can do nothing against the truth, but only for it. If you turn your attention and thought to the actions of men, which are written up, and of which we speak the more freely the more we are driven by our zeal to this side or that, who does not know that even many good deeds ought to be announced only in due time, and evil deeds never, except out of necessity? And this is the field in which most people take their pleasure at this very time. Yet in this very matter, for the sake of charity, we all must strive with one mind, not only because of the authority of the divine word but also because of the gravity of its judgments and the lamentable events which, alas, we see in great number.

units.la: Deinde quàm graue est illud, obsecro, quòd in istis omnibus scriptionum generibus iudices non competentes, non scientes, non æqui, appellantur? Quem enim, amabo te, mihi appellas iudicem, siue de dogmatis aut rebus eò pertinentibus, siue de vita hominum institutas dicere? Nónne appellas plebē? cui nec donum, nec vocationem impertiuit Deus, vt de rebus istis cognoscat, nedū ipsa iudicium faciat. An ignoramus inscientiam plebis aut populi, quem scriptis prouocamus? an ignoramus studia & partes in quas post omnem hominū memoriam plebs quàm facillimè & leuissimè per eiusmodi flabella scissa est ausu temerario? Quin illud fermè in more est populo, si iudicium ad ipsum deferas de rebus grauissimis, vt statim ferat sententiam: siue ex opinione sui, quæ perpetua est ignorantiæ comes; siue ex studiis, quibus inconsulta plebs plurimum traducitur. Hi scilicet quorum non interest de multis cognoscere, qui nec donum habent vt rectè iudicent, nec vocationem vt vel cognoscant, hi (inquam) competentes iudices futuri sunt.
units.tr: Next, how serious is it, I ask you, that in all these kinds of writings the judges appealed to are not competent, not knowing, not fair? For whom, pray, do you call to me as judge, whether you propose to speak about doctrines or matters pertaining to them, or about the lives of men? Do you not appeal to the common people, to whom God has given neither the gift nor the calling to know these things, let alone to pass judgment on them? Or do we not know the ignorance of the populace or the crowd, to which we appeal in writings? Or do we not know the factions and parties into which, since the memory of man, the common people have been most easily and lightly split by such fans of rash daring? Indeed it is almost the custom of the populace, if you refer judgment to them on the gravest matters, that they at once pronounce sentence, either from their own opinion, which is the constant companion of ignorance, or from partisan zeal, by which the ill-advised crowd is very much led astray. Those, forsooth, to whom it is no concern to judge many things, who have neither the gift to judge rightly nor the calling to know, these, I say, are going to be the competent judges?

units.la: Quid verò, quòd hoc ipso facto, dum plebem appellas & cōmoues, viris bonis prudentibusque os planè obstruis? qui operam dant ne aduerso flumini, quo fertur populus, obniti videantur. Nam cur tibi homini tribunitio, & clamoribus fora ac compita implenti, funemq. longum trahenti imperitæ plebis, obloquantur boni intempestiua obmurmuratione? Tu in tuo foro tibi videris dicere: illi in iusto cupiunt. Quid ergo? dixerit fortasse quispiam: túne populum iudicem iniustum dixeris? minimè gentium. nam ne iudicem quidem esse dico: alioquin cuius erit iudex, nisi aut sui ipsius, aut eorum quos habet iudices? utrumque verò absurdum est. Quòd si quis in populo iudicium assumit sibi in plerisque rebus quae traduntur scripto hac licentia temporum; is qua fide, quo iure faciat, viderit; cùm omnes alios anteuertit imprudentia sua; nec Deo ipsi, nec iudicibus vocatis à Deo concedit locum. Nam in rebus dogmaticis, & quæ cum fide coniunctæ sunt, cur potius aliquem de stiuà [?] iudicem audies, quàm eum qui rebus sacris diligenter secundùm Deum operam dederit? Cur potiùs tumultuarium plebis conuentum, aut concursum, ac sibilum anhelantis audies; quàm iustu concilium ex iis hominibus constitutum, quos Deus instruxerit donis & vocatione ad piam & sanctam rerum quæ controuertuntur [?] definitionem? quòd si crimina sunt, conuicia, contumeliæ, aut vitæ male gestæ exprobrationes: primùm Deo iniuriam facis, qui ordine humanum instituit, de rebus male gestis in vita humana cogniturum: Deinde illis ad quos rei cognitio pertinet, iniuriam facis, quàm iniuriam, ut illi diffimulent, nō tamen dissimulabit Deus: prætereà populo iniuriam facis, quem imprudentem excitas, ut copuolet in ius publicum auctoritatemq. magistratus: Denique illi ipsi quem profcindis scripto, iniquus es. Si enim te offendit, habes mandatum Christi, ut arguas inter te & ipsum: Si alium, quis te procuratorem instituit, & gestorem rei alienae? sin autem non offendit te, cur offendis? sin utrumque, cur ita agis, ut palam testatum facias te non salutem, sed perniciem; non honorem, sed ignominiam, id est, non ex charitate, sed ex perturbatione animi à charitate alienissima euersionem illius expetere? Interea verò, ut de tertio capite adiiciam paucula, quis ferat dum populus ita appellatur, silere bonos, qui iusta scientia, imperturbato animo, donisque conuenientibus instructi, aut iudices à Deo sunt istarum rerum instituti, aut à te adhiberi possunt. Haec illa est Christiana ratio, ad quam nos omnes oportet remis velisque (quod aiunt) contendere, non autem ordinem diuinum & humanum eadem opera conturbare. Aut ordinaria insistenda via, aut extra ordinem arbitraria deligenda; nō pro imperio praescribenda à contendentibus: quod est iniquissimum.
units.tr: What then, that by this very act, while you summon and stir up the common people, you plainly stop the mouths of good and prudent men, who take care not to seem to struggle against the stream on which the people is carried? For why should good men object to you, a man playing the tribune, filling the forums and crossroads with shouts and dragging a long rope for the unskilled crowd, with their untimely muttering? You seem to yourself to speak in your own forum; they desire justice. What then? Perhaps someone will say: do you call the people an unjust judge? By no means. For I do not even say they are judges; otherwise whose judge would they be, except either their own or those whom they have as judges? Both are absurd. But if anyone in the populace assumes to himself judgment in most of the matters handed down in writing in this licence of the times, let him see with what good faith and by what right he does so, since his own imprudence outstrips all others; and he yields place neither to God nor to judges called by God. For in dogmatic matters, and those joined with faith, why should you listen to someone from the crowd as judge rather than to one who has diligently devoted himself to sacred things according to God? Why should you hear the tumultuous gathering or rabble of the populace, and the hissing of the panting, rather than a lawful council constituted from those men whom God has equipped with gifts and calling for the pious and holy settling of the matters in controversy? But if these are crimes, insults, abuse, or reproaches for misspent lives: first, you do an injury to God, who has ordered human society so that he himself would sit in judgment on misdeeds in human life; second, you do an injury to those to whom the cognizance of the case pertains, an injury which they may overlook but God will not overlook; moreover, you do an injury to the people, whom you stir up, unwisely, to riot against public law and the authority of the magistrate; and finally you are unfair to the very man you tear apart in writing. For if he has offended you, you have Christ's command to rebuke him between you and himself; if he has offended someone else, who appointed you as agent and manager of another's affair? But if he has not offended you, why do you give offence? And if he has offended you in both ways, why do you act so as openly to show that you seek not his salvation but his ruin, not his honour but his shame; that is, not out of charity but out of agitation of mind, which is most alien to charity, you seek his overthrow? Meanwhile, to add a few words on the third point, who could bear that, while the people are addressed in this way, good men keep silent, men who, with sound knowledge, a calm mind and suitable gifts, have either been appointed judges of these matters by God or could be summoned by you? This is the Christian way, to which we all ought to strive with oars and sails, as they say, and not to disturb the divine and human order at the same time. Either the ordinary way must be followed, or an arbitrary one chosen outside the order; not one dictated by the authority of the contenders, which is most unjust.

units.la: Atque hanc quidem ἀπεξίαν [?] eo indigniorem esse apud omnes constat, quo scripta reuera longiùs à pietate, veritate, & charitate absunt. Sed tamen ne eos quidem ipsos qui tuentur veritatem, peccare velim. fiducia causae suae, & sic eam agere, ut in eadem peccata imprudenter ruant quæ in aliis reprehendunt. Multa enim interdum ad defensionem veritatis humanitus possunt nobis excidere, quæ præstaret inhiberi. Sæpe fit, ut res præter veritatem, præter necessitatem, præter charitatem, præter ossicium ab iis effundantur qui propugnant veritatem. Ignoscat nobis gratiosè Dominus, qui in multis offendimus omnes: sed tamen certissimum illud est, fieri non raro ut plus noceatur veritati, cum ista vitia in causa eius à nobis adsperguntur, quàm accedat adiumenti: nō quòd res ipsa interdum tanti sit momenti, sed quia tanti est quanti legentes esse voluerint: qui rem leviculam, si forte perturbato animo iudicaverint, in gravissimam transformabunt. Quapropter omnes veritatis divinæ sacerdotes, atque administros Christianæ pacis oro & obtestor per sanctissimum nomen Iesu Christi, cui servimus, ut tum ipsi de se & suis sermonibus scriptisque cogitent quàm diligentissimè, ne forte cum veritate, aut charitate, vel in speciem pugnent; tum vero ut in utriusque modo, sermonum inquam & scriptorum, cancellos sibi circumdent quàm prudentissimè, extra quos non patiantur se vel latum pedem abripi, quamuis clamantibus & provocantibus multis. Nam servos Dei armatos esse convenit invicta illa patientia, de qua dicebat apud Salomonem Deus; Melior est longanimis robusto, & qui
units.tr: And it is agreed by all that this kind of ἀπεξία [?] is the more unworthy, the further the writings in fact are from piety, truth and charity. But yet I would not wish even those who defend the truth to sin, by confidence in their cause and by conducting it so that they fall imprudently into the same sins which they rebuke in others. For at times many things may slip from us through human weakness in the defence of the truth, which it would be better to restrain. It often happens that things are poured out by those who champion the truth beyond the truth, beyond necessity, beyond charity, beyond duty. May the Lord graciously pardon us, who all offend in many things; but this is most certain, that it often happens that the truth is harmed more when these faults are sprinkled upon its cause by us than help is added, not because the matter itself is sometimes of such weight, but because it is of the weight the readers wish it to have; who, if by chance they have judged a trifling matter with a disturbed mind, will turn it into a most serious one. Therefore I beg and entreat all priests of divine truth and ministers of Christian peace, by the most holy name of Jesus Christ, whom we serve, both to think as diligently as possible about themselves and their speeches and writings, lest perhaps they fight against truth or charity, or even seem to; and to surround themselves most prudently with boundaries in both of these, I mean in their speeches and writings, beyond which they do not allow themselves to be dragged even a broad step, though many cry out and provoke them. For it is fitting that God's servants be armed with that unconquered patience of which God spoke through Solomon: "Better is the patient man than the strong, and he who"

units.la: dominatur in animum suum eo qui capit civitatem.
units.tr: rules his own spirit than he who takes a city.

units.la: Quid ergo? an non propugnabitur veritas à seruis suis? certè, propugnari oportet, ac non deseri veritatem: sed propugnari volo commodè; non autem imprudenter & sine fructu quasi lacinias veritatis discerpi importunitate hominum, qui veritati seruiunt: propugnari eam à seruis volo, quà loquendo, quà tacendo, & manum Domini (qui Deus veritatis est) expectando. Itaque cùm veritas ipsa commodè velit dici; cuius commoditatis ratio eiusmodi est, vt ex natura ipsa ac fine veritatis, & modo dicendi scribendiqúe, & personis & circumstantiis temporis ac loci, maximè observanda sit: ea omnia si observemus, bene est; si non, in difficultates aut ipsi incidimus, aut alios iniicimus.
units.tr: What then? Will the truth not be defended by its servants? Certainly it must be defended, and the truth must not be abandoned; but I want it defended fittingly, not imprudently and fruitlessly, as if shreds of the truth were torn apart by the importunity of men who serve it. I want it defended by its servants, both by speaking and by keeping silent, and by waiting for the hand of the Lord, who is the God of truth. Therefore, since the truth itself wishes to be spoken fittingly, and the rule of this fittingness is such that it must be observed above all from the very nature and aim of truth, from the manner of speaking and writing, and from persons and the circumstances of time and place, if we observe all these, it is well; if not, we either fall into difficulties ourselves or throw others into them.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem veritatem pro commoditate naturæ ipsius dici existimo, cùm dicitur id quod est; & id quod non est, negatur fide & simplicitate summa, quam suis Dominus Deus veritatis semper imperavit: quemadmodum ostendit Apostolus dicens, Deposito mendacio loquimini veritatem quisq; proximo suo: Nam sumus alij aliorum membra. Enimverò labium veritatis stabilitur in æternum: at donec montem transfigam, lingua falsa. Finem verò huius veritatis charitatem esse tota scriptura testis est. Nam ex charitate docuit nos veritatem hanc Deus: quæ charitas effusa in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis,veritatem nos iubet eloqui,quoad eius fieri in charitate potest & expedit. contra charitatem eloqui veritatem, impium est: præter charitatem,otiosum: neutrū verò approbat Dominus.
units.tr: I hold that truth is best spoken in the way that suits its own nature, when we say what is, and deny what is not, with the utmost plainness and sincerity, which the Lord God of truth has always required of his people. The Apostle shows this when he says: "Putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour, for we are members one of another" (Eph. 4:25). "The lip of truth shall be established for ever, but a lying tongue lasts only for a moment" (Prov. 12:19). Scripture bears witness throughout that the end of this truth is love. God taught us this truth out of love, and that love, poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, bids us speak the truth so far as this can be done in love and is profitable. To speak the truth against love is wicked; to speak it without love is idle; and the Lord approves neither.

units.la: Hæc autem ipsa non raro contingit, vt in mente eius qui dicturus aut perscripturus est, rectè informentur, & tamen peccatum accidat in dicendi aut scribendi modo: præsertim cùm perturbationibus animi aut res obscurantur quodammodo, aut verba obiiciuntur dicenti & scribenti incommoda; nisi accuratè & cum delectu iudicioque maximo dicturus circumspexerit, quæ res ad argumentum, quæ verba ad res, qui modus & ratio ad vtrumque sit adhibendus, vt optata sequatur ex iis ædificatio. Nam verba sapientum non solùm recto & veritati opus est conuenire, sed similia esse aculeis, similia clauis infixis, leétissima, vt ab eodem pastore tradita (vt Ecclesiastes docet) nimirum Domino.
units.tr: It often happens that a man who is about to speak or write has his mind rightly informed, and yet he sins in the manner of his speaking or writing. This is especially so when the matter is somewhat obscured by the disturbance of his feelings, or when words that are unsuitable for the occasion come to the speaker or writer. Unless the one who is about to speak looks carefully and with the greatest discretion at what suits the subject, what words suit the matter, and what manner and method must be used for both, the edification we desire will not follow. For the words of the wise must not only agree with what is right and true, but must be like goads and like nails fixed firmly, given, as Ecclesiastes teaches, by the one Shepherd, the Lord (Eccles. 12:11).

units.la: Adhæc in personis obseruanda multa, citra quæ plurimum offensionis dicentes scribentesque possunt incurrere. Nam & ij ad quos scribitur, & de quibus scribitur, & in quos scribitur, nonnunquam facto nostro ipsorum offenduntur: & (quod grauius est) offensiones illæ quas saltem inter paucos latère oportuisset, eò deueniunt vt omnibus fermè offensioni sint. Quòd si diligenter ad illud dictum Petri in his rebus attenderemus; Ante omnia charitatem alij in alios intensam habete : nam charitas operiet multitudinem peccatorum : item Augustini illud prudentissimum, Vbi natum est peccatum, ibi moriatur peccatum ; neque diffundendis aliorum in fide erroribus, neque divulgandis peccatis ita operam daturi effemus, vt plurimùm datur memoriâ nostrâ.
units.tr: Many things must also be observed concerning persons, lest speakers and writers run into much offence.
