For those to whom we write, those about whom we write, and those against whom we write are sometimes offended by what we do, and (what is more serious) those offences which ought to have remained hidden among a few come to such a pass that they give offence to almost everyone. If we attended carefully to Peter's saying on these matters, "Above all things have fervent charity among yourselves, for charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1 Pet. 4:8), and to Augustine's most prudent saying, "Where sin was born, there let sin die," we would not labour so eagerly to spread abroad the errors of others in matters of faith, nor to publish their sins as we commonly do, so that they are remembered by us for a long time.

units.la: Atque huc maximè pertinet ratio illa circumftantiarum, quam antè diximus : in quibus principes circumstantiæ sunt temporis, & loci, fi à modo quem antè attigimus(quæ summa est actionum circumstantia, etiam non rarò dans speciem actionibus nostris) discesseris. Nam quorsum intempestiua scripta ? quorum gratia omnis eo ipso tempore quo eduntur excidit, & quorum fructus aut damnosus, aut nullus. quemadmodum enim nec acerborum fructuum, nec vetustate putrefcentiu est voluptas neque vtilitas, qui tempestiuè percepti futuri sunt grati & vtiles; sic etiam intempestiuarum fcriptionum solet fe habere ratio.
units.tr: The principle of circumstances, which I mentioned earlier, applies especially here. The chief circumstances are time and place, if one departs from the manner which I touched on before (which is the highest circumstance of our actions and often gives them their character). For why write things at an unseasonable time? Such writings lose all their value at the very time they are published, and their fruit is either harmful or nil. For just as the pleasure and usefulness of sour fruits, or of fruits that have rotted with age, are not those of fruits gathered in season, which will be pleasant and useful, so too is the reckoning of unseasonable writings.

units.la: Nec minus iudicij necesse est adhiberi ad locorum discrimen explorandum: fit enim, vt qui sermo aut quæ scriptura vno in loco prodest, eadem obsit in altero. Sermones & scripta pro ratione locorum ad quæ transmittuntur, vt venti regionibus, ita animis salubria sunt, aut infalubria. Ac propterea iniuriâ faciunt, qui aut suo iudicio, aut suorum[?] temporum locorúmue[?] mo-dulo dulo[?] omnia tempora & loca putant æstimanda. Una quidem est in se veritas, sed quæ sese contemperat generis humani bono, sine sui ipsius detrimento.
units.tr: Equal judgement is needed to discern the differences of places. It happens that a sermon or a writing that does good in one place does harm in another. Sermons and writings, according to the regions to which they are sent, are healthful or unhealthful to minds, just as winds are to regions. Those therefore do wrong who judge all times and places by their own judgement or by the measure of their own times and places. Truth is indeed one in itself, but it adapts itself to the good of mankind without any loss to itself.

units.la: Atque hæc omnia, & alia consimilia quæ adferri possunt, profecto eiusmodi sunt, ut quisquis veritatis administer in charitate est, cogitaturus sit de eis diligentissimè, cùm aut sermonem dicturus, aut scriptum transmissurus est. Medicos omnes peritos & valetudinis humanæ studiosos videmus non solùm de eo laborare, ut veritatem materiarum simplicium, compositarumque & totius artis suæ teneant, (quod theoricorum est) verùm etiam quod practicorum est (ut vocant) ad constitutionem subiecti, id est, corporis humani tum communem, tum singularem attendere; eáque probè exploratâ res secundùm artem iustas, secundùm verò corporis constitutionem modificatas curationis causa admouere. Nos autem qui ad veritatis divinæ supernaturalisque dispensationem vocati sumus, & ad gregem Christi ouesque[?] singulas illius, prout Dominus nobis fuerit admensus, procurandas; an ita desipiemus, ut prudentiam rerum iustarum medicis relinquamus, & inconsideratè loquamur, scribamus, aut ambulemus in domo Domini? Fugiamus procul, ô fratres charissimi, insaniam istam, cùm nobis ipsis, tum aliis damnosissimam; & potiùs à scribenda litera unica totum vitæ huius curriculû abstineamus, quàm vt animâ vllam, vel minimâ & infirmissimâ, percellâmusaut labefactemus officio inofficioso nostro.
units.tr: All these things, and other similar ones that could be adduced, are indeed of such a kind that whoever is a servant of the truth in love will think about them most carefully when he is about to speak a sermon or send out a writing. We see that all skilled physicians who care for human health labour not only to know the truth of simple and compound materials and of their whole art (which belongs to the theoretical side), but also to attend, as they call it, to the practical side, that is, to the constitution of the subject, the human body, both in general and in the particular case. Having carefully investigated this, they apply remedies which are fitting according to the art, but modified according to the constitution of the body, for the sake of healing. But we, who have been called to the divine and supernatural dispensation of the truth, and to care for the flock of Christ and each of his sheep, as the Lord shall have apportioned to us, shall we be so foolish as to leave the wise handling of right matters to physicians, and speak, write, or walk carelessly in the house of the Lord? Let us flee far away, dearest brothers, from that madness, which is most harmful both to ourselves and to others. Rather let us refrain from writing a single letter for the whole course of this life, than strike or weaken any soul, even the smallest and weakest, by our undutiful office.

units.la: Si igitur, quid nónne veritas propugnanda est? dixerit quispiam. Est quidem ea propugnanda, vbi oppugnatur: sed tempus est iustum propugnationis, & tempus cessationis æquè in publico atque in priuato labore nostro à Domino constitutum: quémadmodum in præliis tempus est petendi hostis depellendiquè, & tempus spectandi atque contemnendi, quum solido impingit demens. Tyro consumit operam inaniter, veteranus prudens non nisi vtiliter. Nam, certè si qui naturam veritatis ex doctrina Dei didicerunt, eamque ex officio charitatis ad propinquorum ædificationem cupiunt exponere, vult Deus ad cõuenienté mõdû, ad personas, & ad circumstantias ita ab illis & nobis respici, vt seruiamus paci, & omnem motû cõtrariû paci sanctissima prudentia semper declinemus.
units.tr: "But if so," someone may say, "must not the truth be defended?" Indeed it must be defended where it is attacked; but the time for defence, and the time for silence, are both appointed by the Lord, equally in our public labour and in our private. So in battles there is a time for seeking out and driving off the enemy, and a time for watching and despising him, when the foolish man strikes the solid ground. The raw recruit wastes his effort in vain, but the prudent veteran never does except to good purpose. For surely, if those who have learned the nature of the truth from the teaching of God desire to expound it, out of the duty of love, for the edification of their neighbours, God wills that they and we regard the fitting manner, the persons, and the circumstances, so that we serve peace and always avoid every movement contrary to peace with most holy prudence.

units.la: Quapropter in priuatis institutionibus, redargutionibus, hortamëtis, reprehësionibus, cõsolationibus, & si qua sunt præterea huiusmodi, quid quomodo secundûm rationem personarum & circumstantiarû fieri oporteat, diligentissimè præscripsit Deus. Nam veritatem non solùm expressit secundûm naturam ipsius; verumetiam exprimendæ illius inter nos modum ex charitate circumscripsit, à piis singulis obseruandum, vt sale & gratia conditus sit fermo & scriptura nostra. personarum quoque respectum habere docuit oportere, vt peccantes monéantur, ac non traducantur: monéantur autem ordine charitatis, non inordinata illa imprudentia increpentur, quam cuique dictare solet offensi animi perturbatio: monéantur tempories, dum spes emendationis est; & monéantur locis, ex quibus cognoscant honori suo & saluti consuli; deniq. si repetitis monitis non acquiescerint, sinantur aliquantisper, donec subsederit illa perturbatio animi quæ ipsos transuersos rapit; aut si nunquam resipiscant, sinantur plane, ne discamus cū claudis claudicare, & contentiosi cum hominibus contentiosis & pertinacibus rixando efficiamur. Quid obstat, amabo vos, quo minus eundem ordinem in publicis nostris sermonibus & scriptis obseruemus? Nam hunc ordinem etiam in cathsis publicis nos docuit veritas; & eundem quoque præcipit omnino charitas; cumque natura charitatis ea sit, vt ad commodum respiciat eorum quibuscum agimus, certè & natura eorum postulat vt agamus ex charitatis lege. Cogitemus ergo, fratres dilectissimi, quotquot sumus qui nomen Christo dedimus, qua religione, qua fide prudentiaque in his actionibus publicis versari nos omnes oporteat, qui in priuatis tenemus magis earum modum: & deinceps demus ex animo operam, vt veritatem in charitate, & charitatem in pace ad salutem ædificationemque communé procuremus.recordemur eorum quæ ante de capite illo nostro, typo fidei & coucrfationis nostræ & confessionis Apostolo,Domino Iesu Christo dicebamus:nō litigabit,neq. vociferabitur,&c. Respiciamus ad Pauli monitum;qui hominem etiam hæreticum vult à nobis demum vitari post vnam & alteram admonitionem , quum nouimus eum euersum esse, & ita peccare , vt suopte iudicio fit condemnatus.Meminerimus denique amuleto certissimo nos instrui ab illo dicente , Quòd si quis volet contentiosus esse, non est hic mos noster, neq. Ecclesiarum Dei.
units.tr: Therefore God has most carefully prescribed in private instruction, rebuke, exhortation, reproof, consolation, and whatever else of this kind there is, what ought to be done, and how, according to the nature of persons and circumstances. For he has not only expressed the truth according to its nature, but has also laid down from love the manner of expressing it among us, to be observed by each of the godly, so that our speech and writing may be seasoned with salt and grace (Col. 4:6). He has also taught that regard must be had to persons, so that sinners are admonished and not slandered; and they are to be admonished in the order of charity, not rebuked with that disorderly imprudence which the disturbance of an offended mind usually dictates to each man. They are to be admonished at fitting times, while there is hope of amendment, and admonished in places where they may learn that their honour and salvation are being cared for. Finally, if they do not yield after repeated admonitions, they are to be left alone for a while, until that disturbance of mind which carries them off in a twisted direction has settled down; or if they never come to their senses, they are to be left altogether, so that we do not learn to limp with the lame, and become quarrelsome by wrangling with contentious and obstinate men (cf. Matt. 18:15; Titus 3:10). What hinders us, I ask you, from observing the same order in our public sermons and writings? For the truth has taught us this order also in public teaching, and charity commands the same without exception; and since the nature of charity is to look to the good of those with whom we deal, surely their nature too requires that we act by the law of charity. Let us consider therefore, most beloved brothers, all of us who have given our name to Christ, with what reverence, faith and prudence we ought all to conduct ourselves in these public actions, we who hold to their manner in private. Let us then take pains from our hearts to promote truth in love and love in peace, for the common salvation and edification. Let us recall what we said earlier about that head of ours, the Apostle and High Priest of our faith, conversation and confession, the Lord Jesus Christ: "He shall not strive, nor cry out" (Matt. 12:19). Let us regard the admonition of Paul, who wishes that even a heretic be avoided by us at last after one or two admonitions, since we know that he is perverted and sins in such a way that he is condemned by his own judgement (Titus 3:10–11). Finally, let us remember that we are instructed by him as by a most certain safeguard, who says: "But if any man seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor do the churches of God" (1 Cor. 11:16).

units.la: Neque verò propterea confingendus est nobis inanis metus, desertum hoc pacto iri veritatem ; ac proinde nos diuina, & aliena,& nostra causa teneri scripta accumulare scriptis, & singulis vel oblatrantibus canibus respondere. Nam hoc dictum profectò multorum est μορμολυκεῖον[?], qui suis siue perturbationibus, siue præposteris iudiciis existimant oportere ut alij dextra sua cadant. Longè aliter nos Christus, aliter Prophetæ, aliter Apostoli, aliter denique sancti & prudentes viri inde ab orbe condito docuerunt exemplo & sermone suo.
units.tr: Nor, indeed, should we invent for ourselves an empty fear that the truth will thereby be deserted if we do not, for our own cause and for the cause of others, heap writings upon writings and answer every barking dog. For this saying is surely a bogey of many people, who by their agitations or preposterous judgments think that others must fall at their right hand. Christ taught us quite otherwise, and so did the Prophets, the Apostles, and finally the holy and prudent men from the foundation of the world, both by their example and by their words.

units.la: Veritatem deseri, Deus bone? magnum crimen, si quidem hic crimen est. Sed iam crimen esse definit,ex quo semel aut bis veritatem scripto professus es, ac cultu publico semper doctrinaque communi in Ecclesia testatus palàm. In hanc veritatem velut cippum firmissimum à Deo plantatum instrumento manus tuæ,licet vel millies aduersariis impingere, te stánte & ἀφιλονείκως[?] quiescente. Antecedente facto qui instituit veritatem & præsente mōstrat, is nullo iure posteà dicendus est eam destituisse, si ad singulorū clamores & vociferationes sese non obiecerit. Præposterum hoc iudicium est, de quo sibi maximopere Satanas gratulatur. nouit enim artifex,dum ad clamores & contentiones aures aduertimus, prætermitti à nobis veram ædificationem quæ est in Christo. Adeò veteratorie hic antiquus draco imprudentiæ nostræ nouit illudere.
units.tr: To desert the truth? Good God! That would be a great crime, if indeed it were a crime. But it ceases to be a crime once you have professed the truth in writing once or twice, and have always borne witness to it openly by public worship and common teaching in the Church. You may strike at this truth, planted by God like a firm pillar, with the instrument of your hand a thousand times against your adversaries, while you stand by and remain quiet, without contentiousness. Whoever has first established the truth by his deed, and shows it present, cannot rightly be said afterwards to have abandoned it, if he does not expose himself to the shouts and outcries of individuals. This is a preposterous judgment, and Satan rejoices greatly in it. For the crafty one knows that, while we give our ears to clamours and contentions, we neglect the true edifying that is in Christ. So cunningly does that ancient dragon know how to play upon our folly.

units.la: Quòd si quis dixerit, etsi non veritatis causa, quæ rupes immota est, tamen aliorum causa quos vocat veritas, responderi nonnunquam oportere; Equidé non negauero eiusmodi personas, causas, tempora, loca occurrere,quæ responsionis necessitatem afferant: sed extra hanc necessitatem qui respondet, contentiosus est,aut vt efficiatur contentiosus,itidé metus est. Nam vt breuiter de personis dicam, quorum causa iudicas respondendum?aliena,an tua?si aliena, vtrum illius cui responsandum putas, an verò eorum qui auditores & spectatores futuri. sunt? Si illius causa,cum ipso agendum est, non cum publico. Si aliorum causa , aut eorum qui nihil de re audiuerint, aut qui de re aliquid perceperint. Qui nihil audiuerunt, eos cur commoues? Qui audiuerunt, certè eorum causa oportet inftitui consilium istud,qui firmi in veritate sunt, aut qui infirmi sunt,aut qui in mendacium traducti sunt. Firmorum causa non putem: quid opus est? Infirmorum causa plus habet speciei: sed tamen postquam ex veritate semel, aut bis fuerit dissentientibus fatisfactu; equidem magis metuero, vt infirmentur contentione infirmi,quàm sperauero fore, vt perscriptione noua confirmentur. Et (quod grauius est) multiplex de eodem fcriptio hoc habet incommodi,quòd plerumque siluam offensionis infirmis atque imperitis,calumniæ verò aduersariis fubminiftrat: quia (vt ait Sapiens) multitudine verborum non cessat defectio. Quòd fi eorü causam adduxeris qui iam malo errore implicantur, studium laudo,sed effectum non video. contrà enim plurimùm vfuuenit, vt ea ipsa mala quæ modò ostendimus,miseros confirment in malo, quemadmodum iniecta aqua fabriles carbones solent inardescere.Hoc quotidiana docet experientia; & insignibus duobus exemplis,nimirū suo & alterius cuiufdam Episcopi, Auguftinus optimè demonstrauit,qui ex Manichæorum erroribus nō vllo humano facto,sed fingulari Dei testimonio,tanquam ex peftilentiffima fœtorum sentina erepti sunt: Omnino præstat in hoc genere mali antecedétia scripta & documenta cōmodè & quasi aliud agendo, errantibus subiicere,ad testandâ constantiâ nostram in doctrina veritatis, quū noua multa procudere.
units.tr: But if someone says that, even if it is not for the sake of the truth (which is an immovable rock), yet for the sake of others whom he calls the truth's friends, it is sometimes necessary to answer, I will not deny that persons, causes, times and places arise which bring the necessity of a reply. But whoever replies outside this necessity is contentious, or at any rate there is a danger that he will become so. To speak briefly about persons: for whose sake do you judge that one must answer? For another's, or for your own? If for another's, is it for the sake of the one to whom you think a reply is owed, or of those who are going to be the hearers and spectators? If for the sake of the one, the matter must be dealt with with him, not with the public. If for the sake of others, either of those who have heard nothing of the matter, or of those who have grasped something of it. Those who have heard nothing, why do you stir them up? Those who have heard, surely this plan must be undertaken for the sake of those who are firm in the truth, or of those who are weak, or of those who have been led into falsehood. For the firm I think it is not needed: what is the point? For the weak it has more of an appearance of reason; yet, after the truth has once or twice been made satisfactory to the dissenters, I for my part would fear more that the weak will be weakened by the contention than hope that they will be strengthened by a new writing. And (what is more serious) a multiplicity of writings on the same matter has this disadvantage: that it generally supplies a forest of offence to the weak and unlearned, and of calumny to the adversaries, because, as the Wise Man says, "in the multitude of words there does not fail sin." But if you have brought forward the cause of those who are already entangled in a bad error, I praise the zeal, but I do not see the result. For, on the contrary, it very often happens that those very evils which we have just pointed out confirm the wretched in their evil, just as water thrown on smith's coals is wont to make them blaze up. Daily experience teaches this; and Augustine has excellently demonstrated it by two notable examples, namely his own and that of a certain other bishop, who were rescued from the errors of the Manichaeans not by any human act but by a singular testimony of God, as if from the most pestilential sink of filth. Certainly, in this kind of evil, it is better to set before those who err, conveniently and as if doing something else, the writings and teachings already extant, to bear witness to our constancy in the doctrine of the truth, than to forge many new ones.

units.la: Restat vt dicat is qui scripturus est, sua causa se scriptum publico daturum esse: nempe vt ea aut defendat, aut explicet quae ante scripserit, aut criminationes obiectas diluat. Atqui iam eo peccatum est, si quis sua causa scriptiones eiusmodi immittat publico. Quorsum enim in meis rebus cognoscendis homines occupem? si veritatem quis scripsit & docuit, non sua, sed veritatis causa idem scripturus atque docturus est. Hoc autem officium ab illo amplius non exigit veritas, vt ante ostendimus, eùm vno aut altero scripto fecit satis. Quòd si personarum causa veritatem mentis nostrae opus est explicari (nam aliud est veritatis in se testimonium edere, aliud eius rei quam sentimus cum animis nostris) aut breui additamento, non scriptorum centonibus praestari hoc potest; aut (quod est certissimum) vni & alteri eorum qui rem in dubium vocant, testatam certis literis facere mentem nostram. Alioqui in causa fidei, quid est cur tantopere, si quid singulare credimus, aliis obtrudamus? quid, cur laboremus vt sentiant alij nos hoc aut illud credere, & esse persuasissimos? modò ne ab expressa forma sanorum verborum (vt Paulus vocat) abstinamus, merito omnia susque deq. ferre possumus, quae ab aliis de mente nostra cogitantur, & ipsi nobis (si ita placet) canere sine motu publico.
units.tr: It remains for the one who is about to write to say that he will publish his writing for his own cause: namely, to defend or explain what he has written before, or to dilute the accusations laid against him. But already it is a sin if anyone sends such writings out to the public for his own cause. For why should I occupy people with the examination of my affairs? If someone has written and taught the truth, he is about to write and teach the same not for his own sake but for the truth's. Yet the truth no longer demands this duty of him, as we showed before, since he has done enough with one or two writings. But if for the sake of persons the mind of our heart must be explained (for it is one thing to give testimony to the truth in itself, another to that which we feel with our minds), this can be supplied either by a brief addition, not by patchwork of writings, or (what is most certain) by making our mind plain by sure letters to one or another of those who call the matter into doubt. Otherwise, in a matter of faith, why is it that we press so hard to force on others whatever we believe singularly, why do we labour that others should feel that we believe this or that and are most persuaded of it? Provided only that we do not abstain from the express form of sound words (as Paul calls it), we can rightly bear with equanimity all that others think about our mind, and, if it so pleases them, let them sing to us without public stir.

units.la: Iam vero conuicia sint, iniuriae, criminationes, quibus appetimur palàm, cur non potiùs ferimus, ut Corinthios monet Apostolus; quàm ut eiulationibus & querimoniis eorum aures oppleamus quorum non interest? Aristotelem illum Philosophum celeberrimum narrant historici, cùm à quodam inimico absens grauiter traductus effet, cuidam ad ipsum referenti & exstimulanti [?] respondisse: Etiam licet absentem verberet. Et hos Christianos usque adeò molles & fastidiosos esse, ut res eiusmodi nō possimus contemnere, & quasi pedibus terere? Deinde, an nescimus quod olim prudenter monebat Tacitus, convicia, si irascare, agnita videri: spreta exolescere? Quòd si id ab unoquoque natura exigit, & dictat ratio, quo iure nos serui Christi, qui Spiritu Christi vivimus in corpore Christi, qui armis iustitiae dextrorsum & sinistrorsum per honorē & ignominiam pro Domino nostro debemus contendere, qui etiam beati dicimur hoc ipso fidei & patientiae testimonio, desinemus à sequendo Christo, & salute nostra ipsorum, alienóque propugnanda, ut de rebus studiisque nostris singularibus concertemus, atque in huiusce confirmamus? cur potius non cogitamus, si hic aut ille nos petunt convicis, esse nobis contrà locupletissimum Dei, & animi nostri, & bonorum, apud quos vivimus, testimonium; quo freti acquiescamus, & abstineamus ab ista inani solicitudine? quae si nos torquet, ipsi cum aliis perdimur; si non torquet, perduntur tela contradicentium. Taceo quod ante exposui, iniquè facere eos qui conuicia scriptis passim disseminant: ac proinde etiam iniquitatem eandem ab iis confirmati, qui coram iisdem testibus iudicibusque constituunt respondendum esse, & quasi in foro incompetente (vt vocant) obeunt vadimonium. Si enim purgari me exempli causa ab alicuius hominis contumelia, non dico mea (prius ima dehiscat terra mihi) sed aliena & veritatis ipsius causa necesse est: equidem malim apud eos me legitimè purgare, qui legitimè possunt cognoscere, quàm miseram plebem eo nomine commouere, quæ nec cognitionis instituendæ capax est, nec iudicij faciendi fine cognitione legitima, nec sese denique ex miseris illis & horrendis factionibus, quæ hoc modo exoriri solent, poteft commodè extricare. Prius igitur est, vt contemnamus conuicia: posterius, fi animum noftrum vincere ipsi non possumus, aut res poftulauerit, vt conuiciatores legitima cognitione conuincamus, docendo iustitiam nostram, non iniuriam illorum persequendo. Væ nobis, qui primas eruditionis ambimus, fugimus silentij: in quo tamen etiam Christus, qui veritas est, bonam confessionem coram Pilato confessus est. Qui non responsat, conuiciatorem confundit plane; qui autem conuincit, hanc existimationem sæpe conciliat sibi, vt ex impatientia & animi perturbatione aduersarium persequi iudicetur. id autem, seu verè, seu falsò iudicetur, fructum ministerij impedit vehementissimè, totum non raro intercipit: Et fatis magnas pœnas tum hoc ipso tempore apud bonos, tum futuro in posteritatem conuiciatores reportaturi súnt, nobis tacentibus, & causam nostram committentibus Domino, cui feruimus. De causis verò quibus ad responsandum sæpe adducimur, locus eadem opera explicatus est, cùm de personis diximus.Nam aut ad Deum & veritatem illius,aut ad nos, aut ad alios spectant.
units.tr: Now, as for reproaches, injuries and accusations, by which we are openly assailed, why do we not rather bear them, as the Apostle admonishes the Corinthians, than fill with our wailings and complaints the ears of those who have no concern in it? Historians tell that the famous philosopher Aristotle, when he was grievously slandered by a certain enemy in his absence, and someone reported it to him and urged him on, answered: "Let him even beat me while I am absent." And are we Christians so soft and fastidious that we cannot despise things of this kind and trample them underfoot, as it were? Again, do we not know what Tacitus wisely warned of old: that if you are angered by reproaches, they seem to be admitted; if you scorn them, they fade away? But if nature demands this of everyone, and reason dictates it, by what right, we servants of Christ, who live by the Spirit of Christ in the body of Christ, who ought to contend for our Lord with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, through honour and dishonour, who are even called blessed for this very testimony of faith and patience, shall we cease from following Christ, and, to the neglect of our own salvation and the defence of others, contend about our own private affairs and studies, and confirm this in others? Why do we not rather consider that, if this man or that assails us with reproaches, we have on our side the most abundant testimony of God, of our own mind, and of the good men among whom we live; relying on which we may rest content and abstain from that empty anxiety? If that anxiety torments us, we perish together with the others; if it does not torment us, the darts of the contradictors are wasted. I pass over what I set out before: that those who scatter reproaches abroad in writings act unjustly; and so those who, confirmed by the same iniquity, decide that they must answer before the same witnesses and judges, and, as it were in an incompetent court (as they call it), give bail, do the same. For if I must clear myself, for example, of some man's insult, not of my own (may the earth open beneath me first!) but of another's and of the truth itself, I would rather clear myself lawfully before those who can lawfully take cognizance of it, than stir up the wretched common people on that account, who are neither capable of conducting an inquiry, nor of passing judgment without lawful knowledge of the case, nor finally of extricating themselves conveniently from those wretched and dreadful factions which are wont to arise in this way. Therefore the first course is to despise reproaches; the second, if we cannot ourselves overcome our own feelings, or if the matter demands it, to convict the reproachers by lawful inquiry, teaching our own righteousness rather than pursuing their injustice. Woe to us, who seek the first place of learning and flee silence; yet in silence Christ too, who is the truth, made a good confession before Pilate. He who does not answer plainly confounds the reproacher; but he who refutes him often wins for himself the reputation of pursuing his adversary out of impatience and agitation of mind. And whether this is judged truly or falsely, it very greatly hinders the fruit of the ministry, and not seldom wholly cuts it off. And the reproachers will certainly, both now among good men and in future to posterity, bear sufficiently great penalties, while we keep silent and commit our cause to the Lord whom we serve. As for the causes for which we are often led to answer, the place was explained in the same work when we spoke of persons: for they concern either God and his truth, or ourselves, or others.

units.la: Quapropter iudicium idem fieri de iis necesse est. Præsertim verò seruos Dei per Christum oro, id semper cogitent, non persequendis iniuriis, sed ferendis probari ministerium suum. Cuius probationes optimè demonstrauit Paulus dicens, Nullam in re vlla præbentes offensionem, ne vituperetur ministerium: sed in omnibus nos approbantes vt Dei ministros, tolerantia multa in afflictionibus, in necessitatibus, in verberibus, in carceribus, in exagitationibus, &c. quæ ille fidelissimus imitator Christi nos voluit atq; mandauit imitari. Tempore & loco responderi quoq. interdum oportere antè agnouimus: sed incredibile est quantum fallamur iudiciis, cùm de iis circumstantiis videndū est. Det singulis prudentiam charitatemque Dominus. Et certè, cùm rationem Ecclesiæ Dei, prout nunc se habet, cogito; corpus ita miserè affectum est, vt in plerisque illius malis nihil magis periculosum iudicem, quàm immaimmaturam medicinam. Et tamen hoc vnum à plerisque videtur agi, vt quemadmodum apud Scythas olim & Babylonios per compita ægrotis consulebatur, tot sint Ecclesiæ medici, quot viatores ad. salutandam ipsam quamprimùm accessuri. ita plerumque euenit; vt quod dies curatura effet, vel potiùs Dei gratia successu temporis; id hodie, Deo irato, ad solum aspectum velimus curatum esse, vel ad crepitum digitorum nostrorum: & quod quietè posset consanescere, id commotione intempestiua conturbemus; tanquam prauis humoribus in corpore Ecclesiæ irritatis, quos die & quiete commoda Spiritus Christi curaturus est solus. Atque hæc quidem mala cùm in hunc locum adfero, nemini speciatim maledictum volo. Nam Deus testis est me de singularis cuiusquam hominis, quem quidè nouerim hoc tempore, notando facto minimè cogitare: sed licebit mihi per bonos (spero) deflere publica Ecclesiæ mala, nostras omniù communes culpas, & meas quoque ipsius: qui nos omnes & singulos tam multis intempestiuis & importunis dissidiis iustifsimo Dei iudicio acerbissimoq. agnosco flagellari. Quapropter deprecor, iram flagellaq. Dei communi causa Ecclesiæ, & mea per Christum: orans Dominum Deum nostrum & patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, vt singulorum mentes illuminet in veritate, corda accendat charitate, & omnia simul regat ad finem pacis in vnitate Spiritus obtinendum. Deinde verò quia nos monet Psaltes thronos Dei inter homines ad hunc ipsum finem constitutos esse, vt singuli qui pacem Ecclesiæ experimus, ab illis thronis insta assequamur adiumenta pacis & prosperitatis: vos appello, ô serui Dei, qui ex animo ad thronum spiritualem Christi in Ecclesia procumbitis, & à Deo hauritis mysteria gratiæ & gloriæ, quam Deus timentibus se præparauit: vos itidem[?] appello, ô serui Dei, qui ex officio ad thronum ciuilem in societate humana euecti estis, vt regatis eos in pace quos fidei vestræ commisit Deus: Expetite vos quoque pacem Hierosolymorum[?]: curate vt amantes Ecclesiæ fruantur prosperitate, vt pax sit præmunitioni & prosperitas palatiis eius: facite vt qui non sunt aduersus illam, pro illa habeantur, & in dies illi adiungantur ad vitam æternam per salutis verbum. Nam si hoc cuique de populo, multò magis cuique de numero vestro præceptum est, & impositum hoc munus à Domino. Experimini itaque singuli cum animis vestris pacem illam Domini lætificantem conscientias vestras: procurate vt vestræ illius pacis fructus etiam procedat foras ad eos in quorum societatem vos adduxit Deus.
units.tr: Therefore the same judgment must be made about those things. Above all, I beseech the servants of God through Christ to keep this always in mind: their ministry is to be approved not by pursuing injuries but by bearing them. Paul demonstrated these proofs best when he said: "Giving no offence in anything, that the ministry be not blamed; but in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults," and so on. That most faithful imitator of Christ wished and commanded us to imitate these things. We have already acknowledged that there are times and places when it is right to reply, but it is incredible how much we are deceived in our judgments when the circumstances must be weighed. May the Lord give each of us prudence and charity. Indeed, when I consider the state of the Church of God as it now is, the body is so miserably afflicted that I judge nothing more dangerous in most of its ills than immature medicine. And yet this seems to be the one thing that most people are doing. Just as formerly among the Scythians and Babylonians the sick were consulted at the crossroads, so there are as many physicians of the Church as there are passers-by who are about to greet it. So it commonly happens that what time would cure, or rather what God's grace would cure in the course of time, we now, with God angry, wish to be healed at a mere glance or at the snap of our fingers; and what could quietly grow strong, we disturb by untimely agitation, as if bad humours in the body of the Church were being stirred up, which the Spirit of Christ alone will cure by time and gentle quiet. And although I bring these evils up in this place, I wish to curse no one in particular. God is my witness that I am not thinking, in noting any deed, of any single man whom I know at this time. But I trust that good people will allow me to lament the public evils of the Church, our common faults, and my own too, since I acknowledge that all of us, each one, are scourged by the most just and most bitter judgment of God with so many untimely and troublesome dissensions. Therefore I pray, and beseech God to turn away his wrath and his scourges, for the common cause of the Church and for my own through Christ, asking the Lord our God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ to enlighten the minds of each in truth, to kindle hearts with charity, and to rule all of us together towards the goal of obtaining peace in the unity of the Spirit. Then, because the Psalmist reminds us that the thrones of God were set up among men for this very purpose, namely that each of us who experience the peace of the Church should from those thrones seek the aids of peace and prosperity, I appeal to you, O servants of God, who from the heart fall down before the spiritual throne of Christ in the Church and draw from God the mysteries of grace and glory that God has prepared for those who fear him. I likewise appeal to you, O servants of God, who by your office have been raised to the civil throne in human society, that you may rule in peace those whom God has committed to your trust. Seek the peace of Jerusalem also: take care that those who love the Church enjoy prosperity, that there be peace within its walls and prosperity in its palaces; see that those who are not against it are counted as on its side, and are daily joined to it for eternal life through the word of salvation. For if this is commanded of each of the people, it is much more strongly commanded of each of you, and this duty has been laid upon you by the Lord. Each of you, then, experience with your minds that peace of the Lord which gladdens your consciences, and take care that the fruit of that peace of yours also goes forth to those into whose fellowship God has brought you.

units.la: Studeamus, ô fratres dilestissimi, vt pacem Domini semper cogitemus, semper cupiamus, semper omnibus ostendamus, semper colamus, semperque defendamus strenuè, cùm aduersarium pacis videmus minimè otiantem, sed dies & noctes insidiantem aut appetentem corpus illud Christi,quod ad pacem in veritate & sanctimonia vocatum est. Inuenit quidem aduersarius ille ad pacem Ecclesiae oppugnandam armorum plus satis ( proh dolor) in Ecclesia ipsa,& membris singulis ipsius , quibus, & pastoribus: mortificemus ergo veterem illum hominem , mortificemus membra carnis noftræ paci illi cælesti aduersantia, & omnes aditus veteri illi serpenti,quàm diligentissimè fieri potest,præcludamus;cauentes seriò nobis ipsis, & ad nosipsos attendentes,& ad ouile Christi, & ad oues singulas illius,vt pacem, quam suo sanguine peperit , frendente Satana constantifsimè teneamus. Vos autem,ô viri Principes, qui orbem Christianum videtis tum grauissimis incommodis per infirmitatem ipsius infestari,tum ab iis instrumentis sæpe torqueri & excarnificari miseras animas, quæ Deus sanctificauerat vt pacis instrumenta essent; rogo per sanctissimum nomé Domini nostri Iesu Christi, per amplissimas miserationes illius,ad quarum communionem salutarem vocati estis,per suauissimum illud nomen Christianitatis quo honorauit vos Dominus, & ab aliis cupitis honorari,per fructum illum amplissimum,quem in hac vita spondet, & exhibet, atque in futura consummaturus est Deus; vt miseram Christianitatem , quæ plus satis theatrum dissidiorum & rixarum fuit, consilio & ope vestra allevetis: humano ordine vestro ovibus Christi consulatis: pastores, quicumque tandem illi sint, ad honorem Dei prosequendum & animarum salutem promouendam abiectis aliis cogitationibus, ex verbo Dei, urgeatis: impediatis ne intempestiuis imprudentibusque remediis, vel potius vitiis adnafcentibus vitia accendantur, & pax illa optatissima Christi in mentibus Christianorum omnium, in Ecclesia ipsa (quemadmodum indignissimè adhuc fieri vidimus) tantopere infirmata & debilitata corruat. Vos huic sanctissimo Christianitatis aedificio sustinendo, tanquam tibicines; huic partui alendo & curando, tanquà nutricios; huic corpori tutando, tanquam parentes praefecit Deus. Quandoquidem ergo à Deo est corpus, & à Deo estis huic corpori praepositi, & utriusque Deo rationem redditur[?] in ultimo illo die; ita rerum vestrarum & Ecclesiae totius satagite, ut tanquam oves de instituto vitae, & tanquam pastores de instituto administrationis vestrae possitis Domino illi & Deo omnium refpondere, freti praesidio gratiofiffimo illius cui vos oportet seruire, Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Let us be eager, most beloved brothers, always to think of the peace of the Lord, always to desire it, always to show it to all, always to cultivate it, and always to defend it vigorously, since we see that the adversary of peace is not at all idle, but plots day and night against, or seeks to attack, that body of Christ which is called to peace in truth and holiness. That adversary has indeed found, to assail the peace of the Church, more than enough weapons (alas!) in the Church itself and in its individual members, and in its ministers. Let us therefore mortify that old man, let us mortify the members of our flesh that oppose that heavenly peace, and let us close, as carefully as possible, every access to that old serpent, taking serious heed to ourselves, attending to ourselves, and to the flock of Christ and each of its sheep, so that we may hold most firmly to the peace that he won with his own blood, while Satan gnashes his teeth. But you, O princes, who see the Christian world both troubled by the gravest disadvantages through its own weakness, and the wretched souls, which God had sanctified to be instruments of peace, often racked and tortured by those same instruments: I ask you, by the most holy name of our Lord Jesus Christ, by his most ample mercies, to whose saving fellowship you are called, by that most sweet name of Christian with which the Lord has honoured you and which you desire to be honoured by others, and by that most ample fruit which God promises and offers in this life and will bring to completion in the life to come: help, by your counsel and aid, to relieve the wretched Christianity, which has been more than enough a theatre of dissensions and quarrels. By your human order, look after the sheep of Christ. Let the ministers, whoever they may be, press on, setting aside other concerns, from the word of God, to advance the honour of God and the salvation of souls. Prevent the sores from being inflamed by untimely and imprudent remedies, or rather by vices springing up from vices, and prevent that most longed-for peace of Christ in the minds of all Christians, in the Church itself, from being so greatly weakened and enfeebled that it collapses (as we have unworthily seen happen up to now). God has set you over this most holy building of Christianity as its builders, over this offspring to nourish and care for it as its nurses, and over this body to protect it as its parents. Since therefore the body is from God, and you have been set over this body by God, and an account of both will be rendered to God on that last day, so attend to your own affairs and to the whole Church, that you may be able to answer to that Lord and God of all, both as sheep in the course of your life and as shepherds in the course of your administration, relying on the most gracious protection of him whom you ought to serve, our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: 8. Propter fratres meos & amicos meos, eloquor jam, pax sit tibi.
units.tr: 8. For the sake of my brothers and my friends, I will now speak: peace be upon you.

units.la: 9. Propter domum Jehouæ Dei postri[?], procurabo tibi bonum.
units.tr: 9. For the sake of the house of Jehovah our God, I will seek your good.

units.la: NULLUM genus est docendi communius aut euidentius, quàm quod ab exemplis sumitur. Nam auctoritatem non omnes agnoscunt semper, ad quos habetur sermo; rationem omnes non capiunt. atque hæc duo docendis hominibus attributa sunt, tanquam lumina intus & foris homini præluentia, ut informetur de omnibus rebus quas ab ipso cognosci refert. Sed cùm hæc duo lumina (vtvt[?] homo tenebricosus est) exemplorum lineamentis ante oculos ipsius adumbrantur; tum fit ut humana mens, quibuscumque circumfusa tenebris, quasi propius admota luce videat acutius, & ad reliqua illa ampliora lumina commodè percipienda, velut conspiciliis admotis, plurimum adiuvetur: præsertim si ab iis ipsis qui duas illas faces, auctoritatis & rationis, præferunt, illa exemplorum adminicula simul præbeantur coràm: nempe si iidem typi sint operum, qui sermone docent, & quæ dicunt faciant. Atque hæc causa est, cur ubique Christus de seruis suis sermonem habens, facere & docere, tanquam in unum compegerit; & ipse quoque potentem dictis & factis sese ostenderit. Paulus item se non sermone modo, sed etiam opere docet ouibus Christi praeiuisse, & servos Dei praecipit typos esse bonorum operum & salutaris doctrinae. Iacobus affirmat, si quis audit sermonem & eum non praestat, eum similem esse viro consideranti faciem suam nativam in speculo: ac propterea iubet ut non simus auditores obliuiosi sermonis, sed actores operis. Omnesque denique Apostoli in hoc instituto perstiterunt, ne quando cùm aliis praedicarent, ipsi fierent reprobi, vel reiectanei, ut Pauli utamur verbis. In hunc igitur modum Psaltes, ubi omnes instituit de summo illo pioque studio quo pacem Ecclesiae opus est expeti, & singulos de modo expetendae illius pacis informauit, statuit postremò se ipsum in exemplum sermonum suorum & doctrinae communis statuere. Atque hoc certo consilo[?] facit: tum ut doceret suos, quàm veré & ex animo antegressa illa documenta de laetitia & pace Christiana in commune Ecclesiae proposuerit, tum ut omnes videant & sentiant nos à seruis Dei non doceri res (ut vocant) impossibiles, neq. obrui oneribus difficilibus portatu, quae ipsi digito suo mouere noluerint; sed potiùs ut illius aliorumque Prophetarum exemplis, tamquam nube testimoniorum, circum septi, discamus tandem nos taedere nostri, naturaeque nostrae, & ad officium illud sanctum, quò nos prouocauit, quasi praeeunte eodem duce contendamus.
units.tr: There is no kind of teaching more common or more evident than that which is drawn from examples. For not everyone to whom speech is addressed always acknowledges authority, and not everyone grasps reason. These two things are given to men for teaching, as lights shining upon a man from within and from without, so that he may be formed in all the things that he is told he can know from them. But when these two lights (however shadowy a man may be) are shown before his eyes in the outline of examples, then the human mind, surrounded by whatever darkness, sees more sharply as if brought nearer to the light, and is greatly helped in perceiving those larger lights with ease, as if spectacles were brought up to the eyes. This is especially so if those examples are also offered in person by those very men who bear those two torches, authority and reason, that is, if the same persons are the models of the works that they teach and do what they say. This is the reason why Christ, speaking of his servants everywhere, has joined doing and teaching as if into one, and has himself shown himself powerful in both words and deeds. Paul likewise teaches that he went before the sheep of Christ not only by speech but also by work, and he instructs that the servants of God should be types of good works and of wholesome doctrine. James affirms that if anyone hears the word and does not perform it, he is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror; and therefore he bids us not to be forgetful hearers of the word, but doers of the work. Finally, all the apostles persisted in this practice, lest, while preaching to others, they themselves should become reprobate or castaways, to use Paul's words. In this way the Psalmist, having laid out in general the supreme and pious zeal with which the peace of the Church must be sought, and having instructed each in the manner of seeking that peace, finally determined to set himself up as the example of his words and of the common teaching. He does this with a clear purpose: first, that he might teach his people how truly and sincerely he had set forth those preceding precepts on Christian joy and peace for the common good of the Church; and second, that all may see and feel that we are not taught by the servants of God things that are (as they say) impossible, nor overwhelmed with burdens hard to carry which they themselves have been unwilling to move with a finger. Rather, by the examples of him and of the other prophets, as if surrounded by a cloud of witnesses, we may at last learn to be weary of ourselves and of our nature, and to strive toward that holy duty to which he has summoned us, as if this same leader went before us.

units.la: Hic ergo finis ille est ad quem Propheta spectauit, cùm hos duos versus antecedentibus subiiceret: nimirum vt nobis se sisteret in exemplum, & nos suo ipsius exemplo accenderet confirmaretque in sancto instituto nostro. Summa est, Dauidem velle, certissimis iustissimisque de causis, ac necessariis, sermone expetere & opere procurare pacem Ecclesiae Dei; & hoc officium spondere, dum erat victurus, ad communem ædificationem. Partes itaque duæ sunt: vna est sponsio sermonum orationumque ad pacem Ecclesiae pertinentium: altera, sponsio operum ad eundem finem, si qua vnquam ratione vlla ab ipso poterunt proficisci paci Ecclesiae commoda. Prior locus 8. versu, posterior vltimo proponitur. Quamobrem de utroque distincte nobis videndum est: & quia causæ simul coniunctæ sunt, de illis eadem opera dicendum quod ad hunc locum videbitur pertinere, & ad consilium nostrum.
units.tr: This, then, is the end at which the Psalmist aimed when he added these two verses to what went before: namely, to set himself before us as an example, and to kindle us and strengthen us in our holy purpose by his own example. The sum is that David, for most certain and most just reasons, and necessary ones, wished to seek the peace of God's Church by word and to work for it by deed, and that he pledged this duty, for as long as he should live, for the common edification. There are therefore two parts: the one is a pledge of words and prayers pertaining to the peace of the Church; the other is a pledge of deeds to the same end, if by any means benefits for the peace of the Church could ever come from him. The first is set out in verse 8, the second in the last verse. So we must consider each separately, and since the reasons are joined together, we shall say about them together whatever seems pertinent to this passage and to our purpose.

units.la: Sponsionem igitur sermonum de pace Ecclesiæ Propheta faciens, dicit: Eloquar iam: pax tibi. Causam vero adiicit illis verbis; propter fratres meos, & amicos meos. Ac de causa quidem iam ante diximus. Nam quæcunque ad communionem sanctorum edocti fuimus pertinere, ea fundamento nituntur illius germanitatis seu fraternitatis, & propinquitatis nostræ, quam non solùm inter nos habemus à natura, verùm etiam (quod potentius est) à gratia Dei in Christo, omnes quidem vocante communiter; sed benedictos à Patre vocante singulariter. Hæc conscientia,qua nos fratres & propinquos alios esse aliis novimus ; coniunctissimos efficit, ut tum pacem inter nos procuremus;tum de pace & prosperitate alij aliorum lætemur in Domino. Hæc igitur causa illa est, ad quam Propheta respexit illis verbis. Etsi,quod ante disertis verbis expressimus, non temerè Propheta fratres & amicos distinctè nominauit:sed ut per incrementum elegantissimum oratio assurgeret.quia fratrum appellatione ij solùm proprie continentur ,qui & natura & gratia nobis coniuncti sunt in Ecclesia Dei ; amicorum verò appellatione etiam ij qui foris sunt, & ab Ecclesia absunt : quibus vocandis omnes operam dare tenemur in Domino ; quia (ut ante dicebamus) qui non sunt contra nos,ij pro nobis esse putandi sunt:quemadmodum promissione Deus ostenderat,dicens, Benedicam iis qui benedicent tibi, cùm Abrahamum promissionibus gratiæ instrueret.
units.tr: In making his pledge of words concerning the peace of the Church, the Psalmist says: I will now speak: peace be to you. He adds the reason in these words: for the sake of my brothers and my friends. We have already spoken of this reason before. For whatever we have been taught pertains to the communion of the saints rests on the foundation of that brotherhood or fellowship and kinship which we have not only among ourselves by nature but also (which is more powerful) by the grace of God in Christ, who calls all in common, but calls the blessed ones singularly from the Father. This awareness, by which we know that we are brothers and kinsmen to one another, makes us most closely bound together, so that we both work for peace among ourselves and rejoice in one another's peace and prosperity in the Lord. This, then, is the reason to which the Psalmist looked in those words. And although we have already expressed it in plain words, the Psalmist did not name brothers and friends separately without reason, but so that his speech might rise by a most elegant increase. For by the name of brothers are properly included only those who are joined to us both by nature and by grace in the Church of God; but by the name of friends are included also those who are outside and absent from the Church. We are all bound to labour in the Lord to call these, since (as we said before) those who are not against us are to be thought to be for us, just as God had shown by promise, saying: I will bless those who bless you, when he instructed Abraham with the promises of grace.

units.la: Hanc eandem causam pios omnes indefinenter sibi, præsertim hoc funestissimo perturbatissimoque seculo,necesse est ante oculos ponere;ut non alienationibus (quas videmus)animorum , aut præposteris & iniquis in alios iudiciis studeamus ; sed optima fide & conscientia fratres & amicos singuli cognoscamus,cum illis coalescamus quàm diligentissimè, eosque
units.tr: All the godly must always keep this same reason before their eyes, especially in this most deadly and most troubled age, so that we do not strive for the estrangements of minds that we see, or for prejudiced and unjust judgments of others; but that each of us, in the best faith and conscience, may recognise brothers and friends, join ourselves to them as diligently as possible, and

units.la: omnibus officiis quæ in manu nostra Deus pofuerit, ex charitate ἀνυπκείτῳ [?] prosequamur. Hæc igitur causa, quæ Prophetam excitauit, & nos omnes longè iustius ac vehementius excitare debet ad illa, quę pòst sequuntur, officia præstanda accuratissimè, quàm Themistocles olim se Miltiadis tropæis excitari de nocte prædicabat. Hæc enim tropæa sunt Dauidis & Christianorum omnium clarissima, quòd & cives suos seruauisse, & hostem salutis deuicisse dicuntur à Domino.
units.tr: pursue them with unfeigned [ἀνυπόκριτος] love in all the offices which God has placed in our hands. This reason, then, which stirred up the Psalmist, ought to stir all of us far more justly and vehemently to perform most carefully those duties that follow, than Themistocles once declared that he was stirred by the trophies of Miltiades at night. For these trophies of David and of all Christians are the most famous, since they are said to have been given by the Lord both to save their own citizens and to conquer the enemy of salvation.

units.la: - Officium autem in sermone positum, quod Propheta spondet his iustissimis de causis, duabus in rebus positum est, nimirum in Specie officij, & circumstantiis. Speciem officij Propheta spondet, cùm dicit: Eloquar pacem tibi. Circumstantias, cùm addit, nunc vel iam, vnica voce demonstrauit. Species officij in eloquenda pace Ecclesiæ posita duo membra continet, pro ratione obiectorum siue personarum, apud quas ista ex officio suo eloquuntur pij. Ad vnum pertinent orationes, & preces, gratiarumq. actiones, quibus Deum Ecclesiæ caput appellamus de pace illius: ad alterum communicationes cum Ecclesiæ membris, cum amicis, & cum Ecclesia vniuersa. Nam siue ad Deum respiciamus, pacem oportet spirent animi nostri, & pro ea suspirent coram Domino Deo pacis; siue ad homines qui nos circumstant, oculos & cogitationem conuertamus, proferri à nobis ad pacem oportet omnia;ut qui filij simus illius qui Deus est pacis; alumni Ecclesiæ, quæ domus est pacis; membraque illius corporis quod Christus redemit conciliata cum Deo pace, & constituta inter nos in unitate Spiritus. Atq. hæc quidem omnia jam antè fusius sunt explicata: Sed ea Propheta sibi ipsi nominatim applicavit, ut nostras singulorum conscientias permoveret excitaretque ad idem officium in veritate & charitate præstandum. quod officium si tam diligenter plerique omnes coleremus, quàm diligenter studia & opera carnis colimus, quæ Apo-stolus ad Galatas scribens exprimit copiosissime; jamdiu profectò extinctis mortiferis feminibus Satanæ suavissima pace amplius frucremur.
units.tr: Now the duty set forth in speech, which the Psalmist pledges for these most just reasons, consists of two things, namely the kind of duty and its circumstances. The Psalmist pledges the kind of duty when he says: I will speak peace to you. The circumstances he indicated in one word when he added now or already. The kind of duty in speaking of the peace of the Church contains two parts, according to the nature of the objects or persons to whom the godly speak of it in their office. To the one belong speeches, prayers and thanksgivings, by which we call upon God, the head of the Church, concerning its peace; to the other belong communications with the members of the Church, with friends, and with the whole Church. For whether we look to God, our minds must breathe peace and sigh for it before the Lord God of peace; or whether we turn our eyes and thoughts to the men who surround us, everything must be directed by us toward peace, since we are sons of him who is the God of peace, nurslings of the Church, which is the house of peace, and members of that body which Christ redeemed, its peace with God having been reconciled and its unity established among us in the unity of the Spirit. And indeed all these things have already been explained more fully before; but the Psalmist applied them to himself by name, so that he might move and rouse the consciences of each of us to perform the same duty in truth and love. If most of us cultivated this duty as diligently as we cultivate the desires and works of the flesh, which the Apostle, writing to the Galatians, sets out most fully, we would long since, with the deadly seeds of Satan extinguished, enjoy the sweetest peace much more.

units.la: Sed quid sibi vult illa temporis circumstantia, cùm Propheta dicit & Ecclesia verbis illius, se jamjam eloqui? Respicit quidem ad singularem illam occasionem quam principio Psalmi demonstravimus, quòd Deus locum designasset habitationis suæ, & arca in eum esset importata, ac cultus institutus: sed etiam spectavit ulterius, nempe ostendit se velle prædicare fermonem pacis, & instare tempestivè & intempestivè, adeoque illico sine mora aut cunctatione ulla in eo sancto[?] opere sese occupare. Notum est illud Christi, neminem, qui manu sua admota aratro respexerit ad ea quæ retrò sunt, appositum esse ad regnum Dei. notum & illud Apostoli, quando placuit Deo retegere filium suum in ipso, ut evangelizaret illum inter gentes, non statim praeterea contulisse cum carne & sanguine. Notum & illud elegans Cypriani dictum, cum Aspasio Paterno proconsuli Africae tentanti ipsum, sepe vitae seni facta, respondereret in rebus sanctis non esse deliberationem. Hoc igitur institutum suum citra ullam cunctationem deliberationemque; inde ab illo ipso momento ad ultimum usque spiritum, prositetur Psalmes: ostenditque se (quod praecipit Apostolus) indesinenter oraturum esse pro pace Ecclesiae Dei, & indesinenter cum fratribus atque amicis de pace Ecclesiae sermones habiturum, neque passurum se, ut vel ad mortem[?] abripiatur ab isto sanctissimo officio, tota[?] Deo hominibusque persequendo.
units.tr: But what does that circumstance of time mean, when the Psalmist and the Church in his words say that he will speak already, already? It indeed refers to that singular occasion which we pointed out at the beginning of the Psalm, namely that God had designated the place of his habitation, the ark had been brought into it, and worship had been instituted. But it also looked further, namely it shows that he wishes to preach the word of peace, and to press on in season and out of season, and so to occupy himself in that holy work immediately, without any delay or hesitation. Well known is that saying of Christ, that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back to what is behind is fit for the kingdom of God. Well known too is the saying of the Apostle, that when it pleased God to reveal his Son in him, that he might preach him among the Gentiles, he did not immediately confer with flesh and blood. Also well known is that elegant saying of Cyprian, when, being tempted by the proconsul of Africa, Aspasius Paternus, in his old age he answered that there is no deliberation in holy matters. So the Psalmist professes this purpose of his without any hesitation or deliberation, from that very moment until his last breath; and he shows that (as the Apostle commands) he will pray without ceasing for the peace of the Church of God, and will without ceasing hold talks with brothers and friends about the peace of the Church, and will not allow himself to be dragged away from this most holy duty, even to death, while he pursues it before God and men.

units.la: Hactenus de sermonis ad pacem officiis. Sequitur alter locus, de officiis ad pacem opere praestandis: qui locus duas continet partes, unam, de causa illius officii; alteram, de substantia et specie illius. Causam Propheta expressit his verbis, propter domum Iehova Dei nostri: Officium illis, procurabo quod bonum est tibi, vel exquiram bonum tuum. Respicit autem proprie haec narratio causae ad propositionem illam primam, qua usus est Propheta in principio, dicens piorum coëuntium verbis; Domum Iehovae adeamus: quo ex loco deprompi facile potest horum verborum interpretatio. Ad summam, causam instituti sui vniuersè Propheta ponit domum Iehouæ Dei nostri s. [?] quibus verbis ostendit se ad hoc institutum adlaborare causa Ecclesiæ, non simpliciter quà domus est ex membris humanis coagmentata, sed singulariter quà domus est Iehouæ Dei nostri, ab illo inhabitante sanctificata ad gloriam suam. Proinde cùm Ecclesia non possit recte à nobis considerari, nisi secundùm relationem illam quà ad Deum est ordinata; ex eo sequitur plane, qui Ecclesiæ bene cupit, eundem etiam quodammodo cupere [?] Deo qui Ecclesiâ inhabitat.
units.tr: So far concerning the duties of speech for peace. There follows the second passage, concerning the duties to be performed by deed for peace; this passage contains two parts, one concerning the reason for that duty, the other concerning its substance and kind. The Psalmist expressed the reason in these words: for the sake of the house of Jehovah our God. The duty is in these words: I will seek what is good for you, or I will seek your good. This statement of the reason refers properly to that first proposition which the Psalmist used at the beginning, saying in the words of the godly who gather together: Let us go up to the house of Jehovah; from which place the interpretation of these words can easily be drawn. In sum, the Psalmist sets forth in general the reason for his undertaking as the house of Jehovah our God; by these words he shows that he labours for this undertaking for the sake of the Church, not simply as the house is compacted from human members, but singularly as it is the house of Jehovah our God, sanctified by him who dwells in it for his own glory. Therefore, since the Church cannot rightly be considered by us except according to that relation by which it is ordered to God, it plainly follows that whoever desires well for the Church also desires, in a certain way, the God who dwells in the Church.

units.la: Cupit autem Ecclesiæ pius, tanquàm ad finem propinquiorem & quodammodo συμφυῆ, siue (vt loquuntur) connaturalem respiciens: Deo autem cupit sanquàm ad finem diuinum, in quo Ecclesia ipsa & singuli nostrum in Ecclesia conquiescunt. Nam quemadmodum nos in Ecclesia conquiescimus, non quia domus est, sed quia domus Dei; non quia corpus, sed quia corpus Christi: ita è diuerso, cùm bene Ecclesiæ cupimus, non simpliciter cupimus, quòd domus & corpus sit, sed eò maximè quòd domus Dei viuentis est & corpus Christi.
units.tr: The godly man, however, loves the Church as a nearer end and, so to speak, one that is of one nature with himself (what they call connatural), and he desires good for God as the divine end, in whom the Church itself and each of us rests in the Church. For just as we rest in the Church not because it is a house but because it is the house of God, not because it is a body but because it is the body of Christ, so conversely, when we desire the good of the Church, we do not desire merely that it be a house and a body, but chiefly that it be the house of the living God and the body of Christ.

units.la: Atque hæc causa est, cur Propheta non tantùm in descriptione Ecclesiæ quà est, sed in descriptione Dei, à quo & in quo Ecclesia est, aliquanto pluris hæret, dicens: domum Iehouæ Dei nostri. Nam Iehouam nominando, ad illam efsentiam respicere, nos iubet, quæ sola est per se, & aliis dat ésse, & principium est omnis boni in rerum natura: boni, inquam, tum ex natura, tum ex gratia in nos omnes collati. Deum vero nostrum appellando, respicit ad fœdus illud sanctissimum, quo Deus noster est, & nos vicissim populus illius, & ad demonstrationem fœderis eiusdem perpetuam mentem & operationes gratiæ. Sic enim passim in Scripturis Deus promissiones suas aut operationes afferens, fundamenta naturæ & gratiæ ad confirmationem suæ veritatis in suis solet coniungere. Quo etiam illud pertinet, quod in declaratione suarum promissionum, Vnitatem essentiæ, & personarum Trinitatem in vnitate plurimum denotat: Vnitatem, quam ex natura nouimus naturali appellatione Iehoua: Trinitatem, quam ex doctrina & revelatione gratiæ didicimus, gratioso fœderis elogio significaans, cùm se inscribit Elohim, vel Deum nostrum.
units.tr: This is the reason why the Prophet, in describing the Church, lingers somewhat longer not only on what the Church is but on God, from whom and in whom the Church is, saying: "the house of Jehovah our God." For in naming Jehovah he bids us look to that essence which alone is of itself, gives being to others, and is the source of every good in the nature of things: good, I say, both of nature and of grace bestowed upon us all. But in calling him "our God," he looks to that most holy covenant by which God is ours and we in turn are his people, and to the constant display of the same covenant in the mind and works of grace. For so throughout the Scriptures God, when he sets forth his promises or works, is accustomed to join the foundations of nature and of grace in confirmation of his truth. To this also belongs the fact that in declaring his promises he very often signifies the unity of essence and the Trinity of persons in unity: the unity which we know from nature by the natural name "Jehovah," and the Trinity which we have learned from doctrine and revelation of grace, signified by the gracious title of the covenant when he styles himself "Elohim" or "our God."

units.la: Hæc autem causa quam Prophetæ adfert, profecto eiusmodi est, vt singulos nostrum dies noctesque possit afficere vehementissimè, nisi grauissimo veterno in sentiendis & persequendis bonis, grauissimaque obstinatione in amplexandis malis, ad perniciem nostram teneremur. Cùm autem iam ille Iehoua Deus noster nos à malis vindicauerit, & nobis bona adiudicauerit quæcunque ab ipso ad rem creatam peruenire possent; quid excusationis vel in speciem prætexemus coram Deo atque hominibus, si ab eâdem causa persequenda abstineamus, ex quo Iehouam Deum nostrum & Ecclesiam Dominum Iehouæ Dei nostri per Scripturas sacras didicimus? Quapropter (ut ait Apostolus) expergiscamur qui dormimus, & surgamus à mortuis, & illucescet nobis Christus. Intueamur semper in illam essentiam distinam [?], quæ principium est omnis boni, tum natura communi, tum gratia erga nos singulariter. Intueamur in Patrem illum omnipotentem, qui nos dedit filio in Ecclesiam colligendos: Intueamur in fidei ducem ac perfectorem Iesum, qui pro gaudio sibi propositò pertulit crucem, & ad dextram throni Dei consedit, quò nos euehæret [?]: Intueamur in Spiritu illum patris & filij habitantem in nobis, & testante spiritui nostro nos esse filios Dei, & templa sancta Domino: Intueamur in Ecclesiam, in quam velut templum lectissimum Deus nos convocat, ut per eam ad se contendamus virtute æterni spiritus viuentis in nobis. hæ causæ nos ita moverint, ut cæteras causas dimoveant ex mentibus nostris, & rapiant ad sanctissimum illud studium, cuius hic Propheta meminit, & seipsum exhibet typum in pietate & sanctimonia ad hæc officia præ-tarum.
units.tr: Now the cause which the Prophet brings forward is truly of such a kind that it ought to move each of us day and night most vehemently, unless we were held to our ruin by a most grievous drowsiness in perceiving and pursuing what is good, and a most grievous obstinacy in embracing what is evil. Since that same Jehovah our God has already delivered us from evils and has assigned to us every good that could reach a created thing from him, what excuse, or even a pretext, could we offer before God and men if we refrain from pursuing this same cause, since through the holy Scriptures we have learned that Jehovah is our God and the Church is the house of Jehovah our God? Therefore (as the Apostle says) let us who sleep awake, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon us. Let us always fix our gaze on that essence which is the source of every good, both in common nature and in grace toward us in particular. Let us look to that almighty Father, who gave us to his Son to be gathered into the Church; let us look to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God, whither he would lift us up; let us look to that Spirit of the Father and the Son dwelling in us, and bearing witness with our spirit that we are the sons of God and holy temples of the Lord; let us look to the Church, into which God calls us as a most chosen temple, that through it we may press on toward him by the power of the eternal and living Spirit within us. May these causes so move us that they drive other causes out of our minds and carry us off to that most holy zeal of which this Prophet speaks, and show himself a type of piety and holiness, set before us for these duties.

units.la: Quid ergo est officij, quod Propheta hoc loco prædicat? Quæram [?], inquit, sive procurabe quod bonum est tibi, ô Ierusalem, vel domus Iehouæ. Procurantur quæ adsunt, ut augeantur atque conferconferuentur: procurantur quae absunt, ut inueniantur comparenturq. labore quaerentium nostro. Jam utroq. modo Propheta dicit fe procuratarum quod bonū est Ecclesiæ Dei. Quid autem illud sit quod bonum est Ecclesiæ Dei, in praecedentibus fatis explicauit. Bonū summum Ecclesiæ est, quòd domus est Iehouæ Dei nostri, ad ipsum ordinata constantissimè in Christo per unitatem Spiritus: hoc esse illius. Ex eo bono sequuntur bona omnia, quae deriuantur in nos à Domino: siue percipienda intus à nobis, ut sunt fructus illi Spiritus, quos antè Propheta nominauit, pax & gaudium in Spiritu sancto; siue proferenda à nobis ex quo sumus in Christo insiti, & cōfortes facti pacis laetitiæq. spiritualis illius, ut sunt fructus illi Spiritus, qui in sanctificatione vitæ, & charitate, & pace versantur; siue extrà insuper accedentia per benedictionem Dei, ut sunt pax illa [?] & prosperitas Ecclesiæ, de qua Propheta ante sermonem habuerat. Haec omnia quisquis procurat, procurat Ecclesiæ bonum: qui non procurat, Ecclesiæ officit, ut sibi aliter videatur. Neq. dubium est, quin ad haec omnia Propheta actus Spiritu Dei respexerit. Verumtamen cum illi fructus à forma Ecclesiæ interna externaque sint; nec extra Ecclesiam, sed in Ecclesia, id est, in Domino, qui inhabitat Ecclesiam, sint praesentissima: verius id esse existimo, agere Prophetam maximè de tertio illo bonorum genere, quibus foris benedicit Deus iis quos interna benedictione instruxerit. Omnia igitur bona dat Deus, & omnia quærimus data; quia nec illa ipsa quæ data sunt, nec nos ipsos (adeò cæci sumus infirmitate nostra) inuenturi simus, nisi nos quotidiè exploremus, & bona Dei, tum quæ iâ ex facto dedit, tum quæ porrò gratiosè daturus est, quæramus in Domino. Horum in numero est pax, bonum suauissimum, quod se procuraturum spondebat Psalmes certa Spiritus Dei testificatione, dicentis, Persequimini pacem & sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo Deum visurus est.
units.tr: What, then, is the duty which the Prophet proclaims in this place? "I will seek," he says, "or I will procure, what is good for you," O Jerusalem, or house of Jehovah. What is present is procured so that it may be increased and preserved; what is absent is procured so that it may be found and obtained by the labour of our seeking. Now in both ways the Prophet says that he procures what is good for the Church of God. What that good of the Church of God is, he has explained sufficiently in what precedes. The supreme good of the Church is that it is the house of Jehovah our God, most firmly ordered to him in Christ through the unity of the Spirit: this is its good. From that good all the goods follow which flow down to us from the Lord, whether they are to be received within by us, such as those fruits of the Spirit which the Prophet named before, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit; or whether they are to be brought forth by us, since we have been grafted into Christ and made partakers of that peace and spiritual joy, such as those fruits of the Spirit which consist in holiness of life, love and peace; or whether they come in from outside through the blessing of God, such as that peace and prosperity of the Church of which the Prophet had spoken before. Whoever procures all these things procures the good of the Church; whoever does not procure them hinders the Church, however it may seem to him otherwise. Nor is there any doubt that in all these things the Prophet, moved by the Spirit of God, had regard. Yet since those fruits belong to the inner and outer form of the Church, and are most present not outside the Church but in the Church, that is, in the Lord who dwells in the Church, I judge it more accurate to say that the Prophet is speaking chiefly of that third kind of good, by which God blesses outwardly those whom he has furnished with inward blessing. God therefore gives all good things, and we seek the things given; for neither those very things which have been given, nor ourselves (so blind are we in our weakness), shall we find unless we search ourselves daily and seek in the Lord both the good things God has already given us and those he is yet to give graciously. Among these is peace, the sweetest good, which the Psalmist promised he would procure, by the sure testimony of the Spirit of God, saying: "Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God."

units.la: Quasob res; quotquot sumus qui nomen Deo patri per Christum dedimus in spiritu, qui ad Ecclesiam indulgentissimis promissionibus & gratiosissimo fœdere ipsius provocamur, qui in Christo redempti sumus pretio amplissimo, qui in Ecclesia pedes nostros consistentes agnoscimus virtute Dei, qui testimonio communi gratiæ diuinæ fruimur in domo eius, vt nomen ipsius pro tanta beneficentia percepta celebremus, qui ordine ipsius diuino atque humano ad ius colendum & persequendum deducimur, qui circumsplendente luce testium Dei & Christi sanctissimorum clarissimorumque ad pacem Ecclesiæ procurandam accersimur; qui denique exemplo sanctissimi Prophetæ Dauidis informamur de omnibus illis pietatis charitatisque erga Ecclesiam, & fratres, & amicos omnes officiis: fugiamus, per Deum immortamortalem, omnia illa incommoda, in quæ à natura ferimur præcipites: carnê peccatricem, & membra nostra mortificemus in carne: à studiis carnis, quàm diligentissimè fieri potest, abscedamus: Deum quæramus in Ecclesia: Ecclesiam in Deo, nos & fratres nostros in Deo & Ecclesia simul recognoscamus, & pacem cum omnibus à Deo constitutam colamus constantissimè, fugientem persequamur, oppugnatam propugnemus, amissam quæramus, inuentam teneamus, & obtinentes optimè seruemus in Deo, in Ecclesia, in nobis, & inter nos religiosissimè, expectantes optatissimum illum aduentum Domini & Seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi: qui pacè hîc in se partam, & in nobis inchoatam, illîc in cælis consummaturus est perfecta & æterna consummatione. Amen.
units.tr: Wherefore, all of us who have given the name of God the Father through Christ in spirit, who are called to the Church by his most indulgent promises and most gracious covenant, who have been redeemed in Christ at the highest price, who acknowledge that by the power of God we stand on our feet in the Church, who enjoy the common witness of divine grace in his house, so that we may celebrate his name for so great a kindness received, who are led by his divine and human order to cultivate and pursue justice, who are summoned, with the shining light of the most holy and most illustrious witnesses of God and Christ around us, to procure peace for the Church; who finally are instructed by the example of the most holy Prophet David in all those offices of piety and charity toward the Church, the brethren, and all friends: let us flee, by the immortal God, all those evils into which we are headlong carried by nature: let us mortify our sinful flesh and our members which are in the flesh; let us withdraw from the desires of the flesh as diligently as can be done; let us seek God in the Church, and recognise the Church in God, and recognise ourselves and our brethren together in God and the Church; and let us cultivate with the utmost constancy the peace which God has established with all, pursue what flees, defend what is attacked, seek what is lost, hold fast what is found, and, holding it, keep it most faithfully in God, in the Church, in ourselves, and among one another with the utmost devotion, awaiting the most desired coming of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who will bring to completion, in heaven, with a perfect and eternal consummation, the peace here acquired in himself and begun in us. Amen.

units.la: PARS II. PSALMVS CXXXIII.
units.tr: PART II. PSALM 133.

units.la: I. Canticum excellentissimum, Danidis. Ecce quàm bonum & quàm amœnum est habitare fratres etiam unà.
units.tr: I. A most excellent song of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together, even as one.

units.la: CUM hoc scriptum instituimus, de re pernecessaria, nimirum de pace Ecclesiæ dicturi, hæc summa à nobis fuit proposita instituti nostri: tandem aliquando à pugnis & contentionibus absisti oportere, & pacem quæ sit secundùm Deum procurari, ut fructus illius amplissimos suavissimosque à Deo pacis assequamur. Itaque sermonis instituti ordinem persequentes, cùm ex Prophetæ verbis de procuranda pace & rebus ad eam pertinentibus in Psalmum antecedente dixerimus; nunc videndum nobis est, ut de fructibus illius pacis secundo loco adferamus quæ nobis à Spiritu sancto in breuissimo hoc Psalmo fuerunt dictata. Est enim hic Psalmus perbreuis quidé in speciem indiculus; sed amplissimus argumento, spiritualium fructuum illius pacis, quâ Deus cum Ecclesia sua communicat, certissimam doctrinam conuenientissimo ordine comprehendens. Quapropter etiam, ut alii aliquot Psalmi, quos prisca Ecclesia olim in unum ordinem contulit, Canticum excellentiarum siue excellentissimum appellatur.
units.tr: When we began this work, intending to speak about a matter of the greatest necessity, namely the peace of the Church, we set before ourselves this main aim: that we must at last stop fighting and quarrelling, and seek the peace that is according to God, so that we may obtain from the God of peace its most ample and sweetest fruits.
