Therefore, following the order of our treatise, after we had spoken, from the words of the Prophet in the preceding Psalm, about promoting peace and the things pertaining to it, we must now consider, in the second place, the fruits of that peace, which the Holy Spirit has dictated to us in this very brief Psalm. For this Psalm is indeed, in appearance, a very short index, but in its subject matter it is most ample, comprising in the most fitting order a most certain teaching about the spiritual fruits of that peace by which God shares with his Church. For this reason also, like several other Psalms which the ancient Church once gathered into one group, it is called Canticum excellentiarum, or the most excellent song.

units.la: Cùm autem de hac Cantici inscriptione, quæ, utriusque Psalmi communis est, ea in antecedentem illum dixerimus, quæ ad huius argumenti commodam intelligentiam pertinent, non statuimus hic actum agere, & lectorem in eodem saxo versando occupare. Id nobis suturum est in præsentia satis: auctorem, & rem, & modum æque nobis inscriptione huius cantici atque antecedentis demonstrari. Auctorem Deum esse, qui ipsum dederit, per Davidem virum Dei actum spiritu illius. Rem, quæ hic exponitur auctore spiritu veritatis, esse omnium excellentissimam: Modum denique esse hunc, ut quemadmodum ratione cōmodissima perscriptus est & traditus Ecclesiæ Dei, ita etiam accipiatur ab Ecclesia singulisque membris illius; & auditione, lectione, recordatione, cantu vel modulatione cùm privatim, tum etiam publicè recolatur propter amplissimam eius dignitatem & certitudinem. Quas ad res, non dico si viri sumus, sed (quod amplius est) si filii Dei sumus, oportet nos omnes neruos facultatesque nostras contendere; ut Deo obsequentes ad res excellentissimas religiosè aspiremus, easque indesinenter colamus cum animis nostris, reputantes singularem Dei beneficentiam, qui nos ad excellentissima omnia tam gratiosè provocat, dum stadium huius vitæ decurrimus.
units.tr: Now, although we spoke about this title of the song, which is common to both Psalms, when dealing with the preceding one, and set out what pertains to a convenient understanding of this subject, we have decided not to do that work again here and keep the reader busy going over the same ground. For the present it will be enough that the title of this song shows us equally the author, the subject and the manner: the author is God, who gave it, through David, a man of God, moved by his Spirit; the subject set forth here, under the authority of the Spirit of truth, is the most excellent of all; and finally the manner is this: just as it has been written down and handed over to the Church of God in a most suitable form, so it is also to be received by the Church and by each of its members, and to be recalled, both privately and publicly, by hearing, reading, remembering, singing and chanting, on account of its very great dignity and certainty. To these things, I say, not only if we are men, but (what is greater) if we are sons of God, we ought to direct all our strength and abilities, so that, obeying God, we may earnestly aspire to the most excellent things and cultivate them unceasingly with our minds, reflecting on the singular kindness of God, who so graciously calls us to all excellent things while we run the course of this life.

units.la: Omissa itaq; inscriptione Cantici huius, de verbis & argumento illius speciatim nobis videndum est. Finis, quem Propheta spectauit, cum hoc canticu Deo auctore perscriberet, Ecclesiæque alleruandum [?] & decantandum traderet, hic proprie videtur esse; ut fructus pacis quam Ecclesia à Deo habet, perspicuè exponeret; & contemplatione illorum, animos vniuscuiusque veri membri in Christo Ecclesiaque insiti per fidem, ad utrumque studium, tum fructuum quos singuli natura cupimus, tum pacis quæ nobis datur & fructuosa est per gratiam, eadem opera accenderet. Nam quis fructus excellentissimos videns non appetat? quis arborem illam vel plantam, ex qua fructus progignuntur excellentissimi, non anteponat cæteris rebus, si sapit? Hanc igitur artem adhibuit Psaltes, ut singulos nostrum ad eundem finem persequendum raperet, quem ipse utendum docendumque proposuerat sibi.
units.tr: Setting aside, then, the title of this song, we must now consider particularly its words and subject. The purpose which the Prophet had in view, when by God's authority he wrote down this song and handed it over to the Church to be addressed and sung, seems to be this: to set out plainly the fruits of the peace which the Church has from God; and by contemplating them, to kindle at the same time, in the minds of every true member of Christ and of the Church implanted through faith, both the desire for those fruits, which we all by nature wish for, and the desire for that peace which is given to us and is fruitful through grace. For who, seeing most excellent fruits, does not long for them? Who, if he has any sense, would not prefer above other things that tree or plant from which such excellent fruits come? The Psalmist therefore used this art, so that he might draw each of us to pursue the same end which he himself had proposed to use and to teach.

units.la: Summa autem est, illius pacis, quam in communione sanctorum cum Deo Ecclesiaq; eius obtinemus, fructus esse bonis omnibus commendabiles, & summopere appetendos, tum bonitatis ipsorum, tum suauitatis & iucunditatis nomine. Hos enim fructus nihil in rerum natura adæquare dignitate potest, nedum antecellere: quia ut radix, sic etiā fructus sunt à sola benedictione Domini, qui nobis benedicit omni benedictione spirituali in locis supercælestibus in Christo, vt Ephesiis scribit Apostolus.
units.tr: The sum, moreover, is this: the fruits of that peace which we possess with God and his Church in the communion of the saints are commendable to all good people and greatly to be desired, both for their goodness and for their sweetness and delight. For nothing in the nature of things can equal these fruits in dignity, much less surpass them; because, as with the root, so the fruits too come from the blessing of the Lord alone, who blesses us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, as the Apostle writes to the Ephesians.

units.la: Partes itaque huius Psalmi in vniuersum duæ ponendæ sunt: Nam primum habetur propositio totius argumenti, versu primo. Deinde vero expositio & enarratio illius, duobus sequentibus. Propositionem autem Propheta in hunc modum instituit, vt rem quidem proponat verbis simplicibus, dicendo: Bonum & amœnum est habitare fratres etiam vnà: Sed tamen amplificet dignitatem illius duobus sermonis figurati modis, cùm dicit, ecce, quàm bonum, & quàm amœnum. Primùm itaque de ipsa propositione simpliciter dicturi sumus, deinde vero destringemus illa ornamenta ad amplificandam propositionis dignitatem hoc loco adhibita.
units.tr: The parts of this Psalm, then, must be laid out as two in general: first there is the proposition of the whole subject, in the first verse; then its exposition and explanation, in the two following verses. The Prophet has set out the proposition in this way: he states the matter itself in simple words, saying: Bonum & amœnum est habitare fratres etiam vnà, it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together; but he nevertheless enhances its dignity by two figurative forms of speech, when he says ecce, quàm bonum, & quàm amœnum, behold, how good and how pleasant. First, therefore, we shall speak simply about the proposition itself, and then we shall set out the ornaments used here to enhance the dignity of the proposition.

units.la: Est igitur hæc propositio, communione sanctorum bonam & amœnam vel iucundâ esse. Communio sanctorum denotatur his verbis, Habitare fratres etiam vnà. Quod autem adfirmatur de hac communione, verbis simplicibus & apertis enuntiatum est; bonam videlicet eam & amœnam esse. Ad communionem sanctorum rectè intelligendam duo distinctè opus est obseruari, quid, de quibus dicatur; nempe de sanctis sancta communio: quam communionem in antecedens Canticum copiosè declaranimus. Sancti qui in hac communione sunt, appellatione fratrum denotantur: Communio vero quæ inter ipsos est, communi habitatione per synecdochen Hebræis usitatam hîc adumbrata est.
units.tr: The proposition, then, is this: that the communion of the saints is good and pleasant, or delightful. The communion of the saints is signified by the words Habitare fratres etiam vnà, to dwell together as brothers. What is affirmed of this communion has been stated in simple and plain words: namely that it is good and pleasant. To understand the communion of the saints rightly, two things need to be observed distinctly: what is said, and of whom it is said; namely, the holy communion is said of holy people, a communion which we explained at length in the preceding Song. Those saints who are in this communion are designated by the name fratrum, of brothers; and the communion which exists among them is here shadowed forth, by synecdoche, through the common dwelling which is customary among the Hebrews.

units.la: Ac fratres quidem appellantur sancti qui in Ecclesia sunt, non naturæ ordine, sed gratiæ divinæ instituto. Fratrum enim duo sunt genera, pro ratione principiorum ex quibus efficiuntur fratres. Unum principium natura est; secundum quam fratres appellantur quicunque ex communi parente sunt, sive gradu proximo, ut sunt germani fratres; sive remotissimo, ut sumus omnes filij Adami, ad unam speciem (cuius radix & principium fuit Adam) pertinentes; sive intermediis, prout inter hos duos gradus germanitatis plurimi etiam ex naturæ aut civili ordine τῆς ἀδελφότητ[?] gradus intercurrunt. Cùm autem in Ecclesia non fiant gradus isti, ut qui à natura sint; sed potiùs in ea inveniantur, ut à natura facti; necesse est, ut fraternitatem hanc, de qua agit Psalmes, in Ecclesia non à natura, sed ab instituto aliquo sentiamus proficisci. quod institutum non humanum, sed divinum esse eo cognoscimus, quòd Pater Ecclesiæ, qui dat Ecclesiæ id esse quòd est, idem est membrorum pater, qui dat eis esse in Ecclesia id quod sunt. Sumus autem inter nos fratres, primùm quidem in Christo conciliati Deo; deinde verò inter nos in Christo: quia Christus caput est, cuius vi omnium membrorum inter se compages est coagmentata, & totum corpus ex eis constitutum assurgit in iustam staturam ipsius. Secundùm rationem hanc proximè inter se dicuntur fratres, quicunque in Christo & Ecclesia sunt germani filij Dei Patris in Christo adoptati per gratiam. Verumtamen inter illam fraternitatem naturæ & hanc fraternitatem gratiæ, media quædam est fraternitas, quidam quasi transitus à natura ad gratiam, per vocationem externam hominum à natura ad gratiam transmeantium virtute vocantis Dei. Fratres igitur secundùm carnem & speciem natura faciunt. Fratres secundùm spiritum facit gratia internæ vocationis, quæ singularis est in Christo: Fratres verò communes secundùm participationem aliquam gratiæ facit externa vocatio, quæ communis est mundo & Ecclesiæ, ut omnes à mundo ad Ecclesiam transeuntes cum Christo in ea coalescant. Sed quia de hac ratione fraternitatis nostræ, sanctisq; eius officiis, in Canticum præcedens diximus; nolumus hic longiores esse: modò hoc singuli observent in Prophetæ verbis, proprièque hic de illa fraternitate intima in Christo agi, quæ ut summa est, ita etiam alia illa iustæ fraternitatis genera complectitur. Nam qui frater est hac fraternitate nobiscum in Christo, idem & natura, & externa vocatione frater est: quandoquidem è natura per vocationem externam ad intimam illam & fraternam coniunctionem evocatur, perduciturq;. Huius accessio non est illarum interitus, sed magis perfectio: quemadmodum vnitati si duo adieceris, non tollitur, sed augetur vnitas; nec flammula exstingitur si flammam admoueris.
units.tr: The saints who are in the Church are called brothers, not by the order of nature, but by the institution of divine grace. For there are two kinds of brothers, according to the principle from which they become brothers. One principle is nature; according to it, all who come from a common parent are called brothers, whether in the nearest degree, as full brothers are, or in the most remote, as we are all sons of Adam, belonging to one species whose root and beginning was Adam; or in intermediate degrees, since many degrees of kinship, whether of nature or of civil order, come between these two degrees of relationship [τῆς ἀδελφότητος]. But since in the Church these degrees do not arise as they do from nature, but rather are found in it as made by nature, we must understand that this brotherhood, of which the Psalm speaks, proceeds in the Church not from nature but from some institution. We recognise that this institution is not human but divine, because the Father of the Church, who gives the Church what it is, is also the Father of its members, who gives them to be in the Church what they are. We are brothers among ourselves, first indeed because we are reconciled to God in Christ, and then truly among ourselves in Christ; because Christ is the head, by whose power the joining together of all the members is fitted, and the whole body, constituted from them, grows into its proper stature. According to this reasoning, those who are in Christ and in the Church, the true sons of God the Father, adopted in Christ through grace, are most closely called brothers among one another. Nevertheless, between that brotherhood of nature and this brotherhood of grace there lies a certain intermediate brotherhood, a kind of passage from nature to grace, through the external calling by which men pass from nature to grace by the power of the calling God. Brothers according to the flesh and species, therefore, nature makes. Brothers according to the Spirit, grace makes, through the internal calling, which is singular in Christ. But brothers in common, according to some participation in grace, external calling makes, which is common to the world and the Church, so that all who pass from the world to the Church may grow together in it with Christ. But since we have spoken of this kind of our brotherhood and its holy duties in the preceding Song, we do not wish to be longer here; let each one only observe in the Prophet's words that this is properly a discussion of that inner brotherhood in Christ, which, being the highest, also embraces those other kinds of just brotherhood. For he who is a brother with us in Christ by this brotherhood is also a brother both by nature and by external calling; since he is called out of nature by the external calling and brought to that inner and fraternal union. Its addition does not destroy those other kinds, but rather perfects them: just as if you add two to a unity, the unity is not taken away but increased; and a little flame is not put out when you bring fire to it.

units.la: Quòd si fraterna coniunctio ex natura tantis viribus est, ut nulla voluntate hominum dissolvi pollit, quin semper fratres iure necessitudinis (quod ne tyranni quidem iuis perfringendi habent, ut sese Dionysius Siculus agnoscebat, leges à se latas, posse; à natura, non posse effringere) confunctiinter se teneantur; si fraternitas ex consociatione humanarū vocationum etiam homines inter se obstrictos tenet, quemadmodum prisci illi & prudentes Romani inter cateros diligentissimè observabant, ut scripta illorum & historiæ docent: certè illam fraternitatem, quæ non ex naturæ, aut humano iure est, sed ex divino instituto, & instituto gratiæ; eam (inquam) longè gratiotis momenti ad obstringendos inter se homines dicamus necesse est.
units.tr: If fraternal fellowship is so strongly grounded in nature that no human will can dissolve it, so that brothers are always bound to one another by the right of kinship (which even tyrants do not have the power to break, as Dionysius of Sicily acknowledged: he could repeal the laws he had enacted, but he could not break the laws of nature), then surely the bond of brotherhood that comes from the common ties of human callings also binds men to one another, as the ancient and wise Romans observed with great care above all other peoples, as their writings and histories show. Certainly we must say that the brotherhood which arises not from nature or human law but from divine institution and the institution of grace is far weightier for binding men to one another.

units.la: Quàpropter satis mirari non possum eorum hominum siue audaciam, siue dementiam, qui tantum hoc ius necessitudinis, Deo auctore, divina virtute, & mediis planè divinis constitutum, tam parvi faciunt, ut alios sibi fratres non esse iudicent; aut etiam, si forte in cōmuni noverint nos alios aliis fratres esse, tamen cùm ad singularia venitur, siue in particulari (ut loquuntur) hunc, illum hominem; hanc, illam Ecclesiam nihil secum habere coniunctionis & fraternitatis existimat. Si à natura esset coniun-ctio, ctio[?], natura evinceret non esse penes ipsos, ut ius naturæ perimant arbitratu suo: Si ex humano instituto esset, testaretur ipsorum cōscientia ius illud communionis non posse dissui; nisi per eos quorum auctoritate conciliatum est. Nam vulgatum est illud dictum, Quibus modis conficitur obligatio, iisdem tolli. Iam vero, Deus bone, quid audio? naturæ obligationem homo non perimit: humanam quoq. necessitudinem abolere priuato aut singulari facto suo unus homo non potest: & necessitudo, quam diuinum institutum gratiæ conciliauit, voluntate hominis dissoluatur? O insaniam miserabilem! quà se abripi quicunque fuit, iam prius se Deo & Christo eripuerit, quàm alterum eripiat cogitatione necesse est. Nam quis odit suam ipsius carnem, quod membrum dat operam strincant[?] do[?] corpori suo? Iam non est de corpore Christi, qui præsecare cogitat membrum Christi. Et tamen hic morbus est (ut ita dicam) epidemicus ætatis nostræ: in qua cognoscendis, ꝗbrandis[?], iudicandis, damnandis, & explodendis fratrum nostrorum factis, & ipsis proteruè exluctorandis, sumus plerique omnes audacissimi. Neque dubitamus homines, Ecclesias, regiones totas & potestates à Deo institutas, quasi pro imperio maledictis & anathematis incessere; quamuis[?] Christum sapiant, quia nobiscum[?] non sapiunt per omnia. Manet, mi frater, manet nostra coniunctio: sed tua est (cuius me miseret) alienatio. natio.Si te alienare à me voles , non potes quin prius alienes à Christo , in quo fratres sumus; ego nec volo,nec possum ; quia fratrem me sibi adiunxit Christus,& fratrem effecit tibi. Si fraternitatem rumpis,deintegro nectam:si dilluis, dabo operam ut resarciam: si euertis , erigam denuò:si negas , affirmat Christus, & ego cum Christo:si audire non vis, audiunt tamen boni, & audit Dominus , coram quo miseret me ex animo impotentiæ tuæ . Misericordia ductus feram quicquid non potero corrigere : sed ferens tamen, hæc duo observabo studiosissimè: Unum , ut constanter expectem à Domino curationem miserandæ istius infirmitatis tuæ:Alterum , ut ipse quoque iustas occasiones observem adiuuandi charitate & surrigendi tui , si forte Deus hac mea opera ad salutem tuam aliquando uti voluerit. Cur enim perturbatos animo, vel in causa religionis ,non feramus æquè ac ferimus eos quos ira , odium , & similis de statu mentis demouerint ? Hæc si inter fratres nascatur,nihilominus fratres sunt, nec esse desinunt. Iniquè ergo fecero, si propterea quòd fratrem te esse negas,aut negas officium fratris, ego in idem vitium incidero . nolo malefacto meo accumulare insipientiam tuâ : sed sapientiæ quicquid accepi à Domino, id integrum conferuare, & ex officio restitutionem tuam procurare, aut certè , si nihil aliud, coram Deo hominibusque testari officium meum.
units.tr: For this reason I cannot sufficiently wonder at the audacity or the madness of those men who hold so lightly this right of kinship, established by God as its author, by divine power, and by means that are wholly divine, that they judge others not to be their brothers. Or even if they know in general that we are brothers to one another, yet when it comes to particulars, to this man or that man, this church or that church, they think they have no fellowship or brotherhood with them. If the fellowship were from nature, nature itself would prove that it is not in their power to destroy the law of nature at their pleasure. If it were from human institution, their own conscience would testify that this law of communion cannot be dissolved except by those by whose authority it was made. For it is a common saying: by the same means by which an obligation is created, it is also removed. But good God, what do I hear? A man does not destroy the obligation of nature; one man cannot by a private or single act abolish even human kinship; and yet the kinship that divine institution of grace has established is to be dissolved by a man's will? O miserable madness! Whoever is carried away in this way must, in thought, have already torn himself away from God and Christ before he tears away another. For who hates his own flesh? Who, by such a member, sets himself against his own body? He is no longer of the body of Christ who thinks of cutting off a member of Christ. And yet this sickness, so to speak, is epidemic in our age, in which nearly all of us are most bold in examining, branding, judging, condemning, and rejecting the deeds of our brothers, and in shouting them down shamelessly. We do not hesitate to assail men, churches, whole regions, and powers instituted by God with curses and anathemas, as if by a sovereign decree, even though they hold to Christ, simply because they do not think with us in all things. My brother, our fellowship remains; it is your estrangement that is at fault, and I pity you for it. If you wish to estrange yourself from me, you cannot do so without first estranging yourself from Christ, in whom we are brothers. I neither wish it nor am able to do it, because Christ has joined me to himself as a brother and has made me a brother to you. If you break the brotherhood, I will bind it up again; if you dissolve it, I will take pains to mend it; if you overthrow it, I will raise it up again; if you deny it, Christ affirms it, and I with Christ. If you will not hear me, still good men hear, and the Lord hears, before whom I pity you from my heart for your weakness. Moved by mercy, I will bear whatever I cannot correct. Yet while bearing it, I will observe two things most diligently: first, that I constantly look to the Lord for the healing of this pitiable weakness of yours; second, that I myself also watch for just occasions to help you with love and to raise you up, should God at some time be willing to use my labour for your salvation. For why should we not bear with those who are disturbed in mind, even in matters of religion, as we bear with those whom anger, hatred, and similar disorders of the mind have moved from their right state? If such disputes arise between brothers, they are nonetheless brothers, and they do not cease to be. It would therefore be wrong of me, if, because you deny that you are my brother or deny the duty of a brother, I should fall into the same fault. I do not wish to add to your folly by my own wrongdoing. Rather, with wisdom, I will keep whole whatever I have received from the Lord, and from duty I will seek your restoration; or at least, if nothing else, I will bear witness before God and men to my own duty.

units.la: Est autem officium hoc ad quod præstandum obstricti sumus, nõ solùm in eo positum, nequid faciamus mali; verumetiam in eo maximè, vt quibuscunque modis possumus, alij aliis benefaciamus in Domino: quod officium in symbolo fidei nostræ innuimus, dicentes nos credere cõmunionem sanctorum. 'Hoc à Propheta (quemadmodum antè perstrinximus) locutione commoda designatur, quòd fratres habitent etiam vnà: aut (si ita placet vertere) confideant. Huius autem communionis, de qua Propheta hoc loco instituit agere, ratio commodissimè quatuor vocibus exponitur: prout quatuor sunt capita ad iustam communionis huius intelligentiam necessaria, nam primùm communio iuris est qua fratres sumus, Patris eiusdem filij. tum communio actionum atque bonorû est,qua habitare dicimur. præterea communio principij & typi diuini est,qua etiam dicimur habitare alij cum aliis, puta vt communionem habemus cum Christo,de qua in Psalmo 132. actum est. Postremò harum rerum omnium modus communis est vnio, quam habemus vnitate spiritus in Christo Iesu. Ac de eo quidem quòd fratres sumus, satis antè dictum : De secundo ergo videamus.
units.tr: Now the duty to which we are bound is not only this, that we do no harm, but above all that, in whatever ways we can, we do good to one another in the Lord. We signify this duty in the creed of our faith when we say that we believe the communion of saints. By the prophet (as we have noted above) this is expressed in a fitting phrase: that brothers dwell together also, or, if one prefers to translate it so, trust one another. The nature of this communion, which the prophet in this passage sets out to describe, is most conveniently expressed in four terms, since there are four heads necessary for a right understanding of this communion. First, there is the communion of right, by which we are brothers, sons of the same Father. Then there is the communion of actions and goods, by which we are said to dwell. Besides, there is the communion of the divine beginning and type, by which we are said to dwell also with one another, that is, because we have communion with Christ, of which we spoke in Psalm 132. Lastly, the common mode of all these things is the union which we have in the unity of the Spirit in Christ Jesus. Concerning the fact that we are brothers, enough has been said above; let us therefore look at the second.

units.la: Sanctorum fratrum actiones in communione ipsorum describuntur habitandi vel confidendi verbo. Naturale studium illud est, vt vulgò dicitur, quòd similes similibus facilè aggregantur: ut contrà qui instituti colunt dissimilitudinem, res suas seorsim habere solent. Praeterea & hoc naturale est, ut quibus est conuenientia in vitae genere, illi etiam in occupationibus & actionibus suis eandem cōuenientiam seruent. Tum hoc quoque à natura est, ut qui actionibus vitae communicaturi sunt, ij bonis & commodis quae ad actiones sunt opus, etiam communicent. Deniq. ut hi cōspirant animis, ita opere collaborant. Sicubi autem haec ratio animaduertitur, id potest fieri in iis qui communi domicilio, communi patrefamilias, & communi instituto viuunt: idque maximè in iis qui fratres sunt, prout hoc loco appellamur. Et certè communis est nobis omnibus Pater, Deus: communis habitatio, Ecclesia Dei, quae eadem est habitatio summi illius patrisfamilias, à quo omnis agnatio (ut Apostolus inquit) nominatur in caelo & terra: institutum à patrefamilias vnum esse & typo & modo, nemo, qui quidem Christianus sit, potest ignorare, cùm vnum caput, spiritumq. vnū dederit suis, ut qui se vnum sunt, nō dubitent communicare inter se habitatione. Quòd si quis Hebraea vocem interpretari malit confidendi verbo, id eò amplius doctrinam illa confirmaturũ est quam modò attulimus. Nā demõstratur hoc verbo tranquilla & sedata Christianorũ communi habitatione vtentium ratio: quòd non clamoribus, aut contentionibus, non pugnis aut caedibus, non animorum motum præcipite vehemétia; sed cómoda quadám & cōpofita ratione vitæ res suas instituant coram Domino. Compositus est Christianorum[?] animus,mentes compositæ: ex quibus studia,sermones, conatus, actiones eiusdem modi informantur. Qui secus faciunt, ij eadem opera,patris familias à quo fumus , capitis ex quo fumus, spiritus per quē fumus, & Ecclesiæ habitationis communis nostræ, in qua fumus,rationem videntur negligere.Hæc autem si negligunt, quam rationem habere sui ipsorum dicendi sunt?
units.tr: The actions of the holy brothers in their communion are described by the word dwelling or trusting. It is a natural tendency, as is commonly said, that like easily gathers with like, whereas those who deliberately cultivate dissimilarity usually keep their affairs apart. Moreover, it is also natural that those who share a way of life should keep the same agreement in their occupations and activities. Again, it is from nature that those who are to share in the activities of life should also share the goods and advantages that the activities require. Finally, just as they agree in their minds, so they work together in their deeds. Wherever this principle is observed, it can happen among those who live in a common dwelling, under a common head of the household, and under a common rule, and especially among those who are brothers, as we are called in this passage. And certainly God the Father is common to us all; the Church of God is our common dwelling, which is the house of that supreme Householder, from whom every family (as the Apostle says) is named in heaven and on earth. No one who is truly a Christian can be ignorant that the rule of the Householder is one both in type and in manner, since he has given his own one Head and one Spirit, so that those who are one do not hesitate to share their dwelling with one another. But if anyone prefers to render the Hebrew word by the verb to trust, that will confirm the teaching we have just brought forward all the more. For by this word is shown the calm and settled manner of Christians dwelling together: that they order their affairs before the Lord not with clamours or strife, not with fights or slaughter, not with the headlong violence of passions, but in a fitting and orderly manner of life. The mind of Christians is composed, their thoughts are ordered, and from these come studies, speech, endeavours, and actions of the same kind. Those who act otherwise seem, by that very fact, to neglect the rule of the Householder from whom we come, of the Head from whom we come, of the Spirit through whom we come, and of the common dwelling of the Church in which we are. But if they neglect these, what account of themselves can they be said to have?

units.la: Atque hæ quidem actiones si iudicio nostro aut viribus à nobis instituendæ essent, pessimè sanè nobiscum ageretur: cùm neque certa earum rudimenta informata in nostris mentibus habeamus, neque facultatem vel ea ipsa præstandi quæ nos docet lux naturalis conscientiæ.
units.tr: Indeed, if these actions were to be undertaken by our own judgment or strength, things would go very badly for us, since we have neither certain rudiments of them formed in our minds, nor the ability to perform even those things which the light of natural conscience teaches us.

units.la: Quamobrem tertium illud in hac sanctissima communione nobis erat pernecessarium: nempe ut principium certum, ac immutabile, & typum operum nostrorum Dominus exhiberet; Principium, ut viribus illius ageremur: typum, ut ad exemplum imitationemque illius ageremus. Utrumque, in Ecclesia nobis iniùs & foris suppeditauit Deus, cùm & formam illam internam, quam Psalmo antecedente dicebamus, indidit Ecclesiæ suæ; & formam externam verbi scripti atque prædicati, iustumque ordinem, qui ad constitutionem Ecclesiæ opus est, commisit suis. Ad hæc duo præstantissima Dei beneficia respiciebat Psaltes, cùm diceret etiam de fratribus habitantibus vnà, & communionem suam colentibus. Etenim vox ista, Etiam, ad Psalmum 132. qui proximè præcedit ordinem in libro Psalmorum, referenda est. Expofuerat enim Psaltes Cantico illo singulari excellentissimoque constitutionem Ecclesiæ Dei, qua spectat cum Dominum; & de communione sanctorum, quam cum Deo habent coluntáque animo & facto, dixerat copiosè. Cùm autem communionis ad sanctos pertinentis duplex sit ratio: Vna, qua omnes cum Deo; altera, qua omnes cum fratribus suis inter se communicant: placuerat Propheta de vtroque communionis genere duobus Psalmis continentibus res prædicare summè excellentes. Postquã igitur vim communionis cum Deo explicauit, & rationem totius Ecclesiæ, velut à Deo pendentis relatione perpetua: nunc demum definit hac voce Etiam, se hic sermonem de altera communionis sanctorum parte instituere, qua alij cum aliis vt fratres communicant: idque non suo iudicio (nam sola doctrina Dei Ecclesiam informat, & singula membra eius) non suis viribus (nam Deus est, qui solus facit omnia in omnibus) sed ex sola doctrina & virtute Dei, vt qui solus in Christo sit principium Ecclesiæ & typus absolutissimus. Ab hoc igitur principio & virtute hac diuina in Ecclesia Dei exposita, intus Spi-ritu, ritu, foris ordine sacri ministerij, utrobique falutis verbo: Iam concludit Propheta, quicunque spiritus illius, & ordinis, & verbi participes sunt beneficio Dei[?], eos etiam sic habitare, id est, in unitate spiritus, ordinis, & verbi salutaris sese huic principio & huic typo virtute diuina conformare, ut omnes simul habitent, quemadmodum à Deo uno in unitate spiritus, uno communi ordine, & una salutis doctrina vocati sunt. tanquam si diceret, se de iis demum loqui in hoc loco, qui sunt conscij apud se communis & singularis gratiæ à Deo acceptæ & in Ecclesia expositæ, qui etiam in seipsis hoc principiū sentiunt, hunc typum ante oculos habent, qui toti deniq. etiam feruntur eò unde hoc bonum acceperunt, & porrò accepturi sunt confirmationem illius atque complementum.
units.tr: Therefore that third thing was absolutely necessary to us in this most holy communion: namely, that the Lord should present a certain and unchanging principle and a type of our works. A principle, so that we might be moved by his power; a type, so that we might act after his example and imitation. God has supplied both to us in the Church, inwardly and outwardly: he has implanted in his Church that inner form which we spoke of in the preceding psalm, and he has committed to his own people the outer form of the written and preached Word, and the right order which is needed for the constitution of the Church. The Psalmist had these two most excellent benefits of God in view when he said also of brothers who dwell together and cultivate their communion. For this word also must be referred to Psalm 132, which immediately precedes it in the order of the Psalter. In that singular and most excellent song the Psalmist had set out the constitution of God's Church as it looks to the Lord, and had spoken at length about the communion of the saints which they have with God, cultivated in mind and deed. Since, however, the communion pertaining to the saints is twofold in its nature (one by which all have communion with God, the other by which all share with one another as brothers), the Prophet had chosen to set forth most excellent matters about each kind of communion in two psalms. Therefore, having explained the force of communion with God, and the nature of the whole Church as depending perpetually on God, he now at last marks, by this word Etiam, that he is going to speak here of the other part of the communion of the saints, by which they share with one another as brothers. He does this not by their own judgment (for God's teaching alone forms the Church and its individual members), nor by their own powers (for it is God who alone works all things in all), but from the teaching and power of God alone, since in Christ alone is the principle of the Church and its most perfect type. Therefore, with this principle and this divine power set forth in the Church of God (inwardly by the Spirit, outwardly by the order of the sacred ministry, and in both by the word of salvation), the Prophet now concludes that whoever share in that Spirit, that order and that word by the benefit of God, these also dwell in this way: that is, in the unity of the Spirit, of the order and of the saving word, they conform themselves by divine power to this principle and this type, so that they all dwell together, just as they were called by one God, in the unity of one Spirit, one common order and one doctrine of salvation. It is as if he were saying that in this place he speaks of those who are conscious within themselves of a common and singular grace received from God and set forth in the Church, who also feel this principle in themselves, keep this type before their eyes, and who are at last carried wholly to that source from which they received this good, and who are yet to receive its confirmation and completion.

units.la: Utinam vero quotquot Christiani audire volumus, in eo laboraremus studiosè, & prout didicimus Christum, ita in ipso ambularemus[?], ut verbis utamur Apostoli. Nam Christiani sumus principio illo in nobis habitante, id est, Domino Iesu Christo, per communicationem Spiritus: sed isti principio plerique omnes non secus renunciamus, quàm qui sibi ipsi violentam consciscit mortem, & adimit corpori suo principium vitæ suæ. Christiani sumus typo: sed veritatem ipsam typi plerique oppugnamus, & euertimus in nobis vitiositate nostra, viarumque nostrarum deprauatione. Principium tenemus, & fugimus: typum videmus, & delemus. hoc scilicet Christianorum est. Si ergo Christiani sumus, & communionem illam habemus cum Deo, etiam atque etiam Christiani simus cum fratribus nostris necesse est, colamusque cum eis communionem verè Christianam, quæ nobis hoc loco imperata est.
units.tr: Would that all of us who wish to be called Christians would labour earnestly at this, and, as we have learned Christ, so walk in him, to use the words of the Apostle. For we are Christians through that principle dwelling in us, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, through the communication of the Spirit; yet most people renounce that principle no differently than one who violently takes his own life and deprives his body of the principle of its life. We are Christians by the type; yet most of us oppose the very truth of the type, and overturn it in ourselves by our vice and the corruption of our ways. We hold on to the principle and flee from it; we see the type and destroy it. This, of course, is what Christians do! If therefore we are Christians, and have that communion with God, we must necessarily be Christians also with our brothers, and cultivate with them that truly Christian communion which is enjoined on us in this place.

units.la: Quòd si rerum istarum communionem inter nos instituit Deus; quis adeò demens est, vt non continuò videat modi quoque ad has res pertinentis communionem esse oportere? Hunc autem modum exponit Psaltes, cùm de fratrum habitatione vnà vel pariter instituenda loquitur. Nam qui vnum sunt in Christo, qui vno iure apud Patrem, qui vno principio viuunt, qui ad eundem typum imitandum & eundem finem prehendendum vocati sunt, nō seorsim quidem singuli, sed vnà coiuncti virtute Dei;hi[?] profectò non possunt nō sentire[?] necessitatem coagmentationis suæ, & rebus omnibus inter se communicare, vt optatissimum illum finem ad quem vocati sunt, per gratiam assequantur. Vnum est corpus (inquit Apostolus) & vnus spiritus: sicut & vocati estis in vnam spem vocationis vestræ. vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma, vnus Deus & pater omnium, qui est super omnes, & per omnes, & in omnibus vobis: His denique omnibus vnum commune domicilium & vna statio, Ecclesia Dei; in qua nos versari necesse est, & conuersari prout decet vocationem nostram, primùm Deo seruientes, deinde verò alios aliis secundùm Deum: & vbi singulari ac communi opera, separata & coniuncta, ad vnum illum finem supernæ vocationis, tanquam vnius domini seruos, & domesticos vnius domus, oportet contendere.
units.tr: If God has established these things as a communion among us, who is so mad as not to see at once that the manner of this communion, too, pertaining to these things, ought to be right? The Psalmist sets out this manner when he speaks of brothers dwelling together, or side by side. For those who are one in Christ, who live under one right before the Father, by one principle, who are called to imitate the same type and to lay hold of the same end, not indeed each alone but joined together by the power of God, these surely cannot but feel the necessity of their fellowship, and share all things with one another, so that by grace they may attain that most desired end to which they are called. There is one body, says the Apostle, and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all. To all these there is finally one common dwelling and one station, the Church of God, in which we must dwell and conduct ourselves as befits our calling: serving God first, and then one another according to God. And there, with singular and common effort, separated and joined, we must strive toward that one end of the heavenly calling, as servants of one Lord and members of one household.

units.la: Quid? quòd non solùm vnitas, sed etiam in hac vnitate nostra membrorum & actionum omnium proportio eadem voce imperatur? Ex qua id sequitur boni, quòd neq. à se ipso quisquam diuersus sit in via Domini, neque à suis fratribus, neque à Domino; sed constanter & totus Domino suo fratribusque suis adhæreat, & sequatur Dominum cum fratrum corona religiosissimè. Sed de hac re in Psalmum antecedentem iam satis diximus. Deus ille, qui dat velle & perficere pro bona voluntate sua, gratiosè admoueat paternam manum, vt per eam toto corpore, animo, & mente sanctificemur, & huic officio incumbamus communionis nostræ in timore ipsius.
units.tr: Moreover, is it not only unity but also, within this unity of ours, the proportion of all members and actions that is commanded by the same word? From this follows the good that no one turns aside from himself in the way of the Lord, nor from his brothers, nor from the Lord; but he clings constantly and wholly to his Lord and to his brothers, and follows the Lord most devoutly in the company of the brothers. But we have already said enough about this matter on the preceding psalm. May that God, who gives both the will and the performance according to his good pleasure, graciously guide his fatherly hand, so that through it we may be sanctified in body, soul and mind, and may apply ourselves to this duty of our communion in his fear.

units.la: Postquam verò quænam hæc communio fit audiuimus; tempus est vt ex Dauide cognoscamus quid de ea prædicari possit. Hanc igitur communionē duobus nominibus Psaltes concelebrauit, dicens: Bonum & amœnum esse hanc communionem cœli. Duplex gratia in communione sanctorum proponitur, bonitatis & amœnitatis, vel iucunditatis summæ. hæc autè duo non temerè à Propheta fuerunt posita, sed accommodatè ad naturam & captum hominis. Omnes enim à natura hæc duo expetunt, quod bonum est, & quod iucundum. Sic bonum expetimus vt voluptate coniunctū velimus esse: etiam à medicamento quamuis salubèrrimo[?], si austerum est, abhorremus. Sed bonum & iucundum vulgo cùm dicitur, quamplurimi errores mentibus humanis solent obrepere. Nam bonum aut commune est aut particulare, præterea aut animi aut corporis, tum aut morale in actione positum aut naturale solùm in sensu & contemplatione, postremò aut æternæ illius vitæ aut huius peritura; quorum prius supernaturale atque diuinum est, in spiritu hoc naturale & humanū, in carne & sensu positum. Quid hîc homines faciant iudicij? Certè qui minimè omnium vtuntur ratione, bonum particulare communi, corporale spirituali, naturale & sensuale (vt ita dicam) morali, præsens futuro anteponunt: quia plurimum sensui vt pecudes, rationi perparum, auctoritati Dei in verbo reuelatæ nihil omninò tribuunt. Qui verò calamo rationis solius freti sibi videtur sapere, ij in suis ratiocinationibus euanescentes vmbram boni pro bono amplexantur; & tamen quia sese plurimum cum illis inferioribus comparant, apprimè omnium sibi videntur sapere. Ac proinde neque hi, neque illi vnquam possunt cernere quid bonum & iucundum ex veritate sit.
units.tr: Now that we have heard what this communion is, it is time to learn from David what may be declared about it. The Psalmist therefore celebrates this communion with two names, saying that it is good and pleasant. A twofold grace is set forth in the communion of the saints: that of goodness and that of pleasantness, or supreme delight. The Prophet did not put these two down at random, but suited them to the nature and understanding of man. For all men by nature desire these two things: what is good and what is pleasant. Thus we desire the good in such a way that we want it joined with pleasure; even a medicine, however wholesome, if it is bitter, we shrink from. But when "good" and "pleasant" are spoken of in common usage, very many errors are wont to creep into human minds. For the good is either common or particular, and besides either of the soul or of the body; then either moral, lying in action, or natural, only in sense and contemplation; and lastly either of that eternal life or of this perishable one. Of these, the former is supernatural and divine, lying in the Spirit; the latter natural and human, lying in the flesh and sense. What judgment do men make here? Certainly those who least of all use reason prefer the particular good to the common, the bodily to the spiritual, the natural and sensual (as I may say) to the moral, and the present to the future, because they yield very much to sense like beasts, very little to reason, and nothing at all to the authority of God revealed in the Word. But those who trust in the pen of reason alone and seem to themselves to be wise, these, vanishing in their own reasonings, embrace the shadow of good for good; and yet, because they compare themselves very much with those lower things, they seem to themselves most wise of all. And therefore neither these nor those can ever discern what the good and the pleasant truly are.

units.la: Bonum verò & iucundum, quod quidem verè bonum atque iucundum est, illud appellamus, quod vnam habet constantem veramque symmetriam siue commensum & commoditatem boni: ita vt nec particulare de communi, nec particulare aut commune de vniuersali derogent, nec corporale spiritali impedimentum afferat, nec sensile aut naturale morali obsit, nec denique præsens & caducum futuro æternoque aduersetur; sed inferiora superioribus, omnia summo & vniuersali bono suo ordine & loco inseruiant. Hic demum verè bonum esse & iucundum affirmamus, vbi hæc constitutio rerum animaduertitur.
units.tr: Good and pleasant, in the true sense of the words, is that which has one constant and true symmetry, or proportion, and convenience of good: so that the particular does not detract from the common, nor the particular or the common from the universal; the bodily does not hinder the spiritual; the sensible or natural does not harm the moral; and, finally, the present and perishable does not oppose the future and eternal. Instead, lower things serve higher, and all things serve the highest and universal good in their proper order and place. We affirm that a thing is truly good and pleasant when this arrangement of things is observed.

units.la: Hanc constitutionem, saltem prout in rebus humanis præstari potest, siquis in familia cerneret, incredibiles sui amores excitaret; si in ciuitate, eo gratia amplior, quia commune illud præstat domestico: si in regione, si in mundo denique vniuerso (qui tamen hanc refugit malitia sua) præclarissimè nobiscum ageretur. Sed quod in vniuerso mundo, in regione mundi, in ciuitate, in domo vlla deprehendi non potest, illud totum adeoque amplius in Ecclesia nobis exhibetur beneficio Dei. Nam etsi hoc bonum voluptatemque hanc mundus non videt, nec videt caro aut oculus carnis; vident tamen quicunque oculos habent cordis à Deo illuminatos atque expurgatos, id est, quicunq; in Ecclesia sunt, & in ea adhærent Christo viventi in ipsis atque ambulanti. Hoc illud est quod sibi Propheta voluit, cùm nobis exponeret hanc rem demum bonam & iucundam esse, quòd fratres habitent etiam vel confideant unà.
units.tr: If anyone could see this arrangement, at least as far as it can be achieved in human affairs, within a family, it would arouse incredible affection; within a city, it would be all the more gracious, because the common good surpasses the domestic; and in a region, or finally in the whole world (which nevertheless, by its own malice, shuns this arrangement), we would be dealt with most excellently. But what cannot be found in the whole world, in a region of the world, in a city, or in any house, all this and more is shown to us in the Church by the benefit of God. For although the world does not see this good and this pleasure, and the flesh or the eye of the flesh does not see them, yet all who have eyes of the heart, enlightened and cleansed by God, see them; that is, all who are in the Church and cling in it to Christ living and walking in them. This is what the Prophet meant when he set out to us that this thing is at last good and pleasant, namely that brothers dwell, or even sit together in unity.

units.la: Atque hoc quidem bonum, quamuis diuinitus bonum, & iucundum etiam diuinitus, tamen oculus non videt, auris non audit, homo denique nec palpare manu, nec gustare, nec odorari illud potest, nec sentire vllo pacto viribus naturæ suæ. Sed nō propterea bonū esse desinit, si bonum esse non videtur iis qui bonitatem hanc iucunditatemque non possunt percipere. Nec coloribus, nec sonis, nec odoramentis, nec suauitate rerum, nec tactu afficiuntur mortui, quia mortui sunt, id est, inepti percipiendis rebus quas modò diximus. Odoramentum est odoramentum, etsi in nares pituita obstructas inciderit. Ignis non propterea desinit ignis esse, si ea non vflerit quæ non sunt prædita potentiâ (vt vocant) passiuâ vt igne comburantur. Res omnes tum demum recte agunt actiones suas, rectèq; percipiuntur, cùm ad obiecta cōmoda & conuenientia ipsarum actionibusque peruenerint. Quid tum igitur, si mundus non novit istam bonitatem & iucunditatem, istos fructus Ecclesiæ? Quid tum, si ne Ecclesiam quidem nouerit? Ineptus est his rebus percipiendis. Vitam Ecclesiæ non videt mortuus, odoramentum non sentit frigefactus, ignem Dei in Ecclesia nō sentit lapis. Sed ij demum sentiunt quos Propheta hoc loco vocat & excitat, dicens, ecce, quàm bonum &c. Communiter quidem hoc dicit, sed non omnes in communi audiunt: Ii solùm audiunt, quibus hanc doctrinam in manus tradi, & in animo inscribi voluit Dominus. Quapropter ad pios, qui mysterij huius vere capaces sunt, excitandos duobus argumentis pungit coscientias nostras, cùm propositionem suam exornans atque amplificans, & subiectione utitur, & admiratione vehementissima. Subiectionem dico, qua singulos nostrûm, quasi in rem præsentem vocat, inquiens; Ecce: admirationem verò, qua sibi ipse nō satisfaciens in exponenda amplitudine boni & iucunditatis istius, omnes simul rapit in contemplationem illius, dicendo, quàm bonū & quàm iucundum! perinde enim est atque si diceret, nec ego satis ex officio nosse aut prædicare illud possum, neque nostrûm quisquam, ac ne cuncti quidem, si vires nostras unà coniungamus: sed unica admiratio meo & communi nomine, quod dicturus essem si possem, demonstratura est. silentio meo, quod mihi amplitudo rei ipsius efficit, nolo iniquus esse in gratiam Dei; sed profiteri saltem admirando tenuitatem ieiunitatemq. sermonis mei in rerum tantarum cogitatione.
units.tr: This good, though it is divinely good, and pleasant also divinely, nevertheless the eye does not see it, the ear does not hear it, and man cannot touch it with his hand, taste it, smell it, or perceive it in any way by the powers of his nature. Yet it does not cease to be good because it does not seem good to those who cannot perceive this goodness and pleasantness. The dead are not moved by colours, sounds, odours, the sweetness of things, or touch, because they are dead, that is, unfit to perceive the things just mentioned. A smell is still a smell, even if it falls on nostrils blocked by phlegm. Fire does not cease to be fire if it does not burn things that are not endowed with what they call passive power, so that they may be burned by fire. All things then act their actions rightly, and are rightly perceived, when they reach suitable and fitting objects for their actions. What then, if the world does not know that goodness and pleasantness, those fruits of the Church? What then, if it does not even know the Church? It is unfit to perceive these things. A dead man does not see the life of the Church, a frozen man does not sense the fragrance, and a stone does not feel the fire of God in the Church. But those whom the Prophet calls and stirs up in this place, saying, Behold, how good, etc., are the ones who perceive it. He speaks in general, but not all hear in general: only those to whom the Lord wished this teaching to be handed over and written on the mind hear it. Therefore, in order to rouse the godly, who are truly capable of this mystery, he pricks our consciences with two arguments, using both an address and a most vehement exclamation while he adorns and enlarges his statement. I mean the address, by which he calls each of us as if to a matter present before us, saying, Behold. The exclamation, by which, not satisfied with himself in setting out the greatness of this good and pleasantness, he carries all of us together into contemplation of it, saying, How good and how pleasant! It is just as if he said: I cannot, as my duty requires, know or proclaim it sufficiently, nor can any of us, nor indeed all of us, even if we join our strengths together; but a single exclamation, in my name and in the name of all, will show what I would have said if I could. I do not wish, out of my silence, which the greatness of the thing itself causes in me, to be unfair to the grace of God; rather, I wish at least to profess, by my wonder, the poverty and meagreness of my speech in the thought of such great things.

units.la: Hæc illa insignis est prædicatio, ad quam nos omnes qui Christiani sumus, opus est excitari, in quam opus introspicere, cuius bonitatem & amœnitatem, suavitatemque incredibilem explorare, plorare,quam exploratam admirari & cum admiratione apud omnes pios coram Domino indefinenter testatam facere, quandoquidem (vt ait Apostolus) sic nota fit per Ecclesiæ imperiis ac potestatibus, etiam quæ in cælis sunt, multiformis illa sapientia Dei secundùm propositum æternum, quod constituit in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. Quæ cùm ita sint, primùm omnium Deum oro & patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, nos omnes, quos spiritali vocatione ad fraternam cõiunctionem in Christo primogenito inter multos fratres honorauit, regat Spiritu charitatis & pacis: vt quemadmodum dignatur habitare in nobis, ita nos in ipso etiam habitare vnà studeamus in vnitate corporis & Spiritus sui, & singuli magis ac magis sentiamus, experiamurqué, quàm bonum & quàm iucundum sit sanctissimam illam vnionem, cuius ipse auctor est, conseruare. Deinde verò hortor & oro pios omnes per Christum, & quicunque studio vitæ æternæ suæ gloriæqué diuinæ affecti sunt, tandem aliquando discant, extra hanc communionem recognoscere quàm mala & ingrata omnia: vt hac ratione gloriam cedentes Domino, & ab omni distractione discidicioq.[?] in sanctimonia, pace, modestia, & lenitate spiritus abstinentes; dent operâ diligentissimè optimis & iucundissimis cómunionis huius officiis,quæ Deus hîc & in futuro sæculo, certissimo verissimoq. bono & iucunditate muñeraturus est in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: This is that outstanding proclamation to which all of us who are Christians must be stirred up, into which we must look, whose goodness, delight and incredible sweetness we must explore, having explored it to marvel at it, and with wonder to bear constant witness before all the godly in the presence of the Lord. For, as the Apostle says, through the Church the manifold wisdom of God is made known to the rulers and powers, even those in the heavens, according to the eternal purpose which he established in Christ Jesus our Lord. Since these things are so, first of all I pray to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he, who by spiritual calling has honoured us all to fraternal fellowship in Christ, the firstborn among many brothers, may rule us by the Spirit of love and peace; so that, as he deigns to dwell in us, so we also may study to dwell together in him, in the unity of his body and Spirit, and that each of us may more and more feel and experience how good and how pleasant it is to preserve that most holy union, of which he himself is the author. Then, moreover, I exhort and pray all the godly, through Christ, and whoever is moved by zeal for his eternal life and divine glory, to learn at last to recognise how evil and ungrateful everything is outside this communion; so that, in this way, giving glory to the Lord, and abstaining from all distraction and division, in holiness, peace, modesty and gentleness of spirit, they may apply themselves most diligently to the best and most pleasant duties of this communion, which God, here and in the future age, will reward in Christ Jesus with the most certain and true good and delight.

units.la: 2. Est vt vnguentum illud optimum, superfusum capiti, descendens super barbam, barbam Aharonis; quod descendit ad oram[?] vsque vestimentorum eius.
units.tr: 2. It is like the precious ointment poured on the head, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which runs down to the edge of his garments.

units.la: Etsi verissimum axioma illud est quod antè Propheta enunciauit, de bonitate & amœnitate pacis in communione sanctorum: tamen partim nostra infirmitate & impedimentis aliunde obuenientibus, partimque rei maiestate detinemur, ne veritatem istius enunciati ex officio cognoscamus, nisi Dei Spiritus per administros suos ad tenuitatem nostram sese demiserit. Propterea Psaltes ædificationi publicæ confulturus, deinceps duobus versibus instituit enarratione breuem propositionis illius quam modò diximus: vt & rei veritatem ampliùs videamus, & ab ea quoque afficiamur vehementiùs ad quærendā gloriam Dei & salutem nostram.
units.tr: Although that most true axiom, which the Prophet earlier stated, concerning the goodness and sweetness of peace in the communion of the saints, is indeed true, nevertheless, partly by our weakness and by hindrances arising from elsewhere, and partly by the majesty of the matter, we are held back from knowing the truth of that statement from our duty, unless the Spirit of God, through his ministers, stoops down to our lowliness. Therefore the Psalmist, intending to serve public edification, next sets out in two verses a brief explanation of that proposition which we have just mentioned, so that we may see more fully the truth of the matter, and be moved more strongly by it to seek the glory of God and our own salvation.

units.la: Est autem huius expositionis modus à Propheta institutus duplex: Nam primùm similibus ad declarationem illius enunciati communibus modis vtitur; deinde verò rem simpliciter, prout in se est, apodeictice enuntiat, à causa efficiente supernaturali, necessaria, liberrima, ac non impedita, quæ ex se indesinenter præstat enunciati huius veritatem. Hunc ordinem in ratione docendi conuenientissimum esse natura ipsa ostendit: & Christus non obscurè cùm locis quamplurimis exemplisque frequentibus, cum disertis verbis confirmauit, cùm Nicodemum alloqueretur, dicendo: Si terrena dico vobis & non creditis, quo modo, si dixero vobis cœlestia, credetis? Hæc eloquentia quædam est, ait Augustinus, doctrinæ salutaris, mouendo affectui discentium accommodata, à visibilibus ad inuisibilia, à corporalibus ad spiritalia, à temporalibus ad æterna. Nam ipse animæ motus, quamdiu rebus adhuc terrenis implicatur, pigriùs inflammatur: si verò feratur ad similitudines corporales, & inde ad spiritalia quæ illis similitudinibus figurantur, ipso quasi transitu vegetatur, & tanquam in facula ignis agitatus, accenditur, & ardentiore dilectione rapitur ad quietem suam cognita veritate. Hoc igitur confilio propositionem antegressam Psaltes, primùm quidem similibus illustrauit, deinde verò necessaria demonstratione cōfirmauit. E quibus similia versu secundo & parte tertij, demonstratio verò reliquo versu tertio proponuntur.
units.tr: The method of this exposition, set out by the Prophet, is twofold. For first he uses similes common to illustrate that statement, in ordinary ways; then he states the matter plainly, as it is in itself, demonstratively, from a supernatural, necessary, most free and unhindered efficient cause, which of itself constantly brings about the truth of this statement. Nature itself shows that this order is most suitable in the method of teaching; and Christ, not obscurely but with very many places and frequent examples, and with plain words, confirmed it when he addressed Nicodemus, saying: If I tell you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? This is a certain eloquence of saving doctrine, says Augustine, adapted to move the affection of learners, from the visible to the invisible, from the bodily to the spiritual, from the temporal to the eternal. For the very motion of the soul, as long as it is still entangled with earthly things, is kindled more sluggishly; but if it is carried to bodily likenesses, and from them to spiritual things which those likenesses represent, it is quickened by that very passage, and, as fire stirred in a torch, it is kindled, and is carried with a more ardent love to its rest once the truth is known. With this purpose, therefore, the Psalmist first illustrated the preceding proposition with likenesses, and then confirmed it with a necessary demonstration. Of these, the likenesses are set out in the second verse and part of the third, and the demonstration in the rest of the third verse.

units.la: Cùm autem propositionis illius duo membra habeantur ad communionem sanctorum spectantia: quorum vnum est communionem illam bonam esse; alterum, etiam iucundam esse: vtrumque membrum suæ propositionis illustrare similitudine. Itaque duo similia certo consilio huc fuerunt allata: vnum, quo bonum communionis illius; alterum, quo iucunditas & suauitas eiusdem subiiceretur quodammodo in oculis omnium. Verumtamen, quod in more apud Hebraeos pofitum est, & vetuftiflimi quique auctores granifsimique [?] ad commoditatem iuuandae memoriae obferuarunt, duarum partium illarum expofitionem adhibet similibus ὕστερον πρότερον [?], primùm de amœnitate & suauitate communionis dicendo per similitudinem illius olei siue unguenti unctionis (vt in Lege appellatur) cuius confecturam Moses ex praecepto Dei prisca Ecclesiam docuerat Exodi 30. Deinde verò de bonitate communionis illius, assumpta pluuiae & roris caelestis similitudine.
units.tr: Since the proposition has two parts concerning the communion of saints, one that this communion is good and the other that it is also pleasant, each part is illustrated by its own comparison. Two similes were therefore deliberately brought in: one to show the goodness of that communion, and the other to set its sweetness and pleasantness, as it were, before everyone's eyes. However, as is customary among the Hebrews, and as the most ancient and weighty authors have observed to aid the memory, the Psalmist treats the two parts in reverse order (hysteron proteron [ὕστερον πρότερον]). He first speaks of the charm and sweetness of communion through the simile of that oil or ointment of anointing (as the Law calls it), whose preparation Moses had taught the ancient Church by God's command, Exodus 30. Then he speaks of the goodness of that communion, taking up the simile of the rain and the heavenly dew.

units.la: Potuerat quidem Spiritus Dei ad hoc argumentum alias probationes & illustrationes quoque adhibere; siue exemplis aliunde petitis, siue rationibus ex natura ductis, quae apud auctores ferme innumeros de bono pacis frequentatae sunt. Praeterea ex iis bonis quae de humana pace praedicantur, poterat secundum quandam analogiam, quae à temporalibus ad aeterna obseruatur plurimum, excellentiam fructuum ex diuina illa Ecclesiae pace nascentium ostendere. Sed commodius visum est Prophetae, ex re praesente (vt ita dicamus) similitudines assumere ad argumenti huius declarationem, quàm longè eas arcessere: & prout in prisca Ecclesia Iudaeorum agebat, ita rebus quae ante oculos vel minimi cuiusque versabantur in Ecclesia illa, vti commodissimè ad illustratio-nem nem bonorum quæ Deus in Ecclesiam confert colentem pacis.
units.tr: The Spirit of God could indeed have used other proofs and illustrations for this subject, either examples drawn from elsewhere or arguments from nature, which have been repeated by almost countless authors on the good of peace. Moreover, from the goods that are proclaimed of human peace, he could, by that analogy from temporal to eternal things which is so often observed, have shown the excellence of the fruits springing from that divine peace of the Church. But it seemed more fitting to the Prophet to take his similes from what is present to the matter (as we might say), rather than to fetch them from afar. Just as the ancient Jewish Church did, so he used things that lay before the eyes of even the humblest member of that Church, as most suitable for illustrating the goods God confers on the Church that cultivates peace.

units.la: Horum autem similium duo sunt genera: prius enim Ecclesiæ illius singulare est, sumptum ab instituto diuinæ gratiæ; posterius commune est, à naturæ ordine: vt hac ratione omnes pij sentiant, & videant etiam ignorantes Dei, quæ bona sint expectanda à Domino, si homines pacem coluerint: cùm & per gratiam Deus testatam fecerit voluntatem suam Ecclesiæ suæ, & per naturam aliqué voluntatis istius sensum omnibus sit impertitus. Prius simile ab instituto Dei & obseruatione ecclesiastica sumptum, continetur secundo versu, in quo Propheta amœnitatem illius communionis sanctorum comparat unguento illi præstantissimo atque suauissimo, quo summus sacerdos olim ex lege delibutus est: posterius in parte priore versus 3.
units.tr: There are two kinds of these similes. The first is peculiar to that Church, taken from the institution of divine grace; the second is common, taken from the order of nature. By this means all the godly may perceive, and even those ignorant of God may see, what good things are to be expected from the Lord if men cultivate peace, since God has both testified his will to his Church through grace and imparted some sense of that will to all through nature. The first simile, taken from God's institution and ecclesiastical observance, is contained in the second verse, where the Prophet compares the sweetness of the communion of saints to that most excellent and most fragrant ointment with which the high priest was anointed under the Law. The second is in the first part of verse 3.

units.la: In priore autem simili hic ordo tenendus est, vt primùm intelligamus partes illius, deinde verò accommodationem illarum partium ad hoc argumentum quod agitur. In simili tria distinctè obseruantur: primùm, quid sit quod habet cum illa amœnitate spiritali similitudinem analogicè: Secundò, quis sit ad quem res illa perueniebat instituto Dei; Tertiò, qui vsus & modus istarum rerum ex præscripto Dei. Quid sit, Propheta explicat dicens de vnguento vel oleo optimo, præstantissimoque: ad quem pertineat, exponit iniecto Aharonis nomine & partium illius. Qui usus & modus, demonstrat, cùm superfundi narrat atque descendere.
units.tr: In the first simile the order to be followed is this: first we understand its parts, and then the application of those parts to the matter in hand. Three things are distinctly observed in the simile: first, what it is that has an analogical likeness to that spiritual sweetness; second, to whom that thing was brought by God's institution; third, the use and manner of those things according to God's prescription. What it is, the Prophet explains by saying "of the ointment or oil, the best and most excellent." To whom it pertains, he sets out by introducing the name of Aaron and its parts. The use and manner he shows when he tells of its being poured out and running down.

units.la: De unguento non est cur dicamus multis: tum quia satis expressit Moses quae fuerit illius ratio, tum quia nostris temporibus, vel potius temporum plenitudini non expedit, ut de ea re magnopere laboremus: neque vero est huius instituti.
units.tr: There is no reason for us to say much about the ointment: partly because Moses has expressed well enough what its composition was, and partly because in our times, or rather in the fullness of time, it is not expedient for us to labour greatly over that matter. Nor is it part of this undertaking.

units.la: De persona cui hoc unguentum adhibebatur, ex verbis Prophetae constat: qui non Leui-tam quenquam simpliciter, non sacerdotem, sed Aharonem dicit nominatim; id est, sacerdotem illum summum, principem sacerdotum, cuius unctio Leuitici 8. diserte à Mose perscripta est. Etsi eo in loco de unctione & consecratione non Aharonis solius legitur, sed etiam reliquorum sacerdotum, qui tum auctoritate Dei in ministerio sacro instituti sunt: nêpe quia totus ordo prima illa actione simul fuerat consecrandus Domino, tam eorum qui aderant, tum posteritatis, quae ab ipsis erat ventura, nomine, & successura in idem ministerium. Nam eorum posteri nusquam leguntur fuisse uncti: ac propterea summo sacerdoti specialis est hæc appellatio divinitus attributa, quòd sacerdos unctus est. Sed cùm Aharonis nomen fuit hoc loco positum, exempli causa positū est: pro eo quod est, summus sacerdos ordinarius, quo in ordine princeps fuit Aharon. Est igitur synecdochicū[?]. ronis nomé pro sacerdotibus summis,aut quóuis de numero illorum vsurpari. Vsus verò & modus applicationis;fecundùm quem vnguento vngebatur sacerdos vnctus, demöstratur illis vocibus, quòd vnguentum superfundebatur capiti, quòd descendebat super barbam, & inde ad oram vsque vestimentorum illius, atque hæc de fimili in præsentia fatis. Iā de re,quam Propheta hoc simili adumbratam voluit, videamus.
units.tr: From the Prophet's words it is clear to whom this ointment was applied. He names not any Levite simply, nor a priest, but Aaron by name, that is, the high priest, the chief of the priests, whose anointing Moses describes clearly in Leviticus 8. Although in that place we read of the anointing and consecration not of Aaron alone but also of the other priests who were then appointed to the sacred ministry by God's authority, namely because the whole order was to be consecrated to the Lord in that first action, both those present and the posterity who were to come from them and succeed to the same ministry. For their descendants are nowhere read to have been anointed. Therefore this special title, divinely bestowed, belongs to the high priest, because he was the anointed priest. But when the name of Aaron is placed here, it is placed by way of example, standing for the ordinary high priest, in which order Aaron was chief. It is therefore a synecdoche, and the name of Aaron may be used for the high priests, or for any one of their number. The use and manner of application, by which the anointed priest was anointed with the ointment, is shown by those words: that the ointment was poured on his head, that it ran down upon the beard, and from there to the hem of his garments. So much for the simile for the present. Now let us see what the Prophet wished this simile to foreshadow.

units.la: In hac easdem partes opus est obseruari. Vnguento illi optimo, id est, præstantissimo atque suauissimo sefpondet vnctio spiritualis Dei: id est, donorum omniū suauissima & amœnissima communicatio, qua Deus perfundit ( vt' ita loquamur ) eos qui communionem sanctorum in vnitate Spiritus,& charitate vera,ac pace coluerint. Et certè quæcunque ad commendationem prisci illius vnguenti adferri pössunt, cùm nihil fuerit nisi spiritalium diuinorum. charismatum typus & vmbraculum, ea multò magis de veritate,quā adumbrauit, necesse est prædicari. Dicitur vnguentum, idque præstantissimum: diuinæ igitur benedictiones spirituali modo, adeoque diuino; illud sunt quod istud vnguentum modo corporali prædicatur esse. Cùm autem dicatur primùm quidem vnguentum communi nomine, deinde vero κατ' ἐξοχὴν, vt ab aliis vnguentis discerni quear, optimum ac præstantissimum appelletur, recte exiis appellationibus conficitur, benedictiones Dei, si in ipsis considerétur, vnguenta esse vnguentorum omniū præstantissima: cætera omnia, si ab vnguentis illis Dei separaueris, aut inodora, aut graueolentia dici oportere.
units.tr: In this the same parts must be observed. To that ointment, the best, that is, the most excellent and most sweet, corresponds the spiritual anointing of God: that is, the most sweet and pleasant communication of all gifts, with which God pours out (as we may say) those who cultivate the communion of saints in the unity of the Spirit, in true charity and peace. Certainly, whatever can be said in praise of that ancient ointment, since it was nothing but a type and shadow of the divine spiritual gifts, must much more necessarily be affirmed of the truth it foreshadowed. It is called ointment, and that the most excellent. Therefore the divine blessings are, in a spiritual and so divine manner, what that ointment is said to be in a bodily manner. Since it is first called ointment by a common name, and then, by excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], so as to be distinguished from other ointments, is called the best and most excellent, it is rightly concluded from these appellations that the blessings of God, if they are considered in themselves, are the most excellent of all ointments. All other things, if you separate them from those ointments of God, must be called either odourless or foul-smelling.

units.la: Quo indignior est illorum hominum proteruia, qui documentis naturæ, scripturæq; omnibus modis excitati, non possunt ex veritate animaduertere, quàm sint ipsi putidi, putidaque omnia, aut certè inodora; quibus solent adhærescere, vt saxis ostrea; donec vnguento diuinæ manus perfundantur. In primis autem incredibilis est tenacissimæ illius naturæ obfirmatio in iis quos regenuit Deus semine incorrupto verbi, aut admouit ad aliquam mysterij tanti conscientiam: quòd testes effecti, ac non solùm conscij maximæ illius præstantiæ, quam habet vnguentum benedictionum Dei, tamen aut non afficiuntur conscientia illius, aut affecti nō pofsunt eò vsque assurgere, vt omnem præstantiam in illo solùm diuino vnguento benedictionum Dei spiritalium in Christo positam adiungant sibi, earumque sepositis aliis rebus omnibus teneant constantissimè. De re diximus: Jam de persona videamus, vel potiùs de corpore, cui tanquam obiecto vnguentum illud præstantissimum applicatur à Domino.
units.tr: All the more shameless is the insolence of those men who, though stirred in every way by the evidences of nature and Scripture, cannot perceive from the truth how putrid they themselves are, and how everything putrid or else odourless is. To such things they are wont to cling, like oysters to rocks, until they are drenched with the ointment of the divine hand. The hardening of that most tenacious nature is especially incredible in those whom God has regenerated by the incorruptible seed of the word, or brought to some awareness of so great a mystery. For although they have been made witnesses, and are not only aware of that greatest excellence which the ointment of God's blessings possesses, yet either they are not affected by that awareness, or, being affected, they cannot rise so far as to attach all excellence to that divine ointment of spiritual blessings laid up in Christ alone, and to hold to it most steadfastly, setting aside all other things. We have spoken of the matter; now let us look at the person, or rather the body, to which the Lord applies that most excellent ointment as to its object.

units.la: Nominatur hoc loco Aharon: nominatur autem vt persona quidem; sed velut corpus considerandum est in hac personæ appellatione, quemadmodum illa partium quarundam enumeratio, quæ hoc loco ponitur, demonstrat euidentissimè. Fuit autem Aharon, tanquam sacerdos summus, ex lege institutus, fuit (inquam) vario respectu typus Christi & Ecclesiæ. Nam quisquis mediator est, & inter duas diuersas & differentes partes intercedit, is apud vnum agit personam alterius. Atque hunc in modum Christus defungens τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, id est, partes apud Deum Patrem nostro nomine obeundas, personam gessit Ecclesiæ: cùm verò defungeretur τὰ πρὸς ἡμᾶς, id est, partes apud nos Dei patris nomine perficiendas, personam gessit Dei patris, cuius est imago, sermo, & sapientia æterna. Sic Aharon, cùm de rebus agitur apud Deum obeundis aut percipiendis ab eo, corpus Ecclesiæ corpore suo (vt ita dicamus) adumbrauit: cùm verò de rebus apud nos & erga nos defungendis auctoritate Dei, repræsentauit Deum, pro quo legatus erat in Ecclesia ipsius: ad vtrumque verò speciatim gessit personam Christi, id est, vncti illius summi sacerdotis nostri in æternum. Hic autem agitur quidem de rebus quas Deus in Ecclesiam, vt omnis boni principium, præstiterat, & in Aharonem ipsum, velut institutum Ecclesiæ nomine; sed quas Ecclesia tamen occupare sanctè tenebatur coram Deo & Angelis eius. Propterea hoc loco necesse est, vt nomine Aharonis figurari Ecclesiam intelligamus, fideli obsequio suo sistentem sese coram Domino, & exercentem palàm dona unctionis eius : quemadmodum totam Ecclesiam Christianam in antecedentem Psalmum ostendimus non alia ratione Ecclesiam esse, quàm singulari illa relatione ipsius & ordinatione ad Deum, qua ordinatione sit unctionis illius salutaris particeps, ex qua procedit in singulos omnimoda benedictio.
units.tr: Aaron is named here. He is named as a person indeed, but in this designation of a person the body must be considered, just as that enumeration of certain parts which is set down here demonstrates most clearly. Aaron, instituted as high priest by the Law, was (I say) in various respects a type of Christ and of the Church. For whoever is a mediator, and stands between two different and distinct parties, acts in the person of the one before the other. In this way Christ, discharging the things toward God, that is, the parts to be performed before God the Father in our name, bore the person of the Church. But when he discharged the things toward us, that is, the parts to be carried out before us in the name of God the Father, he bore the person of God the Father, whose image, word and eternal wisdom he is. So Aaron, when the matter concerned things to be performed or received by him before God, foreshadowed the body of the Church with his own body (as we may say). But when it concerned things to be performed toward us and among us by God's authority, he represented God, for whom he was ambassador in his Church. In each case he specifically bore the person of Christ, that is, of our anointed high priest for ever. Here, however, the subject is indeed the things which God, as the origin of all good, had bestowed upon the Church, and upon Aaron himself as instituted in the name of the Church; but which the Church was nevertheless bound to hold with holy care before God and his angels. Therefore in this place we must understand that the Church is figured by the name of Aaron, presenting itself before the Lord in faithful obedience and openly exercising the gifts of his anointing. Just as we showed in the preceding Psalm that the whole Christian Church is the Church by no other reason than that singular relation and ordination to God, by which it shares in that saving anointing, from which all-embracing blessing flows to each individual.

units.la: Sed quia benedictionum Dei in Ecclesiam ipsius ratio est huiusmodi, ut non solùm communiter corpori, sed etiam singulariter in singulas partes tribuantur: propterea optimè Propheta hoc loco ordine etiam partium ad commoditatem benedictionum Dei & communicationem demonstrandam persecutus est.
