Partium autem in homine aliæ sunt innatæ, aliæ adiunctæ: Quæ innatæ, aut sunt necessariæ de natura illius, ut caput; aut non necessariæ, sed de ornamento naturali illius, ut barba est. Quæ adiunctæ, foris aduenient ad commoditatem illius, ut vestimenta sunt: quæ Deus homini sanctificauit ad usum ipsius, ex quo peccati conscientia erubuit miser, & pudefactus est nuditate sua. Atque hæ quoque partes secundùm quandam analogiam obseruantur in Ecclesia Dei, ut eo sit illustrior multiformis illa Dei sapientia, quam in Ecclesia sua coram imperiis & potestatibus explicauit. Ordo est membrorum in Ecclesia Dei; alius superiorum, alius inferiorum; item alius pertinentiū ad necessitatem, alius ad ornatum & decus illius; ut Apostolus ad Corinthios docet.: ordo est praeterea rerum quae commodè ad vsum Ecclesiae adhibentur: quo in numero ij[?] sunt de quibus in praecedentem Psalmum dicebamus; qui non sunt quidem de Ecclesia ipsa, sed tamen Ecclesiae non incommodant, quin potius eam circumuestiunt commodè ad gloriam Dei. Propterea enim fratres ab amantibus Ecclesiae ibi distincti sunt, quia aliud est domesticum esse, aliud vicinum bonum, aut certè minimè malum. In hac igitur persona ad quam pertinet vnctionis diuinae communicatio, tria haec optimè fuerunt distincta: corpus vel vniuersitas Ecclesiae; singula membra eius, etiam quae non ita sunt ad rationem Ecclesiae necessaria; & quae foris ei adiuncta sunt.
units.tr: But because the manner in which God's blessings are bestowed on his Church is such that they are given not only to the body in common but also to each individual part, the Prophet has rightly followed the order of the parts in this place, to show the fitness and sharing of God's blessings. Now among the parts of a man, some are innate and others added. The innate parts are either necessary to his nature, like the head, or not necessary but a natural ornament, as the beard is. The added parts come from outside for the man's convenience, like garments, which God sanctified for man's use, since the wretched man blushed from consciousness of sin and was ashamed of his nakedness. These parts too are observed in the Church of God according to a certain analogy, so that God's manifold wisdom, which he displayed in his Church before principalities and powers, may shine the more clearly. In the Church of God there is an order of members, some superior and some inferior; likewise some belong to what is necessary and others to its adornment and dignity, as the Apostle teaches the Corinthians. There is also an order of the things that are fittingly used for the Church's service. Among these are those things of which we spoke in the preceding Psalm: they are not of the Church itself, yet they do not harm the Church, but rather clothe it fittingly to the glory of God. For this reason the brothers were distinguished there from those who love the Church, because it is one thing to be a member of the household and another to be a good neighbour, or at least not an evil one. In this person, to whom the communication of divine anointing belongs, these three have been very well distinguished: the body or whole Church; its individual members, including those not so necessary to the nature of the Church; and those joined to it from outside.

units.la: Restat nunc locus tertius; de vsu & applicatione (vt vocant) diuini illius vnguenti ad corpus hoc quod modò circumscripsimus. Eam applicationē Propheta fieri à Deo, velut principio omnis boni (quod antè diximus) ordine & modo conuenientissimo demonstrat, seruato decoro similitudinis: cùm ait primùm quidem superfundi, posteaque superfusum descendere; deinde verò ordinem partium distinctè obseruat, dicens superfundi capiti, inde in barbam descendere, ex ea deferri ad oram vestimentorum vsque.
units.tr: There remains now a third point: the use and application (as they call it) of that divine ointment to this body which we have just described. The Prophet shows that this application is made by God, the beginning of all good (as we said before), in the most fitting order and manner, keeping the propriety of the comparison. He says first that it is poured out, and afterwards that, once poured out, it descends. Then he carefully observes the order of the parts, saying: "poured on the head, then it runs down upon the beard, and from there is carried down to the very hem of the garments."

units.la: Sensus igitur est, neminem hominem in Ecclesia esse, qui suauissimâ illam εὐωδίαν[?] vel bonam fragrantiam Christi à Deo Patre in Christo non percipiat: sed vnumquemque suo ordi-ne & ne & loco pro demenso donationum eius: neq. tantùm suauissimum illum amœnissimumque odorem ad germana Ecclesiæ membra pertinere, verumetiam ad vicinos omnes, qui modò nares suas (vt ita dicamus) malitiosè non compresserint,& odoramenta illa Spiritus Dei, quibus Ecclesia perfunditur & perfundit, refugerint. perfunditur enim à Deo cælitus: perfundit, autem in terris secundùm Deum eos omnes, quibus datum est Ecclesiam obseruare; & Spiritui Dei inhabitanti ipsam minimè obsistere. Quapropter ad iustam huius similitudinis intelligentiam optimè distingui ordinem illum necesse est, secundùm quem Propheta causam & effecta amœnitatis suauitatisq. istius in Ecclesia distingui voluit. causa Deus est Ecclesiam perfundens, & quidem actione adeò gratiosa, vt singula membra à capite ad calcem & oras ipsas vestimentorum imbuat odoramento salutari suo. Effecta verò sunt hæc tria: primum, quòd nihil est in Ecclesia, nihil Ecclesiæ, ne adiunctum quidem ipsi, quod in se redditum non sit odoratum benedictione Dei. Secundùm, quòd hanc suauitatem siue εὐωδίαν[?], quæ in nobis est, alij aliis testatam facimus, & communicamus inter nos pro modulo donationis Christi. Tertium, quòd etiam exteros ab Ecclesia, quibus spectaculum facti sumus, afficimus odoratissimis illis vestigiis quæ in nobis impressit Deus.
units.tr: The sense, therefore, is that there is no man in the Church who does not perceive that most sweet fragrance, the good odour of Christ [εὐωδία], from God the Father in Christ; but each one, in his own order and place, according to the measure of God's gifts. Nor does that most sweet and delightful fragrance pertain only to the true members of the Church, but also to all the neighbours who have not, in their malice (so to speak), held their noses shut, and have not fled from those perfumes of the Spirit of God with which the Church is anointed and anoints others. For it is anointed from heaven by God, and it anoints in turn on earth, according to God, all those to whom it has been given to observe the Church and not to resist the Spirit of God dwelling in it. Therefore, for a right understanding of this comparison, it is necessary to distinguish carefully the order by which the Prophet wished the cause and the effects of this delightfulness and sweetness in the Church to be distinguished. The cause is God, who anoints the Church, and indeed by an action so gracious that he imbues each member, from the head to the feet and the very hems of the garments, with his saving fragrance. The effects are these three. First, there is nothing in the Church, nothing belonging to the Church, not even what is merely attached to it, that is not itself made fragrant by God's blessing. Second, we make this sweetness, or fragrance [εὐωδία], which is in us, known to one another and share it among ourselves according to the measure of Christ's gift. Third, we also affect those outsiders, to whom we have become a spectacle, with those most fragrant traces which God has impressed on us.

units.la: Atque hoc quidem in primis ad eos pertinet, & obstringit eos vehementissimè, qui tanquam Aharon ad sacrum ministerium vocati sunt. Hi enim sedulò operam dare debent, ut cum Apostolo dicant ex veritate: Gratia Deo, qui omni tempore triumphum facit nobis in Christo, & manifestat per nos odorem cognitionis sui in omni loco. Sed nullum est tam exiguum membrum, cui pro suo modulo haec quoq; provincia diffundendae illius εὐωδίας[?] non fit demandata.
units.tr: This applies first of all, and binds most strongly, those who have been called like Aaron to sacred ministry. These men ought diligently to take pains that they may say with the Apostle, in truth: "Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and through us makes manifest the fragrance of his knowledge in every place." Yet there is no member so small that this task of spreading that fragrance [εὐωδία] is not also committed to it according to its measure.

units.la: Quid enim? annō omnes etiā minimi in regno caelorū odoramento illo Dei in Ecclesia perfusi sunt? Si sunt, annon odoré illum in Ecclesia perceptū in eadem opus est exhiberi? annon odore illo aërem circumstantem sic impleri, ut exteri sentiant nos in Christo odoratos esse? quàm ridiculum est, si quis odoramentum habere velit, & odorem manibus comprimere? Christianus quisquis appellatur, aut odoramentū factus est in Christo, & odori est aliis; aut si odori non est; iam non est odoramentum Christi: haec suavitas nō potest magis comprimi, quàm suavissimorum odoramentorum odor, quin ad eos dimanet qui circumstant nos. Ecclesia praestantissima est unguentaria; singuli in Ecclesia sunt narthecia pretiosissima, si ad conditionem suam bene aspexerint. Haec unguenta, haec odoramenta cur dissimulemus? cur non colamus? cur muscis iniectis (ut Sapiens in Ecclesiaste loquitur) corrumpamus? Cur disperdamus, proiectis huc illuc & proculcatis aromatis quæ ad confectionem eorum sunt opús? Etenim (ut Propheta inquit) bonum & amœnum est habitare fratres etiam unàsin[?] hac coniunctione sita est amœnitas: ex hac cohabitatione ac veluti confusione & contemperatione aromatum exurgit illud spiritale unguentum optimum, quod Deus olim materiali figurabat, ut Dauide habemus auctorè huius interpretationis. Ad huius unguenti cōstitutionem usqueadeò secundùm Deum communio illa sanctorum & συγκρασία[?] necessaria est, ut insipidum, & inodorum, ac potius fœtidū sit, quidquid in ista communione minimè continetur. Totum odoramentum est Christi, ex quo solo & in quo odorata est communio nostra, prout in Cantico Canticorum docemur passim. huius odoramenti ea natura est, ut tanquam oleum stillet per totum Ecclesiæ corpus à capite ad calces illius. qui in hac cōmunione Christi versari cupit, eum in communione Ecclesiæ sese opus est cōtinere, quam præcedente Psalmo ex Dauide cognouimus, & membris sibi adunatis in Christo constanter adhærere. Solus Christus seorsim odoratus est, atque adeò odoramentū ipsum: nemo nostrum sine Christo & sine fratribus esse odoratus potest: sine Christo, quia odoramento est, & nos in eo bona fragrantia sumus coram Domino: sine fratribus, quia corpus simul totum, nō autem fastuosum, confidens, aut fastidiosum membrum seorsim perfunditur odore Christi.
units.tr: For what then? Are all, even the least, in the kingdom of heaven anointed with that ointment of God in the Church? If they are, must not that fragrance perceived in the Church also be displayed in the Church? Must it not fill the air around, so that outsiders perceive that we have been made fragrant in Christ? How ridiculous it is, if someone wishes to have a perfume and to hide its odour with his hands! Whoever is called a Christian is either made a perfume in Christ and is an odour to others, or if he is not an odour, he is no longer a perfume of Christ. This sweetness cannot be suppressed any more than the smell of the most precious perfumes can be kept from spreading to those who stand around us. The Church is the most excellent perfumer's shop; each of its members is a most precious flask of ointment, if they have looked well to their own condition. Why should we conceal these ointments and these perfumes? Why should we not honour them? Why should we spoil them by throwing in flies (as the Wise Man says in Ecclesiastes)? Why should we destroy them, scattering and trampling the spices that are the materials for their making? For (as the Prophet says) it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together also; this pleasantness lies in their union, and from this living together, and as it were blending and mixing of spices, there arises that spiritual ointment, the best, which God once prefigured by a material one, as we have David as the author of this interpretation. For the making of this ointment that fellowship of the saints and the mixing [συγκρασία] according to God is so necessary that whatever is not contained in that fellowship is tasteless, odourless, and rather foul. The whole perfume belongs to Christ, from whom alone our fellowship is fragrant and in whom it is fragrant, as we are taught throughout the Song of Songs. Such is the nature of this perfume that it drips like oil through the whole body of the Church, from its head to its feet. Whoever wishes to dwell in this fellowship with Christ must keep himself in the communion of the Church, which we learned from David in the preceding Psalm, and cling constantly to the members united to him in Christ. Christ alone is fragrant by himself, and so he is the perfume itself; none of us can be fragrant without Christ and without the brothers. Without Christ, because he is the perfume, and we are a good fragrance before the Lord only in him; without the brothers, because the whole body, not a proud, self-confident, or disdainful member standing apart, is anointed with the odour of Christ together.

units.la: Omnino perfectionem amœnitatis huius instituit Deus: amœnitate facit odoramentorum communio, communionem charitas, quæ persectionis vinculum à Paulo dicitur: pax necessarium est charitatis instrumentum.
units.tr: Surely God established the perfection of this delightfulness: fellowship makes the perfumes delightful, love makes the fellowship, which Paul calls the bond of perfection, and peace is the necessary instrument of love.

units.la: Quid ergo putamus, miseri? quid fingimus, cùm tanto supercilio alij alios quasi furcilla extrudimus, & censoriam quandam virgulam in hos, in illos promiscuè adhibemus, tanquam si nobis solùm esset iudicij nasus; aut Christus hanc facultatem cessisset nobis, qua ad libidinem animi nostri abutamur? Id sanè faciant Satanæ stabularij: at oues Christi non decet, pastores minimè. Quin potiùs Christo cedimus, nos & illos in communionem corporis & Spiritus sui gratiosissimè adhibenti? Quin potiùs odores amœnissimos ab illo in nos deriuantem manu ipsius animaduertimus? quin potiùs unguento illo odoratissimo fratres communiter nobiscum sentimus delibutos? quin potiùs etiam amicos ad participationem suauissimi eiusdem odoris ab illo capite in corpus unum adscitum iri confidimus? quin potiùs & continendis iis qui iam vocati sunt, & vocandis qui absunt, damus operam diligentissimè; ab omni fœtore abstinentes, quo crepant animi nostri, & omnem suauissimum odorem illis exhibentes, qui ad Christum & ad nos per Christum unà perducantur? O beatum studium eorum, qui in hoc pietatis officio consumunt operam! beatas mentes quæ de hoc studio cogitant! beatos homines, qui ita statuunt cum animis suis, eo se odoratiores fore, quo cõiunctiores cum Christo & suis fratribus futuri sunt! Contrà verò, quàm perditum & deploratú studium,in quod funestis hisce temporibus plerique abripiuntur! qui se odoratos fore tum demű arbitrantur, cùm alios à se abalienauerint, aut etiam sordibus & inquinamentis indignè commaculauerint. Ab improbo,inquiebat Dauid,prodeat improbitas:& tu, miser, itáne statuisti desipere, ut improbitatem vomens,& pacem oppugnáns & odoramentum fratrum tuorum , meliorem te fore iudices? aut odoratiorem fore, cùm à fonte odorû purissimo, à Christo ita discesseris? non cogitas sordes à te in proximum excreári non posse,quin prior sordeas? aut spargi venenum, quin venenatus sis?
units.tr: What then do we think, wretches that we are? What do we imagine, when with such haughtiness we thrust others away from us, as with a fork, and apply a sort of censor's rod to these and those indiscriminately, as if we alone had the nose of judgment, or as if Christ had yielded this power to us, so that we might abuse it for the lust of our minds? Let Satan's stable-boys do that; but it is not fitting for Christ's sheep, nor at all for ministers. Rather should we yield to Christ, who most graciously brings us and them into the communion of his body and Spirit? Rather should we notice with our own hands the most delightful odours that he pours upon us from himself? Rather should we feel together with our brothers anointed with that most fragrant ointment? Rather should we trust that friends too will be taken by him from that head into the one body, to share in that most sweet fragrance? Rather should we, both in holding fast those who have already been called and in calling those who are absent, labour most diligently, abstaining from all the stench with which our minds reek, and offering the sweetest fragrance to those who are to be brought together with us to Christ through Christ? O blessed zeal of those who spend their labour in this duty of piety! Blessed minds that think upon this zeal! Blessed men who so resolve in their hearts that they will be the more fragrant the more closely they are joined to Christ and to their brothers! On the contrary, how lost and desperate is the zeal into which many are swept in these deadly times! They think they will be fragrant only when they have estranged others from themselves, or even defiled them unworthily with filth and pollution. "Let wickedness," David said, "come forth from the wicked"; and you, wretch, have you so decided to be foolish, that, vomiting wickedness and attacking peace and the fragrance of your brothers, you think yourself the better, or the more fragrant, when you have departed so from the purest fountain of fragrance, Christ? Do you not reflect that you cannot cast filth out upon your neighbour without first becoming filthy yourself? Or that you cannot scatter poison without being poisoned?

units.la: Agite ergò, ô fratres dilectissimi, participes unctionis illius pretiosæ Christi,& in communionem sanctissimi illius corporis vocati virtute Spiritus, amœnitatem istius communionis nostræ recognoscite mecum , per Deum immortalem; in qua communione Deus ungit, Christus à Patre unctus est,membra unguntur in Christo , & minimi etiam quique in regno cælorum tanquam barbæ ipsius pili (si ita placet) odoramento perfunduntur , ipsæ denique vestes,& quicunque nos circumstant, afficiun-turtur odoris istius amœnissimi conscientia. Ne si-namus ergo tanti illius, non privati, sed catholici vel universalis boni sensum, aut usum, aut fructum nobis intercidere: ne sinamus nos ab eo excidere in quo odorati sumus: ne sinamus abiis nos divelli quibuscum odorati sumus, & odoratiores amplius efficimur, quo amplius ipsis in Christo adhæremus: odorem illic invenimus, non intulimus; quem si oppugnemus in ullo, non illum, sed nosmet ipsos extrudimus: ne sinamus vel minimi cuiusquam membri fastidium aut contemptum in animis nostris invalescere: ne sinamus denique vel eos ipsos qui foris sunt, fœtorem nostrum sentire ex contemptu sui: sed quem odorem gratiose communicavit nobiscum Christus, eundem summo studio & alacritate cum illis communicemus, si fieri potest, ut ille ipse odor noster tum in illis, qui in peccatis mortui ac fœtentes erat, tum in nobis qui a morte & corruptione per Christum vindicati sumus, sit Deo gloriosus, & Ecclesiæ illius salutaris. Si fecerimus, bene est; officium fecerimus Christo & Ecclesiæ eius debitum: si non, jam non odor, sed fœtor futurus est, quem coram Deo, Ecclesia, & universo mundo erubescabimus: quod malum avertat Dominus. In eos homines optimè quadrabit illud sanctissimum Augustini dictum: Magnum istis hominibus consilium vindicandi est libido moriendi, non in corpore, sed in corde: ubi funus occultè priusʃuo putore sentitur, quàm mors nostrâ cogitatione prospicitur :hos ante fœtentes sentimus, quàm mortuos nouimus. Hoc verò non laudi cuiquam nostrûm, sed fraudi & perditioni acerbissimæ futurum est; si pro odore etiam exteros ad Christum pellecturo fœtorem edamus fugaturum.
units.tr: Come then, most beloved brothers, you who are partakers of that precious anointing of Christ and called by the power of the Spirit into fellowship with that most holy body, let us together consider the sweetness of this fellowship of ours, by the immortal God. In this fellowship God anoints, Christ is anointed by the Father, the members are anointed in Christ, and even the least of those in the kingdom of heaven are drenched with fragrance, as the very hairs of his beard (if I may put it so). Finally, the garments and all who stand around us are touched by the awareness of that most pleasant odour. Let us not allow the sense, the use, or the fruit of this great good, which is not private but catholic or universal, to be lost to us. Let us not allow ourselves to fall away from him in whom we have been made fragrant. Let us not allow ourselves to be torn away from those with whom we have been made fragrant, and we become all the more fragrant the more closely we cling to them in Christ. We have found the fragrance there; we did not bring it in. If we attack it in anyone, we are not attacking it but thrusting ourselves out. Let us not allow contempt or disdain for the least of any member to grow strong in our minds. Let us not allow even those who are outside to perceive our stench through our contempt for them. Rather, the fragrance that Christ has graciously shared with us, let us share with them with the utmost zeal and eagerness, so that, if possible, that very fragrance of ours may be glorious to God and healthful to his Church, both in those who were dead and stinking in sins and in us who have been rescued from death and corruption through Christ. If we do so, it is well; we will have performed the duty owed to Christ and to his Church. If not, what will be there is no longer a fragrance but a stench, of which we shall be ashamed before God, the Church, and the whole world. May the Lord avert that evil. That most holy saying of Augustine fits such people very well: "The desire to die is a great counsel for these men to take vengeance, not in the body but in the heart, where the corpse is secretly perceived by its stench before death is foreseen by our thought. We smell these men as dead before we know them as dead." Yet this will be no praise to any of us, but a deceit and most bitter ruin, if we, while intending to draw outsiders to Christ by our fragrance, give off a stench that drives them away.

units.la: 3. Ut ros Hermonis, ut qui descendit super montes Sionis. Nam illic mandauit Iehoua benedictionem, vitam usque in sae- culum.
units.tr: 3. As the dew of Hermon, and as the dew that descended upon the mountains of Zion: for there the LORD commanded the blessing, even life for evermore.

units.la: AMOENITATEM, quam in communione sanctorum Dominus collocauit, cuius pij sunt apud se conscij, & quam exteri utcunq. sentiunt virtute Dei, ex praecedente versu, Dauide teste, cognouimus. Cùm verò duobus nominibus sanctissimam illam communionem Propheta celebrauerit, amoenitatis & boni:tiani[?] nobis ratio illius boni, quod in Ecclesia & communione sanctorum in Christo deposuit Deus, videnda est. Videnda autem, non accumulatis & arcessitis hinc inde testimoniis; sed ex his ipsis Prophetæ verbis, quæ modò exscripsimus: ut certissimum hunc ductum secuti, de pace illa, quam nobis dedit Christus, continenda, seruanda, atque colenda indies magis ac magis cogitemus.
units.tr: From the preceding verse, with David as witness, we have learned the sweetness that the Lord has placed in the communion of the saints, of which the godly are conscious among themselves, and which outsiders in some measure perceive by the power of God. Since the Prophet has praised that most holy fellowship with two names, that of sweetness and that of good, we must now see the nature of that good which God has deposited in the Church and the communion of the saints in Christ. But it must be seen not by heaping up and summoning testimonies from here and there, but from the very words of the Prophet which we have just copied out. Following this most certain guide, we may think more and more each day about how to keep, guard, and cherish that peace which Christ has given us.

units.la: Bonum itaque communionis sanctorum, pacisin hac communione à Christo imperatæ; duobus modis hoc loco describitur : primùm quidem simili à naturæ ordine sumpto, vt antè dicebamus:deinde verò simplice enunciatione tum boni, tum causæ,vnde emanat bonum, & ad communionem sanctorum peruenit.Simile quo Propheta vtitur,quamuis specie duplex atque circumstantiâ , ratione tamen vnum est; cùm hoc modo dicit, est vt ros Hermonis, vt qui descendit super montes Sionis. Agitur enim de vno rore,cuius naturam fiue rationem non variat subiecti loci,in quem decidit, constitutio. Propria autem boni illius descriptio ἀπολαυκῶς[?] à Psalte subiicitur, dicente verbis sequentibus, Nam illic mandat Iehoua benedictionem,&c.
units.tr: Therefore the good of the communion of the saints, and of the peace commanded by Christ in this communion, is described here in two ways. First, by a likeness taken from the order of nature, as we said before; and then by a plain statement both of the good and of the cause from which the good flows and comes to the communion of the saints. The likeness the Prophet uses, though double in appearance and circumstance, is one in reason, since he says: "It is as the dew of Hermon, as that which descends upon the mountains of Zion." For it concerns one dew, whose nature or reason is not changed by the situation of the place on which it falls. The proper description of that good is then given by the Psalmist in the words that follow: "For there the LORD commands the blessing," and so on. [ἀπολαυκῶς]

units.la: Quòd autem Propheta ad rei eiusdem circumfcriptionem duobus his similibus vtitur,id certo consilio ab ipso factum est: quod confilium ante exponi à nobis opus est,quàm ad explicationem argumenti ipsius veniamus. Hermonem montem,vel potiùs montana Hermonis,ex Scripturis constat pascuis illis Bafanis fertilitate summa nobilibus esse imposita: montes verò Sionis in ipsa vrbe fuisse constat,& proximè vrbem Hierosolymorum,admodum siticulofos : adeò vt neminem, ne puerulum quidem, fugere posset cognitio commoditatis illius quæ proximo agro ex rore cælitus accidebat. His rebus animaduersis, facilè iam omnes vifuri sunt, cur duo similia argumento eadem, loco differentia Propheta hoc loco adscripserit. Prius simile ad copiam amplissimam bonorum à Deo in Ecclesia ad extremos usque terminos pertinentium respicit: posterius ad vim illam benedictionis Dei, qua loca etiam arentia & fiticulosa (unde Sion Hebraeis appellatus est) ac fermè inepta edendis fructibus, efficiuntur ferendis illis habilia. Nunc de argumento ipso videamus.
units.tr: Why the Prophet uses these two similes to describe the same thing, he did with a definite purpose, which we must explain before we come to the explanation of the argument itself. From the Scriptures it is clear that Mount Hermon, or rather the heights of Hermon, were named for those Bashan pastures, famous for their great fertility. It is also clear that the mountains of Zion were in the city itself, and close to the city of Jerusalem, very dry and parched, so that no one, not even a little child, could fail to know how great the benefit was that came from heaven as dew to the nearby land. With these things noticed, everyone will easily see why the Prophet, in this place, has added two similar things on the same subject, differing in location. The first simile looks to the very ample abundance of good things that God gives in the Church, reaching to the furthest borders; the second to that power of God's blessing by which even dry and parched places (whence Zion was called by the Hebrews) and nearly unfit for bearing fruit are made apt for bearing them. Now let us look at the argument itself.

units.la: In hoc itaque simili eosdem partes sumus observaturi, quas in præcedente ostendimus. Primùm enim videndum quid sit quòd analogiè cum illo spiritali bono, de quo hîc sermo est, habere dicitur similitudinem: Secundò, ad quem ras ille perveniebat naturæ ordine (nam hoc exemplum naturale est)& ductu singulari Dei: Tertiò, qui usus & modus sistarum rerum ex instituto illius. Quid sit cum bono illo comparatum, palàm est, dicente Propheta, est ut ros. Quò perveniat, demonstratur verbis illis, super montes Hermonii, & super montes vel montana Sionis. Qui usus & modus docetur eo quòd Propheta rorem ait descendere.
units.tr: In this simile, then, we shall observe the same parts that we pointed out in the preceding one. First, we must see what it is that is said to have a likeness by analogy to that spiritual good of which he speaks here. Second, to what place the dew came by the order of nature (for this example is natural) and by the singular guidance of God. Third, what use and manner of these things follows from its appointment. What is compared with that good is plain, since the Prophet says, "it is as the dew." Where it comes is shown by the words, "upon the mountains of Hermon, and upon the mountains or heights of Zion." The use and manner are taught by the Prophet's saying that the dew "descends."

units.la: Ac rorem quidem naturâ bonum esse nouerunt omnes, cùm fructus illius quotidie ab hominibus percipiantur amplissimi ad commoditatem præsentis vitæ. Quod autem de rore secundùm naturâ à vulgo percipitur diciturque, idemà piis de bono spiritali dicitur percipiturq. in communione sanctorum: ab aliis propterea non percipitur (vt antè dicebamus) quia percipiendis illis planè inepti sunt, donec regeniti fuerint à Domino.
units.tr: Everyone knows that dew is by nature a good thing, since its very ample fruits are daily received by men for the convenience of the present life. But what is perceived and said of dew according to nature by the common people, the same is said and perceived by the godly of the spiritual good in the communion of the saints. Others, therefore, do not perceive it (as we said before), because they are altogether unfit to perceive it until they have been born again by the Lord.

units.la: Neque verò hic necesse est, vt amplissimum illum latiffimumq. campum bonorum (piritalium decurramus, & percenseamus scriptis. Hæc bona, etiamsi chartis innumeris statueremus perrexere, nemo tamen perceptus esset, nisi qui iam per Dei gratiam insitum habeat in se & ingeneratum bonum. Hæc bona (inquâ) omninò intus sentiri præstat, quàm perscribi multis: quia singulis suo ordine sua sunt bona à Deo distributa virtute Spiritus, quæ in conscientia leguntur digito Dei exarata, nō autè in charta humanisve tabulis. Sed quia vbique in Scripturis sacris verbum Dei, quod potentia est eius ad salutem omni credenti, cum rore comparatum est, velut instrumentum vitæ æternæ à Deo in has terras demissum cælitùs, quo perinde animi nostri irrorentur, humectentur, & inebrientur gustu ac potu salutis æternæ, ac rore aluntur gramina atque recreantur: propterea non dubitamus, quin hoc etiam loco ad illud sanctissimum verbum vitæ æternæ Psaltes respexerit, cùm bonum communionis sanctorum describeret. Nam Deus cùm omnis boni in natura auctor, rorem suum defundit in agros ad infirmæ huius naturæ fustentationem, tum verò maximè, vt boni spiritualis in Ecclesia auctor, verbum fuû defundit in Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Nor is it necessary here that we run through and list in writing that very ample and broad field of spiritual goods. Even if we should go on setting them out in countless pages, no one would have grasped them, except one who by the grace of God already has inborn and engendered good in himself. I say that it is better to feel these goods wholly within than to describe them at length to many, because each has its own goods distributed by God through the power of the Spirit, which are read in the conscience, written by the finger of God, and not on paper or in human tablets. But since everywhere in the holy Scriptures the Word of God, which is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes, is compared with dew, as an instrument of eternal life sent down from God from heaven to this earth, by which our minds are likewise watered, moistened, and made drunk with the taste and drink of eternal salvation, just as the grasses are nourished and refreshed by dew, we do not doubt that in this place too the Psalmist, in describing the good of the communion of the saints, had regard to that most holy word of eternal life. For God, being the author of all good in nature, pours out his dew upon the fields to sustain this weak nature; but much more, as the author of spiritual good in the Church, he pours out his word into the Church.

units.la: suam, quæ ratio est vineaque ipsius, ut singula quæ in ea sunt, roris[?] illius communicatione alantur, augescant, & ad iustam matutitatem virtute ipsius perducantur. Ac proinde quemadmodum rorem non solùm secundùm se, & respectu principij sui nouimus esse bonum, verumetiam his rebus inferioribus bonum; id est, utilem & necessarium; omnibusque modis commodum (id enim omnes comperimus usu & experientia communi) ita verbum quoque Domini cùm in se & secundùm principium ipsius spirituali modo bonũ esse docemur hoc loco, tum summè nobis utile ac necessarium, qui ad arvum vineamque illius pertinemus.
units.tr: His own field, which is also his vineyard, so that each thing in it may be nourished, grow, and be brought by the power of God to its due ripeness through the communication of that dew. And so, just as we know dew to be good not only in itself and with respect to its source, but also good for these lower things, that is, useful and necessary and in every way convenient (for we all learn this from use and common experience), so too we are taught in this place that the word of the Lord is good in itself and in its spiritual manner of origin, and also most useful and necessary to us, who belong to his field and vineyard.

units.la: 2 Hanc autem hæreditatem Domini, in qua & nos sumus; Propheta circumscribit montium Hermonũ & Sionis appellatione: quorum illi ad fines regionis sanctæ Orientem & Aquilonem versus pertinebant, hi velut ad umbilicum eius: illi ad feraces valles agrosque irrigandos commodè impositi; hi arentes & siticulosi vix subiectis vallibus alimentum subministraturi esse videbantur. Quapropter his duabus appellationibus, tanquam ex re præsente, priscam Ecclesiam instituit David non esse curtam aut infirmam Dei manum, quin ab uno fine Chananæ ad alterum potentissimè rorem suum diffunderet, & peræque loca arentia & siticulosa ac pinguia arua & valles uberes fecundaret. Quod autem hoc modo aspectabili Deus Ecclesiæ in typo Chananæ testificatus est, idem nos sine typo habemus testimonium , & virtutem Dei experimur. Nam cōmunio hæc sanctorū, ad quam vocati sumus , culta est hæreditas illius, quam Christus suo sanguine comparauit.In hoc aruo Christi hæreditario sunt herbæ,frutices,virgulta,arbusta,arbores;quas tum sua paterna manu colit Deus in Christo,tum Christus in sese infitas alit & conseruat diligentissimè,quas indesinenter temperato veluti calo, rore , consimilibusque adiumentis curat & prouehit scientifsimus fidelissimusq. agricola; & studiosissimus salutis nostræ:neç curat nos nimborum impetu, quo futurum esset vt eorrumperemur præ tenuitate & infirmitate nostra; sed rore lenissimo ,stillante commodissimè in nos, quamuis infirmissimos; vt paulatim singulj possimus in ipso augescere. Ita fit, vt omnes, velut rami in vnum truncum insiti atque in vnum corpus, vnum Spiritum , & vnam communionem vocati, tum bono à Deo erga nos collato vtamur ipsi salutariter , tum idem bonum ad gloriam ipsius & ad communionem sanctorum proeo ac possumus ædificandam oeçupemus.
units.tr: This inheritance of the Lord, in which we also stand, the prophet describes by the names of the mountains Hermon and Zion. Of these, Hermon lay toward the edges of the holy land, toward the east and north, while Zion lay, as it were, at its navel. Hermon was conveniently placed for watering fertile valleys and fields, whereas Zion, dry and thirsty, seemed able to supply nourishment only to the valleys lying beneath it. By these two names, as if pointing to something present, David taught that the ancient Church was not a short or weak hand of God. God could pour out his dew mightily from one end of Canaan to the other, and make both the dry, thirsty places and the rich fields and fertile valleys fruitful alike. What God attested to the Church in this visible type of Canaan, we also have, without a type, as testimony, and we experience the power of God. For this communion of the saints, to which we are called, is the cultivated inheritance that Christ bought with his own blood. In this field of Christ's inheritance there are herbs, shrubs, bushes, trees and great trees. God tends them with his own fatherly hand in Christ, and Christ, grafted into himself, nourishes and preserves them most diligently. The most skilled and faithful farmer, who is most eager for our salvation, constantly tends and promotes them with a mild and temperate warmth, with dew and similar aids. Nor does he treat us with the force of storms, by which we would be ruined because of our frailty and weakness, but with the gentlest dew, falling upon us most conveniently, however weak we are, so that each of us may gradually grow in him. And so it comes about that all of us, like branches grafted into one trunk, called into one body, one Spirit and one communion, both make use of the good that God has bestowed on us for our own salvation, and devote that same good, as far as we can, to the glory of God and the building up of the communion of the saints.

units.la: Propterea enim in ipso Cantici huius ingrefsu Psaltes dicebat, Ecce; vt nos testes illius boni in communione sanctorum appellaret : & moneret simul nostram ab aliis spectari atque obseruari in communione hac , quàm alij à nobis obseruantur: ideoq. necessarium esse, vt totum illud bonum quod à Deo accepimus,tum quia bonum est,tam[?] quia nobis ipsis bonum , in ædificatione & salute occupemus aliena & nostra. Etenim cum in terris nulla tam exigua herba fit, quæ, rorem à Deo nō sentiat, quæ non utatur, & quæ non occupet eum ad testificationem gloriæ Deo auctori omnis boni tribuendæ: indignissimum illud est, si nos tam multis à natura bonis instructi, & aucti gratia copiosa atque infinita segnescamus in officio hoc, & Deo palàm proclamante, Ecce, & Angelis hominibusq. in Ecclesia, extraque Ecclesiam spectantibus, non demus operam, vt bonum hoc à Deo collatum ad Dei gloriam & communionem corporis, quod Christus sanguine suo redemit, & in quo sumus ipsi, vicissim referamus.
units.tr: For this reason the Psalmist, at the very beginning of this song, said Behold, so as to call us witnesses of this good in the communion of the saints. He also warns us that in this communion our conduct is watched and observed by others, just as we observe others. Therefore it is necessary that we devote all that good which we have received from God, both because it is good and because it is good for us, to the building up and salvation of others and of ourselves. For on earth there is no herb so small that it does not feel the dew of God, does not use it, and does not devote it to bearing witness to the glory of God, the author of every good. It is most unworthy that we, endowed with so many natural goods and enriched with abundant and infinite grace, should grow slack in this duty. When God proclaims aloud Behold, and angels and men, both within the Church and outside it, look on, we do not take pains to return to God's glory and to the communion of his body, which Christ redeemed with his blood and in which we ourselves are, this good that God has given us.

units.la: Enimuerò cur segnescamus, aut aliud agamus in hoc opere sanctissimo, quod Deus nobis imperat Prophetæ verbis? Deus non segnescit benefaciendo, dat omnibus, nemini exprobrat, suppeditat omnia, suggerit commodè velut rorem herbæ: idque non semel, sed indesinenter stillantibus è cælo benedictionibus eius. Quid est, siue in nobis, siue extra nos, quod ab officio hoc sanctissimo nos auocare possit, cum Deus aduocat, & omnia quæ sunt opus ad hoc ossicium nostrum sapientissimè, commodissimè, & utilitate summa communicat? Si alienū vitium offensasq. esse nobis impedimento querimur; quid nos vulneramus alieno vulnere? quid cadimus in alieno casu? quid aliena macula infami maculamur? alienum malum curemus potiùs, quàm vt participemus: malū non curatur malo. At bonum nostrum nunquam omittamus, aut illius utendi commoditatem sinamus eripi e manibus nostris. Sin autem vitium a nobis est; an ergo putamus idem etiam foras effundi oportere? annon praestaret intus suffocari, quam ad alios impotentia animi nostri aut imprudentia dimanare? Euellendum, exstirpandum malum, non propagandu est. id-iusta [?] communio postulat, ut bonis communicemus inter nos, non malis. haec enim ubi sunt, atq. adeo ubicunque, quumprimu nascuntur, praestat extingui & quasi suffocari: bona vero cum in nobis ipsis, tum in aliis semper in communione sanctorum procurari.
units.tr: Why, then, should we grow slack, or do anything else in this most holy work, which God commands us in the words of the Prophet? God does not grow slack in doing good. He gives to all, reproaches no one, supplies all things, and conveys them conveniently, like dew to the herb. And he does this not once but without ceasing, with his blessings falling from heaven. What is there, whether in us or outside us, that could call us away from this most holy duty, when God summons us and supplies, most wisely, most conveniently and with the greatest usefulness, all that is needed for this task? If we complain that another's fault or offence is an obstacle to us, why do we wound ourselves with another's wound? Why do we fall through another's fall, or stain ourselves with another's infamous stain? We should rather take care of another's evil than share in it, for evil is not cured by evil. But let us never neglect our own good, nor allow the opportunity of using it to be snatched from our hands. If, however, the fault is ours, do we think it should therefore be poured out abroad too? Would it not be better to be stifled within, than for the lack of self-control or the folly of our mind to flow out to others? Evil must be uprooted and torn out, not propagated. Such is what the just communion demands: that we share good things among ourselves, not evil ones. For where evil things arise, and indeed wherever they first spring up, it is better to put them out and, as it were, stifle them. Good things, however, must always be cultivated in the communion of the saints, both in ourselves and in others.

units.la: Atque hoc officium eo studiosius fieri a nobis necesse est, quo amplius procliue esse Deum animaduertimus ad beneficiorum suorum communicationem. Nam ut rorem videmus descendere; nec semel descendere, sed subinde; nec uno in loco, sed in tota aratione Domini; nec frustra, sed effectu certissimo: ita etiam de rore illo bonorum spiritualium iudicium nos oportet facere. semper decidit ros ille beneficiorum Dei, descendens commodissime in omni tempore & loco, continuatissimus divina efficacitate, quemadmodum olim per Prophetam Deus pronunciauerat. Verum ut amor descendit magis a parentibus in liberos, quam ascendit retro, ita haec efficacitas. Non enim assurgit a nobis ad Deum usque, ut capiat fructum de nobis: sed in communione sanctorum tota est a nobis occupanda; ut filij simus patris Illius nostri cælestis qui facit ut sol suus exoriatur super malos & bonos, & pluit super iustos ac iniustos, non ulla dignitate aut virtute nostra adductus, sed sola benignitate & munificentia sua. quid enim terra ad rorem supernè obtinendum facit? Deus idem auctor est & faciendi & demittendi roris: eam non terra meretur; sed largitur gratia, qua naturæ ordinem constituit Deus. Vt itaq. nec Hermon, nec Sion fecerunt quidquam ad habendum rorem; ita etiam de nobis profiteamur coram Domino necesse est. Descendit amor infinitus illius ad nos vehementissimè; at non vicissim ad illum ascendit pusillus noster: efficit ille amor & rorem benedictionum & effecta singula ex rore illo procedentia. Nos igitur, qui tam gratiosa benignitate patris cælestis nostri in communione sanctorum participes efficimur roris cælestis illius; quo studio, qua contentione tenemur laborare, obsecro, ut istas benedictiones Dei refundamus, & gratum animum nostrum omni officio ac potius pietate Deo testatum faciamus?
units.tr: And we must perform this duty all the more eagerly, the more we see that God is inclined to share his benefits. For as we see the dew descend, and not once only but repeatedly, and not in one place only but over the whole field of the Lord, and not in vain but with the most certain effect, so we ought to judge concerning that dew of spiritual goods. That dew of God's benefits always falls, descending most conveniently at every time and place, unbroken by divine efficacy, just as God once declared through the Prophet. Yet this efficacy flows, as love descends from parents to children more than it rises back up. For it does not rise from us up to God, so that he may receive fruit from us. Rather, it must be taken up by us within the communion of the saints, so that we may be sons of that heavenly Father of ours, who makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust, moved not by any worth or virtue of ours, but by his own kindness and bounty alone. For what does the earth do to obtain the dew from above? God is the author both of making and of sending down the dew. The earth does not earn it, but God bestows it by the grace by which he has established the order of nature. Therefore, just as neither Hermon nor Zion did anything to have the dew, so we too must confess before the Lord. His infinite love descends upon us most vehemently, while our little love does not rise back up to him in return. That love produces both the dew of blessings and each effect that proceeds from that dew. We, then, who through the so gracious kindness of our heavenly Father are made partakers of that heavenly dew in the communion of the saints, with what zeal and what effort ought we to labour, I beg you, to pour back these blessings of God, and to show our grateful mind to God by every duty and rather by piety?

units.la: - At non refundit terra, nec reppendit cælo, à quo perfusa est. bene est: Nam eadem quoque ratione res à se acceptas per nos Deus refundi postulat; Nec terra refundit cælo, nec nos Domino refundimus; sed cum terra refundat creatis rebus aliis, in quarum commodum fructus ipsius instituti sunt, ac proinde hominibus ipsis sit parens & altrix benefica; utrumque nobis tenendum est; nec posse nos Deo beneficia accepta cepta refundere, ut terra cælo non potest: nec posse nos non refundere, vel potiùs profundere in eos tanquâ vicarios, quibus destinauit Deus omnes fructus à nobis prodituros. Proinde ut terra animantibus, ac præsertim humano genere, fœcunda est; ita nos fœcundari necesse est humanæ societatis vniuersæ, & maximè Ecclesiæ bono. De hoc bonorum diuinorum vsu dies & noctes oportet cogitemus, in hoc laboremus, hoc vnum agamus coram Domino, denique toti in hoc simus: cùm Dominum illum, qui solus est αὐτάρκεστος[?], in hoc totum esse videamus, vt communioni sanctorum benedicat, & per nos etiam, quoscunque honore isto dignatur, quotiescunque fieri potest, benefaciat.
units.tr: But the earth does not pour back the rain, nor return it to the heaven from which it was soaked. That is well. For by the same reasoning God requires that things received from him be returned through us. The earth does not return to heaven, and we do not return to the Lord. But since the earth returns its fruits to other created things, for whose benefit its produce has been ordained, and so is a beneficent parent and nurse to men themselves, we must hold both points. We cannot pour back the benefits received to God, as the earth cannot to heaven. Nor can we fail to return them, or rather pour them out upon those people, as God's representatives, for whom God has destined all the fruits that are to come forth from us. Therefore, as the earth is fruitful for living creatures and especially for the human race, so we must be made fruitful for the good of the whole human society and above all of the Church. Day and night we ought to think about this use of divine goods, labour at it, make this one thing our business before the Lord, and in short be wholly given to it. For we see that the Lord, who alone is self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης], is wholly intent on this: that he may bless the communion of the saints, and through us also do good to whomever he deigns to honour in this way, as often as it can be done.

units.la: Ad hunc finem nos prouocaturus vehemen-tiùs Psaltes, simpliciter exponit quæ duobus antegressis illis similibus ad institutionem nostram pronunciauerat, altera parte huius versus dicens; Nam illic mandat Iehoua, &c. Cùm enim verba illa adhibet αἰτιολογικῶς[?], perinde est atque si diceret: Optimo consilio & ex veritate, sebonum[?] ad communionem sanctorum pertinens cum rore cœlitùs demisso comparauisse.
units.tr: To urge us more strongly toward this end, the Psalmist simply restates what he had laid down for our instruction in the two preceding similar clauses, using the second half of this verse: For there the LORD commands, etc. By using those words in an explanatory way (αἰτιολογικῶς), he is saying, as it were, that the good thing pertaining to the communion of the saints was obtained with the best counsel and in truth, like dew sent down from heaven.

units.la: Nam certissimam esse analogiam inter opera naturæ & gratiæ, corporalia & spiritalia; visibilia & inuisibilia, temporalia & æterna Dei. Erenim rerum à Deo esse, & amandari ab eo ad res creatas, præsertim verò ad hæreditatē suorum: & consimiliter bonū illud quòd de communione sanctorum prædicatur; & ab eo esse, & ab eodem amandari, & speciatim communicari cum Ecclesia ipsius, in qua est illa communio sanctorum, de cuius causa laboramus. Hæc summa sententia est sermonum, quibus Propheta in fine huius Psalmi utitur.
units.tr: For there is a most certain analogy between the works of nature and of grace, the bodily and the spiritual, the visible and the invisible, the temporal and the eternal works of God. Just as all things are from God and are sent by him to created things, and above all to the inheritance of his own people, so likewise the good that is proclaimed concerning the communion of the saints is from him, is sent by the same God, and is specifically shared within his Church, in which the communion of the saints exists, and for whose sake we labour. This is the main sense of the words the Prophet uses at the end of this Psalm.

units.la: In hac autem propria enunciatione illius, quatuor distincte ponuntur ista, de quibus iam antea ex parte diximus: auctor, obiectum, modus, & species actionis illius siue bonorum spiritalium in Christo Iesu. Auctor est Iehoua: obiectum, Ecclesia & communio sanctorum in illa: modus, mandatum seu verbum ipsius: species, benedictio eius & vita æterna.
units.tr: In this proper statement of his, four things are set out distinctly, which we have already discussed in part: the author, the object, the manner, and the kind of that action, that is, of the spiritual goods in Christ Jesus. The author is the LORD; the object is the Church and the communion of the saints in it; the manner is his command or word; the kind is his blessing and eternal life.

units.la: Auctorem Iehouam esse natura & Scriptura docent euidentissimè: natura quidè, auctorem esse omnis naturalis boni; quanto magis illius quo natura quàm longissimè superatur? Scriptura verò auctorem esse omnis supernaturalis boni: quandoquidem nemo res creatas supra naturam potest euehere atq. transmittere, quàm qui supra naturā est. Utrumq. appellatione Iehoua ostenditur, qua Hebraei solum significant verum & viuentem Deum, ut qui est à se, in se, per se, & propter se; & à quo, in quo, per quem; & propter quem sunt omnia quæ sunt, quæque futura sunt; denique à quo facta sunt omnia, & sine quo factum est nihil quod factum est: quibus verbis Ioannes diuinitatem Christi affirmauit.
units.tr: Nature and Scripture teach most evidently that the LORD is the author. Nature teaches that he is the author of every natural good, and how much more of that by which nature is surpassed by far? Scripture teaches that he is the author of every supernatural good, since no one can lift created things above nature and convey them beyond it except him who is above nature. Both are shown by the name LORD, which the Hebrews use to signify only the true and living God, who is of himself, in himself, through himself, and for himself; from whom, in whom, and through whom, and for whose sake, all things are, and all things that will be; and by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made that was made. In these words John affirmed the divinity of Christ.

units.la: Hic verò summus & summè reuerendus auctor etsi res omnes creatas colit & curat arbitratu suo, tamen obiectum illud secreuit à reliquis creatis rebus,quod Ecclesiam appellamus, ut in ea omnes vires effectaq; suæ illius gratiæ per infinitam dilectionē suam in Christo exereret. Hoc autem corpus est quidē ex hominibus, atq. etiam (si ita placet) Angelis constitutum; sed alium non habet quem Græci vocant ὑπάρξεως[?], id est existendi modū in forma & esse suo (vt loquuntur) quàm illū ipsum quem confitemur in symbolo Apostolorū, dicentes ; Credo communionem sanctorū; communionem, inquam (vt præcedente Psalmo ostendimus) primùm quidem cum Deo nostro, deinde verò inter nos, prout in Christo vnū corpus & vnus spiritus effecti sumus. Illic ergo, id est, in illa Ecclesia illaq. communione sanctorum, quam hæreditatem sibi in Christo per gratiam æternam adsciuit Pater, obiectum diuinæ gratiæ & misericordiæ oportet recognoscamus : neq. solùm vt communio spiritualis est, quā communionem habēt Angeli & Spiritus iustorum consecratorum in cælis; verum etiam ptout hic in terris haberi potest, spiritualis & corporalis, interna externaq. secundùm ordinē & relationē interternam, externamque, à Deo sancitam in verbo ipsius. Illic ergo, vbi Ecclesia est ; vbi communio sanctorū fratrū vnā habitantium ; vbi Christus communionis illius fundamentū inexpugnabile; vbi Christiani huic fundamento impositi per verbum, quod Prophetæ & Apostoli tradiderunt; vbi à nobis quidē imperfectiones quàm plurimæ, mentes dissentientes ; animi diuersi, conatus aduersi, opera ad impietatē & iniustitiam plus satis adspirātia infirmitate nostra; sed perfectio maxima in fundamēto & radice nostra: illic, inquam, thesaurus totus benedictionum Dei certissimē est depositus. Quo fit, vt quenquam hominem in hac cōmunione neque nouimus, neq. iudicamus secundum carnem: nam vetera præterierūt, omnia noua facta sunt (vt antecedente Psalmo dicebamus) sed secundum Christū agnoscimus, quamuis adhuc laboret grauissimè ex vitiofitate sua qui in Christo & in hac communione est.
units.tr: This highest and most reverend author, although he cherishes and cares for all created things according to his own pleasure, nevertheless has set apart from the rest of created things that object which we call the Church, so that in it he might display all the powers and effects of his grace through his infinite love in Christ. This body is indeed made up of men and, if it be so pleased, of angels; but it has no other mode of existence (which the Greeks call ὑπάρξεως, that is, the mode of existing, in its form and being, as they say) than that very one which we confess in the Apostles' Creed when we say: I believe the communion of the saints. The communion, I say, which, as we showed in the preceding Psalm, is first indeed with our God, and then among ourselves, inasmuch as we have been made one body and one spirit in Christ. There, therefore, that is, in that Church and that communion of the saints, which the Father has adopted for himself as an inheritance in Christ through eternal grace, we ought to acknowledge the object of divine grace and mercy. And this is not only as a spiritual communion, such as the angels and the spirits of the consecrated righteous have in heaven, but also as it can be had here on earth, both spiritual and bodily, internal and external, according to the order and relation between the internal and the external, which God has sanctioned in his Word. There, then, where the Church is; where is the communion of the saints dwelling together as brothers; where Christ is the impregnable foundation of that communion; where Christians are built upon this foundation through the Word which the Prophets and Apostles handed down; where, indeed, on our side there are very many imperfections, divided minds, different affections, hostile endeavours, works far too inclined to impiety and injustice because of our weakness; but the greatest perfection lies in our foundation and root: there, I say, the whole treasure of God's blessings is most certainly laid up. Hence we neither know nor judge any man in this communion according to the flesh. For the old things have passed away, and all things have become new (as we said in the preceding Psalm); but we acknowledge him according to Christ, although he who is in Christ and in this communion still struggles very grievously with his own faultiness.

units.la: Modus harum rerū à Propheta vnico verbo ostenditur, cum Iehoam præcepisse siue mandasse narrat. Si quis enim roget quem modū adhibere Deus in præstandis actionibus suis, respondebimus ex Prophetæ verbis, Deum sine motu suo agere, & solo dicto siue mandato suo, id est, voluntate apud se conceptā actiones suas potentissimè efficere. Quòd si alias hoc modo efficit, certè multo magis eas quas sibi soli vindicat, & quarū gloriam cum nemine homine aut creatura vlla communicat. Huius generis autem sunt bona spiritualia, quæ ad Ecclesiam peruenīunt cœlitus, & immediatè à Deo perficiuntur in corpore Christi, quod est Ecclesia.
units.tr: The manner of these things is shown by the Prophet in a single word, when he says that the LORD commanded or ordered. For if anyone asks what manner God uses in carrying out his actions, we shall answer from the Prophet's words that God acts without any movement of his own, and that by his word alone, or command, that is, by the will conceived within himself, he most powerfully brings his actions to effect. And if in other cases he works in this way, then certainly much more so in those works which he claims for himself alone, and whose glory he shares with no man or creature. Of this kind are the spiritual goods which come to the Church from heaven and are accomplished immediately by God in the body of Christ, which is the Church.

units.la: Accedit alterum infigne & pernecessarium, in hoc præsertim tempore, documentū: quòd nimirū omnia illa bona quæ Deus timentibus se præparauit, præcepto eius semel ita fuerūt constituta, vt nunquā quicquam eorum quæ instituit Deus & præcepit volūtate sua ineluc-tabili,sit futurum irritum. Nam(vt ait Efaias) Iehoua exercituum iniuit consiliū,& quis irritum faciat? & manum eius extentam quis auertat? Quòd si in hac misera constitutione nostra æquè in nobis ac in aliis fratribus nostris & seruis Domini nostri Iesu Christi interdū quàm plurima animadvertimus abesse longissimè ab illa ratione quam salutari consilio suo constituit Deus; immò etiā nonnullos qui ex cösilio̸[?] eius ad hanc, communione pertinent, indignissimè hanc ipsam communionē dissuere, & atrocissimè perrumpere: tamen non ad præsens illorū factum, sed ad æternum Dei consilij atq. mandatū gratiæ referre animos nostros oportet constantissimè;vt tū ipsi de nobis infirmissimis vasis spem concipiamus in Domino, tum etiā de aliis meliora speremus omnia: in quibus superciliosè damnandis atq. expungendis partim facto ipsorum, partimq. studiis & infirmitatibus plus æquo operam (proh dolor) consumimus.
units.tr: There is also another notable and most necessary lesson, especially in this present time: namely, that all those good things which God has prepared for those who fear him have been so established once for all by his command that nothing of what God has ordained and commanded by his unchangeable will can ever come to nothing. For (as Isaiah says) the LORD of hosts has formed a counsel, and who will make it void? And his outstretched hand, who will turn it back? But if in this wretched condition of ours we often see, both in ourselves and in our other brothers and servants of our Lord Jesus Christ, that very many are far removed from that order which God has set up by his saving counsel; indeed, even that some who belong to this communion by his counsel shamefully dissolve this very communion and most atrociously break it apart: nevertheless we ought steadfastly to direct our minds not to their present conduct but to the eternal counsel and command of God's grace; so that we may both conceive hope in the Lord concerning ourselves, who are most feeble vessels, and also hope for all better things concerning others. Yet in condemning and blotting out these others with arrogance, we spend (alas!) our effort, partly on their deeds, partly on our own zeal and weaknesses, more than is right.

units.la: Itaq. si hic hominem male agentem video, illic tamen Deum bene ordinantem contemplor in eadem communione sanctorum, & illa ipsa mala quæ ab homine sunt plenitudine infinitæ gratiæ obtegentem, vt extincto peccato seruetur homo ad vitam in die illo obtinendam. Atq. hic demùm circumfulget nos illa infinitas gratiæ & beneficentiæ diuinæ, cùm in homine misero & peccatis dante operā miserrimè animaduerto simul, tum fidem decreti illius & consilij æterni, quod
units.tr: Therefore, if here I see a man behaving badly, yet there I contemplate God ordering well in the same communion of the saints, and covering those very evils which come from man with the fullness of infinite grace, so that, sin being put to death, man may be preserved to obtain life on that day. And here at last that infinite grace and divine beneficence shines round about us, when I observe at once in wretched man, who labours most miserably at sin, and the faith of that eternal decree and counsel which God has proposed in himself; and also the man's unfitness, or (as we may say) his incapacity. And this is no wonder, because God alone is the one who makes us fit and worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light, as the Apostle wrote to the Colossians. Therefore, since nothing comes from us except our own evil, and whatever good there is, both in us and in the communion of the saints itself, comes from God, it remains for us to learn about those goods from the words of David.

units.la: Deus proposuit in se[?],tum hominis ἀνυαρόπυτα[?] sive (ut ita dicamus) ineptitudinem. Nec mirum: quia solus Deus est qui nos aptos sive idoneos faciat ad participandam fortem sanctorum in luce, quemadmodū ad Colossenses scribebat Apostolus. Quapropter cùm nihil à nobis, sit nisi malum nostrum, & quidquid boni est tum in nobis, tum in ipsa communione sanctorum, à Deo sit; restat ut de bonis illis ex Dauidis sermone cognoscamus.
units.tr: God has determined in himself to remedy man's unfitness, or (as we may say) his ineptitude. This is no wonder, since God alone makes us fit and suitable to share in the lot of the saints in light, as the Apostle wrote to the Colossians. Therefore, since nothing in us is anything but our own evil, and whatever good there is, both in us and in the communion of saints itself, comes from God, we must learn from David's words what those good things are.

units.la: Bonorum ergo quæ ad nos in communione sanctorum pertinent, & in quibus magis magisq. à Deo prouehimur, duo genera à Psalte posita sunt: cùm benedictionem Dei & vitam æternam nominat. Ac vita quidem æterna summus est terminus, vbi nos oportet conquiescere in præsentissima contemplatione & fructu gloriæ Dei, in quo cum Christo victuri sumus: benedictio vero universè omnia bona comprehendit antecedentia, quibus Deus benedicit assiduè nobis, donec ad summā illam vitæ æternæ metam perfectè transmittamur. Hæc igitur bona sunt, quæ in communione sanctorum à Deo exponi fidelibus Propheta narrat: quorum hæc in cursu, illud in meta positum est, postquam benedictiones illas in vitæ huius decursu percepimus.
units.tr: Of the goods that pertain to us in the communion of the saints, and in which we are advanced more and more by God, the Psalmist sets out two kinds, when he names the blessing of God and eternal life. Eternal life is the highest goal, where we ought to rest in the most immediate contemplation and enjoyment of the glory of God, in which we shall live with Christ. The blessing, however, comprehends in general all the preceding goods by which God blesses us continually, until we are fully carried over to that highest goal of eternal life. These, then, are the goods which the Prophet declares God sets forth to the faithful in the communion of the saints: the former placed in the course, the latter in the goal, once we have received those blessings in the course of this life.

units.la: Harum autem benedictionum potentissimum caput inter cætera illud est, quod in symbolo fidei nostræ cum Apostolis & sanctis omnibus profitemur, nos credere remissionem peccatorum. Sic enim ostendimus nos, qui fide Christum prehendimus & iustitiam eius qua iustificati sumus coram Deo, non aliter vivere in Christo, quàm si nobis moriamur: mori autem nos nobis coram Domino, cùm peccatum nostrum remissione aboletur; vivere, cùm peccati nostri loco iustitia Christi vivétis in nobis safficitur[?]: quam iustitiam quisquis prehendit & conscius est eius apud se per fidem, is omnino vitam æternam adepturus est.
units.tr: Of these blessings, the most powerful chief is that which we profess in the creed of our faith with the Apostles and all the saints: that we believe in the forgiveness of sins. For thus we show that we, who by faith lay hold of Christ and of his righteousness by which we are justified before God, live in Christ only as if we had died to ourselves; we die to ourselves before the Lord when our sin is blotted out by remission, and we live when the righteousness of Christ is supplied in us in place of our sin. Whoever lays hold of that righteousness, and is aware of it within himself through faith, will certainly obtain eternal life.

units.la: At qui[?] bona? amabo vos; quantopere expetenda? Benedictionem Dei & vitam æternam. Benedictio enim Dei, quam hîc Propheta docet, non levis benedictio est, sed omnes benedictiones quæ in rebus creatis possunt existere, omnino superans: Auctore, nam Deus auctor est, & non homo: Quantitate, si qua est infiniti cùm finito comparatio, nam omnis benedictio est in omnem plenitudinem, infinita in infinitum; non autem hæc aut illa re seorsim: Modo; nam spiritualis est, ac non corporalis benedictio, proinde momentanea: Sede, nam benedictio est in cælis excelsissima, non autem in terris abiectissima: Fundamentis materiaque, nam benedictio est in Christo, non autem in nobis à Deo deposita, ut certò sciamus neminem de iis quos Pater dederit in manům illius, periturum: quæ omnia sanctissimè verbis paucissimis Apostolus complexus est, cùm ad Ephesios scriberet. Hac benedictione in vitam illām æternam perducimur infinito bono & amœnitate præditam cõstantissimè, & gloriâ immutabili in Christo Iesu: cuius infinitas sic præcurrit mentes nostras, vt hic non possit comprehendi: sic rapit, vt illic comprehendenda sit, vbi comprehendere habere est.
units.tr: But what good things? Pray, how greatly to be desired? The blessing of God and eternal life. For the blessing of God, which the Prophet teaches here, is no slight blessing, but one that far surpasses all the blessings that can exist in created things. (As to its author: God is its author, and not man. As to its quantity: if there can be any comparison of the infinite with the finite, for every blessing is unto all fullness, infinite unto infinity, and not this or that thing separately. As to its manner: it is spiritual and not bodily, and therefore not momentary. As to its seat: the blessing is in the heavens, most high, and not on earth, most low. As to its foundation and matter: the blessing is in Christ, and not laid up in us by God, so that we may know for certain that none of those whom the Father has given into his hand will perish; all of which the Apostle comprised most holily in very few words when he wrote to the Ephesians.) By this blessing we are led into that eternal life, endowed with infinite good and delight, most constantly, and with immutable glory in Christ Jesus; its infinity so runs ahead of our minds that it cannot be grasped here, and so carries us off that it is to be grasped there, where to grasp is to have.

units.la: Quapropter tempus est, vt iam à somno expergiscamur, & ab omnibus illis auocamentis carnis atque impedimentis foris obuenientibus animos nostros & cogitationes abducamus, vt toti in colenda hac sanctorum communione occupemur in Christo & in Ecclesia, alij aliis bene facientes, bene iudicantes, bene sperantes, bene cupientes, & ad omnem bonorum quæ à Deo accepimus, communicationem secundùm Deum contendentes.
units.tr: Therefore it is time that we now awake from sleep, and draw our minds and thoughts away from all those distractions of the flesh and impediments that come from outside, so that we may be wholly occupied in cultivating this communion of the saints in Christ and in the Church, each doing good to the others, judging well, hoping well, desiring well, and striving according to God for the sharing of all the good things we have received from God.

units.la: Hoc Deus semper beneficus erga nos facto docet, sermone iubet, spiritu efficit: efficit autem in communione sanctorum, ad quam vocati sumus. Huic communioni benedictionem suam, vitámque æternam consilio instituit, promisit verbo, præstat opere; & in exoptatissimo illo die secundi aduentus Christi consummaturus est.
units.tr: God teaches this always, showing kindness to us by his deed, commanding by his word, and effecting by his Spirit; he effects it, moreover, in the communion of the saints, to which we have been called. For this communion he has established his blessing and eternal life by counsel, promised by his word, and bestows by his work; and he will bring it to completion on that most longed-for day of the second coming of Christ.

units.la: Videamus ergo, ô fratres in Christo dilectissimi, videamus obsecro, vt deinceps religioso studio ad benedictionem Dei vitámque æternam attendamus: ad Iehouam auctorem illius respiciamus: cõquiescamus in mandato & beneplacito voluntatis eius ineluctabili: in Ecclesia & communione sanctorum hos thesauros gratiæ depositos in dies recolamus: rorem & cultura Domini quàm fidelissimè agnoscamus in corpore Ecclesiæ & membris singulis illius, abdicata omni animorum perturbatione quæ nos occæcat indignissimè: odoremur optimam illam fragrantiam Christi odoremque suauissimum ad membra singula in Ecclesia permeantem; neque persentiscendis[?] priuatis fœtoribus infirmitatibusque hominum inuestigandis & consequendis incumbamus; quicquid ad communionem sanctorum farciendam, alendam, & continendā pertinet, quàm diligentissimè procuremus: deniq. quantum nobis cordi est quidquid boni, quidquid amœni in Ecclesia, in Christo, in gloria Dei est, id vnanimes in communione sanctorum, ad quam vocati sumus, procuremus; vt decurso hoc misero & laboriosò stadio præsentis vitæ, in illa vita tandem conquiescamus, vbi quies sine interturbatione, gloria sine labe, & vita sine fine fine æternùm futura est, in Christo Iesu vnico Seruatore nostro.
units.tr: Let us therefore see, O brethren most beloved in Christ, let us see, I beseech you, that henceforth with religious zeal we attend to the blessing of God and eternal life; let us look up to Jehovah, its author; let us rest in the command and in the unshakable good pleasure of his will; let us daily call to mind in the Church and the communion of the saints these treasures of grace laid up; let us most faithfully acknowledge the dew and the cultivation of the Lord in the body of the Church and in each of its members, having put aside all disturbance of mind that blinds us most unworthily; let us savour that best fragrance of Christ and that most sweet odour which pervades each member in the Church; let us not busy ourselves with perceiving private stenches and with searching out and pursuing men's weaknesses; let us most diligently provide for whatever pertains to filling, nourishing and sustaining the communion of the saints; and finally, as much as we hold dear whatever is good and whatever is pleasant in the Church, in Christ, and in the glory of God, let us, being of one mind, promote it in the communion of the saints to which we have been called; so that, the course of this wretched and laborious race of present life being run, we may at last rest in that life where there is rest without disturbance, glory without stain, and life without end, to be forever in Christ Jesus, our only Saviour.

units.la: Te autem, ô Deus & Pater miserationum, qui propter sanctissimum filium dilectionis tuæ gratiosissimè misertus nostri voluisti nos in cōfortium pacis & gaudij spiritualis adducere, quod Ecclesiæ tuæ in eodem filio tuo æternùm præparauisti, supplex oro condones omnia peccata nostra, quia peccauimus in te; & mortificans carnem nostrā cum eius concupiscentiis, veram lætitiam illam spiritualem ex vera charitatis sanctæ conscientiā proficiscentem cùm in me ipso, tum in omnibus nobis ingeneres, faciasque vt nunquam alij aliis inuideamus, aut impeimpedimento simus, aut etiã labefactemus, aut deturbemus de cõmunione illa quam imperas, aut ordini tuo aduersentur, aut paci obsistamus, aut bonum & amœnitatem, quam in communione sanctorū posuisti, interuertamus per malitiam, infirmitatem, imprudentiã, aut ignorationem nostram mente, animo, sermone, aut facto: sed potius quidquid bonum, sanctum, iustum, & cõueniens charitati est, illud virtute Spiritus tui acti cogitemus, studeamus, eloquamus, seruemus, faciamusq. ad gloriam tui nominis: da, ô cælestis Pater, ut te Iehouam cognoscamus, & domum tuam in te, quæ spelunca foret sine te; da, ut adeuntes domum tuam, & cõsistentes in ea, sanctissimo zelo agnoscamus, semperque lætemur de iis qui dicunt, & consilia capiunt de Ecclesia tua adeunda, studio gloriæ tuæ & salutis suæ: da, ut Ecclesia optimè cõstructa sit; & refecta labe illius, quæ hoc tempore amplissima est, coagmenta lapides viuos illius pariter: fac, ut omnes ascendant eò ad petcipiendum[?] testimonium verbi salutaris tui, & celebrationem nominis tui exercendam: effice, ô Deus ordinis, ut iustus ordo in misera Christianitate obtineat: ut qui rebus sacris præsunt, eas procurent sanctè, abiecta rerum aliarum omnium cogitatione, & adiecto animo ad salutem gregis illius, quem filius dilectus tuus sanguine pretioso suo comparauit: ut qui rebus ciuilibus & humanis præfecti sunt; suis patribus tum in res publicas sibi commissas, tum in te, à quo omnis potestas est, fidelissimè perfungantur, tuóque ordini inseruiant: inde omnibus simul, præfectis & subditis, superioribus & inferioribus, verù studium pacis publicæ in societate humana & in Ecclesiastica sanctorum communione persequendæ, tùm propter fratres & amicos omnes, tùm propterea quòd hæc domus tua est, ô Deus, qui dignatus es Ecclesiam capi, quamuis cæli cælorum non capiant te: da, ut bonum amœnitatemque communionis illius omnibus documentis naturæ & gratiæ discamus cognoscere, & rerum istarum comprehensione possimus omnia fugere, auersari, oppugnare, vincere, perrumpere, quæ illâ communionem sanctorum, bonumque & amœnitatem illius præripiunt Ecclesiæ tuæ. Attende, ô Deus, è cælo, & respice, & mandata tua consiliaque gratiosè de nobis ab æterno capta etiam atque etiam perfice; ut renunciantes omni malo, & amplexi benedictiones tuas hîc vivamus fecundùm te, certaque fiducia & spe optatissimum illum diem expectemus, quo æternum sumus victuri in te per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: But to you, O God and Father of mercies, who, for the sake of your most holy beloved Son, graciously had mercy on us and willed to bring us into the fellowship of peace and of spiritual joy, which you have prepared for your Church forever in that same Son of yours, I humbly pray: forgive all our sins, for we have sinned against you; and, mortifying our flesh with its lusts, produce and work in me and in all of us that true spiritual joy which springs from the conscience of true holy charity; and grant that we never envy one another, nor be a hindrance, nor even weaken, cast down from that communion which you command, nor oppose your order, nor resist peace, nor overturn the good and the pleasantness which you have placed in the communion of the saints, through our malice, weakness, imprudence or ignorance, in mind, heart, speech or deed; but rather that whatever is good, holy, just and befitting charity, we may think, strive for, speak, keep and do by the power of your Spirit, to the glory of your name. Grant, O heavenly Father, that we may know you as Jehovah, and your house in you, which would be a den without you; grant that those who approach your house and stand in it may recognise it with most holy zeal, and may always rejoice over those who speak and take counsel to approach your Church, with zeal for your glory and their own salvation. Grant that the Church may be built up most well; and, its ruin being repaired, which at this time is very great, join together its living stones alike; bring it about that all may ascend there to receive the testimony of your saving word and to carry on the celebration of your name. Effect, O God of order, that right order may obtain in miserable Christendom; that those who preside over sacred things may manage them holily, having cast aside all thought of other things, and having set their minds on the salvation of that flock which your beloved Son purchased with his precious blood; that those who are set over civil and human affairs may most faithfully discharge their duties, both towards the commonwealths entrusted to them and towards you, from whom all power comes, and may serve your order; then, for all alike, both rulers and subjects, superiors and inferiors, grant a true zeal for pursuing public peace in human society and in the ecclesiastical communion of the saints, both for the sake of all brothers and friends, and because this is your house, O God, you who have deigned to be contained in the Church, though the heavens of heavens cannot contain you. Grant that we may learn to know the goodness and pleasantness of that communion by all the lessons of nature and grace, and by grasping these things may be able to flee, shun, assail, overcome and break through all those things which snatch away from your Church that communion of the saints and its goodness and pleasantness. Look down, O God, from heaven, and regard, and graciously bring to completion again and again your commands and counsels concerning us, which were taken from eternity; that, renouncing every evil and embracing your blessings, we may live here according to you, and with certain confidence and hope may await that most desired day on which we shall live forever in you, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: Etiam atque etiam Amen.
units.tr: Again and again, Amen.
